0.title: About this report · B0004
0.text: Prepared by Little Orange Fish, Huntsville, Alabama, in its role as backbone organization for the North Alabama Mental Health Coalition. Version 2 supersedes the June 2025 edition (v250603). The text on this site (v261003.1) is the 3 October 2026 draft after a claim-by-claim check against its cited sources, carried out the same day. What that check corrected is recorded in the change log, and what could not be confirmed is listed in Appendix D.

1.title: About this report · B0005
1.text: How to read this report. Part I is a short guide for advocates and planners. Part II describes the system through eight domains adapted from the World Health Organization's health-system building blocks, each read through two lenses: the continuum of care (promotion → prevention → outpatient → crisis → inpatient and forensic → recovery supports) and, where the justice system touches the domain, the Sequential Intercept Model. Part III adds four sections on the systems that sit outside the Department of Mental Health but shape mental health outcomes: children and families, justice, housing and social determinants, and payers. Part IV holds the cross-domain dependency map, a table of actors by sector, a baseline of Alabama indicators and the appendices; the sources are on the References page. Each domain section ends with a line showing which goals of the Alabama Department of Mental Health's Strategic Plan 2025–2028 it touches, so the report can be read alongside the state's own plan. The "Gaps and opportunities" bullets in each section are this report's analytical reading of the evidence, offered for planners and advocates to weigh; they are not positions of Little Orange Fish or of any coalition.

2.title: About this report · B0006
2.text: Status and intended use. This is a draft for review. It has not been approved by Little Orange Fish, and it is published here so that reviewers can test it against its sources; on approval it will be published on NorthAlabamaMentalHealthCoalition.org. Nothing in it is a position of the North Alabama Mental Health Coalition or of any coalition member organization. It contains no clinical guidance and no political advocacy; where it describes policy choices, it describes them as the public record does.

3.title: About this report · B0007
3.text: A note on method and AI. The June 2025 edition was drafted with ChatGPT as a research-synthesis tool. This edition was revised with Claude, which was used to locate and read primary sources, to compare the prior text against them, and to draft replacement text; the Executive Director of Little Orange Fish is responsible for the content. Where the 2025 text described institutions whose names could not be confirmed, those passages have been replaced or removed. On 3 October 2026 the draft was then checked claim by claim, again with Claude: the text was split into about 1,900 individual claims, every cited source was opened, and each claim was marked as confirmed, corrected, updated, moved to the source that actually carries it, given a source it lacked, or left open. The sources were read through an automated reader that returns extracts, so quoted passages should be treated as the reader returned them. Appendix D lists what remains unverified, and the Methods page of this site gives the counts.

4.title: Why this report exists · B0012
4.text: Alabama's mental health system is not one system. It is a set of systems — a state agency and its contracted community centers, Medicaid and commercial insurers, hospitals and emergency departments, schools, courts and jails, housing coalitions, veterans' services, and nonprofits and faith communities — that together determine whether a person in Alabama can find help, afford it, reach it, and keep it. No single office sees all of it. This report is an attempt to describe all of it in one place, in plain language, so that people who want to improve it can see where they stand.

5.title: Why this report exists · B0013
5.text: The report has three uses. For advocates, it supplies verified, dated figures and the name of the body responsible for each part of the system, so that a request to a legislator, a county commission or a foundation can be specific. For planners in nonprofits, providers and coalitions, it offers a common structure for deciding where to invest and for recognizing which partner owns the adjacent piece. For the coalition itself, it gives a baseline against which later editions — and a planned North Alabama regional edition built on the same template — can measure change.

6.title: How the system is described · B0015
6.text: The analysis uses eight domains adapted from the World Health Organization's six "building blocks" of a health system, plus two that this report adds, on equity and on community engagement [1]:

7.title: How the system is described · B0016
7.text: Governance, policy and legal foundations — who decides, under what law, with what accountability.

8.title: How the system is described · B0017
8.text: Financing and resource allocation — where the money comes from and how it moves.

9.title: How the system is described · B0018
9.text: Service-delivery continuum — what services exist, where, for whom.

10.title: How the system is described · B0019
10.text: Workforce development and well-being — who delivers care and whether there are enough of them.

11.title: How the system is described · B0020
11.text: Medicines, technology and infrastructure — buildings, beds, data pipes, telehealth, medications.

12.title: How the system is described · B0021
12.text: Information, data and quality improvement — how the system knows what it is doing.

13.title: How the system is described · B0022
13.text: Equity, inclusion and cultural responsiveness — who the system reaches and who it misses.

14.title: How the system is described · B0023
14.text: Community engagement, education and advocacy — how the public shapes the system.

15.title: How the system is described · B0024
15.text: Two lenses run through the report. The continuum-of-care lens asks, at each point, whether Alabama has promotion and prevention, outpatient treatment, crisis response, inpatient and forensic care, and recovery supports — a range drawn from the National Academies' spectrum of promotion, prevention, treatment and maintenance and from the state mental health directors' association's argument that a full continuum of psychiatric care is necessary [2] [3]. The justice lens uses the Sequential Intercept Model's six intercepts, from community services through community corrections [4] [5], because in Alabama the justice system is a regular point of contact for people with mental illness [6].

16.title: How the system is described · B0025
16.text: Four sections in Part III describe systems that lie outside the Department of Mental Health: children, youth and families (using the national System of Care principles) [7]; the justice interface; housing and social determinants (using the Healthy People 2030 framework) [8]; and payers, including the Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic transition that is reshaping how community care is funded.

17.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0027
17.text: The findings below are the ones a reader should carry away. Each is developed in its section. Figures are for state fiscal year 2025 (October 2024–September 2025) unless noted; bracketed numbers point to the source list, and on this site each one opens a summary of the source and the passage that supports the sentence. Three terms recur: 988 is the national suicide and crisis line, answered in Alabama by four in-state call centers [9]; a CCBHC (Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic) is a community clinic paid a daily Medicaid rate to provide a defined set of services including 24/7 crisis response [10]; and Hunter is the federal consent decree governing how long people may wait in jail for competency evaluation and restoration [11].
17.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

18.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0028
18.text: Crisis response has been Alabama's major structural gain since 2020, and it is now under scrutiny. Six regional crisis centers, four in-state 988 call centers and fourteen mobile crisis teams now operate [12] [9] [13]; the first crisis center opened in 2021 and 988 launched in July 2022 [14] [15]. In FY2025 the crisis centers performed 9,929 evaluations and the 988 call centers handled 40,053 calls, with an in-state answer rate of 87.4 percent for the year that reached 90.9 percent in May 2025 [16]. The FY2027 budget, as reported, withholds the last two quarterly installments of the $42 million for crisis diversion and rural crisis-care centers until the Department "reports the status of the programs" to the budget chairs, the Finance Director and the Legislative Fiscal Officer [17] [18]; the Senate committee's version had tied third- and fourth-quarter payments for the six crisis centers to reporting of costs, staffing and persons served and to evaluator access [19]. The conditions followed a preliminary report of September 2025 in which the state's independent evaluator said it "cannot verify" the emergency-room and jail-diversion figures the Department had reported [14].
18.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

19.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0029
19.text: The funding surge did not continue. The FY2027 General Fund appropriation of $240.9 million is slightly below FY2026's $244.5 million [18] [20]. For FY2026 the Department had been considering, in December 2024, a request for a 22.9 percent increase in its total state appropriation (28.8 percent in General Fund terms) [21]; the enacted General Fund increase was about 2 percent [20] [22]. Alabama's state mental health agency spent $133 per resident in FY2024 against a national average of $179 [23].
19.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

20.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0030
20.text: The biggest structural change under way is payment reform, not new buildings. In June 2024 Alabama was named one of ten states added to the federal CCBHC Medicaid demonstration [24] [25]. Four clinics have moved to the model — two certified by the state in July 2024 and two approved by SAMHSA in October 2025 and April 2026 [26] [27] — and ADMH's CCBHC directory lists a fifth, which the Department's May 2026 release does not name [28]; six more providers received grants in August 2026 to pursue certification [29], and the Department's stated goal is a statewide transition [24] [27]. The first two clinics served 30,275 people in FY2025 [16].
20.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

21.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0031
21.text: Beds remain far below the planning benchmark. Alabama had 15.1 involuntary (civil-commitment) beds per 100,000 people in January 2026 — 771 beds, up from 698 beds (13.7 per 100,000) in August 2025 — against the 30 per 100,000 that the Treatment Advocacy Center calls the minimum and the Department uses as its planning benchmark [30] [31]. The Department prices closing the 779-bed gap to that benchmark at $226.4 million [30]; the House General Fund budget chair has put the cost of replacing 787 beds at about $590 million in construction alone [32] [33]. The two are separate estimates, not reconciled in the sources. The forensic waitlist — people waiting in county jails for psychiatric evaluation or treatment — stood at 291 in July 2026, under a federal consent decree [32] [11].
21.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

22.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0032
22.text: Workforce is a binding constraint on every other domain. 2.9 million Alabamians live in federally designated mental-health shortage areas; the state meets 28 percent of the estimated need for psychiatric care in those areas, as of December 2025 [34]. Mental Health America ranks Alabama 51st of 51 for workforce availability, at one provider per 740 residents [35].
22.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

23.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0033
23.text: Coverage is the equity issue. Alabama has not expanded Medicaid [36]. The coverage gap is put at up to 155,000 people by Alabama Arise [36] [37] (KFF's July 2026 estimate is 86,000 uninsured adults in the gap itself and 147,000 who would become eligible if the state expanded [38]), and roughly 95,000 people left the ACA marketplace in 2026 after enhanced subsidies expired [36] [39]. Among adults with mental illness, 14.1 percent are uninsured against 9.2 percent nationally [35].
23.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

24.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0034
24.text: Children's access to care is where Alabama ranks worst. On Mental Health America's youth measures Alabama ranks 50th of 51; nearly two-thirds (66.4 percent) of Alabama youth with major depression receive no treatment, the worst rate in the country [35]. The state's own plan lists child and family services second among its five priorities [40], and the pediatric crisis unit in Huntsville — the state's first [41] — performed 520 evaluations in FY2025 [16].
24.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

25.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0035
25.text: The data to manage the system is improving but still thin. The 2025 federal reporting shows a public-system penetration rate of 18.3 per 1,000 residents against 22.9 nationally (18.3 and 23.5 in 2024) [42] [43]. The state's evaluation commission, created in 2019, published a preliminary evaluation of the crisis centers in September 2025 [44] [14], and Alabama's health information exchange listed the Department's connection as a work in progress as of December 2025 [45].
25.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

26.title: Using the report for advocacy · B0037
26.text: Cite the figure and its owner. Each section names the responsible body. The Department's own annual report shows 637 people served in its mental-illness facilities in FY2025, and the Department told the Joint Mental Health Task Force in August 2026 that its forensic waitlist stood at 291 in July carries more weight than a general claim of shortage [16] [32].

27.title: Using the report for advocacy · B0038
27.text: Match the ask to the domain. A county can act on jail screening (Section 10) [46] and transit (Section 11) [47]; the Legislature acts on appropriations (Domain 2) [18] and licensure compacts (Domain 4) [48]; the Department acts on certification and crisis-system design (Domains 1 and 3) [49] [50].

28.title: Using the report for advocacy · B0039
28.text: Use the state's own plan. Every domain section lists the goals of the ADMH Strategic Plan 2025–2028 it touches [40] (the goal numbering is Little Orange Fish's own, from its alignment analysis of the full plan). Framing a request as support for a goal the state has already adopted is both accurate and effective.

29.title: Using the report for advocacy · B0040
29.text: Acknowledge gains. Crisis centers, 988, CCBHC, the pediatric crisis unit and the Taylor Hardin expansion are real [12] [9] [27] [41] [32]. Advocacy that credits them and then shows the next gap is harder to dismiss.

30.title: Using the report for advocacy · B0041
30.text: Keep to what is verified. Appendix D lists what this report could not confirm. Do not fill those gaps with estimates in public materials. The "Gaps and opportunities" bullets are this report's reading of the evidence, not positions.

31.title: Using the report for planning · B0043
31.text: Find your slot. The eight domains plus four cross-sector sections are a map of who does what. A new program should be able to say which domain it strengthens and which existing actor it depends on.

32.title: Using the report for planning · B0044
32.text: Plan across the continuum. A program that adds crisis capacity without a step-down or follow-up partner adds readmissions. The continuum-lens paragraphs in Domains 2 and 4 to 8 show which neighbors a program needs [3].

33.title: Using the report for planning · B0045
33.text: Measure against the baseline. Appendix B gives Alabama's standing on 17 national indicators and the federal Uniform Reporting System measures. Later editions will use the same table.

34.title: Using the report for planning · B0046
34.text: Build regionally on the same frame. The North Alabama edition planned to follow this report will keep the same domains and lenses, so that regional findings can be compared with the state picture — and so that the template can serve other regions.

35.title: What changed from the 2025 edition · B0048
35.text: The June 2025 edition organized its analysis into eight domains, and this edition keeps those same eight. Three things are different.

36.title: What changed from the 2025 edition · B0049
36.text: First, the 2025 edition's opening guide described a different list of eight domains (for example "Prevention & Early Intervention" and "Crisis & Acute Care") from the ones the analysis actually used, so a reader could not match the guide to the report. In this edition the guide and the analysis use one list.

37.title: What changed from the 2025 edition · B0050
37.text: Second, every figure has been re-checked against its cited source — a primary document wherever one could be read — and dated, and fourteen passages in the 2025 text that named programs, offices or laws that could not be confirmed have been corrected or removed.

38.title: What changed from the 2025 edition · B0051
38.text: Third, four sections have been added for the systems outside the Department of Mental Health that the 2025 edition touched only in passing — children and families, justice, housing and social determinants, and payers — together with the two cross-cutting lenses and a baseline indicator table. The References page lists the sources; Appendix D lists what remains open.

39.title: Scope · B0055
39.text: Governance is the set of laws, institutions and decision rights that determine who is responsible for mental health in Alabama, how they are held to account, and what rights people with mental illness can assert. It includes the state mental health authority and its board, the Legislature's budget and policy committees, the Governor, the courts that enforce constitutional standards of care, and the interagency bodies that coordinate across health, education, justice and human services. A strong governance frame gives the rest of the system direction, legitimacy and accountability; a weak one leaves gaps that courts eventually fill.

40.title: Alabama's structures · B0057
40.text: The Alabama Department of Mental Health (ADMH) is the state mental health authority, created by statute in 1965 and governed by Title 22, Chapter 50 of the Code of Alabama, which authorizes it "to act in any prudent way to provide mental health services" to Alabamians [51]. The Governor appoints the Commissioner, who serves at the Governor's pleasure [51]. Kimberly G. Boswell has been Commissioner since December 2020 [50].

41.title: Alabama's structures · B0058
41.text: The Department is organized into three divisions. The Division of Mental Health and Substance Use Services (Associate Commissioner Nicole Walden) holds the offices of Certification; Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics; Child and Family Services; Deaf Services; Facility Operations; Forensic Mental Health Services; Forensic Outpatient Services; Mental Illness Community Programs; Peer Programs; Quality Improvement and Risk Management; and Substance Use Services [16] [52]. The Division of Developmental Disabilities (Associate Commissioner Camille Cumuze) serves people with intellectual and developmental disabilities [53]. The Division of Administration (Associate Commissioner Brooke Hibbard) runs finance, certification administration, policy and planning, information systems and facilities [16] [54]. Both the Developmental Disabilities and Administration associate commissioner positions changed hands in 2025; the board's November 2025 minutes record the retirements and introduce the successors [55] [56].

42.title: Alabama's structures · B0059
42.text: The 2025 edition of this report described separate associate commissioners for "mental illness" and "substance abuse". That structure no longer exists; mental health and substance use are one division [16] [52].

43.title: Alabama's structures · B0060
43.text: The ADMH Board of Trustees has sixteen members. The Governor chairs it; the Speaker of the House, the Lieutenant Governor and the Commissioner (as secretary) sit ex officio, with seven congressional-district and five at-large appointees. The board meets quarterly and publishes its minutes [57] [55] [26].

44.title: Alabama's structures · B0061
44.text: The ADMH Strategic Plan 2025–2028 sets five priorities [40]. (The goal numbering used in this report — A1 to E3 — follows Little Orange Fish's alignment analysis of the full plan document; the Department's strategy page shows the five priority headings [40].)

45.title: Alabama's structures · B0062
45.text: System of Care Transformation — "transform the system of care to ensure services are accessible, integrated, and responsive." [40]

47.title: Alabama's structures · B0064
47.text: Workforce Health and Wellness — recruit and retain a skilled workforce. [40]

48.title: Alabama's structures · B0065
48.text: Resources — seek and secure sustainable funding. [40]

49.title: Alabama's structures · B0066
49.text: Awareness and Knowledge — empower Alabamians with clear, relevant information. [40]

50.title: Alabama's structures · B0067
50.text: The numeric targets associated with the plan in public discussion — civil psychiatric beds from 13.4 to 30 per 100,000, mobile crisis teams from 14 to 23, crisis centers from 6 to 11, and crisis coverage from 24 counties to all 67 — come from the Commissioner's February 2025 budget presentation, as reported by Alabama Daily News, rather than the strategy document itself, and should be cited that way [33]. (The Department's annual report gives 13.7 beds per 100,000 for the start of FY2025, and its August 2025 presentation gives the same figure; its FY2027 budget presentation, counting beds as of 13 January 2026, gives 15.1 [16] [31] [30].) The 2025 edition of this report stated that ADMH had no single strategic plan or annual report; both exist, and the FY2025 annual report (posted April 2026) is this report's most-used source [16] [40].

51.title: Alabama's structures · B0068
51.text: The Legislature enacts the General Fund and Education Trust Fund appropriations that are among the Department's largest state revenues (Domain 2) [16] [20] [58], and in the 2026 session attached conditions to them: as reported on final passage, the FY2027 General Fund budget withholds the last two quarterly installments of the $42 million for crisis diversion and rural crisis-care centers until the Department reports the status of the programs to the General Fund budget chairs, the Finance Director and the Legislative Fiscal Officer [17] [18]; the Senate committee's version of the bill had required reports of each crisis center's operating expenses, employees and persons served, and access for the state evaluator [19]. The House General Fund budget chair, Rep. Rex Reynolds, has been a prominent legislative voice on crisis-system funding [33]. Legislation in the 2025 session touching mental health included SB101, raising the age of independent consent for medical and mental-health treatment from 14 to 16 (Act 2025-455, effective 1 October 2025) [59] [60]; SB236 (Act 2025-366), which requires the executive committee of a regional mental health authority board with more than sixteen directors to include a sheriff (or the sheriff's representative) and a probate judge where those officials serve on the board [61] [62]; SB200 (Act 2025-183), which renamed drug courts "accountability courts" and extended their eligibility to defendants with mental illness and to veterans [63] [62]; SB40, the Houston Hunter Act, creating voluntary firearm-hold agreements as a suicide-prevention measure [64]; and SB70, creating a Veterans Resource Center [22]. No comparable mental-health statute from the 2026 session was identified in the sources read for this report (as of October 2026).

52.title: Alabama's structures · B0069
52.text: Independent evaluation now extends to the crisis system. The Alabama Commission on the Evaluation of Services (ACES), created by Act 2019-517 (Code of Alabama §29-2A-1) to advise the Legislature and the Governor [44], evaluated the state's suicide-prevention programs, including the Department's, in 2020 [65] and published a preliminary evaluation of the crisis centers in September 2025 [14]; the FY2027 appropriation conditions followed [19].

53.title: Legal foundations · B0071
53.text: Three bodies of law frame the system.

54.title: Legal foundations · B0072
54.text: Civil commitment (Code of Alabama §22-52) allows any person to petition the probate court; the standard is clear and convincing evidence of mental illness and a real and present threat of substantial harm, and the court must order the least restrictive alternative necessary and available [66]. Initial orders run up to 150 days and renewals up to one year [66]. Outpatient commitment is available where a designated facility consents [66]. No annual count of commitments was found in the Department's published reports as of October 2026 (Appendix D).

55.title: Legal foundations · B0073
55.text: Constitutional standards of care were set in Alabama. Wyatt v. Stickney (M.D. Ala., 1971) established a right to adequate treatment for people confined in state psychiatric institutions and kept the Department under federal court supervision until 2003 [67] [68]. Its successors are active today. In Hunter v. Beshear (settled 2018; now captioned Hunter v. Boswell), a consent decree governs the time people may wait in jail for competency evaluation and restoration; the decree's inpatient-restoration term, extended in March 2025, runs to 31 January 2027, with the Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program, an associational plaintiff, monitoring compliance [11]. In Braggs v. Commissioner, Alabama Department of Corrections (the Eleventh Circuit's caption; the case is now styled Braggs v. Lovelace), a 2017 ruling found that mental health care in state prisons violated the Eighth Amendment; on 24 June 2026 the Eleventh Circuit affirmed that finding and the system-wide injunction but reversed the specific correctional-staffing mandate, some suicide-resistant cell requirements and the application of relief to Tutwiler, and returned those questions to the district court [69] [70] [71]. A separate U.S. Department of Justice suit against the Department of Corrections is set for trial in November 2026 [72].

56.title: Legal foundations · B0074
56.text: Federal program law — the Mental Health Block Grant, Medicaid's state plan and waivers, and since 2024 the Section 223 CCBHC demonstration — carries its own planning, reporting and consumer-participation requirements, including the federally required state mental health planning council [73] [24] [74] [26].

57.title: Key actors and how decisions move · B0076
57.text: Actor Role in governance Governor Appoints the Commissioner; chairs the ADMH board; proposes the executive budget; signs appropriations and bills [51] [57] [18] [64] ADMH Commissioner and divisions Sets standards, certifies and contracts providers, operates state hospitals, administers federal grants and the CCBHC demonstration [16] [49] [24] ADMH Board of Trustees Quarterly oversight; receives budget and program reports [57] [26] [56] Legislature (General Fund and ETF committees) Appropriates; attaches reporting conditions; enacts policy (consent age, courts, boards) [18] [58] [17] [59] [61] [63] Probate courts Civil commitment hearings and orders [66] Federal courts and monitors Enforce Hunter and Braggs; DOJ litigation against ADOC [11] [69] [72] ACES Independent program evaluation advising the Legislature and the Governor [44] [14] Alabama Medicaid Agency Sets covered services, rates and waivers that determine what providers can bill [49] [75] Regional (310) mental health authority boards Govern the 19 community mental health centers; executive committees now include a sheriff and a probate judge where SB236 applies [31] [49] [61] Interagency councils Alabama Opioid Overdose and Addiction Council (annual report, 2025) [76]; Reentry Task Force (SJR80, 2025) [77]
57.section: Key actors and how decisions move

58.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0078
58.text: Accountability now runs through appropriations. The FY2027 conditions on crisis-center funds show the Legislature using the budget as its oversight tool [17] [19]. The opportunity is to agree, in advance, on a small set of published measures (Domain 6) so that conditions are met with data rather than negotiated after the fact.

59.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0079
59.text: Coordination across sectors is ad hoc. No standing statewide body dedicated to mental health that joins the Department, the courts, the Department of Corrections, Pardons and Paroles, Human Resources, Youth Services and Education was identified for this report; the Reentry Task Force created by SJR80 (2025) is the nearest thing on the justice side [77], and for children state law provides two bodies with wider remits, the State Team for multiple-needs children [78] and the Children's Policy Council [79]. According to Little Orange Fish's alignment analysis of the full plan, the ADMH plan's child-and-family priority includes identifying shared objectives with child-serving agencies (goal B4 in this report's numbering), which implies such a forum (Section 9).

60.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0080
60.text: Court orders still substitute for policy. More than twenty years after Wyatt ended, Alabama operates its forensic and prison mental-health systems under two federal decrees [68] [11] [69]. Meeting the Hunter timelines by January 2027 is a governance deadline as much as a clinical one (Section 10) [11].

61.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0081
61.text: Coverage policy is unresolved. The Legislature has not expanded Medicaid [36], and no alternative coverage program was found to have been enacted as of October 2026; the 2025 federal budget law ended, from January 2026, the temporary enhanced federal match offered to states that newly expand and limits state provider taxes (Section 12) [80] [81]. Coverage policy affects more sections of this report than any other single decision.

62.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0082
62.text: Regulatory modernization continues. Alabama belongs to seven interstate licensure compacts (Domain 4) [82] [48] [83] [84] [85] [86] [87] and permits audio-only Medicaid telehealth at parity (Domain 5) [88]; keeping rules current with practice remains a standing task.

63.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0083
63.text: ADMH plan goals touched: A1, A2, A3, A6, D1, D2.

64.title: Key information assets · B0085
64.text: Asset What it provides mh.alabama.gov Program pages, provider directories, board minutes, annual reports, strategic plan [13] [57] [16] [40] ALISON (alison.legislature.state.al.us) Bills, enacted budgets, LSA comparison sheets, budget-hearing presentations [59] [18] [31] evidence.alabama.gov ACES evaluations [14] Alabama Administrative Code portal ADMH and Medicaid rules (e.g., 560-X-47 rehabilitative services) [49] Court dockets and the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse Hunter and Braggs filings and monitor reports [11] [69]

65.title: Key data sources · B0087
65.text: ADMH Annual Report FY2025 [16]; ADMH Strategic Plan 2025–2028 [40]; LSA FY2026 and FY2027 enacted budget comparisons [20] [18] [58]; ACES crisis-center evaluation [14]; Braggs opinion [69]; Hunter consent decree record [11]; enrolled texts of SB101 and SB236 [59] [61].

66.title: Scope · B0090
66.text: Financing covers where the money for mental health care comes from — state appropriations, Medicaid and other federal funds, commercial insurance, local and philanthropic sources — and how it is allocated across hospitals, community programs, crisis services and the workforce. The question for planners is not only how much Alabama spends, but which payer pays for which service, because that determines which services can grow.

67.title: The Department's budget · B0092
67.text: ADMH's total operating revenue in FY2025 was $1.43 billion. The state's share was 40.9 percent: General Fund $239.8 million (16.8 percent), the Special Mental Health Fund $236.4 million (16.5 percent), the Education Trust Fund $79.1 million (5.5 percent), and other state sources $30.7 million, of which the Opioid Treatment Fund was $12.5 million. The remaining 59.1 percent was federal, local and miscellaneous, dominated by Medicaid: $568.0 million for community developmental-disability services, $125.9 million for community mental-illness services, $14.2 million for facilities and $9.5 million for community substance-use services. Federal grants added $64.2 million and federal block grants $33.8 million [16].

68.title: The Department's budget · B0093
68.text: Expenditures were $1.45 billion, of which 87.4 percent went to community services — $772.1 million developmental disabilities, $400.9 million mental illness, $89.9 million substance use — 8.5 percent (about $123 million) to the state hospitals (Bryce $55.9 million, Taylor Hardin $34.7 million, Mary Starke Harper $30.7 million, East Alabama adolescent unit $1.5 million), 2.6 percent to administration and the balance to special services [16].

69.title: The Department's budget · B0094
69.text: Two points follow. First, more than half of ADMH's budget is developmental-disability services funded largely by Medicaid; the mental-illness share of community spending is about $401 million [16]. Second, the General Fund — the line the Legislature debates each spring — is one-sixth of the whole [16], but it is the part that pays for what Medicaid does not: crisis centers, state hospitals for the uninsured, and services for adults without coverage.

70.title: What the Legislature did, FY2026 and FY2027 · B0096
70.text: In December 2024 the Department was considering a request for a General Fund increase of $68.6 million (28.8 percent) for FY2026 — $23.4 million for civil-commitment beds, $11.5 million to expand crisis care toward a goal of eleven crisis centers, $2 million for detoxification and $1 million for school-based mental health programs — as part of a tentative total state request of $389.6 million, 22.9 percent above FY2025 [21]. The Legislature did not fund an increase on that scale. The FY2026 enacted General Fund appropriation was $244.5 million, an increase of about $4.7 million (2 percent) [20] [22], with the six existing crisis diversion centers funded at $36 million, $8 million for civil-commitment and residential beds, $1 million for CIT training and provider rate increases [20]. The ETF appropriation was $84.0 million [58] [89].
70.section: What the Legislature did, FY2026 and FY2027

71.title: What the Legislature did, FY2026 and FY2027 · B0097
71.text: For FY2027 (Act 2026-383, signed April 2026) the General Fund line is $240.9 million, slightly below FY2026 [18] [90]. The main lines are set out below; the 988 call-center line fell from $500,000 to zero [18], and the last two quarterly installments of the $42 million for crisis diversion and rural crisis-care centers are withheld until the Department "reports the status of the programs" to the General Fund budget chairs, the Director of Finance and the Legislative Fiscal Officer, in the Alabama Reflector's account of the enacted budget [17] [18]. The Senate committee's version of the bill had tied third- and fourth-quarter payments of the $36 million for the six crisis centers to reporting each center's operating expenses, employees and persons served and to giving the Commission on the Evaluation of Services (ACES) access [19].
71.section: What the Legislature did, FY2026 and FY2027

73.title: What the Legislature did, FY2026 and FY2027 · B0099
73.text: Source: LSA enacted comparisons [20] [18]; the FY2027 sheet restates the FY2026 total as $244.6 million [18]. The FY2027 ETF line is $84.1 million ($84.0 million in FY2026), including $5.5 million for the school-based mental health collaboration [58].
73.section: What the Legislature did, FY2026 and FY2027

74.title: What the Legislature did, FY2026 and FY2027 · B0100
74.text: Opioid-settlement funds have become a second channel. Act 2025-255 directed $27.9 million to ADMH, including $5 million for civil beds, $3.5 million for 988, $2 million for Medicaid match and $1 million for naloxone [91]. HB487, passed by the Legislature in April 2026 [90] [92], appropriates a further $43.1 million across agencies, including $26.4 million to ADMH (of which $4 million is for the 988 crisis line, $7.5 million for co-occurring civil-commitment beds and $1 million for naloxone), $3 million to the Administrative Office of Courts for specialty courts, $2 million for a UAB psychiatry residency and $1.5 million to Pardons and Paroles [92] [93].
74.section: What the Legislature did, FY2026 and FY2027

75.title: What the Legislature did, FY2026 and FY2027 · B0101
75.text: In August 2026 the House General Fund budget chair, Rep. Rex Reynolds, put the cost of replacing 787 civil-commitment beds — the 2010 budget cuts closed 725 — at roughly $590 million in construction alone ($750,000 a bed), and the Commissioner said "We've got to have a new revenue stream" [32] [33]. A separate estimate, in ADMH's January 2026 budget presentation, prices closing the 779-bed gap to 30 beds per 100,000 residents at $226.4 million as a five-year goal [30]; the two estimates are not reconciled in the sources.
75.section: What the Legislature did, FY2026 and FY2027

76.title: Benchmarks · B0103
76.text: Alabama's state mental health agency spent $133.15 per resident in FY2024, ranking 30th of 52 jurisdictions (the 50 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico), against a U.S. average of $179. Of $685.2 million in SMHA-controlled spending, 84.8 percent went to community programs and 14.2 percent to state hospitals — a community-heavy mix by national standards [23]. The public system's penetration rate — people served per 1,000 residents — was 18.31 in 2025, unchanged from 2024, against 22.94 nationally (23.46 in 2024) [42] [43].

77.title: Payers other than the state · B0105
77.text: Medicaid is the largest single funder of ADMH-contracted care [16]. Alabama's standard federal match (FMAP) is 72.63 percent for FY2026 and 72.55 percent for FY2027 [95]; the federal government pays about 78 percent of Alabama Medicaid's $7.9 billion annual spending, and children are about half of enrollment [96]. Alabama has not expanded eligibility to low-income adults; the coverage gap is put at up to 155,000 people by Alabama Arise [36] [37]; KFF's July 2026 estimate is 86,000 uninsured adults in the gap itself and 147,000 who would become eligible if the state expanded [38]. Medicaid covers rehabilitative mental-health and substance-use services delivered by ADMH-certified providers (Admin. Code 560-X-47) [49], mobile crisis response since October 2023 [75], and, for adults aged 21–64, inpatient psychiatric care in institutions for mental disease located in Mobile and Baldwin counties under a Section 1115 waiver running to May 2027 [97]; a substance-use 1115 waiver has been pending at CMS since July 2023 [98]. Section 12 describes the CCBHC prospective-payment model now layered on top.

78.title: Payers other than the state · B0106
78.text: Employer-sponsored insurance covers half of Alabamians [99]; Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama holds 84 percent of the commercial market, and the American Medical Association ranks Alabama's commercial health-insurance market the least competitive in the nation [100]. The state has no published mental-health parity enforcement actions, according to ParityTrack's Alabama page (last modified in March 2021) [101].

79.title: Payers other than the state · B0107
79.text: Federal block grants to ADMH totaled $33.8 million in FY2025 [16]. The FY2026 federal appropriation (bill text released in January 2026, signed 3 February 2026) kept SAMHSA's funding roughly level [102] [103].

80.title: Payers other than the state · B0108
80.text: Local and philanthropic funding was not quantified for this report. Separately, the federally funded Alabama Rural Health Transformation Program awarded eight community mental health centers more than $8 million in its first round, in August 2026, including $4.4 million to six providers to pursue CCBHC certification [29]; a second round of 34 grants totaling nearly $55 million, to providers of all kinds and none described as being for CCBHC certification, followed on 1 October 2026 [104].

81.title: Key actors · B0110
81.text: Actor Financing role Legislature (General Fund and ETF committees) Appropriates state funds; sets conditions; directs opioid-settlement funds [18] [58] [17] [92] Governor and Department of Finance Executive budget; allotments [89] ADMH Division of Administration Allocates to state facilities and to 19 CMHCs and other contractors; manages block grants [54] [31] Alabama Medicaid Agency Eligibility, covered services, rates, waivers; CCBHC prospective payment [49] [97] [105] CMS and SAMHSA Match, waivers, block grants, demonstration oversight [95] [97] [16] [27] BCBS of Alabama and other insurers Commercial behavioral-health benefits and networks [100] ADECA Rural Health Transformation Program awards [29] Examiners of Public Accounts; ACES Audit and program evaluation [14]

82.title: Continuum lens · B0112
82.text: State dollars concentrate at two ends of the continuum — crisis and inpatient — while outpatient and recovery supports depend on Medicaid and therefore on coverage. The FY2027 budget illustrates it: $36 million for crisis centers, $6 million for rural crisis programs and $10.5 million for civil-commitment beds and residential services, against a 988 line reduced to zero [18]. CCBHC prospective payment is the first mechanism that pays the same clinic for prevention, outpatient, crisis and follow-up together.

83.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0114
83.text: Flat state funding after a growth period. The FY2026 draft request was the system's own estimate of what the five-year plan needs [21]; it received 2 percent [20] and FY2027 is lower [18]. The Legislature's conditions show that further funding will follow evidence of results (Domain 6) [17].

84.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0115
84.text: The coverage gap is also a financing gap. Every uninsured adult in crisis is a state-funded encounter. Section 12 gives the coverage figures.

85.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0116
85.text: Settlement funds are one-time. Opioid-settlement appropriations have paid for 988, beds and naloxone [91] [92]; none of these recur without a base appropriation.

86.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0117
86.text: Crisis-center cost per bed-day is now public. ACES's preliminary evaluation reported an FY2024 average of $2,193 per bed-day and 27 percent utilization, and could not verify the diversion figures [14]. The centers' case for continued funding depends on producing those numbers.

87.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0118
87.text: Conditioned appropriations are an opening. Agreeing a standard quarterly report for crisis centers and extending it to mobile crisis and 988 would turn a sanction into a management tool [17] [19].

88.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0119
88.text: ADMH plan goals touched: A1, A2, A3, D1, D2, D3, D4.

89.text: Asset What it provides LSA budget comparison sheets (ALISON) Line-item General Fund and ETF appropriations, enacted and proposed, by agency [20] [18] [58] ADMH Annual Report, financial section Revenue and expenditure by source and division [16] ADMH budget-hearing presentations The Department's own case, with program metrics [31] Alabama Medicaid provider manuals and alerts Covered services, codes and rates [106] NRI SMHA expenditure reports Per-capita spending comparisons across states [23] KFF state indicators FMAP, enrollment, coverage [95] [96]

90.title: Key data sources · B0123
90.text: ADMH Annual Report FY2025 [16]; LSA enacted comparisons FY2026 and FY2027 [20] [18] [58]; NRI SMHA Expenditures FY2024 [23]; SAMHSA URS 2024 and 2025 [43] [42]; KFF [95] [96]; Alabama Political Reporter on the 2025 session, HB487, bed costs and rural-health grants [22] [93] [32] [29]; Alabama Reflector on the FY2026 draft request, the FY2027 General Fund and HB487's passage [21] [17] [90].

91.title: Scope · B0126
91.text: This domain describes what services exist in Alabama, who provides them, and how a person moves between them: from promotion and prevention, through outpatient treatment, crisis response, inpatient and forensic care, to the supports that keep recovery going. The organizing question, borrowed from the National Academies' continuum and from the state mental health directors' Beyond Beds analysis, is whether each level exists at enough scale and whether the hand-offs between levels work [2] [3].

92.title: Who was served · B0128
92.text: In FY2025 the public system served about 232,000 people: 141,631 adults and 31,847 adolescents for mental illness, 48,860 adults and 4,506 adolescents for substance use (figures the Department marks as estimated for FY2025), and 4,817 adults and 340 adolescents for developmental disabilities. Community mental health center programs served 96,062 people, and the two then-certified CCBHCs served 30,275 [16]. The federal Uniform Reporting System counts 94,410 Alabamians served by the state mental health authority in its 2025 reporting year (October 2024 to September 2025), up from 93,506 in 2024, a penetration rate of 18.31 per 1,000 residents in both years against 22.94 nationally (23.46 in 2024); 618 were served in state hospitals during the year (645 in 2024) [42] [43].

93.title: The community base: 19 centers becoming CCBHCs · B0130
93.text: Alabama's community mental health system rests on 19 community mental health centers (CMHCs) [31], each governed by a regional "310" board [49] and together covering all 67 counties: ADMH's emergency-contact page lists a community provider for every county [107]. (ADMH's FY2025 report counts 23 CMHC programs [16], reflecting providers that operate more than one program; 19 is the number of organizations.) They are the entry point for outpatient therapy, psychiatric medication management, case management, Assertive Community Treatment, day programs, residential care, supported housing and supported employment for adults with serious mental illness and children with serious emotional disturbance. The March 2026 contract service delivery manual lists the residential tiers ADMH will fund — among them supported housing, adult residential care homes, three-bed residential, semi-independent apartments, crisis residential units, transitional-age residential and foster care [108].
93.section: The community base: 19 centers becoming CCBHCs

94.title: The community base: 19 centers becoming CCBHCs · B0131
94.text: The centers are in the middle of a structural change. In June 2024 Alabama was named one of ten states added to the federal Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic (CCBHC) Medicaid demonstration [24] [25]. A CCBHC must provide nine services, including 24/7 crisis response, outpatient mental-health and substance-use treatment, primary-care screening, targeted case management, psychiatric rehabilitation, peer and family support and services for veterans, and is paid a daily prospective rate rather than fee-for-service [10]. WellStone (Huntsville) and AltaPointe (Mobile) were certified in July 2024 [26]; Mountain Lakes Behavioral Healthcare (Jackson and Marshall counties) received federal approval in October 2025 and Highland Health Systems (Calhoun and Cleburne) in April 2026 [27]. ADMH's CCBHC service directory also lists a fifth clinic, South Central Alabama Mental Health, which the May 2026 release does not name [28] [27]. Six more providers — Integrea, Northwest Alabama Mental Health Center, Carastar, CarePath, Central Alabama Wellness and JBS — received rural-health grants in August 2026 to pursue certification [29]. ADMH's stated goal is a statewide transition [24] [27]. Section 12 describes the payment model.
94.section: The community base: 19 centers becoming CCBHCs

95.title: The community base: 19 centers becoming CCBHCs · B0132
95.text: Three first-episode psychosis (coordinated specialty care) programs operate under the NOVA name — at JBS Mental Health Authority in Birmingham, AltaPointe in Mobile and WellStone in Huntsville [109]. Statewide in the 2025 reporting year, 897 people were in Assertive Community Treatment, 234 in supported employment and 259 in supported housing (779, 205 and 240 in 2024) [42] [43].
95.section: The community base: 19 centers becoming CCBHCs

96.title: Crisis response: someone to contact, someone to respond, a safe place for help · B0134
96.text: Alabama built its crisis system almost from nothing after 2020. It now has the three elements of the national model [110] [13], and in 2025 its crisis centers came under independent evaluation by the Alabama Commission on the Evaluation of Services [14].
96.section: Crisis response: someone to contact, someone to respond, a safe place for help

97.title: Crisis response: someone to contact, someone to respond, a safe place for help · B0135
97.text: Someone to contact. Alabama answers 988 through four in-state call centers operated by AltaPointe (Mobile), JBS and the Crisis Center (Birmingham), SpectraCare (Dothan) and WellStone (Huntsville) [9]. The centers handled 40,053 calls in FY2025, up from 34,027 in FY2024; texts and chats were still routed to a national center. The in-state answer rate — calls answered by an Alabama counselor rather than routed to a national backup — rose from 82.5 percent in FY2024 to 87.4 percent in FY2025 and reached 90.9 percent in May 2025; average speed to answer was 22 seconds by September 2025 [16]. Between the July 2022 launch and ADMH's release of 16 July 2025, crisis counselors received 132,713 contacts, counting calls, texts and chats [15]. The FY2027 General Fund line for 988 call centers is zero, after $500,000 in FY2026 [18]; opioid-settlement appropriations carried $3.5 million for the 988 crisis line in 2025 and $4 million in the 2026 supplemental appropriation the Legislature passed in April (HB487) [91] [92].
97.section: Crisis response: someone to contact, someone to respond, a safe place for help

98.title: Crisis response: someone to contact, someone to respond, a safe place for help · B0136
98.text: Someone to respond. ADMH funds 14 mobile crisis teams at 11 CMHCs [13]; in February 2025 the Department's five-year plan was to grow from 14 teams to 23, and 24 counties were then covered by mobile teams and crisis centers taken together [33]. Five child-and-adolescent teams at three centers (AltaPointe, JBS, WellStone) [111] served 936 young people in FY2025, the first year that figure was reported [16]; the General Fund has carried a $5 million child-and-adolescent mobile-crisis pilot line since at least FY2025, unchanged in FY2027 [20] [18]. Mobile crisis became a Medicaid-billable service in October 2023 [75]. A co-responder program pairing officers with clinicians was running in Huntsville by early 2022 [112], and Mobile police announced a one-precinct pilot with AltaPointe in May 2022 [113] (Section 10).
98.section: Crisis response: someone to contact, someone to respond, a safe place for help

99.title: Crisis response: someone to contact, someone to respond, a safe place for help · B0137
99.text: A safe place for help. Six crisis diversion centers (the state budget's term; ADMH's own pages call them crisis centers [20] [12]) operate — AltaPointe (Mobile), Carastar (Montgomery), JBS (Birmingham), Indian Rivers' Hope Pointe (Tuscaloosa), WellStone (Huntsville) and SpectraCare (Dothan, operational from 17 February 2025) [12] [114] — plus WellStone's 24-bed pediatric crisis unit (ages 12–18) in Huntsville, the state's first, opened in late September 2024 [41] [115]. The centers accept walk-ins and law-enforcement drop-offs around the clock [12] and provide crisis stabilization, clinical evaluation and psychiatric care, with temporary and extended observation beds [12] [31]; the opioid council's 2025 report describes them as "detox-capable" [76]. They performed 9,929 evaluations in FY2025 and more than 1,000 in August 2025, a new monthly high; the pediatric unit performed 520 [16]. ADMH's five-year plan of February 2025 called for eleven centers [33]; the FY2026 and FY2027 General Fund budgets fund the "Existing Six Crisis Diversion Centers" and carry no line for a seventh [20] [18]. The 2025 edition of this report gave the centers' catchment as 20 of 67 counties; ADMH's crisis-centers page now lists 60 counties as served by one of the six centers and leaves out seven (Butler, Coffee, Colbert, Covington, Crenshaw, Franklin, Lauderdale) [12] [13] — a measure of responsibility rather than travel distance (the 24 counties reported in February 2025 counted counties then covered by mobile teams and crisis centers together [33]). ADMH's own pages disagree on the detail: that page lists five counties for the Dothan center, while the Department's February 2025 release says it serves 20 [12] [114].
99.section: Crisis response: someone to contact, someone to respond, a safe place for help

100.title: Crisis response: someone to contact, someone to respond, a safe place for help · B0138
100.text: What the evaluator found. The Alabama Commission on the Evaluation of Services said in a preliminary report of September 2025 that the centers then operating had logged 16,414 interactions from 2021 to the end of 2024 and that the state had dedicated $175 million to the six centers since FY2021; that the FY2024 average was $2,193 per bed-day and 27 percent utilization; that capital costs ranged from $3.3 million to $12.6 million per center; and that it "cannot verify" the emergency-room and jail-diversion figures the Department had reported, because centers counted them inconsistently and one never reported a jail diversion. The Department's response, printed with the evaluation, questions how utilization and average daily bed costs were calculated and says "most centers function at capacity most days" [14]; at a public meeting that September the Commissioner and her staff pushed back on the analysis, saying the Department cannot turn over protected health information [19]. The FY2027 budget then attached conditions to the crisis money: the Senate committee's version made the third- and fourth-quarter payments for the six centers depend on reporting of each center's operating expenses, employees and persons served, and on evaluator access [19]; the enacted budget, as reported, withholds the last two quarterly installments of the $42 million for crisis centers and rural crisis care until the Department "reports the status of the programs" to the budget chairs, the Finance Director and the Legislative Fiscal Officer [17]. Provider-level examples remain available — SpectraCare reported 485 emergency-room diversions and 43 law-enforcement drop-offs in the part of FY2025 after it opened [16] — but the 2025 edition's statewide diversion totals should no longer be cited.
100.section: Crisis response: someone to contact, someone to respond, a safe place for help

101.title: Inpatient and forensic care · B0140
101.text: Alabama operates three state psychiatric facilities: Bryce Hospital (Tuscaloosa; 337 people served in FY2025), Taylor Hardin Secure Medical Facility (forensic; 189) and the Mary Starke Harper Geriatric Psychiatry Center (94), plus an adolescent unit at East Alabama Medical Center (17), for a combined 637 individuals served in FY2025 as reported by ADMH [16]; the federal tables count 618 people served in state hospitals during the 2025 reporting year and 645 in 2024 [42] [43].

102.title: Inpatient and forensic care · B0141
102.text: Capacity is the system's most-cited gap. ADMH's FY2027 budget presentation, with data as of 13 January 2026, counts 771 involuntary (civil-commitment) beds — 285 at Bryce and Harper, 234 contracted in community hospitals and 252 crisis residential beds at certified providers, which ADMH lists among its involuntary beds — or 15.1 per 100,000 residents against the 30 per 100,000 (1,550 beds) that the Treatment Advocacy Center calls the minimum and the Department uses as its planning benchmark; the presentation prices closing the 779-bed gap, as a five-year goal, at $226.4 million [30]. The earlier count was 698 beds (13.7 per 100,000), both at the start of FY2025 and in August 2025 — 285 at Bryce and Harper, 225 contracted and 188 crisis residential — plus 180 voluntary observation beds at crisis centers; the Department's stated intention then was to add 57 beds over the following year, to 755 (14.8 per 100,000), funded from the Opioid Settlement Fund and legislative appropriation [16] [31]. In August 2026 the House General Fund budget chair, Rep. Rex Reynolds, put the cost of replacing 787 beds at about $590 million in construction alone; the 2010 cuts had closed 725 [32] [33]. The $226.4 million and the $590 million are two separate estimates, not reconciled in the sources.

103.title: Inpatient and forensic care · B0142
103.text: On the forensic side, Taylor Hardin has expanded from 140 to 225 beds, with about 200 filled by August 2026 [32] [115]. The forensic waitlist — people waiting in county jails for psychiatric evaluation or treatment, the population covered by the Hunter consent decree — fell from 327 in January 2026 to 291 in July 2026, against a goal of 100 by year-end [32]; the average wait was "well over a year" in November 2025 [116]. A jail-based restoration program had enrolled 31 people and completed 23 by September 2025 [16]; the Department has also begun a telehealth restoration program in county jails, and forensic navigators now work the list [32]. Section 10 treats this in full.

104.title: Inpatient and forensic care · B0143
104.text: Community hospitals and emergency departments remain the default for many people in crisis — ADMH names reducing "the burden on EDs/Hospitals" among the goals of crisis care [13] — but emergency-department boarding of psychiatric patients is not measured statewide: no such measure was found in the Department's published reports as of October 2026. Children's of Alabama said in January 2025 that it would add eleven beds to its inpatient behavioral-health unit that month [117]; UAB's child and adolescent psychiatry division, which describes a strong on-site affiliation with the hospital, lists 50 inpatient beds (12 child, 38 adolescent) on an undated page [118].

105.title: Promotion, prevention and early intervention · B0145
105.text: School-based mental health. ADMH's collaboration with the State Department of Education brings CMHC services into 122 school systems through all 19 centers [119], funded at $5.5 million in the FY2027 ETF [58]; separately, local education agencies that apply receive roughly $40,000 each for a Mental Health Services Coordinator under an ALSDE program [120]. The sources disagree on that program's FY2026 funding: ALSDE's memo says the FY2026 ETF appropriated $6.36 million [120], while the Legislature's FY2027 ETF sheet shows the line at $4.69 million budgeted for FY2026 and $9.25 million in the FY2027 ETF [58]. Since 2022 schools must obtain written parental opt-in consent for mental-health services, at first for students under 14 [60] [121]; since October 2025 students under 16 cannot consent to ongoing counseling on their own [59] [60].

106.title: Promotion, prevention and early intervention · B0146
106.text: Suicide prevention. ADMH employs the state's suicide prevention coordinator, the Alabama Suicide Prevention and Resources Coalition is the state coalition, and the state plan runs 2021–2026 [122]; 834 Alabamians died by suicide in 2024, a rate of 16.2 per 100,000 [123]. The Houston Hunter Act (2025) adds voluntary firearm-hold agreements as a lethal-means tool [64].

107.title: Promotion, prevention and early intervention · B0147
107.text: Substance-use prevention and treatment. The Opioid Overdose and Addiction Council's 2025 report counts at least 1,151 overdose deaths in 2024, a floor drawn from emergency-department cases, and an estimated 1,052 in 2025, a provisional figure [76]; ADMH distributed 48,179 boxes of naloxone between 1 November 2024 and 31 October 2025 (40,733 kits in fiscal year 2025) [76] and certifies 104 detoxification beds statewide, including a 16-bed unit in Huntsville [16].

108.title: Promotion, prevention and early intervention · B0148
108.text: Primary care. Alabama's federally qualified health centers are a primary-care platform for integrated behavioral health: the state's 17 federally funded health centers served 316,993 patients in 2025, 15,696 of them for mental health [124]. Alabama Medicaid pays for live-video and audio-only telehealth at parity, which supports collaborative-care models [88]. No statewide count of integrated-care sites was found as of October 2026. Alabama Medicaid is a fee-for-service program with no comprehensive managed-care plans [125] [49], with care coordination through the Alabama Coordinated Health Network [126], so behavioral-health benefits are set by the state plan and ADMH certification rather than by health plans [49] (Section 12).

109.title: Promotion, prevention and early intervention · B0149
109.text: Peer support. ADMH's Office of Peer Programs trains and certifies peer specialists [127]; a current statewide count was not found on its page or in the Department's other published sources read as of October 2026 (Appendix D).

110.title: Recovery supports · B0151
110.text: Supported employment reached 234 people and supported housing 259 in the 2025 reporting year (205 and 240 in 2024), small numbers against 94,410 served [42] [43]. The Individual Placement and Support program, run with the Department of Rehabilitation Services, expanded in February 2025 from three sites to five (Central Alabama Wellness, AltaPointe, Carastar, Indian Rivers, JBS) under a five-year federal grant [128]. In 2025, 91.4 percent of people served (all ages) lived in a private residence and 2.7 percent were homeless or in a shelter at the reporting point (92.7 and 1.9 percent in 2024); among adults the 2025 figures were 87.6 and 4.1 percent. Of adults served, 21.0 percent were employed against 28.8 percent nationally (21.7 and 28.9 percent in 2024) [42] [43]. Section 11 covers housing and employment as systems.

111.title: Continuity of care · B0153
111.text: Thirty-day readmission to state hospitals was 1.5 percent in the 2025 reporting year (9.0 percent nationally) and 180-day readmission also 1.5 percent (19.8 percent nationally), down from 6.8 and 9.5 percent in 2024; the rates rest on very small numbers — one readmission among 68 civil discharges in 2025, five among 74 in 2024 [42] [43]. The 2025 edition's figure of 3.4 percent reflected an earlier year. No statewide seven-day follow-up measure was found in the Department's published reports or the federal tables as of October 2026; the CCBHC billing manual allows follow-up interventions for up to 72 hours after a mobile-crisis response [105].

112.title: Key actors · B0155
112.text: Actor Role in the continuum 19 CMHCs (4 CCBHCs named in ADMH's May 2026 release; 5 in its service directory) [31] [27] [28] Outpatient, case management, ACT, residential, school-based, mobile crisis, crisis centers [108] [119] [13] [12] ADMH state facilities Bryce, Taylor Hardin, Harper; contracted community-hospital beds [16] [31] 988 centers (AltaPointe, JBS/Crisis Center, SpectraCare, WellStone) Someone to contact; triage to mobile teams and centers [9] Hospitals and emergency departments; Children's of Alabama; UAB Acute and inpatient care; pediatric intake and consult lines [117] [129] [130] [118] Federally qualified health centers Primary-care integration [124] Law enforcement and co-responder programs Transport and diversion (Section 10) [12] [112] [113] ADRS Supported employment partner [128] ACES Independent evaluation of crisis services [14]

113.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0157
113.text: Measure the crisis system the way the evaluator asked. Reporting to the Legislature on the crisis programs is now a condition of the last two quarterly payments [17]; the Senate committee's version specified operating costs, staffing and persons served, plus evaluator access [19]. The evaluator found no common way of counting diversion among the centers [14], and no uniform definitions of follow-up or readmission were found in the Department's published reports as of October 2026. Extending common definitions to mobile crisis and 988 would give Alabama a crisis dashboard for the first time.

114.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0158
114.text: Fill the middle of the continuum. Beds and crisis centers have grown; step-down residential, intensive outpatient and supported housing have not. The 2025 figures of 259 people in supported housing and 234 in supported employment measure the gap [42].

115.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0159
115.text: Reach the counties without teams. In February 2025 mobile crisis teams and crisis centers together covered 24 counties [33]; the five rural crisis-care programs, first funded in FY2021 [111] and carried at $6 million a year in the General Fund [18], and the $5 million child-and-adolescent pilot, in the budget since at least FY2025 [20] [18], are the current increments toward the 23-team goal [33].

116.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0160
116.text: Finish the forensic repair. Reaching the Department's goal of 100 on the waitlist by the end of 2026 [32], within the decree's inpatient-restoration term that runs to 31 January 2027 [11], depends on filling Taylor Hardin's remaining beds and scaling jail-based restoration.

117.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0161
117.text: Use CCBHC to join the pieces. The CCBHC rate pays for crisis, outpatient and follow-up in one bundle [10] [105]; as more centers convert, the hand-offs that now fail between separately funded programs can become one provider's responsibility.

118.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0162
118.text: ADMH plan goals touched: A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, B3.

120.title: Key data sources · B0166
120.text: ADMH Annual Report FY2025 [16]; ADMH crisis and 988 pages [12] [13] [9] [15]; ACES evaluation [14]; SAMHSA URS 2025 and 2024 [42] [43]; ADMH summer 2025 budget deck and January 2026 budget presentation [31] [30]; CCBHC releases and manuals [24] [27] [10] [105]; Alabama Political Reporter on the forensic waitlist and rural-health grants [32] [29].

121.title: Scope · B0169
121.text: The workforce domain covers the people who deliver mental health care — psychiatrists, psychiatric nurse practitioners, psychologists, licensed counselors and social workers, nurses, case managers, direct-support staff, peer specialists — and the pipeline, licensure, incentives and working conditions that determine how many there are and where they practice. It also covers the wider network of first responders, educators and faith leaders trained to recognize and respond to mental health needs. Every other domain depends on this one.

122.title: Alabama's shortage, measured · B0171
122.text: Alabama has 67 federally designated mental health professional shortage areas covering 2,934,202 people — more than half the state's population of 5.19 million [34] [133]. Federal data as of December 2025 show Alabama meeting 28.4 percent of the need for psychiatric care in those areas, with 128 additional practitioners required to lift the designations [34]. Mental Health America's 2025 ranking places Alabama 51st of 51 for mental health workforce availability, at one provider for every 740 residents against a national ratio of one to 320 [35]. In this report's reading, the shortage falls hardest on the 42 percent of the population that lives in rural areas [134].

123.title: Alabama's shortage, measured · B0172
123.text: Inside the public system, ADMH reported in 2024 that its mental health provider network had 752 vacancies at the end of FY2023 against a need of 4,678 full-time positions — about 3,926 filled, or about 84 percent staffed [135]. No later statewide staffing or vacancy figure was found in the Department's published reports as of October 2026; its 2025 and 2026 budget presentations did not update it, and this report does not estimate one (Appendix D). The Commissioner told the board in August 2024 that only about half of the forensic hospital's technician and nursing positions were filled [116] [136].

124.title: How Alabama develops its workforce · B0174
124.text: Licensure compacts. Alabama has joined most of the interstate compacts that let licensed clinicians practice across state lines, in person or by telehealth: the Psychology Interjurisdictional Compact (PSYPACT, effective June 2021) [48], the Counseling Compact (member; ten states were issuing privileges by 1 October 2026, Alabama not yet among them) [82], the Nurse Licensure Compact (January 2020) [83], the Interstate Medical Licensure Compact [84], the EMS Compact (2017) [85] and the Occupational Therapy Compact (member, not yet issuing privileges in Alabama) [86]. Alabama joined the Social Work Licensure Compact in 2024 [87]; that compact had 35 member states by July 2026 but had not yet begun issuing multistate licenses [137].

125.title: How Alabama develops its workforce · B0175
125.text: Training pipeline. The University of Alabama's College of Community Health Sciences announced a psychiatry residency with its first class to start in June 2026 and six residents a year [138], and HB487 (2026) directs $2 million of opioid-settlement funds to a UAB psychiatry residency [92] [93]; UAB's child and adolescent psychiatry division trains eight fellows [118]. Alabama's universities — UAB, the University of Alabama, Auburn, the University of South Alabama, Alabama A&M, Alabama State and others — supply counseling, social work, psychology and nursing graduates; no statewide behavioral-health graduate-output series was found as of October 2026.

126.title: How Alabama develops its workforce · B0176
126.text: Incentives. Federal National Health Service Corps loan repayment is available at approved shortage-area sites [139]. In FY2024 the Legislature funded $15 million for mental-illness providers and $2.86 million for substance-use providers as workforce investments through higher provider rates, and the rate increases it funded for developmental-disability providers lifted the average direct-support-professional wage from $9.91 an hour in FY2022 to $15.17 by March 2024; ADMH added shift differentials and attendance bonuses for state-hospital staff [135] [140]. The FY2026 budget carried provider rate-increase lines for intellectual-disability programs, raised by $2.5 million, and for substance-use programs, held at the FY2025 level [20]. No direct-support wage later than March 2024 was found in the Department's published reports as of October 2026 (Appendix D).

127.title: How Alabama develops its workforce · B0177
127.text: Peer and community workforce. ADMH's Office of Peer Programs trains and certifies peer support specialists [127]; the CCBHC model requires peer and family support as one of its nine services, which will expand demand for certified peers as centers convert [10]. The Agency for Substance Abuse Prevention, with ADMH, has certified more than 400 faith leaders as Faith-Based Support Specialists since 2022 [141]. The Alabama Peace Officers' Standards and Training Commission has listed a two-day Crisis Intervention Team class for 16 continuing-education units but mandates no mental-health hours in officers' continuing education [142] [143]; NAMI Alabama's CIT Division coordinates the regional CIT programs and its pages give no statewide count of trained officers [144] [145]; ADMH's July 2024 budget presentation reported "1375 plus CIT trained officers" [135], and no current or agency-level count was found as of October 2026 (Section 10).

128.title: How Alabama develops its workforce · B0178
128.text: Strategic plan. Workforce Health and Wellness is the third of ADMH's five priorities [40]; according to Little Orange Fish's alignment analysis of the full plan, its goals are to support staff well-being, build trauma-related skills, train supervisors and widen the applicant pool through alternative qualifications.

129.title: Well-being and retention · B0180
129.text: The Department's plan, as read in Little Orange Fish's alignment analysis, names well-being first among its workforce goals, a recognition that turnover, not only recruitment, drains capacity. Public evidence is thin: no statewide turnover rate, burnout survey or exit data was found for the mental health provider network or the state hospitals in the Department's published reports as of October 2026; its FY2026 budget presentation says only that Alabama was "one of the states with the largest decrease in staff turnover" in 2022–2023 National Core Indicators data [140]. The Legislature's 2025 resolution (HJR273) commissioned a study of PTSD among first responders [22]. What can be said is that pay has moved — the direct-support wage rose by half between 2022 and 2024 [135] — and that the forensic system's staffing shortfall is the most visible well-being problem in the system, because it determines how long people wait in jail.

130.title: Continuum lens · B0182
130.text: Workforce shortages fall unevenly along the continuum. Crisis centers and 988 have been staffed because they were funded first [135]; outpatient and children's services carry the longest waits because they depend on licensed clinicians in shortage areas [34]; the forensic hospital, which needs nurses and mental health technicians in Tuscaloosa [16] [135], is the system's weakest link. Telehealth and the compacts ease the outpatient end; they do not help inpatient units.

131.title: Key actors · B0184
131.text: Actor Workforce role ADMH (Peer Programs; Human Resources; Facility Operations) Certification of peers; state-hospital staffing; provider workforce funding [127] [54] [52] [135] Licensing boards (Medical Examiners, Nursing, Psychology, Counseling, Social Work) Licensure, compact participation, supervision rules [83] [84] Universities and ACCS Degree programs, residencies, fellowships [138] [118] HRSA / National Health Service Corps Shortage designations; loan repayment [34] [139] NAMI Alabama CIT Division; APOSTC Law-enforcement training [145] [142] Agency for Substance Abuse Prevention Faith-Based Support Specialist certification [141] Professional associations Advocacy on reimbursement, telehealth and scope

132.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0186
132.text: Publish the staffing picture. The 2023 vacancy count (752) [135] was presented alongside the FY2024 workforce funds; an annual update would let the Legislature see what those funds bought.

133.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0187
133.text: Use the compacts. Alabama's membership in seven compacts is a real asset [82] [48] [83] [84] [85] [86] [87]; the practical constraint is that the Counseling and Social Work compacts are not yet operational in Alabama [82] [137]. Tracking the number of out-of-state clinicians practicing under PSYPACT and the Nurse Licensure Compact would show whether they are reaching rural counties.

134.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0188
134.text: Grow the non-licensed tiers. Certified peers, community health workers and bachelor's-level case managers can carry work that now waits for licensed clinicians; under CCBHC payment a certified peer specialist's service is enough to trigger the clinic's daily rate [105].

135.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0189
135.text: Grow the psychiatry pipeline. The UA residency announced for June 2026 and the UAB residency money the Legislature passed in 2026 would be the first state-funded pipeline steps in years [138] [92]; the state's three first-episode programs [109] and the pediatric crisis unit [41] show where graduates are needed.

136.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0190
136.text: Forensic staffing first. Every unfilled position at Taylor Hardin is measured in jail days under a federal decree [11].

137.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0191
137.text: ADMH plan goals touched: C1, C2, C3, C4, A5.
