139.title: Key data sources · B0195
139.text: KFF HPSA and HRSA data [34] [139]; MHA 2025 [35]; compact sources [82] [48] [137] [83] [84] [85] [86] [87]; ADMH budget presentations of July 2024 and FY2026 for FY2022–2024 staffing and wage figures [135] [140]; ADMH Strategic Plan [40] and Little Orange Fish's alignment analysis of it; Alabama Political Reporter on 2025 session and HB487 [22] [93] and the enrolled HB487 [92]; WSFA and Alabama Reflector on forensic staffing [116] [136]; FY2026 General Fund comparison sheet [20]; ADMH reports, pages and CCBHC manuals [16] [10] [105] [109] [52] [54] [127] [146]; other sources cited in this section [142] [143] [11] [133] [134] [144] [145] [118] [141] [41] [138].

140.title: Scope · B0198
140.text: This domain covers the physical and technical capacity behind services: hospital and crisis-center buildings, residential beds, the information systems that carry client records and claims, telehealth, broadband, and access to psychiatric medications. Infrastructure decisions are slow and expensive; they set the ceiling on what the other domains can deliver for a decade.

141.title: Facilities · B0200
141.text: State hospitals. Bryce Hospital was rebuilt in 2014 on a new Tuscaloosa campus [147]. Taylor Hardin Secure Medical Facility, the forensic hospital, has grown from 140 to 225 beds; about 200 were in use by August 2026, with the remaining 25 awaiting a plumbing repair that the Commissioner expected in the first week of October 2026 [32]. No report that those beds had opened was found as of 3 October 2026. The Mary Starke Harper Geriatric Psychiatry Center serves older adults [16]. Together with the adolescent unit at East Alabama Medical Center, the three hospitals served 637 people in FY2025 [16]. State hospital operations cost about $123 million in FY2025 [16].

142.title: Facilities · B0201
142.text: Crisis infrastructure. The six crisis centers [14] and the pediatric unit [41] are the state's newest buildings. ACES's preliminary evaluation of September 2025 found capital costs ranged from $3.3 million to $12.6 million per center and that FY2024 utilization averaged 27 percent — meaning the physical capacity exists to absorb growth before new construction [14]. The Department's response, printed with the evaluation, questions how utilization and average daily bed costs were calculated and says "most centers function at capacity most days" [14]; at a public meeting that September the Commissioner and her staff pushed back on the analysis, saying the Department cannot turn over protected health information [19]. The Legislature's FY2027 line of $36 million is for the "Existing Six Crisis Diversion Centers" [18]; this report reads it as operating money, not capital.

143.title: Facilities · B0202
143.text: Beds. Involuntary bed capacity — 698 at the start of FY2025, 13.7 per 100,000 [16]; 771, or 15.1 per 100,000, in the Department's January 2026 count, against the 1,550 beds (30 per 100,000) that the Department, citing the Treatment Advocacy Center, treats as the minimum [30] — is the system's defining infrastructure gap. The Department prices the 779 further beds at $226.4 million among its five-year financial goals [30]; the $590 million estimate for replacing 787 beds, given in August 2026 at a Joint Mental Health Task Force meeting by Rep. Rex Reynolds, the House General Fund budget chair [32] [33], is a construction-only figure that the Commissioner said cannot be met from current revenues [32]. The two are separate estimates, not reconciled in the sources. Residential step-down capacity (the residential categories in ADMH's contract service delivery manual) is contracted rather than built [108]; no statewide count of those beds was found in the Department's published reports as of October 2026.

144.title: Facilities · B0203
144.text: Detoxification. ADMH certifies 104 detox beds statewide, including River Crossing in Huntsville (16 beds) [16].

145.title: Facilities · B0204
145.text: Corrections. The 4,000-bed Governor Kay Ivey Correctional Complex in Elmore County, built at about $1.25 billion with specialized medical and mental-health units, is due to be completed by 15 October 2026; the Department of Corrections flagged a "reasonable concern" of delay in July 2026 (Section 10) [148]. No report of completion, opening or a revised date was found as of 3 October 2026.

146.title: Information systems · B0206
146.text: ADMH runs two provider-reporting systems: the Alabama Community Services Information System (ACSIS) for mental-illness and CCBHC providers — client, episode, staff and 837P billing submissions — and the Alabama Substance Abuse Information System (ASAIS) for substance-use providers [149] [150]. The 2025 edition of this report used several other names for these systems; none was correct. The Department's certification process moved to an automated platform (ACAP) in November 2025 [16].

147.title: Information systems · B0207
147.text: One Health Record, the Alabama Medicaid health information exchange, announced in April 2023 that it planned to join the eHealth Exchange QHIN under the federal TEFCA framework [151], and reports that in 2023 it was the "first HIE to successfully exchange data across the TEFCA QHIN framework" [45]; as of December 2025 it connected 57 hospitals (16 more in progress), more than 800 clinics and 15 FQHC, rural-health, health-information-network and CMHC organizations (more than 300 sites). ADMH's own connection was listed as a work in progress ("ADMH W-I-P") [45]. CCBHCs must report federally specified outcome measures; ADMH's board minutes reference a Netsmart system for that purpose [26].

148.title: Information systems · B0208
148.text: Clinical data sharing remains constrained by federal substance-use confidentiality rules (42 CFR Part 2) [152] and by the fact that each CMHC runs its own electronic health record [153].

149.title: Telehealth and broadband · B0210
149.text: Alabama Medicaid reimburses live-video and audio-only telehealth at parity with in-person visits and allows patients to be served at home (originating sites receive a $20 fee; the home does not); the Center for Connected Health Policy finds no private-payer telehealth parity law [88]. The CCBHC provider manual permits telehealth for eligible services on a HIPAA-compliant platform with documented client preference, following Medicaid's telehealth chapter [10]. 988 text and chat are available [9], and a federal rule effective October 2025 requires nationwide carriers to georoute 988 texts within 18 months (36 months for smaller carriers), so that texts reach the nearest 988 center [154] [155].

150.title: Telehealth and broadband · B0211
150.text: Broadband is the constraint on telehealth's reach. About 87.5 percent of Alabama households had a broadband subscription in 2020–2024, leaving one in eight without [133]. Alabama's final BEAD proposal, approved in March 2026, commits nearly $460 million across 63 projects to reach roughly 92,000 unserved locations; 71 percent of the projects will use fiber and 24 percent low-earth-orbit satellite [156].

151.title: Medicines · B0213
151.text: Psychiatric medication for people in the public system is paid for by Medicaid where they are enrolled and otherwise through the state's Indigent Drug Program, dispensed through the community mental health centers, and manufacturer assistance [157]; the FY2025 report does not publish a prescriptions count. Medication-assisted treatment for opioid use disorder is a Medicaid benefit [158] [159], and ADMH distributed 48,179 boxes of naloxone between 1 November 2024 and 31 October 2025 (40,733 kits in fiscal year 2025) [76]. The Prescription Drug Monitoring Program is run by the Department of Public Health's Pharmacy Division under Code of Alabama §20-2-210 [160]. The 2025 edition's statement that Alabama had enacted prescriptive authority for psychologists was incorrect; Alabama is not among the nine jurisdictions that have enacted it [161], and no such Alabama statute was found.

152.title: Medicines · B0214
152.text: Medication continuity at transitions — hospital discharge, jail release, loss of coverage — is, in this report's reading, a reason the CCBHC model's provision for up to 72 hours of follow-up after a crisis response matters [105].

153.title: Transportation · B0216
153.text: Alabama Medicaid operates a Non-Emergency Transportation program [47] [162]. As of ALDOT's 2023 study, twenty-eight rural (Section 5311) transit providers serve 58 of 67 counties; nine counties, including several urban ones served by city systems, have no rural provider [47]. The only mental-health-specific transport support identified is the transportation voucher within the IPS supported-employment program [128].

154.title: Continuum lens · B0218
154.text: Alabama's infrastructure investment since 2020 has gone to the crisis and forensic ends of the continuum [14] [32]. The middle — residential step-down, supported housing, outpatient clinic space in rural counties — has no capital program that was found for this report. Telehealth and broadband are the cheapest way to extend the outpatient end; they do nothing for beds.

155.title: Key actors · B0220
155.text: Actor Infrastructure role ADMH Division of Administration; Facility Operations State hospitals, capital projects, ACSIS/ASAIS, ACAP [54] [16] Alabama Medicaid Agency / One Health Record HIE, telehealth policy, NEMT, pharmacy benefit [45] [88] [162] [159] ADECA BEAD broadband; Rural Health Transformation awards [163] [164] CMHCs / CCBHCs Own clinics, crisis centers, residential sites, EHRs [12] [108] [153] ADPH Pharmacy Division PDMP [160] ALDOT and local transit agencies Rural and urban transit [47] Department of Corrections Prison medical and mental-health facilities [148]

156.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0222
156.text: Use the capacity already built. Crisis-center utilization of 27 percent, as ACES measured it for FY2024 [14], means the first growth can come from referrals and transport, not construction.

157.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0223
157.text: Decide the bed question. A $590 million capital estimate that the Commissioner says cannot be met from current revenues [32] is the system's largest open item (Chairman Reynolds's August 2026 figure for replacing 787 beds; the Department's own January 2026 estimate for closing the 779-bed gap to 30 per 100,000 is $226.4 million, and the two are separate estimates [30]); a phased plan tied to the Department's own five-year bed goal — its 755-bed interim target [16] was overtaken by the 771 beds counted in January 2026 [30] — would make the bed question legible to the Legislature.

158.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0224
158.text: Connect ADMH to the exchange. One Health Record's TEFCA status and hospital coverage make it the natural spine for discharge notification and follow-up; the Department's connection is the missing link [45].

159.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0225
159.text: Pair BEAD with telehealth access points. Libraries, extension offices and CMHC satellite rooms in the 92,000 unserved locations' counties can bring telepsychiatry to people before fiber arrives [156].

160.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0226
160.text: Build the step-down middle. Residential care and supported housing are the cheapest beds in the system and the least visible in the budget.

161.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0227
161.text: ADMH plan goals touched: A1, A2, A6, D4.

163.title: Key data sources · B0231
163.text: ADMH Annual Report FY2025 [16]; ACSIS page [149]; ACES evaluation [14]; One Health Record briefing [45]; CCHP [88]; Census QuickFacts [133]; Governor's BEAD release [156]; ALDOT rural transit study [47]; Alabama Political Reporter on Taylor Hardin and beds [32].

164.title: Scope · B0234
164.text: This domain covers how the system knows what it is doing: the data providers report, the measures the state publishes, the surveys of people served, the evaluations that test whether programs work, and the quality processes that turn findings into change. Alabama's 2025 crisis-center evaluation made this domain the pivot of the state's mental-health politics: funding is now conditioned on reporting [14] [17].

165.title: What Alabama measures today · B0236
165.text: Federal reporting. Through the Mental Health Block Grant, ADMH submits the Uniform Reporting System tables each year. The 2025 tables (published July 2026, covering October 2024 through September 2025) give the public system's clearest performance picture; 2024 values (published July 2025) are shown for comparison [42] [43]:

167.title: What Alabama measures today · B0237+1
167.text: Alabama's readmission rates rest on very small numbers: one readmission among 68 civil discharges in 2025 and five among 74 in 2024 [42] [43].

168.title: What Alabama measures today · B0238
168.text: The 2025 edition of this report misread two of these: it gave 17.4 percent as the share of Alabama clients who are Black (that is the national figure in the 2022 tables; it was 17.3 percent in 2023, 17.6 percent in 2024 and 18.1 percent in 2025; Alabama's is 38.3 percent) and an employment rate of 45.5 percent, which in the 2022 tables is the share employed among adults in the labor force, not among all adults with known employment status (20.5 percent in 2022, 21.0 percent in 2025) [165] [166] [43] [42]. Both corrections change the equity analysis (Domain 7).

169.title: What Alabama measures today · B0239
169.text: Departmental reporting. The FY2025 Annual Report publishes people served by division, crisis-center evaluations, 988 calls and answer rates, individuals served at each state hospital, and financial tables [16]. Budget-hearing presentations add bed counts and targets [31] [30]. The Office of Quality Improvement and Risk Management collects stakeholder input on care and outcomes and coordinates performance-improvement efforts [52]. ACSIS and ASAIS carry the underlying service data (Domain 5) [149] [150].

170.title: What Alabama measures today · B0240
170.text: Public-health surveillance. The Department of Public Health publishes vital statistics (834 suicides in 2024, 16.2 per 100,000) [123], runs the Alabama Violent Death Reporting System [167] and CDC-funded overdose surveillance [168] [169], and maintains the maternal mortality review [170]. The Opioid Council's annual report compiles overdose deaths and naloxone distribution [76].

171.title: What Alabama measures today · B0241
171.text: Independent evaluation. The Alabama Commission on the Evaluation of Services, created by statute in 2019 to advise the Legislature and the Governor on the evaluation of services [44], delivered a preliminary evaluation of the crisis centers in September 2025. It found the Department's reported diversion outcomes could not be verified because centers used inconsistent definitions, that FY2024 utilization averaged 27 percent and cost per bed-day $2,193, and that there was "insufficient data" to judge the centers' effectiveness [14]. The Department's response, printed with the evaluation, questions how utilization and average daily bed costs were calculated and says "most centers function at capacity most days" [14]; at a public meeting that September the Commissioner and her staff pushed back on the analysis, saying the Department cannot turn over protected health information [19]. The FY2027 appropriation now conditions crisis-center payments on reporting [17].

172.title: What Alabama measures today · B0242
172.text: Youth data. Alabama returned federal funds for the Youth Risk Behavior Survey in 2023; the last state survey is from 2021 [171]. VOICES for Alabama's Children has moved its Kids Count indicators, including a mental-health theme, to an online data center [172] [173] [174].

173.title: What Alabama does not publish · B0243+1
173.text: As of October 2026, no published source was found for any of the following:

174.title: What Alabama does not publish · B0244
174.text: A public dashboard of crisis-system metrics (988 answer rate, mobile-crisis response times, crisis-center diversions and follow-up) comparable to the 988 data dashboards that ten states had posted by September 2024 [175].

175.title: What Alabama does not publish · B0245
175.text: A seven-day follow-up-after-discharge rate across hospitals and crisis centers.

176.title: What Alabama does not publish · B0246
176.text: Provider-network staffing, vacancy and turnover later than the end of FY2023, when the Department reported 752 vacancies against 4,678 positions at mental health providers [135] (Domain 4).

177.title: What Alabama does not publish · B0247
177.text: Annual civil-commitment counts; jail mental-health screening and suicide counts.

178.title: What Alabama does not publish · B0248
178.text: Outcomes for CCBHCs beyond people served and one clinic's access times: the Department's January 2026 budget presentation gives WellStone's days to initial evaluation and to first clinical service [30]. The Department's CCBHC quality manual says it will develop an annual CCBHC Quality Report [153]; none was found.

179.title: What Alabama does not publish · B0249
179.text: Disaggregated outcomes by race, county and age beyond the federal tables.

180.title: Quality improvement · B0251
180.text: The Department reviews critical incidents [176] and requires providers to run internal quality programs [177]; readmission and consumer-survey results, in the federal tables, are its published outcome measures [42]. CCBHC certification adds a required quality framework with standard measures and an outcomes platform [26] [153]. As a condition of the block grant, the state must maintain a planning council that reviews the state's plan, evaluates the adequacy of services each year, and includes people with lived experience [73].

181.title: Continuum lens · B0253
181.text: Data coverage follows funding: the crisis end is the best measured (because the Legislature asked) and the recovery end the least (employment and housing appear only in federal tables) [42]. Children's outcomes are the thinnest of all — the state lacks a current youth survey [171] and reported child mobile-crisis counts for the first time in FY2025 [16].

182.title: Key actors · B0255

183.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0257
183.text: Standardize crisis definitions now. The ACES finding is specific: centers counted "diversion" differently [14]. A common data dictionary across the six centers [16], mobile teams and 988 — and quarterly publication — would satisfy the FY2027 conditions [17] and end the dispute.

184.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0258
184.text: Publish a small dashboard. About ten measures, updated quarterly — 988 answer rate and speed, mobile-crisis responses, center evaluations and utilization, 30-day readmission, forensic waitlist, people served, CCBHC enrollment, school systems covered, naloxone distributed — would cover most of what advocates and legislators ask [16] [14] [42] [76].

185.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0259
185.text: A youth survey. Without YRBS or an equivalent, the state cannot track adolescent depression and its treatment; on treatment of youth with major depression it ranks worst nationally [171] [35].

186.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0260
186.text: Disaggregate. The federal tables show a public system that serves Black Alabamians at a higher share than their population [42] [133]; the next question — whether outcomes differ by race, county or age — can be answered only in part from published data: the federal tables break out consumer-survey results, homelessness and state-hospital readmissions by race, but not employment, and give nothing by county (Domain 7) [42].

187.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0261
187.text: Evaluation by agreement. The evaluation commission has existed since 2019 [44], but its crisis-center report drew a dispute [14]. Agreeing the next evaluation's questions and data in advance would make its findings usable.

188.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0262
188.text: ADMH plan goals touched: A6, D2, D3, E2.

191.title: Scope · B0269
191.text: Equity asks who the system reaches, who it misses, and whether the care people receive fits their language, culture, disability and circumstances. In Alabama the relevant dimensions are race, rurality, income and insurance, language and hearing, veteran status, age, and involvement with the justice and child-welfare systems. This domain reports what the data show and names the programs built for specific communities; it makes no clinical claims and takes no policy position.

192.title: Who Alabama is · B0271
192.text: Alabama's population of 5.19 million is 25.9 percent Black and 6.5 percent Hispanic [133]; 42 percent of residents live in rural areas, among the ten highest shares nationally [134]. In 2024, 15.2 percent of residents lived below the poverty line (child poverty 20.2 percent) [179], and the state's median household income of $63,999 in the 2020–2024 five-year estimate is well below the national figure [133]. The Poarch Band of Creek Indians, the state's only federally recognized tribe [180], operates its own health department with behavioral-health services at the Buford L. Rolin Health Clinic in Atmore [181]. Alabama is home to roughly 300,000–377,000 veterans, depending on the count used [182] [183].

193.title: What the data show · B0273
193.text: Race. The public mental health system serves Black Alabamians at a higher share (38.3 percent of people served in the 2025 reporting year; 37.8 percent in 2024) than their share of the population (25.9 percent) [42] [43] [133], the reverse of what the 2025 edition of this report stated: its 17.4 percent was the national figure in the 2022 tables, not Alabama's [165]. No explanation was found in the federal tables or in the Department's published reports as of October 2026; plausible contributors are higher uninsurance and poverty rates, which route people to the public system, and the justice and crisis pathways that feed it. Whether outcomes differ by race is reported only in part (Domain 6): the federal tables break out consumer-survey results, homelessness and state-hospital readmissions by race, but not employment. In the 2025 tables, 84 percent of Black adults and 81 percent of White adults surveyed reported positive outcomes, and 2.9 percent of Black and 2.7 percent of White clients with a known living situation were homeless [42]. Outside mental health, the disparity is stark: Alabama's pregnancy-related mortality rate for Black women was 77.0 per 100,000 live births against 28.2 for White women in 2020–2021, the latest review to publish rates by race [170].

194.title: What the data show · B0274
194.text: Rurality. Fifty-five of 67 counties are deemed rural [111] [184], and 42 percent of Alabamians live in rural areas [134]. In this report's reading, rural residents face the longest distances to the six crisis centers [12] [111], the thinnest provider supply, nine counties with no rural transit provider, several of them urban counties with city systems [47], and the largest broadband gaps (87.5 percent of households statewide have a broadband subscription) [133]. The five rural crisis-care programs, first funded in FY2021 [111] and carried at $6 million a year in the General Fund, and the $5 million child-and-adolescent mobile-crisis pilot, in the budget since at least FY2025, are the state's current response [20] [18].

195.title: What the data show · B0275
195.text: Income and insurance. Among Alabama adults with any mental illness, 14.1 percent are uninsured (U.S. 9.2 percent), and 30.0 percent of adults reporting 14 or more mentally unhealthy days could not see a doctor because of cost (U.S. 26.6 percent) [35]. The Medicaid coverage gap is put at up to 155,000 people by Alabama Arise [36] [37]; KFF's July 2026 estimate is 86,000 uninsured adults in the gap itself and 147,000 who would become eligible if the state expanded [38]. About 95,000 people left marketplace coverage in 2026 [36] [39]. These figures are the equity face of the financing gap in Domain 2 and Section 12.

196.title: What the data show · B0276
196.text: Children. Alabama ranks 50th of 51 on Mental Health America's youth measures; 66.4 percent of Alabama youth with major depression received no treatment, the highest rate in the country, and 18 percent of youth with private insurance had plans that did not cover mental health (U.S. 8.6 percent) [35] (Section 9).

197.title: What the data show · B0277
197.text: Justice involvement. People waiting in county jails for psychiatric evaluation or treatment — 291 in July 2026 [32] — are the population whose access to care is governed by a federal consent decree [11]; ADOC's mental health caseload was about 3,400 of 19,500 people in custody when the Braggs suit was filed in 2014 (Section 10) [69].

198.title: Programs built for specific communities · B0279
198.text: Deaf and hard-of-hearing Alabamians. ADMH's Office of Deaf Services provides linguistically specific care through regionally based clinicians and communication-access staff [52] [185].

199.title: Programs built for specific communities · B0280
199.text: Veterans. Alabama has four VA medical centers (Birmingham, Tuscaloosa, Montgomery and Tuskegee) and four Vet Centers; a 2024 training deck prepared for ADMH lists 17 community-based outpatient clinics (three of them in Georgia) plus two outpatient clinics [183]; the Veterans Crisis Line is reached through 988 (press 1) [9]. ADMH's veterans mental-health plan was funded at $12 million in 2025 [186], the Alabama Veterans Resource Center opened in Montgomery in February 2026 under SB70 [187] [188] [189], and the Houston Hunter Act created voluntary firearm-hold agreements after 139 Alabama veteran suicides in 2022 (more than 85 percent of Alabama veteran suicides involve a firearm) [186] [64]. Fox Army Health Center at Redstone Arsenal serves the active-duty community in North Alabama [190].

200.title: Programs built for specific communities · B0281
200.text: Faith communities. More than 400 faith leaders have been certified as Faith-Based Support Specialists since 2022 through the Agency for Substance Abuse Prevention, which ADMH funds in part [141].

201.title: Programs built for specific communities · B0282
201.text: Mothers and infants. Alabama Medicaid covers twelve months of postpartum care [106], an extension that KFF's tracker of 15 July 2026 lists as implemented under a state plan amendment approved on 13 January 2023 [191]; ADMH's infant and early-childhood programs support young children and the adults who care for them [192], and the Postpartum Support International Alabama chapter addresses perinatal mental health (Section 9) [193].

202.title: Programs built for specific communities · B0283
202.text: Language access. ADMH's program rules require certified providers to offer free language assistance to people with limited English proficiency or who are deaf, and allow telephone or video interpreting for spoken languages [194]; no ADMH language-access plan or CLAS-standards assessment was found as of October 2026 (Appendix D).

203.title: Programs built for specific communities · B0284
203.text: Tribal. The Poarch Band's Tribal Health Improvement Plan (2015–2020) set diabetes, obesity and hypertension as its priorities; it lists behavioral health among the tribal clinic's services and mental-health awareness among its community recommendations [195]. Coordination with the state system was not found in public documents as of October 2026.

204.title: Programs built for specific communities · B0285
204.text: LGBTQ+ Alabamians. Supportive programming exists through community organizations such as Birmingham's Magic City Acceptance Center [196]; no state data or program specific to this population was found as of October 2026.

205.title: Continuum lens · B0287
205.text: Equity gaps widen toward the ends of the continuum. Prevention and outpatient care depend on coverage and transport, which fall hardest on rural, low-income and uninsured residents; crisis and forensic care are where the justice system's racial disparities enter. The middle — supported housing and employment — serves so few people (259 and 234 in 2025) that its distribution cannot yet be assessed [42].

207.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0291
207.text: Report outcomes by race, county and age. The system now knows who it serves; beyond a few federal tables by race, it does not publish whether they fare equally [42].

208.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0292
208.text: Track coverage alongside outcomes. Coverage status is the variable most consistently associated with the access figures in this domain (Section 12) [35] [36].

209.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0293
209.text: Measure the rural crisis layer by distance. The five rural crisis-care programs [111] [18] could be assessed against distance-to-care rather than catchment assignment.

210.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0294
210.text: A youth survey. The state's worst national ranks are for children [35], and it has no current instrument to track them [171].

211.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0295
211.text: Document language access and CLAS. The Department's rules require free language assistance [194]; a published plan and CLAS assessment would let providers and the public know what to expect.

215.title: Scope · B0303
215.text: This domain covers how the public shapes the system: awareness and anti-stigma education, training of lay and professional responders, the organizations that carry the voice of people with lived experience and their families, regional coalitions, the press, and the advocacy that moves budgets and law. ADMH's fifth strategic priority — Awareness and Knowledge — commits the Department to giving Alabamians information that raises awareness and connects them to services [40]; this report reads that as recognizing public engagement as a system function, not an add-on.

216.title: Who engages · B0305
216.text: NAMI Alabama and its eleven listed affiliates (one still forming) run family and peer education and support groups [197] [199], and its CIT Division coordinates the state's regional Crisis Intervention Team programs (Section 10); the Division's 2024–2026 strategic plan organizes its regional coordinators into six regions matching the boundaries of the six crisis centers [145]. The Alabama Suicide Prevention and Resources Coalition (ASPARC), which began as a task force chosen to help the Department of Public Health with suicide-prevention strategy and is now a nonprofit, works to prevent suicide through education, advocacy and awareness and trains people in suicide prevention [200]; it is the state coalition listed alongside ADMH's suicide prevention coordinator and the 2021–2026 state plan [122]. The Alabama Council of Community Mental Health Boards (which also uses the name Alabama Council for Behavioral Healthcare) represents its members, 22 community mental health providers by its own count [201]. The Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program protects rights [202] and monitors the Hunter decree [11]. Alabama Arise, through its Cover Alabama campaign, a coalition of more than 130 organizations, advocates coverage expansion [36] [203]. VOICES for Alabama's Children compiles child well-being data [172] [174]. Regional coalitions — including the North Alabama Mental Health Coalition, formed in 2015, which meets monthly and brings together mental-health providers, law enforcement, local officials, probate judges, advocates and social-service agencies [204] — connect these statewide bodies to local practice; the 2025 edition of this report recommended creating "a united Mental Health Coalition" without noting that such coalitions already exist.

217.title: Who engages · B0306
217.text: Public education and training. Each May ADMH joins organizations across the state in observing Mental Health Awareness Month, with events such as its annual Strike Out Stigma game and Capitol Art Showcase [205]; ADMH's Prevention Day drew about 100 attendees in April 2025 [16]. Mental Health First Aid, which ADMH, NAMI Alabama and more than 90 certified instructors offer to audiences that include houses of faith, schools and human-resource staff [206], and the Faith-Based Support Specialist program, an addiction-recovery training that has certified more than 400 faith leaders since 2022 [141], extend recognition and referral skills into congregations and workplaces. Schools now host both CMHC services and Mental Health Services Coordinators (Section 9) [119] [120].

218.title: Who engages · B0307
218.text: Press. The Alabama Reflector, Alabama Political Reporter, Alabama Daily News and regional outlets have covered the crisis-center evaluation, the forensic waitlist, the prison litigation and the coverage gap in detail during 2025–2026 [19] [32] [116] [70] [72] [37] [39]; this report cites them where they report primary documents.

219.title: What advocacy has achieved and where it stands · B0309
219.text: The crisis-system build-out of 2020–2024 is the clearest case of advocacy, data and executive leadership aligning: local advocates pressed for a crisis center (in North Alabama, a 2019 petition signed by probate judges, police chiefs and sheriffs) [204], the Department made a specific request, $18 million for three crisis centers [207], the Governor made it a priority and the Legislature funded it, beginning with the FY2021 budget [208] [14]. The 2025 and 2026 sessions show the next phase. The Legislature did not fund the five-year plan's increase [33] [21] [20] [18], and in the FY2027 budget conditioned crisis-center money on reporting [17] [19] and cut the 988 General Fund line [18], while separately directing opioid-settlement funds to 988, beds and naloxone [91] [92] and passing targeted bills on consent age, accountability courts, veterans and regional boards [59] [63] [22] [61]. Advocacy that worked by showing need now has to work by showing results — which makes Domain 6 the advocacy domain.
219.section: What advocacy has achieved and where it stands

220.title: Continuum lens · B0311
220.text: Community engagement is strongest at the crisis end (CIT, 988 awareness) [145] [15] and the promotion end (awareness months, school programs) [205] [119] and weakest in the middle: supported housing, step-down residential care and outpatient wait times have no organized constituency comparable to the one that built the crisis system.

221.title: Key actors · B0313
221.text: Actor Engagement role NAMI Alabama and affiliates Family/peer education, support groups, CIT, advocacy [199] [197] [145] ASPARC Suicide-prevention education, training and advocacy; the state coalition [200] [122] Regional coalitions (e.g., NAMHC) Local convening across sectors [204] Alabama Council of Community MH Boards Provider voice [201] ADAP Rights advocacy and litigation monitoring [202] [11] Alabama Arise / Cover Alabama Coverage advocacy [36] [203] VOICES for Alabama's Children Child data and advocacy [172] [174] Faith communities; Agency for Substance Abuse Prevention Faith-Based Support Specialists [141] Press Public accountability [17] [19] [32] State planning council (block grant) Consumer and family input to ADMH planning [73]

222.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0315
222.text: Organize around results. A shared set of about ten published measures (Domain 6) would give every advocate the same facts and let the Legislature see conditions met [17].

223.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0316
223.text: Build the missing constituencies. Supported housing, employment and step-down care need the organized voice that crisis services had.

224.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0317
224.text: Keep lived experience in the room. Peer-run organizations are few in Alabama — ADMH's peer-support page lists three (Wings Across Alabama for mental illness; PEIR and ROSS for substance-use recovery) [209]; CCBHC's peer-support requirement and the planning council are the existing footholds [10] [73].

225.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0319
225.text: Count the trained. No current or agency-level count of people trained in CIT or Mental Health First Aid was found on NAMI Alabama's CIT pages or ADMH's Mental Health First Aid page as of October 2026; the latest figures located are in ADMH's July 2024 budget presentation, which reported "1375 plus CIT trained officers" and more than 1,250 other officers trained in Mental Health First Aid for first responders [135]. Publishing current counts would show coverage and gaps by county.

226.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0320
226.text: Use the regional template. Little Orange Fish plans a North Alabama edition of this report, built on the same domains, as a planning instrument for the region.

230.title: Scope and frame · B0329
230.text: Children's mental health in Alabama is delivered by at least six public systems — the Department of Mental Health, schools, Medicaid, child welfare, juvenile justice and early-childhood education — plus pediatric medicine. The national System of Care framework, adopted by the federal government since the 1980s and updated in 2010 [7] and again in 2021 [210], holds that services for children should be family-driven and youth-guided, community-based, culturally and linguistically competent, and coordinated across agencies, with early identification, individualized planning and smooth transitions to adulthood [7]. The 2021 update keeps each of these values and principles, with some rewording (the first value is now "Family and Youth Driven"), and adds principles on trauma-informed care, health–mental health integration, a public health approach and mental health equity [210]. This section describes Alabama's pieces against that frame. Child and Family Services is the second of ADMH's five strategic priorities [40].

231.title: Where Alabama stands · B0331
231.text: Alabama ranks 50th of 51 on Mental Health America's composite youth measures. An estimated 18.9 percent of Alabama youth (about 75,000) had a major depressive episode in the latest data — close to the national rate — but 66.4 percent of them received no treatment, the highest share in the country (U.S. 50.8 percent). Eighteen percent of Alabama youth with private insurance had plans that did not cover mental health (U.S. 8.6 percent), also the worst in the country; 13.5 percent reported serious thoughts of suicide (U.S. 12.9 percent); and only 1.5 per 1,000 students had an emotional-disturbance designation for special education, the lowest reported rate in the country (two states reported no data) [35]. Teen (15–19) suicide was 9.9 per 100,000 in 2021–2023, slightly below the national rate [211]. Alabama's Youth Risk Behavior Survey was last conducted in 2021, and in 2023 the state returned the federal funds for it [171]; no later state survey was found as of October 2026.

232.title: The Department's children's system · B0333
232.text: ADMH created the Office of Child and Family Services in October 2023 [212], consolidating child and adolescent mental-illness treatment, adolescent substance-use treatment, autism services, infant and early-childhood mental health, early intervention, intensive in-home services, prevention and school-based mental health [131] [212]. In FY2025 the public system served 31,847 adolescents for mental illness and an estimated 4,506 for substance use [16], compared with 29,796 and 2,739 in FY2024 [115]; because ADMH footnotes its FY2025 substance-use figures as estimated after a system transformation, the two years may not be like-for-like [16]. Five child and adolescent mobile-crisis teams at three centers — AltaPointe, JBS and WellStone [111] — served 936 young people, the first year that count appeared in the Department's annual report [16]; WellStone's 24-bed pediatric crisis unit (ages 12–18) in Huntsville — the first in the state, opened in late September 2024 — performed 520 evaluations [41] [115] [16]. Adult crisis centers may not admit children [14], and the Huntsville unit is the only pediatric crisis unit on the Department's list of crisis centers [12]. The General Fund has carried a $5 million child-and-adolescent mobile-crisis pilot line since at least FY2025, unchanged in FY2027 [20] [18].

233.title: The Department's children's system · B0334
233.text: Services for children with serious emotional disturbance — crisis, outpatient, outreach, day treatment and residential care — are offered by the state's treatment providers, with at least one of these offered in every county; intensive home-based services are a separate program of the office [131]. Infant and early-childhood programs include consulting therapists in child-care and pediatric settings; PATHS (Pediatric Access to Telemental Health Services), a behavioral-health consultation line for primary-care practices run with Children's of Alabama under a federal grant; and PPEER, a 2024–2028 federally funded program for children up to age 12 who are at risk for or engaged with child protective services in Jefferson, Jackson and Mobile counties [192] [130]. ADMH's page links a Child and Family Services resource directory, a file uploaded in August 2025 [131]. Eleven certified providers treat adolescent substance use [131].

234.title: The Department's children's system · B0335
234.text: The 2025 edition of this report referred to wraparound and therapeutic-foster-care programs under names that could not be confirmed; therapeutic foster care in Alabama is a DHR-contracted service [213], and this edition does not attribute programs to ADMH that its own pages do not list.

235.title: Schools · B0337
235.text: Schools are the largest point of contact. Two programs run in parallel:

236.title: Schools · B0338
236.text: ADMH–ALSDE School-Based Mental Health Collaboration (since 2010) brings CMHC services into 122 of Alabama's school systems through all 19 centers [119], funded at $5.5 million in the FY2027 Education Trust Fund [58].

237.title: Schools · B0339
237.text: ALSDE Mental Health Services Coordinators: local education agencies that apply receive about $40,000 a year for a coordinator who links students to services [120]. The sources disagree on the program's FY2026 funding: ALSDE's memo says the FY2026 ETF (Act 2025-270) appropriated $6.36 million [120], while the Legislature's FY2027 ETF sheet shows the line at $4.69 million budgeted for FY2026 and $9.25 million in the FY2027 ETF [58]. It began as a 102-district pilot in 2020–21 and was due to reach every district in 2022–23 [214], when Act 2022-442 required each local education agency to employ a coordinator [60] [121].

238.title: Schools · B0340
238.text: Since 2022 (Act 2022-442), schools must give annual written notice, keep mental-health records separate from academic records and obtain written opt-in consent from a parent before mental-health services, surveys or assessments, at first for students under 14 [121] [60]; since 1 October 2025, SB101 (Act 2025-455) raises that age to 16, so that students under 16 cannot consent to ongoing counseling on their own [59] [60]. The statute excepts an imminent threat to the health of the student or others, suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, and an immediate need for grief counseling [59], and ALSDE's guidance treats instruction, advisement and occasional interventions as outside the opt-in requirement [60] [121]. The practical effect on school-based service volume is not reported: no before-and-after count of school-based services was found in the sources read for this section as of October 2026. Alabama's school-counselor ratio was about 401 students per counselor in 2024–25 (398 in 2023–24) against a recommended 250 [215] [216].

239.title: Child welfare · B0342
239.text: The Department of Human Resources had 5,900 children in out-of-home care in May 2025, 576 of them with relatives. In its federal case review, DHR rated mental and behavioral health needs as a strength in 48 percent of cases reviewed (11 of 23) in FY2024, and it funds a psychotropic-medication review team for children in foster care from adoption savings [217]. Therapeutic foster care and its enhanced tier (Therapeutic Foster Care-Enhanced) are DHR-contracted services [213]. No published figure giving the share of foster youth with behavioral-health needs, and no joint DHR–ADMH protocol, was located for this report as of October 2026; the APSR has a section on Family First Prevention Services Act transition grants (section IV.E.3) [217].

240.title: Juvenile justice · B0344
240.text: The Department of Youth Services operates three secure campuses (Mt. Meigs, Vacca, Autauga) and funds diversion grant programs that serve all 67 counties [218]; its FY2024 report counts nine contracted custodial community facilities and 51 diversion programs (ten community programs and 50 diversion programs in FY2023) [219] [218]. In FY2024 the diversion programs served 2,430 youth, and 87 percent of the 972 evaluated six months after discharge had not reoffended [219]; in FY2023, 2,629 youth were in diversion with 78 percent completing and 86 percent not reoffending within six months, while 108 youth were awaiting beds in mid-2023 [218]. Juvenile probation is run through the courts: in counties of 99,000 or fewer people at the 1990 census — a group to which the statute adds Mobile County and, from 1 October 2024, Shelby County — probation officers are state employees supervised by the presiding juvenile judge [220]. Neither the FY2023 nor the FY2024 DYS annual report gives clinical or mental-health service counts [218] [219]. According to Little Orange Fish's alignment analysis of the full plan, ADMH's strategic plan includes strengthening collaboration with juvenile justice (goal B5 in this report's numbering).

241.title: Early childhood and maternal mental health · B0346
241.text: First Teacher Home Visiting (Alabama Department of Early Childhood Education) delivers Nurse-Family Partnership, Parents as Teachers and HIPPY in all 67 counties, prenatal to kindergarten, though families may be on waiting lists; maternal mental health is an explicit focus [221].
241.section: Early childhood and maternal mental health

242.title: Early childhood and maternal mental health · B0347
242.text: Help Me Grow Alabama, run by the Alabama Partnership for Children, provides developmental screening for children up to age five and a half [222].
242.section: Early childhood and maternal mental health

243.title: Early childhood and maternal mental health · B0348
243.text: Alabama Medicaid covers twelve months of postpartum care (since October 2022) [106], an extension that KFF's tracker of 15 July 2026 lists as implemented under a state plan amendment approved on 13 January 2023 [191].
243.section: Early childhood and maternal mental health

244.title: Early childhood and maternal mental health · B0349
244.text: Postpartum Support International's Alabama chapter connects families to PSI's national helpline and provider directory [193].
244.section: Early childhood and maternal mental health

245.title: Early childhood and maternal mental health · B0350
245.text: Maternal mortality review. Alabama's review found 78 percent of pregnancy-related deaths in 2020–2021 preventable (82.4 percent in 2022), with a Black maternal death rate nearly three times the White rate in 2020–2021 [170] [223]; the 2020–2021 summary does not break out mental-health or substance-use contributions [170], while the 2022 key findings list mental health conditions among the leading causes, at 11.8 percent of pregnancy-related deaths [223].
245.section: Early childhood and maternal mental health

246.title: Pediatric medicine · B0352
246.text: Children's of Alabama runs the PIRC psychiatric intake line (8 a.m.–11 p.m., seven days) [129] and said in January 2025 that it would add eleven beds to its inpatient behavioral-health unit that month [117]; UAB's child and adolescent psychiatry division, which describes a strong on-site affiliation with the hospital and trains eight fellows, lists 50 inpatient beds (12 child, 38 adolescent) on an undated page that does not mention the expansion [118]. Emergency-department boarding of children awaiting psychiatric placement is not measured statewide: no such measure was found in the published reports read for this section as of October 2026.

247.title: Reading Alabama against selected System of Care principles · B0354
247.text: Principle Alabama today Broad array of services Crisis, outpatient, outreach, day and residential services, at least one of them in every county [131]; one pediatric crisis unit [41] [12]; five youth mobile-crisis teams at three centers [111]; three first-episode programs [109] Family-driven, youth-guided Opt-in parental consent now governs school services [121] [59] [60]; no statewide youth or family advisory body identified Early identification CMHC services in schools (122 systems) [119], coordinators (required in every LEA) [60] [121], PATHS consult line [192] [130], Help Me Grow [222], home visiting [221] Cross-agency coordination ADMH goal B4 names it; no standing interagency body dedicated to children's mental health identified — state law provides two bodies with wider remits, the State Team for multiple-needs children [78] and the Children's Policy Council [79] Data-driven accountability Youth mobile-crisis counts reported for the first time in FY2025 [16]; no youth survey since 2021 [171] Transitions to adulthood Transitional-age residential is a funded CMHC service [108]; no published outcomes

248.text: Actor Role ADMH Office of Child & Family Services The Department's office for children's behavioral-health services [131] [212] ALSDE School coordinators; consent and notification policy [120] [60] 19 CMHCs School-based services [119]; youth mobile crisis (five teams at three centers) [111]; pediatric crisis unit (WellStone) [41] Alabama DHR Foster care; therapeutic foster care; medication review [217] [213] Alabama DYS; juvenile courts Secure care, diversion, probation [218] [220] ADECE; Alabama Partnership for Children Home visiting; Help Me Grow [221] [222] Children's of Alabama; UAB PATHS, PIRC, inpatient beds, training [130] [129] [117] [118] Alabama Medicaid Postpartum coverage [106] [191]; children's benefits (about half of enrollment) [96] ADPH Youth suicide prevention materials [224]; maternal mortality review [170] VOICES for Alabama's Children; PSI Alabama; ASPARC Data and advocacy [172] [193] [122]

249.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0358
249.text: A forum for the child-serving agencies. ADMH, ALSDE, DHR, DYS, ADECE and Medicaid each run a piece; according to Little Orange Fish's alignment analysis of the full plan, the state plan's goal B4 (shared objectives with child-serving agencies) points toward a standing forum. State law already provides two bodies with wider remits — the Children's Policy Council and the State Team for multiple-needs children [79] [78]; none dedicated to children's mental health was identified.

250.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0359
250.text: Measure what the consent law does. The 2022 opt-in rule, tightened in 2025, is the largest recent policy change affecting children's access; school-based service volumes before and after would show its effect [121] [59] [60].

251.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0360
251.text: Facility-based crisis care for minors beyond Huntsville. The state has one pediatric crisis unit, with 24 beds for ages 12–18 [41] [115] [12].

252.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0361
252.text: A youth survey. Without it, the state cannot track the measures on which it ranks last or next to last [171] [35].

253.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0362
253.text: Publish DYS and DHR mental-health data. Neither agency's public reporting, as read for this report, includes service counts for the children it holds [218] [219] [217].

254.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0363
254.text: ADMH plan goals touched: B1, B2, B3, B4, B5, A2, A5.

255.title: Key data sources · B0365
255.text: ADMH Annual Report FY2025 and Child & Family Services pages [16] [131] [192]; ADMH school-based page [119]; ALSDE memos [120] [60] [121]; SB101 [59]; DHR APSR 2026 [217]; DYS FY2023 and FY2024 reports [218] [219]; ADECE [221]; Children's of Alabama and UAB [130] [129] [117] [118]; Help Me Grow and PSI [222] [193]; MHA 2025 [35]; ADPH [170] [223]; America's Health Rankings [211]; ACES on children in crisis centers [14].

256.title: Scope and frame · B0368
256.text: In Alabama, the justice system is a regular point of contact for people with mental illness: Lee County's sheriff says some sheriffs describe their jails as a "de facto center" for people with mental-health conditions, and the director of Alabama's Crisis Intervention Team program estimates that 20 to 30 percent of the calls law enforcement fields involve a person in a mental-health crisis [6]. This section follows the Sequential Intercept Model, which maps the points at which a person can be diverted from the justice system into care: Intercept 0 (community and crisis services), 1 (law enforcement), 2 (initial detention and court hearings), 3 (jails and courts), 4 (reentry) and 5 (community corrections) [4] [5]. Alabama's forensic and prison mental-health systems both operate under federal court oversight [11] [69], which makes this the area where the state's obligations are most explicit.

257.title: Intercept 0 — Community and crisis response · B0370
257.text: The crisis system described in Domain 3 is the first intercept: four in-state 988 centers [16] [9], fourteen mobile crisis teams [13] and six crisis diversion centers that accept law-enforcement drop-offs around the clock [12]. Co-responder programs pair officers with clinicians: in Huntsville, Huntsville Police with WellStone, funded in 2021, had two master's-level clinicians by early 2022 [112]; in Mobile, the police announced a one-precinct pilot with AltaPointe in May 2022 [113]. No published figures on the current staffing or outcomes of these programs were found as of October 2026. Under a 2022 law (HB70, Act 2022-202) that took effect in July 2022, officers may transport a person in crisis to a crisis center rather than jail [225] [226] [227].

258.title: Intercept 1 — Law enforcement · B0372
258.text: Crisis Intervention Team (CIT) training in Alabama is coordinated by NAMI Alabama's CIT Division, under a statewide administrative coordinator, named in the Division's 2024–2026 plan as John (Johnny) Hollingsworth [145] [144], with a $1 million General Fund line through ADMH in FY2026 and FY2027 [20] [18]. The 2024–2026 strategic plan started from five regional programs — WellStone with Huntsville Police, JBS with the Jefferson County Sheriff, Hope Pointe with Tuscaloosa Police, Carastar with Opelika Police (Montgomery under development) and AltaPointe with Mobile Police and the Baldwin County Sheriff — and aims for six regions aligned with the six crisis centers, for the International Association of Chiefs of Police "One Mind" campaign (all sworn officers trained in mental-health response, at least 20 percent CIT-trained), and for APOST credit for all CIT courses [145]. The Peace Officers' Standards and Training Commission has listed a two-day CIT class for 16 continuing-education units [142]; it requires 12 hours of continuing education a year with no mental-health subject mandated [143], and it raised the basic academy's Mental Health Awareness block from four to eight hours from January 2018 [228]. NAMI Alabama's CIT pages give no statewide count of CIT-trained officers; ADMH's July 2024 budget presentation reported "1375 plus CIT trained officers" [135], and no current or agency-level count was found as of October 2026 (Appendix D).

259.title: Intercept 1 — Law enforcement · B0373
259.text: Lethal means. The Houston Hunter Act (SB40, 2025) created voluntary firearm-hold agreements with licensed dealers and the SAFER program, against a background of 139 veteran suicides in Alabama in 2022; more than 85 percent of the state's veteran suicides involve a firearm [64].

260.title: Intercept 2 — Initial detention and initial court hearings · B0375
260.text: Jail screening. No statewide standard for mental-health screening at booking was found for Alabama as of October 2026. Morgan County's jail, for example, employs two licensed counselors who logged 6,338 inmate visits in 2025, and its Sheriff's Office says mental-health crisis issues occur in about half of inmates [229]. No statewide count of jail suicides was found as of October 2026 (Appendix D).
260.section: Intercept 2 — Initial detention and initial court hearings

261.title: Intercept 2 — Initial detention and initial court hearings · B0376
261.text: Civil commitment. Under Code of Alabama §22-52 any person may petition the probate court; the standard for inpatient commitment is clear and convincing evidence of mental illness and a real and present threat of substantial harm to self or others, together with findings that the person will continue to deteriorate without treatment and cannot make a rational decision about treatment, and the court must order the least restrictive alternative necessary and available; initial orders run up to 150 days [66]. Outpatient commitment exists where a designated facility consents [66]. No annual count of commitments was found in the Department's published reports as of October 2026.
261.section: Intercept 2 — Initial detention and initial court hearings

262.title: Intercept 2 — Initial detention and initial court hearings · B0377
262.text: Specialty courts. SB200 (Act 2025-183) renamed drug courts "accountability courts," extended eligibility to defendants with mental illness and to veterans, and directed the Administrative Office of Courts to set statewide policy, effective 1 October 2025 [63] [62]; HB487, passed in April 2026, directs $3 million of opioid-settlement funds to the AOC for specialty courts [92] [90]. Before SB200, mental-health and veterans courts were local initiatives: Cullman County's circuit added a mental health court to its drug and veterans court dockets in 2022 [230], and Shelby County's district attorney's office lists a mental health court and a veterans court [231]; no count of the circuits now operating them was found as of October 2026.
262.section: Intercept 2 — Initial detention and initial court hearings

263.title: Intercept 2 — Initial detention and initial court hearings · B0378
263.text: Regional boards. SB236 (Act 2025-366, effective 1 October 2025) requires the executive committee of a regional (310) mental health authority board with more than sixteen directors to include a sheriff (or the sheriff's representative) and a probate judge where those officials serve on the board (the officials may opt out), formalizing the justice system's seat at the community mental health table [61] [62].
263.section: Intercept 2 — Initial detention and initial court hearings

264.title: Intercept 3 — Jails and courts: competency and forensic care · B0380
264.text: This is Alabama's most litigated intercept. Under the 2018 Hunter v. Beshear consent decree (now captioned Hunter v. Boswell), the state must evaluate and restore defendants found incompetent within set times [11] (60 days for evaluation and 30 days for admission to restoration, as the Associated Press describes the decree's terms [116]); the decree's inpatient-restoration term, extended in March 2025, runs to 31 January 2027, with the Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program, an associational plaintiff, monitoring compliance [11]. The forensic waitlist — people waiting in county jails for psychiatric evaluation or treatment [32] — was 273 in August 2025 (the Associated Press's count of men waiting for Taylor Hardin) [116], 327 in January 2026 and 291 in July 2026, against a Department goal of 100 by the end of 2026 [32]; in 2025 the average wait exceeded a year and more than thirty people had waited more than two years [116].
264.section: Intercept 3 — Jails and courts: competency and forensic care

265.title: Intercept 3 — Jails and courts: competency and forensic care · B0381
265.text: The Department's response has four parts: the expansion of Taylor Hardin from 140 to 225 beds [32] [115] (about 200 of the 225 in use in August 2026, with the last 25 awaiting a plumbing repair then expected in the first week of October 2026 [32]; no report that they had opened was found as of 3 October 2026); jail-based competency restoration, including a telehealth program that had restored 32 people between summer 2025 and August 2026 [32] (the Department's jail-based program had 31 people enrolled and 23 completed as of September 2025 [16]); forensic navigators who work the list [32]; and outpatient forensic evaluations contracted to JBS under the Office of Forensic Mental Health Services [232]. The Commissioner told the board in August 2024 that only about half of Taylor Hardin's technician and nursing positions were filled [136] [116].
265.section: Intercept 3 — Jails and courts: competency and forensic care

266.title: Intercept 3 — Jails and courts: competency and forensic care · B0382
266.text: Stepping Up Alabama, the state's version of the national county jail initiative, funded eight county sites through four CMHCs in its fourth round of grants (sites starting between January and July 2021), with awards originally capped at $50,000, and screened 6,926 people in jails, 261 of them positive for serious mental illness [233]; a map ADMH posted in April 2026 shows Stepping Up in 48 counties and 19 without [234]. The 2025 edition of this report attributed Stepping Up to ADMH as a state program; it is a national initiative sponsored by the National Association of Counties, the American Psychiatric Association Foundation and the Council of State Governments Justice Center that ADMH has administered locally [46] [233].
266.section: Intercept 3 — Jails and courts: competency and forensic care

267.title: Intercept 4 — Reentry · B0384
267.text: Prisons. In Braggs v. Commissioner, Alabama Department of Corrections (the Eleventh Circuit's caption; the case is now styled Braggs v. Lovelace), a federal court in 2017 found mental health care in Alabama prisons "horrendously inadequate" and in violation of the Eighth Amendment [69] [71]. On 24 June 2026 the Eleventh Circuit affirmed the liability finding and the system-wide injunction but reversed the specific correctional-staffing mandate (the state had about 1,600 qualifying officers against about 3,600 required under the order), some suicide-resistant cell requirements and the application of relief to Tutwiler, and returned those questions to the district court [69] [70]. When the suit was filed in 2014, the record put ADOC's mental-health caseload at about 3,400 of roughly 19,500 people in custody [69]. The U.S. Department of Justice's separate suit, which alleges unconstitutional conditions in the men's prisons, is set for trial in November 2026 after a government motion for summary judgment in September [72]. ADOC announced on 29 April 2026 that it had terminated its $1.06 billion medical and mental-health contract with YesCare, which was to run through September 2027, and said it was working to execute an emergency agreement with NaphCare, with the transition set for 3 May 2026 (the release's headline describes a 24-month agreement) [235] [236]. The 4,000-bed Elmore County complex, which includes a 720-bed medical and mental-health area, was due to be completed by 15 October 2026, with ADOC warning in July of possible delay [148]; no report of completion or of a new date was found as of 3 October 2026. At least 277 people died in Alabama prisons in 2024 [237] and at least 202 in 2025 [238].

268.title: Intercept 4 — Reentry · B0385
268.text: Reentry programs. The Bureau of Pardons and Paroles operates the Perry County PREP Center in Uniontown [239] [77], announced in November 2025 a CARE Center for women in Thomasville, for an initial cohort of 20, to open in spring 2026 [240] (no report that it had opened was found as of 3 October 2026, and the Bureau's locations page did not list it [241]), opened a new skills facility at the PREP Center in September 2026 [242], and runs five Day Reporting Centers (Birmingham, Huntsville, Mobile, Montgomery, Tuscaloosa) with contracted mental-health and substance-use treatment [243], along with six "Day Reporting Center Lite" sites (Baldwin, Fort Payne, Jasper, Opelika, Sand Mountain, Calera) [241]. A Unite Us referral pilot with ADMH and the Alabama Department of Veterans Affairs, funded from opioid settlements, began at about five of the day-reporting centers in early 2026 [244]. The Reentry Alabama plan, developed with the Council of State Governments Justice Center [77], and the Reentry Task Force created by SJR80 (2025) [77] and chaired by the Bureau's director [245] are the statewide coordinating instruments; in September 2026 the task force advanced a proposed recidivism definition for a vote at its next meeting [245]. No approved or pending Medicaid reentry waiver for Alabama was identified: the state is not mentioned in KFF's August 2024 review of such waivers or in the text of its waiver tracker as of 30 September 2026 [246] [247] (Appendix D). Alabama law provides that people held in state prisons and county jails have their Medicaid eligibility suspended, not terminated [248].

269.title: Intercept 5 — Community corrections and parole · B0387
269.text: Thirty-eight community corrections programs cover 52 counties; fifteen counties have none, on ADOC's map dated 1 April 2023 [249]. The parole grant rate was 16 percent in November 2025 and 17 percent for the fiscal year to date, down from 29 percent a year earlier [250]; the Bureau's later monthly reports show 23 percent in June, 29 percent in July and 12 percent in August 2026, with 20 percent for the fiscal year through August [251] [252]; the Bureau's director reports recidivism falling from 34 to 27 percent [245]. No published figures on dedicated mental-health supervision caseloads were found as of October 2026.
