270.text: Intercept What exists Published measure Gap 0 Community/crisis 988 [16] [9]; 14 mobile teams [13]; 6 crisis centers [12]; co-responders in Huntsville (as of 2022) and a pilot announced in Mobile [112] [113] 988 calls and answer rate; center evaluations [16] Diversion counts unverified [14]; mobile teams and crisis centers together in 24 counties (February 2025) [33] 1 Law enforcement NAMI AL CIT, 5 regional programs (goal 6) [145]; $1M state line [20] [18]; Houston Hunter Act [64] One statewide count: 1,375-plus CIT-trained officers (July 2024) [135] No current or agency-level trained-officer count; no APOST continuing-education mandate [143] 2 Detention/court County jail mental-health services (Morgan County example) [229]; probate commitment [66]; accountability courts (SB200) [63]; SB236 boards [61] Morgan Co. example [229] No screening standard found; no commitment or jail-suicide counts found 3 Jails/courts Taylor Hardin 225 beds; jail-based restoration; navigators [32]; Stepping Up [233] [234] Waitlist 291 (Jul 2026) [32] Inpatient-restoration term of the decree to Jan 2027 [11]; goal of 100 by end-2026 [32]; technician and nursing staffing about half (2024) [136] [116] 4 Reentry ADOC care under Braggs [69]; PREP, CARE (announced), DRCs [239] [240] [243]; Reentry Alabama [77]; Unite Us pilot [244] ADOC caseload ~3,400 (at filing, 2014) [69]; at least 277 deaths 2024 [237], at least 202 in 2025 [238] DOJ trial Nov 2026 [72]; no Medicaid reentry waiver identified [246] [247] 5 Community corrections 38 programs / 52 counties [249]; parole supervision [250] Parole rate 16–17% (Nov 2025) [250]; 12% in August 2026 and 20% FY2026 through August [252] 15 counties uncovered [249]; no MH caseload data found

271.title: Key actors · B0391
271.text: Actor Role ADMH Office of Forensic Mental Health Services; Taylor Hardin Evaluations, restoration, forensic beds [232] [32] NAMI Alabama CIT Division; APOSTC Officer training [145] [143] Probate courts; AOC (accountability courts) Commitment; specialty-court policy [66] [63] Sheriffs and county jails; co-responder units Custody, screening, transport [229] [233] [227] [112] Alabama Department of Corrections; NaphCare (announced as health-care contractor from May 2026; YesCare before) Prison health care; mental-health care under Braggs [69] [236] [235] Bureau of Pardons and Paroles; Reentry Task Force PREP, CARE (announced), day reporting, parole [243] [77] [245] ADAP; SPLC; EJI; U.S. DOJ Litigation and monitoring [11] [71] [253] [72] ACES Evaluation [14] [44] Regional (310) boards with sheriff and probate seats Local governance [61]

272.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0393
272.text: The Hunter timeline. Filling Taylor Hardin's last 25 beds and staffing them, and scaling jail-based restoration, are the Department's stated path to a waitlist of 100 by year-end [32].

273.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0394
273.text: Set a jail screening standard. A statewide booking screen, with counts reported, would give Intercept 2 its first data.

274.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0395
274.text: Count CIT. Publishing trained-officer numbers by agency — ADMH's 2024 presentation gave only a statewide total [135] — would show which of the 67 counties have a CIT-capable force.

275.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0396
275.text: Use SB200. Accountability courts now have a mental-health remit [63] and, in the supplemental appropriation the Legislature passed in April 2026, settlement funding [92]; the AOC's statewide policy and circuit coverage should be published.

276.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0397
276.text: Document Medicaid at release. Alabama law suspends rather than terminates Medicaid eligibility for people in state prisons and county jails, and lets the Department of Corrections renew or establish eligibility before release [248]; how often that happens was not found in the sources read for this report (as of October 2026).

277.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0398
277.text: ADMH plan goals touched: A1, A2, A5, B5.

278.title: Key data sources · B0400
278.text: Braggs opinion [69]; Hunter record [11]; Alabama Political Reporter on the forensic waitlist and parole [32] [250]; Alabama Reflector on the ruling, DOJ suit, Elmore and law-enforcement practice [70] [72] [148] [6]; WSFA [116]; NAMI Alabama CIT plan [145]; APOSTC [142] [143]; SB236 [61] [62]; Stepping Up Year 4 [233]; Pardons and Paroles [243] [77]; ADOC community corrections map [249]; Morgan County Sheriff [229]; co-responder sources [112] [113]; ADMH forensic primer and annual report [232] [16].

279.title: Scope and frame · B0403
279.text: Mental health outcomes depend on conditions outside the clinic: housing, income and work, transport, connectivity, food, education and social connection. Healthy People 2030 groups these into five domains of social determinants — economic stability, education access and quality, health care access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context [8]. This section describes Alabama's systems in each, with a focus on housing and homelessness, where the mental health system's own gap is clearest.

280.title: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness · B0405
280.text: The count. Alabama's 2024 Point-in-Time count found 4,601 people experiencing homelessness [254] [255], a 39 percent increase on 2023 [255] but still one of the lowest rates in the country at 8.9 per 10,000 residents (U.S. 22.6) [256]. The 2025 count found 4,137 people, about 10 percent fewer, according to the National Alliance to End Homelessness's fact sheet on HUD's 2025 count and HUD's own state report [257] [258]; nationally, overall homelessness fell 3 percent from 2024 to 2025 while chronic homelessness has risen 81 percent since 2013 [259]. HUD's state report for the 2025 count lists 502 of the people counted in Alabama as severely mentally ill [258]; in the public mental health system, 2.7 percent of people served (all ages) and 4.1 percent of adults served were homeless at the 2025 reporting point, up from 1.9 and 3.0 percent in 2024 [42] [43].
280.section: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness

281.title: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness · B0406
281.text: The system. Nine HUD Continuums of Care plan the local homelessness response and set priorities for federal Continuum of Care funds [260] [261] [262]: AL-500 One Roof (Jefferson, St. Clair, Shelby); AL-501 Homeless Coalition of the Alabama Gulf Coast (Mobile, Baldwin); AL-502 Homeless Care Council of Northwest Alabama; AL-503 North Alabama Coalition for the Homeless (Madison, Limestone, Morgan); AL-504 Mid-Alabama Coalition for the Homeless (Montgomery region); AL-505 Homeless Coalition of Northeast Alabama; AL-506 West Alabama Coalition for the Homeless (Tuscaloosa); AL-507 Alabama Rural Coalition for the Homeless (balance of state); and AL-508 Southeast Alabama Coalition for the Homeless [260]. ADECA passes through federal Emergency Solutions Grants [263] — $2.7 million to eleven grantees in December 2025, including $450,000 to Huntsville [264]. Jefferson County's housing authority wound down a CoC rental-assistance program that had once helped 585 people (370 households), in stages between October 2024 and May 2025, saying HUD had not provided enough funding to sustain it [265].
281.section: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness

282.title: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness · B0407
282.text: Mental-health housing. ADMH funds a ladder of residential services through CMHC contracts — including supported housing, adult residential care homes, three-bed residential, semi-independent apartments, crisis residential and transitional-age residential [108] — but no statewide count of those beds was found in the Department's published reports as of October 2026; 259 people were in supported housing in the 2025 reporting year (240 in 2024) [42] [43]. A $500,000 ADMH contract with Navigate Affordable Housing Partners, which was approved to run through 30 September 2026, was to coordinate supportive-housing development for people with mental health problems who are homeless, in jails or in emergency departments [266]; no report of a renewal was found as of 3 October 2026. The Department's anti-eviction defense program is funded at $650,000 in the FY2027 General Fund, the level the Legislature kept after the Governor proposed halving it [18]. No state supportive-housing subsidy program was found as of October 2026; neither Section 811 project rental assistance through the Alabama Housing Finance Authority nor a Shelter Plus Care program could be confirmed by name (Appendix D). Birmingham's unsheltered-services roadmap includes 350 added shelter and transitional beds, with most of its strategies due by the end of 2026 [267].
282.section: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness

283.title: Economic stability: income, work and food · B0409
283.text: Poverty. 15.2 percent of Alabamians (about 760,000) lived in poverty in 2024, the lowest rate in American Community Survey data going back to 2010; child poverty was 20.2 percent [179]; median household income was $63,999 in the 2020–2024 five-year estimate [133].
283.section: Economic stability: income, work and food

284.title: Economic stability: income, work and food · B0410
284.text: Disability income. In December 2025, 179,658 Alabamians received Social Security disability benefits as disabled workers and 138,832 received SSI (130,122 for disability), at an average SSI payment of about $736 a month (this report's division of the month's total payments by the number of recipients) [268]; a year earlier the counts were 185,048 and 140,811 [269].
284.section: Economic stability: income, work and food

285.title: Economic stability: income, work and food · B0411
285.text: Work. The Department of Rehabilitation Services' Vocational Rehabilitation Service served 45,793 people, of 72,236 served across all the Department's programs in its 2025 annual report, and closed 3,999 cases in competitive integrated employment [270]. The ADMH–ADRS Individual Placement and Support program, the evidence-based supported-employment model for people with serious mental illness [128] [271], expanded in February 2025 to five sites under a federal grant [128]; 234 people were in supported employment in the 2025 reporting year (205 in 2024), and 21.0 percent of adults served by the public system were employed against 28.8 percent nationally (21.7 and 28.9 percent in 2024) [42] [43].
285.section: Economic stability: income, work and food

286.title: Economic stability: income, work and food · B0412
286.text: Food. 17.8 percent of Alabamians were food-insecure in 2024 [272]. SNAP enrollment fell from about 722,000 in October 2025 to about 678,000 in April 2026 [273] and about 650,000 by July 2026, after the 2025 federal budget law tightened work requirements [274]; the state faces a projected cost of about $174.3 million from October 2027, a 10 percent share of benefit costs, unless its payment-error rate (9.52 percent in FY2025) falls below 8 percent in FY2026 [274]. State officials had earlier put the range at $174–261 million for a 10–15 percent share [273].
286.section: Economic stability: income, work and food

287.title: Health care access · B0414
287.text: The coverage picture is set out in Domain 2 and Section 12: 8.4 percent of Alabamians uninsured [99], up to 155,000 people in the Medicaid coverage gap by Alabama Arise's count [36] [37] (KFF's July 2026 estimate is 86,000 uninsured adults in the gap itself and 147,000 who would become eligible if the state expanded [38]), and a 23 percent fall in marketplace enrollment in 2026 [39]. Thirty percent of Alabama adults reporting 14 or more mentally unhealthy days could not see a doctor because of cost [35]. Alabama Medicaid pays for live-video and audio-only telehealth at parity, which extends access where broadband allows [88].

288.title: Health care access · B0415
288.text: Transport. Alabama Medicaid operates a Non-Emergency Transportation program [47] [162]; as of ALDOT's 2023 study, 28 rural transit providers serve 58 of 67 counties, with nine counties lacking a rural provider [47]. The only mental-health-specific transport support identified is the transportation voucher within the IPS program [128].

289.title: Health care access · B0416
289.text: Connectivity. 87.5 percent of households had a broadband subscription in 2020–2024 [133]; on a different measure, the Black Belt's average high-speed access rate was 76 percent on the FCC's 2024 map, against 87 percent statewide [275]; the March 2026 BEAD award of nearly $460 million targets about 92,000 unserved locations [156].

290.title: Education access · B0418
290.text: 88.6 percent of Alabama adults have a high-school diploma and 28.4 percent a bachelor's degree [133]. School mental-health services — CMHC services in 122 school systems [119] and a coordinator that state law requires every district to employ [60] — are described in Section 9.

291.title: Social and community context · B0420
291.text: Alabama ranks 44th among states on America's Health Rankings' social and economic factors composite [276]. Forty-two percent of residents live in Census-defined rural areas [134]. Faith communities are the network the mental-health system has most deliberately engaged, through more than 400 faith leaders certified as Faith-Based Support Specialists since 2022 [141]. Alabama's 300,000-plus veterans [182] [183] have access to four VA medical centers, two VA outpatient clinics, 17 community-based outpatient clinics (three of them in Georgia) and four Vet Centers [183], and the Veterans Crisis Line [277]; ADMH's $12 million veterans plan [186] and the Veterans Resource Center, which opened in February 2026 [187], add state capacity. The Houston Hunter Act's firearm-hold agreements, signed into law in April 2025, are a recent lethal-means intervention [64]. No all-ages measure of social isolation was found as of October 2026; America's Health Rankings publishes a risk index for ages 65 and over [278].

301.title: Scope · B0436
301.text: Who pays determines what gets delivered. This section describes Alabama's payer mix — Medicaid, commercial insurance, Medicare, the marketplace, federal and state direct funding — and the single largest change in how community mental health care is paid for in a generation: the Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic model.

302.title: The coverage picture · B0438
302.text: In 2024, 50.0 percent of Alabamians had employer coverage, 20.8 percent Medicare, 14.7 percent Medicaid or CHIP (each person counted under one coverage type), 6.2 percent individual-market coverage and 8.4 percent were uninsured [99]. Medicaid enrolls about 1.1 million people, half of them children, with the federal government paying 78 percent of the program's $7.9 billion, according to KFF's May 2025 fact sheet [96].

303.title: The coverage picture · B0439
303.text: Alabama is one of ten states that have not expanded Medicaid to low-income adults [281] [38]; its income limit for parents is about 18 percent of the federal poverty level [282], and childless adults without a disability are not eligible [283]. The result is a coverage gap — adults who earn too much for Alabama's narrow Medicaid eligibility and too little for marketplace subsidies [38] — put at up to 155,000 people by Alabama Arise in a September 2026 statement [36] [37]. KFF's July 2026 estimate, using 2024 data, is 86,000 uninsured adults in the gap itself and 147,000 who would become eligible if the state expanded [38]. Adult uninsurance in non-expansion states ran 16.2 percent in 2025 against 9 percent in expansion states [36] [37]. The "ALLHealth" proposal to use expansion funds for private coverage, unveiled by the Alabama Hospital Association and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama in December 2024, has not been adopted [284] [38]. The 2025 federal budget law (H.R.1) ended, from January 2026, the temporary enhanced federal match offered to states that newly expand [80] and limits state provider taxes [81] [80]; were Alabama to expand, its 6 percent hospital provider tax would have to fall to 3.5 percent by FY2032, an estimated $118 million loss of hospital-tax revenue in that year [81]. The law's work requirements apply to expansion populations and so do not directly reach Alabama [81]. Separately, the expiry of enhanced marketplace subsidies at the end of 2025 cut Alabama's marketplace enrollment by about 95,000 people, or 23 percent, in 2026 [39].

304.title: The coverage picture · B0440
304.text: For people with mental illness the gap is visible in the national data: 14.1 percent of Alabama adults with any mental illness are uninsured (U.S. 9.2 percent), 14.2 percent of those with private insurance have plans that do not cover mental health (U.S. 9.6 percent), and 30 percent of adults reporting 14 or more mentally unhealthy days could not see a doctor because of cost (U.S. 26.6 percent) [35].

305.title: Medicaid behavioral health · B0442
305.text: Alabama Medicaid is a fee-for-service program with no comprehensive managed-care plans [125]: benefits and provider qualifications are set by the state plan and ADMH certification and rates by the Agency's fee schedule [49], and the Alabama Coordinated Health Network provides care coordination in seven regions [126]. That is why the CCBHC rate could be introduced by state action and why there is no health plan to hold to parity on the Medicaid side. Medicaid covers rehabilitative mental-health and substance-use services under Administrative Code 560-X-47, delivered by ADMH-certified community mental health centers, certified substance-use providers and, for children, state agencies [49]. Behavioral-health-specific developments:

306.title: Medicaid behavioral health · B0443
306.text: Mobile crisis became a Medicaid benefit on 1 October 2023 under State Plan Amendment AL-23-0009, which qualifies for an enhanced federal match for 24/7 two-person teams with follow-up [75].

307.title: Medicaid behavioral health · B0444
307.text: Inpatient psychiatric care in institutions for mental disease for adults aged 21–64 with serious mental illness is covered under a Section 1115 waiver running from 20 May 2022 to 19 May 2027, limited to facilities in Mobile and Baldwin counties — enrollees may use them regardless of their county of residence — with a 30-day average-stay cap [97].

308.title: Medicaid behavioral health · B0445
308.text: A substance-use disorder 1115 waiver, submitted in July 2023, remains pending at CMS [98].

309.title: Medicaid behavioral health · B0446
309.text: Twelve months of postpartum coverage has been in effect since October 2022 [106]. Alabama Medicaid's March 2023 alert called the extension a pilot [106]; KFF's tracker of 15 July 2026 lists it as implemented under a state plan amendment approved on 13 January 2023 [191].

310.title: Medicaid behavioral health · B0447
310.text: Telehealth is reimbursed at parity for live video and audio-only, with the home as an allowed site [88].

311.title: The CCBHC transition · B0449
311.text: What it is. A Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic must deliver nine services — screening and assessment; person- and family-centered treatment planning; outpatient mental-health and substance-use treatment; primary-care screening and monitoring; targeted case management; psychiatric rehabilitation; peer and family support; intensive community-based care for veterans and service members; and 24/7 crisis services with mobile response and 72-hour follow-up — and is paid a prospective daily rate (Alabama uses PPS-1) for each Medicaid enrollee on any day a qualifying service is delivered, instead of fee-for-service [10] [105]. The rate is set for each clinic from a cost report of the total cost of operating the CCBHC [285], which is why it can fund crisis response, peer support and care coordination that fee schedules under-pay.

312.title: The CCBHC transition · B0450
312.text: Alabama's path. ADMH received a $1 million federal planning grant in March 2023 to write state criteria [286], and on 4 June 2024 the federal government named Alabama one of ten states added to the Section 223 demonstration [25] [24] [74]. Only ADMH-designated CMHCs may apply, with quarterly entry points; a clinic may contract with designated collaborating organizations but must deliver at least 51 percent of encounters itself [10]. In the model so far: WellStone (Huntsville and Cullman) and AltaPointe (southwest and east Alabama), certified by the state effective July 2024 [26] [27] [28]; Mountain Lakes Behavioral Healthcare (Jackson, Marshall), approved by SAMHSA in October 2025; and Highland Health Systems (Calhoun, Cleburne), approved in April 2026 [27]. ADMH's CCBHC service directory also lists a fifth, South Central Alabama Mental Health, which the May 2026 release does not name [28], and the Department's board was told in November 2025 that five centers "will become CCBHCs in 2026" [56]. In August 2026 six providers — Integrea, Northwest Alabama Mental Health Center, Carastar, CarePath, Central Alabama Wellness and JBS — received $4.4 million in first-round Rural Health Transformation grants specifically to pursue certification [29]; a second round of 34 grants totaling nearly $55 million, to providers of all kinds and none described as being for CCBHC certification, followed on 1 October 2026 [104]. The Department's stated aim is a statewide transition [27] [287]; the 2025 edition of this report's phrase "convert all 19 CMHCs" does not appear in any ADMH source and is replaced here.

313.title: The CCBHC transition · B0451
313.text: Early results. The first two CCBHCs served 30,275 people in FY2025 [16]. ADMH has adopted an outcomes platform for CCBHC reporting [26]. The Department's January 2026 budget presentation reports that at WellStone the wait for an initial evaluation fell from 18 days in January 2025 to less than one day in December 2025, and the wait for a first therapy session from 33 days to eight [30]. No clinical outcome measures — hospitalization, emergency use, employment, housing — were found in the Department's published reports for the Alabama demonstration as of October 2026 (Appendix D).

314.title: The CCBHC transition · B0452
314.text: Why it matters for the rest of the system. CCBHC changes the financing logic of Domains 2 and 3. Crisis response and follow-up, now funded by General Fund lines the Legislature conditions and cuts [17] [20] [18], become Medicaid-reimbursable services inside a clinic's rate; a certified peer specialist's service is enough to trigger the daily payment, and case management is carried as a cost inside the rate [288] [285]; and the clinic, not the state, carries responsibility for the hand-offs between crisis, outpatient and recovery supports. The limit is the same as everywhere else in this report: the rate applies to Medicaid enrollees [105], and Alabama's uninsured adults — the coverage-gap population — are outside it.

315.title: Commercial insurance, Medicare and other payers · B0454
315.text: Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama held 84 percent of the state's commercial market in 2024, with the second carrier at 6 percent; the American Medical Association's 2025 study ranks Alabama the least competitive health-insurance market in the country [100]. ParityTrack's Alabama page, last modified in 2021, reports no published mental-health parity enforcement actions in the state [101]. Medicare covers one in five Alabamians [99]. Employer assistance programs, TRICARE and the VA, which has four medical centers in the state [183], complete the picture; this report did not compile Alabama-specific figures for them.
315.section: Commercial insurance, Medicare and other payers

316.title: Spending benchmarks · B0456
316.text: Alabama's state mental health agency spent $133 per resident in FY2024, 30th of 52 jurisdictions (the 50 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico), against a U.S. average of $179; about 85 percent of that went to community care [23]. The Department's FY2025 revenue of $1.43 billion was 41 percent state and 59 percent federal and other, with Medicaid the largest line (Domain 2) [16]. Enacted General Fund appropriations were $244.5 million for FY2026 and $240.9 million for FY2027 [20] [18].

327.title: Cross-Domain Dependency Map · B0472
327.text: Read together: a well-governed and well-financed system (1, 2) with enough staff (4) and built capacity (5) can deliver the full continuum (3) and measure it (6); housing and coverage (11, 12) decide who that system reaches (7); and organized communities (8) sustain the funding. In this report's reading, the binding constraints in Alabama in 2026 are coverage [36] [38], workforce [34] and data [14].

339.title: Appendix C. Source Register · B0493
339.text: The source register of the PDF edition listed 117 entries, several of which bundled a number of documents under one code. On this site each document is a reference of its own, numbered in the order it is first cited (sources used only for the maps and glossary follow at the end), and the References page is the register: it gives each document's publisher, date and address, a short summary, how fully it could be read, and where a newer edition exists. Hovering over a bracketed number in the text shows the same summary together with the passage that supports the sentence.

340.title: Appendix D. Verification notes and open items · B0619
340.text: This appendix lists what the report could not establish when it was checked claim by claim against its cited sources on 3 October 2026. The items are grouped by the reason: a document could not be read; a statement could not be confirmed; a figure or record was not found in any published source; or the answer depends on a date that had not yet arrived. In the body each is left out, attributed to the source that makes it, worded as something this review did not find, or, in the few cases noted below, kept without a source.
340.section: Appendix D. Verification notes and open items

435.title: Version history · B0634
435.text: Version Date Change v250603 3 June 2025 Original report (eight domains; white paper; cross-domain map). Produced with ChatGPT research synthesis. v261003 (the 3 October draft) 3 October 2026 Verification and refresh of the figures; reconciled white paper to the analysis; corrected 14 hedged or incorrect passages; added two cross-cutting lenses (continuum of care; Sequential Intercept Model); added four new sections (children, youth & families; justice interface; housing & social determinants; payers & CCBHC); added Alabama baseline indicators and a source register. Produced with Claude; reviewed by the Executive Director. [DRAFT — For Review] v261003.1 (this text) 3 October 2026 Claim-by-claim re-verification of the 3 October draft against every cited source; corrections, updates and re-attributed citations logged in the site's change log; source register split into individual documents; open items rebuilt.

436.title: [1] Monitoring the Building Blocks of Health Systems: A Handbook of Indicators and Their Measurement Strategies
436.text: World Health Organization. WHO's 2010 handbook of indicators for monitoring health systems. Only the cover, contents pages and WHO's catalogue description could be read; the full text on WHO's repository refused the fetch. Its six chapters follow the six building blocks: health service delivery, health workforce, health information systems, access to essential medicines, health systems financing, and leadership and governance. Equity and community engagement are not among the six.

437.title: [2] Preventing Mental, Emotional, and Behavioral Disorders Among Young People: Progress and Possibilities — chapter 3, 'Defining the Scope of Prevention' (NCBI Bookshelf copy)
437.text: National Research Council and Institute of Medicine; National Academies Press. Chapter 3 of the 2009 National Academies report edited by Mary Ellen O'Connell, Thomas Boat and Kenneth E. Warner, read on the NCBI Bookshelf because the publisher's own site (register item S60) could not be opened. It sets out the spectrum of mental health interventions the report uses: promotion; universal, selective and indicated prevention; treatment (case identification and standard treatment); and maintenance (long-term treatment and after-care, including rehabilitation). It is a national framework and says nothing about Alabama. Only this chapter and the contents page were read.

438.title: [3] Beyond Beds: The Vital Role of a Full Continuum of Psychiatric Care
438.text: National Association of State Mental Health Program Directors and Treatment Advocacy Center. A 31-page policy paper arguing that inpatient psychiatric beds are only one part of a working system and that states need a complete continuum of psychiatric care. Its ten recommendations begin with funding a comprehensive continuum and include justice diversion, emergency treatment, bed capacity, data, linkages between systems with warm hand-offs, technology, workforce and partnerships. It is a national paper and does not assess Alabama.

439.title: [4] The Sequential Intercept Model (SIM)
439.text: SAMHSA. SAMHSA's web page for the Sequential Intercept Model, which it says details how people with mental and substance use disorders come into contact with and move through the criminal justice system. It lists six intercepts: 0 Community Services, 1 Law Enforcement, 2 Initial Detention/Court Hearings, 3 Jails/Courts, 4 ReEntry and 5 Community Corrections. The page is a national framework and says nothing about Alabama.

440.title: [5] The Sequential Intercept Model: Advancing Community-Based Solutions for Justice-Involved People with Mental and Substance Use Disorders (brochure, PEP19-SIM-BROCHURE)
440.text: SAMHSA's GAINS Center. The GAINS Center's brochure on the Sequential Intercept Model, developed in the early 2000s by Mark Munetz, Patricia Griffin and Henry Steadman. It describes six intercept points along which people with mental and substance use disorders flow through the criminal justice system, and says communities use the model to identify gaps, resources and opportunities at each. Intercept 0 covers crisis response and proactive policing that can divert people from the justice system. It does not discuss Alabama.

441.title: [6] Alabama law enforcement looks for new ways to address mental health crises
441.text: Alabama Reflector. Feature article, part of a Reflector series on mental health care, on how Alabama police and sheriffs respond to people in mental-health crisis. Lee County Sheriff Jay Jones says jails have become what 'some sheriffs describe as a de facto center' for people with mental-health conditions. John Hollingsworth, director of Alabama Crisis Intervention Training (CIT), estimates that 20% to 30% of the calls law enforcement fields involve people in a mental-health crisis. The article describes CIT training, mobile crisis and co-responder models, and notes there is no statewide standard for crisis response.

442.title: [7] Updating the System of Care Concept and Philosophy
442.text: Georgetown University Center for Child and Human Development, National Technical Assistance Center for Children's Mental Health. A 12-page issue brief that restates the system of care approach for children's mental health, first published in 1986 after the federal Child and Adolescent Service System Program began in 1984. It gives three core values (family driven and youth guided, community based, culturally and linguistically competent) and thirteen guiding principles, among them individualized service planning, linkages across child-serving agencies, early identification and support for the transition to adulthood. It is a national framework and does not discuss Alabama.

443.title: [8] Social Determinants of Health — Healthy People 2030
443.text: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion. The federal Healthy People 2030 page defining social determinants of health as the conditions where people are born, live, learn, work, play, worship and age that affect health and quality of life. It groups them into five domains: economic stability, education access and quality, health care access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context. It is a national framework and carries no Alabama data.

444.title: [9] 988 in Alabama (988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline)
444.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's public information page on the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, read on 3 October 2026. It explains that 988 has been the national three-digit crisis number since 16 July 2022 and frames Alabama's crisis system as someone to call, someone to respond and somewhere to go. It says call centers are located at AltaPointe Health in Mobile, at JBS in collaboration with The Crisis Center Birmingham, at SpectraCare Health Systems in Dothan and at WellStone in Huntsville, and it links to the six crisis centers by name. It contains no statistics: no contact volumes, answer rates, evaluation counts or number of mobile crisis teams.

445.title: [10] Alabama Comprehensive Provider Manual for Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics (CCBHCs), version 1
445.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's operating manual for clinics in Alabama's CCBHC Medicaid demonstration, version 1, published 29 August 2025 (about 75 pages). It says only the designated community mental health center for a region may become a CCBHC, that clinics may join at the start of any fiscal quarter, and that each must be able to deliver nine required services, directly or through designated collaborating organizations, while providing at least 51 percent of service encounters itself. Payment is a daily prospective rate under the PPS-1 method. Telehealth must use a HIPAA-compliant platform with documented client preference and follow Medicaid Policy Manual Chapter 112. Only pages 1 to 36 could be read for this check; the crisis-services detail, the designated-collaborating-organization section and the quality-improvement and reporting sections were not reached.

446.title: [11] Demontray Hunter v. Kimberly Boswell, Commissioner of the Alabama Department of Mental Health, 2:16-cv-00798 (M.D. Ala.)
446.text: Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse (University of Michigan Law School). Case summary page for the class action filed 30 September 2016 over delays in court-ordered competency evaluations and restoration treatment for people held in Alabama jails. It reports a settlement and consent decree approved 25 January 2018, requiring evaluations, treatment and therapy within 45 days by the end of the first year, with compliance monitoring by ADAP (also an associational plaintiff) and regular reports to the court. In March 2025, on joint motion, the decree's term was extended to 31 January 2027 'specifically as to inpatient mental competency restoration treatment'. The page shows the case as ongoing; its docket listing stops in 2017 and it records nothing after March 2025.

447.title: [12] Crisis Centers
447.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's public page listing the state's crisis centers, read on 3 October 2026. It says six centers currently operate, with access around the clock every day of the year, and that people can walk in or be brought in by law enforcement, first responders and EMS. For each center it gives a phone number, an address and the counties it serves: AltaPointe in Mobile (7 counties), Carastar in Montgomery (11), JBS Craig Crisis Care Center in Birmingham (11), Indian Rivers' Hope Pointe in Tuscaloosa (11), SpectraCare in Dothan (5) and WellStone Emergency Services with WellStone Pediatric Crisis Care in Huntsville (15). The lists add up to 60 of Alabama's 67 counties; Butler, Coffee, Colbert, Covington, Crenshaw, Franklin and Lauderdale are not listed. The page gives no opening dates, bed counts or ages served, and says nothing about 988 call centers or mobile crisis teams.

448.title: [13] Alabama Crisis System of Care
448.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's overview page for the Alabama Crisis System of Care, read on 3 October 2026. It describes the system as 988, mobile crisis teams and crisis centers, says the Governor, the Legislature and ADMH have funded six crisis centers, and names each with the counties it serves. It states that there are now 14 mobile crisis teams at 11 community mental health centers. A map caption says all counties are covered by the six centers except Butler, Coffee, Colbert, Covington, Crenshaw, Franklin and Lauderdale. The page carries no dates, no count of counties with mobile-crisis access, no target number of teams and no mention of the Division of Developmental Disabilities.

449.title: [14] An Evaluation of the Alabama Department of Mental Health Crisis Centers (listed by ACES as 'A Preliminary Report on the Evaluation of ADMH Crisis Centers')
449.text: Alabama Commission on the Evaluation of Services (ACES). ACES's evaluation of the six ADMH-funded crisis centers, cover-dated August 2025 and sent to the Commission on 4 September 2025 with a letter asking that it be treated as a preliminary report. It finds that the state has put $175 million into the centers since FY21 ($42 million a year now), that 16,414 interactions had taken place by the end of 2024, and that in FY24 average utilization was 27% and the average cost per bed day $2,193. It says centers collect the emergency-department and jail-avoidance measures inconsistently (one always reports zero jail avoidances), so ACES cannot verify the key performance indicators, and that there is insufficient data to judge effectiveness. ADMH's attached response questions the methodology behind the utilization and bed-cost figures and says most centers run at capacity most days.

450.title: [15] Alabama Department of Mental Health Celebrates Three Years of 988
450.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. An ADMH press release of 16 July 2025 marking the third anniversary of 988. It says that since the launch on 16 July 2022 a total of 132,713 contacts have been received by crisis counselors, that the in-state answer rate reached 87.9 percent in June 2025 (up from 64 percent in July 2022) and that the average speed to answer is 23 seconds. It also says Alabama has opened six regional crisis centers and expanded mobile crisis teams. It does not name the call centers.

451.title: [16] Innovative Solutions, Enduring Impact: Annual Report FY25
451.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. The Alabama Department of Mental Health's annual report for fiscal year 2025 (October 2024 to September 2025), a 31-page illustrated report addressed to the Governor by Commissioner Kimberly G. Boswell. It carries feature articles on the year's work, including the 988 line's in-state answer rate, the new Dothan crisis center and Tuscaloosa expansion, and a five-year plan for civil-commitment beds. It describes the Department's divisions and their offices, and prints the FY25 operating revenue ($1,429,209,064) and expenditures ($1,445,681,218) by line. Its closing data pages count individuals served by population, by community mental health center, by state facility, and, for the first time, by crisis center, 988 call center, child/adolescent mobile crisis team and certified community behavioral health clinic. The document prints no publication date; the month comes from the ADMH upload path (2026/04).

452.title: [17] Alabama Legislature gives final approval to $3.7 billion General Fund budget
452.text: Alabama Reflector. News report on final passage of SB 146, Alabama's $3.7 billion General Fund budget for fiscal year 2027. The Senate concurred 20-0 on Wednesday 8 April 2026 with House changes that included a slight increase for the Department of Mental Health (ADMH), sending the bill to Gov. Kay Ivey. It reports that ADMH, DHR and Corrections have conditional appropriations, and that the last two quarterly installments of ADMH's collective $42 million for existing Crisis Diversion and Rural Crisis Care centers will not be paid until the department reports the status of the programs to the budget chairs, the Finance Director and the Legislative Fiscal Officer. It does not give ADMH's total appropriation, the 988 line, an act number, or any detail of what must be reported.

453.title: [18] State General Fund Appropriations Comparison Sheet for FY 2027 - SB146 (Act 2026-383), 2026 Regular Session
453.text: Alabama Legislative Services Agency, Fiscal Division. The Legislative Services Agency's line-by-line comparison sheet for Alabama's FY2027 General Fund budget (SB146, Act 2026-383), 20 pages. For each agency it shows FY2026 budgeted, the Governor's recommendation, the Senate-passed and the House-passed/enacted amounts, and the difference. The Department of Mental Health is enacted at $240,864,549 against $244,569,847 budgeted for FY2026 (-$3,705,298), with earmarks including $36,000,000 for the six existing crisis diversion centers, $6,000,000 for five existing rural crisis care programs, $5,000,000 for a child and adolescent mobile crisis pilot, $8,000,000 for civil commitment/residential services plus $2,500,000 for additional civil commitment beds, $650,000 for anti-eviction defense, $1,000,000 for crisis intervention training and no 988 line. It is a table of amounts only: it carries no proviso or condition language, no agency-request column and no signing date.

454.title: [19] Senate committee passes '27 General Fund budget with more money, requirements
454.text: Alabama Daily News. News report on the Senate committee's approval of a $3.72 billion FY2027 General Fund bill put forward by Sen. Albritton, which attached reporting requirements to several agencies. It says the bill allocates $36 million for ADMH's six crisis centers and that the Department will not receive that funding in the third and fourth quarters unless it reports each center's operating expenses, number of employees and persons served, and allows the Commission on the Evaluation of Services access to the centers. It notes the Commission's evaluation the previous year found inconsistent data reporting and that ADMH pushed back on that analysis. It describes the bill at committee stage, a month before enactment, and does not mention the rural crisis-care line, the ADMH total, 988 funding or the Act number.

455.title: [20] State General Fund Appropriations Comparison Sheet for FY 2026 - HB186 (Act 2025-251), 2025 Regular Session
455.text: Alabama Legislative Services Agency, Fiscal Division. The Legislative Services Agency's line-by-line comparison sheet for Alabama's FY2026 General Fund budget (HB186, Act 2025-251), 15 pages, showing FY2025 budgeted, the Governor's recommendation, House-passed, Senate-passed/enacted and the difference from FY2025. The Department of Mental Health is enacted at $244,467,967, up $4,705,298 from $239,762,669 in FY2025 (the Governor had recommended $248,162,669). Earmarks include $36,000,000 for the six existing crisis diversion centers, $6,000,000 for five existing rural crisis care programs, $5,000,000 for the child and adolescent mobile crisis pilot, $8,000,000 for civil commitment/residential services, $1,000,000 for crisis intervention training, $650,000 for anti-eviction defense, $500,000 for 988 call center capacity and $200,000 for a Veteran's PTSD Program. It has no agency-request column and no proviso language.

456.title: [21] ADMH mulls budget request with 23% increase to address mental health needs
456.text: Alabama Reflector. News report on the draft fiscal year 2026 budget request that Commissioner Kimberly Boswell presented to the ADMH board on Friday 13 December 2024. The department was considering a $389.6 million budget, 22.9% above the current $317 million, including an increase of $68.6 million (28.8%) from the General Fund and $4.6 million from the Education Trust Fund. Tentative items were $23.4 million for civil commitment beds, $11.5 million to expand crisis care (Boswell said Alabama needs 11 crisis centers), $2 million for detox services and $1 million for school-based mental health programmes. The article stresses that the request was tentative and might change.

457.title: [22] A look at the 2025 session's impacts on mental healthcare
457.text: Alabama Political Reporter. A news round-up by the Alabama Political Reporter, published 28 May 2025 (updated 29 May), of what the 2025 legislative session did for mental health. It lists the bills passed: SB70 (Alabama Veterans Resource Center), SB101 (medical and mental-health consent age raised from 14 to 16), SB236 (regional mental health authority boards), SB40 (firearm hold agreements) and HJR273 (a study commission on PTSD in first responders). On money, it says the Department of Mental Health received a $4.7 million, or 2 percent, increase, bringing its budget to $244 million, and that the 2026 budget included a combined $10 million for community mental health centers. It does not mention the Department's budget request, provider rate increases, 988, crisis-center conditions, accountability courts or bed counts.

458.title: [23] State Mental Health Agency Expenditures and Funding Sources: FY'2001 to FY'2024
458.text: NRI, Inc. (NASMHPD Research Institute). A nine-page NRI profile of what state mental health agencies spent and where the money came from, based on 50 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico. Table 1 gives Alabama $685,168,334 in FY2024 agency-controlled mental health spending, $133.15 per resident, ranked 30th; the report says states averaged $179 per resident. Table 2 splits Alabama's spending 14.2 percent state hospitals, 84.8 percent community programs and 1.0 percent central office, against 24.2, 73.3 and 2.5 percent for all states together.

459.title: [24] Alabama Selected for Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic Medicaid Demonstration Program
459.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. An ADMH press release dated 5 June 2024 announcing that Alabama is one of ten states selected by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, with SAMHSA, for the CCBHC Medicaid Demonstration Program. It says Alabama's behavioral healthcare system will begin its transition to the CCBHC business model and quotes Commissioner Boswell's vision that every Alabamian in all counties will have access to 24/7 mental health and substance use treatment. It does not name the other nine states, the first Alabama clinics, the start date of the demonstration or the federal statute.

460.title: [25] Biden-Harris Administration Expands Access to Mental Health and Substance Use Services with Addition of 10 New States to CCBHC Medicaid Demonstration Program
460.text: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. The federal announcement, dated 4 June 2024, that ten states were being added to the CCBHC Medicaid Demonstration Program: Alabama, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Rhode Island and Vermont. It explains that the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act lets the Department of Health and Human Services add ten states every two years, and that SAMHSA awarded 15 state planning grants in March 2023. It does not give a start date for the new states.

461.title: [26] ADMH Board of Trustees meeting minutes, 16 May 2025 (approved 15 August 2025)
461.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. Four pages of approved minutes of the ADMH Board of Trustees meeting of 16 May 2025, called to order by the Commissioner as Secretary with the Governor's proxy present; sixteen members or proxies are listed as present or absent. The CCBHC update says AltaPointe and WellStone were certified by the state effective July 2024, that CCBHCs must offer nine core services and are paid through a Prospective Payment System rate, that 15–17 federal outcome measures must be reported, and that ADMH has invested in a platform called Netsmart to report outcomes. The minutes also say the leadership team is working on a strategic plan to present at the next meeting.

462.title: [27] Alabama Continues Statewide Transition to Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic Model – Expanding into Two New Areas of the State
462.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. An ADMH press release of 28 May 2026 announcing that two more community mental health centers have been approved to move to the CCBHC model. Mountain Lakes Behavioral Healthcare (Jackson and Marshall counties) and Highland Health Systems (Cleburne and Calhoun counties) received approval from SAMHSA in October 2025 and April 2026 respectively, joining AltaPointe and WellStone, which moved to the model in 2024. It lists the nine core services a CCBHC must provide and says becoming a CCBHC can take six to eighteen months. It gives no figures for people served, does not describe the payment system and does not mention other centers preparing to convert.

463.title: [28] Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics: For Individuals Seeking Services (CCBHC service directory)
463.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's directory of CCBHC locations, read on 3 October 2026. It lists five organizations with their access numbers and addresses: AltaPointe Health, Highland Health Systems, Mountain Lakes Behavioral Healthcare, South Central Alabama Mental Health and WellStone, marking which sites offer the full scope of CCBHC services and which offer limited services. A map image on the page is dated July 2026 by its file path. The page gives no certification or approval dates, and ADMH's release of 28 May 2026 names only four of the five (not South Central).

464.title: [29] Alabama mental health centers receive more than $8 million in rural health grants
464.text: Alabama Political Reporter. A news report published 7 September 2026 saying eight Alabama community mental health providers received 11 grants totalling more than $8 million in the first round of the Alabama Rural Health Transformation Program, which Governor Ivey announced on 24 August. About $4.39 million goes to six centers working toward certification as Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics: Carastar, CarePath, Central Alabama Wellness, Integrea, the Jefferson-Blount-St. Clair Mental Health Authority and Northwest Alabama Mental Health Center. The article notes these grants help the six prepare for certification but do not confer it. The rest goes to AltaPointe, WellStone and Central Alabama Wellness for school-based care, integrated access points and technology.

465.title: [30] FY27 Budget Presentation (Alabama Department of Mental Health, legislative budget hearing)
465.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. The Commissioner's slide deck for the Legislature's FY2027 budget hearings. Its bed slide, with data as of 13 January 2026, totals 771 involuntary beds, 15.1 per 100,000 residents. A five-year goals slide proposes raising civil-commitment beds to 30 per 100,000 (779 more beds, $226.4 million) and putting crisis services and Stepping Up in all 67 counties ($41 million), $312.4 million in all. Two slides give results for one CCBHC, WellStone: days to initial evaluation fell from 18 in January 2025 to less than one in December 2025, and days to first clinical service from 33 to eight. As read, it gives no count of civil commitments, no staffing vacancy or turnover figures and no 988 answer rate.

466.title: [31] Federal Impacts to Mental Health (ADMH legislative budget hearing presentation, summer 2025)
466.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health, posted by the Legislative Services Agency. A 30-slide deck Commissioner Kimberly Boswell presented at the Legislature's summer budget hearings on 26 August 2025, mostly about how federal changes affect ADMH's budget, the CCBHC model and rural health transformation funds. Its bed slides give 698 involuntary beds as of 19 August 2025 (285 at Bryce and Harper, 225 contracted at hospitals, 188 crisis residential) and 180 voluntary crisis-center observation beds, and say Alabama has 13.7 beds per 100,000 residents against the Treatment Advocacy Center's 'absolute minimum' of 30. One slide is headed 'Nineteen Community Mental Health Centers'. It contains no plan or target for adding beds, no cost estimate for new beds, and no counts of crisis centers or mobile crisis teams.

467.title: [32] Alabama Department of Mental Health works to reduce forensic waitlist
467.text: Alabama Political Reporter. A news report published 18 August 2026 (updated 19 August) on what the Department of Mental Health told a Joint Mental Health Task Force meeting the week before. It reports 291 people waiting in jails in July, down from 327 in January, and a goal of 100 by the end of 2026, under the 2018 federal consent decree in Hunter v. Beshear. It says Taylor Hardin's capacity rose from 140 to 225 beds, with about 200 filled and the remaining 25 waiting on a plumbing repair, and that a jail-based telehealth restoration program has restored 32 people since summer 2025. It also reports that budget cuts in 2010 led to the loss of 725 beds, that 'Chairman Reynolds' put the cost of replacing 787 beds at $590 million, and that Commissioner Kim Boswell said a new revenue stream is needed.

468.title: [33] Plan to double Alabama's mental health beds, crisis services achievable, budget chair says
468.text: Decatur Daily (Alabama Daily News story). A news report on Commissioner Kim Boswell's presentation to lawmakers in the first week of February 2025 of a five-year ADMH plan: civil-commitment beds from 13.4 to 30 per 100,000 residents, mobile crisis teams from 14 to 23 and crisis centers from 6 to 11. For FY2026 ADMH asked for $248 million from the General Fund, including about $23.4 million for new beds and $11.5 million to extend mobile crisis teams and crisis centers to the whole state; 'today, only 24 counties are covered'. Rep. Rex Reynolds, chair of the House General Fund budget committee, is reported as calling the plan achievable but costly and dependent on later budget cycles.

469.title: [34] Mental Health Care Health Professional Shortage Areas (HPSAs)
469.text: KFF (State Health Facts). A KFF State Health Facts table that republishes the federal Health Resources and Services Administration's quarterly summary of designated mental health shortage areas, as of 31 December 2025. For Alabama it shows 67 designations covering 2,934,202 people, 28.4% of need met and 128 more practitioners needed to remove the designations. Need met and practitioners needed are counted in psychiatrists only. The national figure for need met is 27.3%.

470.title: [35] The State of Mental Health in America 2025
470.text: Mental Health America. Mental Health America's annual report ranking the 50 states and the District of Columbia on 17 measures of mental illness prevalence and access to care, published October 2025. Most measures combine 2022 and 2023 federal survey data; the workforce measure is 2024. Alabama ranks 49th overall, 18th for adults, 50th for youth, 18th on prevalence and 51st (last) on access to care. It ranks last on three individual measures: mental health workforce availability (740 residents per provider against 320 nationally), youth with major depression who received no services (66.4%) and youth whose private insurance did not cover mental health (18.0%).

471.title: [36] New Census data emphasizes need to expand health coverage in Alabama
471.text: Alabama Arise (Cover Alabama campaign). A short Alabama Arise news release dated 16 September 2026 carrying a statement by Debbie Smith, director of Arise's Cover Alabama campaign, in response to new Current Population Survey data. It says Alabama is one of 10 states yet to expand Medicaid, that adult uninsurance in non-expansion states last year (16.2%) was nearly twice that in expansion states (9%), that the state's refusal to expand leaves up to 155,000 low-income people in a coverage gap, and that more than 95,000 Alabamians lost ACA coverage this year (a 23% enrollment decline) after Congress did not renew enhanced premium tax credits. It does not define the coverage gap in income terms and gives no Alabama uninsured rate.

472.title: [37] Alabama's uninsured rate exposes Medicaid expansion gap
472.text: Alabama Political Reporter. A news report published 17 September 2026 on Census Bureau Current Population Survey figures released that week. It says the uninsured rate among adults aged 19 to 64 was 16.2 percent in states that have not expanded Medicaid and 9 percent in states that have. It quotes Debbie Smith of Alabama Arise's Cover Alabama campaign saying Alabama's refusal to expand leaves up to 155,000 low-income people in a coverage gap. It also says Alabama is one of 10 non-expansion states and that more than 95,000 Alabamians lost marketplace coverage this year, a 23 percent decline.

473.title: [38] How Many Uninsured Are in the Coverage Gap and How Many Could be Eligible if All States Adopted the Medicaid Expansion?
473.text: KFF. A KFF brief estimating, from 2024 survey data, how many uninsured adults in the ten states without Medicaid expansion fall in the coverage gap, defined as people whose incomes are too high for their state's Medicaid program but too low for marketplace subsidies. It counts 1.2 million people in the gap across the ten states. Its state table gives Alabama 86,000 adults in the gap and a further 61,000 between 100 and 138 percent of the poverty level, or 147,000 uninsured adults who would become eligible if the state expanded. It also notes that the 2025 federal budget law eliminated the financial incentive for states to adopt expansion. The state table is an embedded chart, read in the browser.

474.title: [39] Alabama Obamacare enrollment drops 23% after tax credits expire
474.text: Alabama Reflector. News report, based on a late-July 2026 KFF analysis, that Affordable Care Act marketplace enrollment in Alabama dropped by 95,000, about 23%, after the enhanced premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025. It states that Alabama is one of ten states that has not expanded Medicaid and quotes Cover Alabama's director on the effect of a larger uninsured population on hospitals. It refers to the Medicaid coverage gap but gives no number of people in it.

475.title: [40] Strategic Plan: Priorities & Goals (Alabama Department of Mental Health Strategic Plan 2025-2028)
475.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's web page for its Strategic Plan 2025-2028. It gives a short introduction, five priorities each with a one-sentence statement (System of Care Transformation; Child & Family Services; Workforce Health & Wellness; Resources; Awareness & Knowledge) and three foundational principles (Trauma-Responsive Care, Peer & Family Engagement, Partnerships). As read, the page lists no goals beneath the priorities, carries no goal numbering, gives no numeric targets and links to no fuller plan document.

476.title: [41] The ribbon is cut on WellStone's 24/7 pediatric unit
476.text: WellStone. A news post on WellStone's own website, dated 23 September 2024 by its URL, about the ribbon-cutting for the WellStone Emergency Services Pediatric Unit in Huntsville. It describes a 24-bed, 12,000-square-foot, $9 million crisis care center, calls it the first of its kind in the state, and says Huntsville was 'just days from opening' it. Governor Ivey and WellStone's chief executive are quoted. It does not give the ages served or an opening date, and it does not mention the other crisis centers.

477.title: [42] 2025 Uniform Reporting System (URS) Output Tables: Alabama
477.text: SAMHSA. The 2025 Uniform Reporting System tables for Alabama, published by SAMHSA on 31 July 2026 and covering 1 October 2024 to 30 September 2025. They report how many people the state mental health authority served, penetration and utilization rates, state-hospital readmissions, employment and living situation, evidence-based practices and consumer-survey results, each beside the national figure. They supersede the 2024 tables the report first used.

478.title: [43] 2024 Uniform Reporting System (URS) Output Tables — Alabama (2024 Mental Health National Outcome Measures)
478.text: SAMHSA, Center for Behavioral Health Statistics and Quality. SAMHSA's annual 32-page state table for Alabama's public mental health system, built from data the state mental health authority reports under the Community Mental Health Services Block Grant. This edition covers 1 October 2023 to 30 September 2024 and was posted on 25 July 2025. It shows 93,506 people served (18.31 per 1,000 residents against 23.46 nationally), 645 people served in state hospitals during the year, and Alabama-versus-U.S. figures for readmission, employment, living situation, evidence-based practices, consumer surveys and the race of people served. Several headline rows (penetration, living situation, readmission, race) cover all ages, not adults only.

479.title: [44] Code of Alabama §29-2A-1: Alabama Commission on the Evaluation of Services, creation and purpose
479.text: State of Alabama (2025 Code of Alabama, as published by Justia). The section of the Code of Alabama that creates the Alabama Commission on the Evaluation of Services. It says the Commission 'is created for the purpose of advising the Legislature and the Governor regarding the evaluation of services, which may include evidence-based policymaking, within the state'. The history line shows it was enacted by Act 2019-517. Only this section of the chapter was read.

480.title: [45] Alabama One Health Record: Alabama's Health Data Interstate — A Primer on Alabama's Health Information Exchange
480.text: Alabama Medicaid Agency (slides hosted by the Health Leaders Association of Alabama). A 36-slide briefing by Gary D. Parker, Alabama Medicaid's chief data officer and director of Alabama One Health Record, dated 23 February 2026 and prepared for the Health Leaders Association of Alabama conference on 5 March 2026. It describes One Health Record as the state's health information exchange, launched by the Alabama Medicaid Agency. A connections table headed December 2025 shows 57 hospitals (16 more as work in progress), 800+ ambulatory clinics and care sites, and 15 FQHC, rural health clinic, health information network and community mental health center organizations (300+ sites); the Department of Mental Health appears only as "ADMH W-I-P". A timeline slide says that in 2023 it was the first HIE to successfully exchange data across the TEFCA QHIN framework.

481.title: [46] Stepping Up Alabama
481.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. The Department's page on Stepping Up Alabama. It describes the national Stepping Up initiative as sponsored by the National Association of Counties, the American Psychiatric Foundation and the Council of State Governments Justice Center, in partnership with the federal Bureau of Justice Assistance. It says Stepping Up received its first state appropriation in fiscal year 2021 and that ADMH awarded annual grants of $50,000 to centers through a request for proposals. It lists the national criteria, which include using a validated mental-health screening tool on every person booked into jail, and notes that Mobile and Shelby counties hold national Innovator designations. It gives no count of participating counties.

482.title: [47] Statewide Rural Transit Study
482.text: Alabama Department of Transportation (prepared by Sain Associates, Inc.). A consultant study for ALDOT, dated 13 March 2023, of Alabama's rural (FTA Section 5311) public transit. It says Alabama has 28 rural transit providers serving 58 of 67 counties, offered as on-demand service that must be booked in advance, and its gap analysis names the nine counties with no rural transit service: Bullock, Butler, Crenshaw, Elmore, Montgomery, Limestone, Mobile, Fayette and Tuscaloosa. It notes in one sentence that Alabama Medicaid operates non-emergency medical transportation. It does not classify counties as rural or urban, give a rural population share, or mention crisis centers, mental-health providers or broadband.

483.title: [48] PSYPACT map / participating states
483.text: PSYPACT Commission. PSYPACT's list of participating states with each state's enabling bill and dates. Alabama's entry reads 'AL SB 102 (Enacted 3/18/2021; Effective 6/1/2021)' under 'PSYPACT participating states'. The register's home-page URL (psypact.gov) carries no state data; the map page does.

484.title: [49] Alabama Administrative Code chapter 560-X-47, Rehabilitative Services
484.text: Alabama Medicaid Agency (Alabama Legislative Services Agency, Administrative Code). Alabama Medicaid's rules (.01 to .11) for rehabilitative services for people with mental illness or substance abuse diagnoses, issued under the State Plan for Medical Assistance, Attachment 3.1-A. Providers must be DMH-certified 310-board community mental health centers, DMH-certified substance abuse treatment organisations, or, for children under 21, state agencies (DHR, DYS, DMH for ASD, and DCS). Payment is a statewide maximum per procedure code on the Agency's published fee schedule. The chapter says nothing about fee-for-service versus managed care or about the ACHN.

485.title: [50] Office of the Commissioner
485.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's biography page for its Commissioner, read on 3 October 2026. It says Kimberly G. Boswell was sworn in as Commissioner on 16 December 2020, quotes Governor Kay Ivey on her selection, and says that since 2021 she has created and expanded the Alabama Crisis System of Care, offering services 'not previously available in the state'. It does not state how the Commissioner is appointed or the terms of the office.

486.title: [51] Code of Alabama, Title 22, Chapter 50 (Department of Mental Health): §§22-50-2, 22-50-9 and 22-50-16
486.text: State of Alabama (2025 Code of Alabama, as published by Justia). Three sections of the chapter of the Code of Alabama that sets up the Department of Mental Health, read in the 2025 edition. Section 22-50-2 creates the Department as a department of state government made up of the Commissioner and the divisions the Commissioner directs. Section 22-50-9 authorizes the Department, through its Commissioner, 'to act in any prudent way to provide mental health services and mental retardation services for the people of Alabama'. Section 22-50-16 says the Governor appoints the Commissioner, who serves at the Governor's pleasure, and that the Commissioner may appoint associate commissioners. All three trace to Acts 1965, No. 881. Only these three sections of the chapter were read.

487.title: [52] Division of Mental Health & Substance Use Services
487.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's page for its Division of Mental Health and Substance Use Services, read on 3 October 2026. It names Nicole Walden as Associate Commissioner and says the division contracts for, monitors and certifies community services and manages the three state facilities (Bryce, Mary Starke Harper and Taylor Hardin). The body of the page describes eight offices; the division's menu lists eleven, adding Facility Operations, Forensic Mental Health Services and Forensic Outpatient Services. It describes the Office of CCBHC as responsible for a statewide transformation of the behavioral health system using the CCBHC model.

488.title: [53] Division of Developmental Disabilities
488.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's page for its Division of Developmental Disabilities, read on 3 October 2026. It names Camille Cumuze as Associate Commissioner and says the division serves individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities and their families. It lists the division's offices, among them Support Coordination, Supported Employment, Quality & Planning and waiver management. It does not mention crisis services.

489.title: [54] Division of Administration
489.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's page for its Division of Administration, read on 3 October 2026. It names Brooke Hibbard as Associate Commissioner and says the division provides support services for the Department's facilities and central office staff. It lists ten offices and programs: Administrative Support Services, Certification Administration, Finance, Human Resources Management, Information Technology, Land & Asset Management, Life Safety & Technical Services, the Nurse Delegation Program, Pre-Admission Screening, and Policy & Planning.

490.title: [55] ADMH Board of Trustees meeting minutes, 14 February 2025 (approved)
490.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. Six pages of approved minutes of the ADMH Board of Trustees meeting of 14 February 2025, chaired by Vice Chair Donna Foster. The Commissioner reports that two CCBHCs have opened under the demonstration at WellStone and AltaPointe, that 'the first pediatric crisis center' opened in Huntsville in October, and that the goals are more civil-commitment beds and statewide crisis services. The associate commissioners named are Nicole Walden (Mental Illness & Substance Use), Kathy Sawyer (Developmental Disabilities) and LaVonda Blair (Administration). The Developmental Disabilities report describes its incident-investigation system; the next meetings are listed as 16 May, 15 August and 21 November 2025.

491.title: [56] ADMH Board of Trustees meeting minutes, 21 November 2025 (signed 20 February 2026)
491.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. Three pages of signed minutes of the ADMH Board of Trustees meeting of 21 November 2025, called to order by Vice Chair Donna Foster. The Commissioner announced that Associate Commissioners LaVonda Blair (Administration) and Kathy Sawyer (Developmental Disabilities) were retiring and introduced their replacements, Brooke Hibbard and Camille Cumuze; the attendance list already gives the two successors those titles. She also reported an increase in special mental health funds at the end of FY2025, that five community mental health centers will become CCBHCs in 2026, and that the crisis centers had exceeded 1,000 evaluations a month for three months. The next meetings are listed as 20 February, 15 May, 14 August and 20 November 2026.

492.title: [57] Board of Trustees
492.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's page for its Board of Trustees, read on 3 October 2026. It lists sixteen members: the Governor (Kay Ivey) as chair, the Speaker of the House (Nathaniel Ledbetter), the Lieutenant Governor (Will Ainsworth) and Commissioner Kimberly Boswell as secretary, all ex officio, plus one member for each of the seven congressional districts and five at-large members. It says members are appointed by the Governor and that the board meets quarterly, and it links to a page of meeting minutes.

493.title: [58] Education Trust Fund Comparison Sheet for FY 2027 - HB238 (Act 2026-380), 2026 Regular Session
493.text: Alabama Legislative Services Agency, Fiscal Division. The Legislative Services Agency's line-by-line comparison sheet for Alabama's FY2027 Education Trust Fund budget (HB238, Act 2026-380), 22 pages, showing FY2026 budgeted, Governor's recommendation, House-passed, Senate-passed/enacted and the difference. The Department of Mental Health receives $84,107,489 (up $95,660 from $84,011,829), including a $5,500,000 earmark for the School-Based Mental Health Services Collaboration. In the State Department of Education section, the School-Based Mental Health Service Coordinator line rises from $4,690,000 budgeted in FY2026 to $9,250,000 enacted for FY2027.

494.title: [59] SB101, 2025 Regular Session, enrolled (consent to medical treatment)
494.text: Alabama Legislature. Enrolled text of Alabama SB101 (2025), which amends Code sections 16-22-16.2, 22-8-4, 22-8-6, 22-8-9 and 22-8-10 and adds 22-8-12 to 22-8-14. It raises from 14 to 16 the age at which a minor may consent to his or her own medical, dental and mental health services, and bars public K-12 students under 16 from ongoing school counseling without specific written parental permission. It requires school mental-health records to be treated as health-care records and kept separately from academic records, and takes effect 1 October 2025. The enrolled PDF does not print an act number.

495.title: [60] Memo FY25-1021: Updates to Mental Health Services Notification
495.text: Alabama State Department of Education. A memorandum from the State Superintendent to local superintendents, dated 29 September 2025, on how Act 2025-455 changes the school mental-health consent rules. It restates that Act 2022-442 requires each local education agency to employ a mental health services coordinator and to adopt a parental opt-in policy with annual written notice to parents, mental-health records stored separately from academic records, and written parental permission. It says Act 2025-455 requires written parental permission for students under 16 to take part in ongoing school counseling or mental health services, and widens the definition of mental health services to include surveys and assessments. Instruction, advisement and occasional interventions are stated to be outside the opt-in requirement. The memo does not name SB101, give an effective date, or mention grief support.

496.title: [61] SB236, 2025 Regular Session, engrossed (regional mental health authority boards)
496.text: Alabama Legislature. Engrossed text of Alabama SB236 (2025), amending Code sections 22-51-8 and 22-51-9 on regional mental health authority ('310') boards; the enrolled version (SB236-enr.pdf) was also read and carries the same operative wording. Boards with more than 16 directors may appoint a nine-member executive committee, which must include one sheriff (or representative) and one judge of probate if those officials serve on the board; any of them may opt out and keep board membership. Effective 1 October 2025. Neither version prints an act number.

497.title: [62] Goat Hill Report, 2025 Regular Session Edition (final)
497.text: Association of County Commissions of Alabama. The county commissions association's end-of-session digest of 2025 Alabama acts affecting counties. It lists Act 2025-366 ('Representation on Local Mental Health Boards', Sen. Barfoot and Rep. Bedsole), requiring a probate judge and a sheriff or representative on the executive committee of any 310 board that has one, and Act 2025-183 ('Renames Drug Courts to Accountability Courts', Sen. Jones), extending those courts to veterans and people needing substance-abuse or mental-health services. Both are shown as effective 1 October 2025. Entries give act numbers and sponsors, not bill numbers; SB101 does not appear.

498.title: [63] SB200, 2025 Regular Session, enrolled (accountability courts)
498.text: Alabama Legislature. Enrolled text of Alabama SB200 (2025), amending Code sections 12-23A-1 to 12-23A-13. It renames 'drug courts' as 'accountability courts' and widens whom they serve to include veterans and offenders whose offence involved mental illness or who need mental health services. Effective 1 October 2025. The register gives no URL for this bill; this is the Legislature's own enrolled PDF. It does not print an act number.

499.title: [64] Gov. Ivey signs bill promoting veteran mental health
499.text: Alabama Public Radio. Short news report that Gov. Kay Ivey signed Senate Bill 40, the Houston Hunter Act, sponsored by Sen. Keith Kelley and Rep. Russell Bedsole and named for veterans Houston Tumlin and Hunter Whitley, who died by suicide. The law promotes voluntary, temporary firearm storage: it establishes firearm hold agreements between individuals and federal firearm licensees and creates the SAFER (Storing Ammunition and Firearms to Enhance Resilience Together) Program. Citing the Governor's office, it says 139 Alabama veterans died by suicide in 2022 and that more than 85 percent of Alabama veteran suicides involve a firearm.

500.title: [65] Suicide Prevention Programs: Program Evaluation
500.text: Alabama Commission on the Evaluation of Services. An evaluation of Alabama's suicide-prevention programs published by the Alabama Commission on the Evaluation of Services in September 2020. It 'looked primarily at the three agencies overseeing various aspects of the suicide prevention framework': the Departments of Mental Health and Public Health and the State Department of Education. A response from the Department of Mental Health is attached from page 37. It is used here only to show that the Commission had evaluated the Department's programs before its 2025 crisis-center report; its findings were not read in detail.

501.title: [66] Code of Alabama, Title 22, Chapter 52, Article 1 (civil commitment): §§22-52-1.2, 22-52-10.1, 22-52-10.3, 22-52-10.4, 22-52-10.5 and 22-52-10.6
501.text: State of Alabama (2025 Code of Alabama, as published by Justia). Six sections of Alabama's civil-commitment law, read in the 2025 edition of the Code. Any individual may petition the probate court of the county where the person is located for another person's involuntary commitment. The judge may order inpatient treatment on clear and convincing evidence that the person has a mental illness, poses a real and present threat of substantial harm to self or others, will continue to deteriorate without treatment and cannot make a rational decision about treatment; the least restrictive alternative necessary and available must be ordered. Inpatient and outpatient orders may not exceed 150 days, and a renewal may not exceed one year. Outpatient treatment may be ordered only if the designated mental health facility has consented. Probate judges must report commitment orders to the state law enforcement agency for firearms background checks.

502.title: [67] Wyatt v. Stickney, 325 F. Supp. 781 (M.D. Ala. 1971)
502.text: U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Alabama (as published by Justia). The first opinion in the class action brought on behalf of patients at Bryce Hospital in Tuscaloosa, decided on 12 March 1971. The court held that people involuntarily committed for treatment 'unquestionably have a constitutional right to receive such individual treatment as will give each of them a realistic opportunity to be cured or to improve his or her mental condition'. It describes Bryce Hospital as part of Alabama's mental health service delivery system. Later orders in the case, including the 1972 standards and the 2003 termination, are not in this document.

503.title: [68] Wyatt v. Stickney
503.text: Encyclopedia of Alabama (a program of Auburn University Outreach). A reference article on the Wyatt litigation. It says the suit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Alabama on 23 October 1970 and that on 12 March 1971 the court ruled that committed patients have a constitutional right to treatment giving them a realistic opportunity to be cured or to improve. It says that on 5 December 2003 Judge Myron Thompson held a fairness hearing and terminated the lawsuit after finding the state had complied with the settlement, more than 33 years after the case began. It is a reference work, not a court document.

504.title: [69] Braggs v. Commissioner, Alabama Department of Corrections, No. 22-10292 (11th Cir.)
504.text: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit (read on Justia and on the court's own PDF).
