Published opinion of the Eleventh Circuit, filed 24 June 2026 (Document 139-1, 73 pages), on Alabama's appeal from the district court's 2017 liability ruling and December 2021 remedial order in the prison mental-health class action (D.C. No. 2:14-cv-00601-MHT-JTA). The court found no factual or legal error in the district court's finding that ADOC was deliberately indifferent to prisoners' serious mental-health needs. Per Justia's summary on the same page, it affirmed most of the system-wide remedial and monitoring orders, reversed provisions on suicide-proofing cells, some staffing requirements and relief as applied to a women's facility, and remanded for modification in those respects. The opinion records about 19,500 prisoners and about 3,400 receiving mental-health treatment when the suit began. Only pp. 1-59 of the opinion text could be read; the disposition wording comes from Justia's summary, not the opinion's own final pages.

505.title: [70] Federal court ruling on Alabama prison mental health care could lower staffing requirements
505.text: Alabama Reflector. Follow-up news report on the 11th Circuit panel decision in Braggs v. Lovelace (formerly Braggs v. Dunn), the class action over mental health care in Alabama prisons. It says the panel 'largely sustained' Judge Myron Thompson's ruling that inadequate mental health care in ADOC is cruel and unusual punishment, but reversed three parts of the remedial order and told the district court to review them: required staffing numbers, suicide-proofing of cells, and the inclusion of Tutwiler Prison for Women. It reports that ADOC has about 1,600 qualifying officers against about 3,600 needed under Thompson's order. The article dates the ruling only as 'Friday' and does not give caseload or prison-population figures.

506.title: [71] Braggs, et al. v. Lovelace, et al. (case page)
506.text: Southern Poverty Law Center. The Southern Poverty Law Center's page for the class action over medical and mental-health care in Alabama prisons, filed on 17 June 2014 in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Alabama. It says the SPLC and the Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program filed the suit. It quotes the June 2017 ruling that 'ADOC's mental-health care is horrendously inadequate'. The page styles the case 'Braggs, et al. v. Lovelace, et al.'; its web address still carries the earlier defendant's name.

507.title: [72] Federal government seeks summary judgment against Alabama Department of Corrections
507.text: Alabama Reflector. News report on a 260-page motion for summary judgment filed by the U.S. Department of Justice in its lawsuit against Alabama over violence in the state's men's prisons. The DOJ sued in December 2020 alleging Eighth Amendment violations; the motion asks U.S. District Judge Harold D. Mooty III to rule for the government on failure to protect prisoners from physical violence, sexual violence and excessive force. The article refers to 'the November trial' coming nearly six years after the suit was filed. It does not discuss the Braggs mental-health case.

508.title: [73] 42 U.S.C. § 300x-3, State mental health planning council
508.text: United States Code (text as published by Cornell Legal Information Institute). The federal law that makes a planning council a condition of the Community Mental Health Services Block Grant. A state taking the grant must "establish and maintain a State mental health planning council". The council reviews the state's block-grant plans and recommends changes, advocates for adults with serious mental illness and children with severe emotional disturbance, and at least once a year monitors, reviews and evaluates the allocation and adequacy of mental health services in the state. Members must include adults who receive or have received mental health services and family members, and at least half must be people who are neither state employees nor providers. It is the general federal rule; it says nothing specific about Alabama's council.

509.title: [74] Section 223 Medicaid CCBHC Demonstration and State Programs
509.text: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA). SAMHSA's page on the federal demonstration under which states pay certified community behavioral health clinics through Medicaid. It names the program the 'Section 223 CCBHC Medicaid Demonstration' and says it began in 2017 with 67 clinics in eight states. The part of the page that could be read did not list the states that joined later or set out the reporting requirements, so it is used here only for the program's name.

510.title: [75] Alabama State Plan Amendment AL-23-0009 (mobile crisis services), approval package
510.text: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. CMS approval letter, CMS-179 form and state plan pages for Alabama Medicaid SPA 23-0009, approved 20 November 2023 with an effective date of 1 October 2023. The amendment allows mobile crisis services to be offered statewide through the Alabama Department of Mental Health, with two-person teams available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week and follow-up for up to 72 hours. It states the section 1947(b) requirements that must be met to claim enhanced federal match (eFMAP), and estimates a federal budget impact of $15 million in each of FFY 2024 and 2025.

511.title: [76] 2025 Annual Report: Alabama Opioid Overdose and Addiction Council
511.text: Alabama Opioid Overdose and Addiction Council (co-chaired by ADMH, ADPH and the Attorney General); posted by ADMH. The Council's annual report to the Governor, dated 31 December 2025 and posted by ADMH in January 2026. It reports that of 12,545 overdose cases seen in emergency departments in 2024, at least 1,151 were confirmed fatal, and it states that Alabama 'documented 1,052 overdose deaths' in 2025, alongside other provisional counts for different periods. On naloxone it gives two different figures: 48,179 boxes distributed by ADMH between 1 November 2024 and 31 October 2025, and 40,733 kits distributed by ADMH in fiscal year 2025. It also covers treatment expansion, medication treatment in jails and prisons, training and prescribing trends. It contains no count of detoxification beds and no statement about Medicaid coverage of medication-assisted treatment.

512.title: [77] Alabama's Leaders Release Plan to Drive Down State Recidivism Rate
512.text: Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles. Bureau news release announcing the Reentry Alabama report of the Alabama Reentry Commission, chaired by Bureau Director Cam Ward. It says the Council of State Governments Justice Center guided the process and gave technical assistance, and that under SJR80 a new Reentry Task Force will take over from the Commission, implement the report and meet quarterly through 2030. Commission members listed include the Bureau, Labor, the community colleges, ALEA, Mental Health, Human Resources, Medicaid, Corrections, Veterans Affairs, Youth Services and the District Attorneys Association. It names the Perry County PREP Center as a success; it does not mention day reporting centers, the CARE Center, Unite Us or a recidivism definition.

513.title: [78] Code of Alabama §12-15-505: State Team established; membership; term; duties; hiring authority (multiple needs children)
513.text: State of Alabama (text as published by Justia). The section of Alabama's juvenile code that sets up a State Team for children with multiple needs. Its members represent the Department of Education, the Department of Human Resources, the Department of Mental Health, the Department of Public Health, the Department of Youth Services and the chief probation officers' association. The team must meet at least monthly, develop interagency plans, set guidelines for allocating resources, advise the county teams created by the same article and report to the Alabama Children's Policy Council. Only the statute was read; it does not show whether the team is active today or how much of its work concerns mental health.

514.title: [79] Code of Alabama §26-24-30: Alabama Children's Policy Council
514.text: State of Alabama (text as published by Justia). The statute creating the Alabama Children's Policy Council. Its members include legislators, the Chief Justice, and the heads of the state's child-serving agencies: the Departments of Human Resources, Early Childhood Education, Mental Health, Youth Services, Education, Public Health and Rehabilitation Services and the Medicaid Agency, along with advocacy groups such as VOICES for Alabama's Children. The Secretary of Early Childhood Education chairs it; it must meet at least once a year and make recommendations to the Governor and Legislature by 1 October. Its remit is children's services in general, not mental health in particular, and only the statute was read.

515.title: [80] Health Provisions in the 2025 Federal Budget Reconciliation Law
515.text: KFF. KFF's section-by-section summary of the health provisions of the federal budget reconciliation law signed on 4 July 2025. On Medicaid expansion its entry for section 71114 reads 'Eliminates the temporary incentive for states that newly adopt the Medicaid expansion', effective 1 January 2026; that incentive was the extra federal match offered under the American Rescue Plan Act. On provider taxes it says section 71115 bars all states from creating new provider taxes or raising existing ones and, for states that have expanded Medicaid, lowers the permitted tax rate by half a point a year from fiscal year 2028 until it reaches 3.5 percent in 2032. Only these two provisions were read.

516.title: [81] Continued Financial Costs of Alabama's Inaction on Medicaid Expansion
516.text: Families USA. A Families USA fact sheet dated March 2026 arguing that Alabama would still gain financially from expanding Medicaid after the 2025 federal budget law (H.R. 1). It says H.R. 1 limits states' ability to raise provider-tax revenue, and that expanding would require Alabama to cut its 6% hospital provider tax to 3.5% by fiscal year 2032, losing $118.33 million in hospital tax revenue in 2032. It notes that federal law now imposes work reporting requirements on expansion populations and estimates 154,800 low-income adults could gain coverage. It does not mention the ALLHealth proposal or the end of the enhanced federal match for newly expanding states.

517.title: [82] Counseling Compact map and news
517.text: Counseling Compact Commission. The Counseling Compact Commission's member map and news feed. Alabama is listed as a member state. The map page's text still says the compact is live for licensees in Arizona, Minnesota and Ohio, but the Commission's news shows privileges being issued since late 2025/January 2026 and, on 1 October 2026, ten states issuing them (Arizona, Minnesota, Ohio, Louisiana, Georgia, Indiana, Arkansas, Wyoming, Tennessee, Oklahoma). Alabama is not among the states issuing or receiving privileges and no Alabama go-live date is given.

518.title: [83] Nurse Licensure Compact
518.text: Alabama Board of Nursing. The Alabama Board of Nursing's page on the Enhanced Nurse Licensure Compact. It says that effective 1 January 2020 applicants who meet the requirements may apply for multistate licensure, and the Board issues multistate RN and LPN licences. The register gives no URL for this item; this is the Board's own page.

519.title: [84] Board Resumes Issuing Letters of Qualification for Interstate Medical Licensure Compact
519.text: Alabama Board of Medical Examiners and Medical Licensure Commission. A short press release from Alabama's medical licensing bodies. It says the Board's status as a State of Principal Licensure under the Interstate Medical Licensure Compact has been reinstated and that it is again issuing Letters of Qualification so that Alabama physicians can obtain licenses in other compact states. It shows that Alabama takes part in the compact. As read, it carries no date and does not say when Alabama joined or when and why its status had been suspended.

520.title: [85] Member States (EMS Compact)
520.text: Interstate Commission for EMS Personnel Practice. The EMS Compact commission's list of member states. Alabama's entry reads 'Enacted 2017'. The page says the compact has been enacted in 28 states and is operational in 27, and that it creates a privilege to practice for EMS clinicians across state lines.

521.title: [86] Before You Apply (Occupational Therapy Compact state table)
521.text: Occupational Therapy Compact Commission. The Occupational Therapy Compact Commission's table of member states, showing for each whether it is accepting applications for compact privileges. Alabama is listed as a member with 'Not Yet' in the accepting-applications column and fees still to be set. Eight states are shown with start dates in 2026 (Indiana, Maryland, Minnesota, Ohio, Tennessee, Virginia, West Virginia, Wisconsin; the first on 12 January 2026). The page says states not listed are not members; it does not give the year Alabama enacted the compact.

522.title: [87] Social Work Compact
522.text: National Center for Interstate Compacts, Council of State Governments. The Council of State Governments' reference page for the Social Work Licensure Compact, which 'allows eligible social workers to practice in all compact member states'. It lists member states with the year each joined; Alabama's entry is 'Alabama (Joined 2024)'. The page listed 33 states when read, so it lags the 35 reported by the compact commission in July 2026, and it says nothing about whether multistate licenses are yet being issued.

523.title: [88] Alabama: State Telehealth Laws and Reimbursement Policies
523.text: Center for Connected Health Policy. The Center for Connected Health Policy's running summary of Alabama telehealth law and Medicaid policy, last updated 29 June 2026. It reports that Alabama Medicaid pays for telemedicine by audio-and-video and by audio-only at parity with face-to-face services, that services can be delivered to a recipient at home, and that Medicaid pays a $20 origination-site facility fee that the home is not entitled to. For private payers it finds no reference to a telehealth definition, service parity or payment parity. It lists federally qualified health centers only as eligible originating sites and says nothing about integrated behavioral health.

524.title: [89] Education Trust Fund Budget Summary (FY 2027 Governor's recommendation handout)
524.text: Alabama Department of Finance, Executive Budget Office. A 15-page Executive Budget Office handout summarising the Governor's recommended FY2027 Education Trust Fund budget. Its columns are FY2026 ETF appropriations, FY2027 agency budget requests, the FY2027 Governor's recommendation, and dollar and percent change. For the Department of Mental Health it shows $84,011,829 appropriated for FY2026, $87,011,829 requested and $84,107,489 recommended (+$95,660, 0.11%), with $5,500,000 for the School Based Mental Health Services Collaboration in all three columns. It is a recommendation published before the Legislature acted, not the enacted appropriation.

525.title: [90] What passed in the Alabama Legislature: April 7-9, 2026
525.text: Alabama Reflector. Weekly roundup of bills passed. Its entry for HB 487 (Rep. Rex Reynolds), listed under Tuesday 7 April in the House, says the bill makes supplemental appropriations of $43.1 million from the Opioid Treatment and Abatement Fund, that the House concurred with Senate changes 104-0, and that it goes to Gov. Kay Ivey. The entry gives no breakdown of the $43.1 million and does not mention the Administrative Office of Courts or specialty courts. (Identified as the register's 'final passage of HB487 (10 April 2026)' item by date; 10 April is the publication date, the vote was 7 April.)

526.title: [91] Oversight Commission on Alabama Opioid Settlement Funds (ADMH presentation)
526.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. A 29-slide presentation by ADMH Commissioner Kimberly Boswell to the Oversight Commission on Alabama Opioid Settlement Funds on 22 October 2025. It sets out the opioid-settlement money appropriated to the Department by year: $8.5 million under Act 2023-384, $20.51 million under Act 2024-426 and $27.86 million under Act 2025-255. The 2025 lines include $8.93 million for prevention, treatment and recovery grants, $5 million for co-occurring civil commitment beds, $5 million for a therapeutic community model project, $3.5 million for the 988 crisis line, $2 million for Medicaid state match, $1.3 million for a statewide marketing campaign, $1 million for residential detox and $1 million for naloxone.

527.title: [92] HB487, 2026 Regular Session, enrolled (supplemental appropriations from the Opioid Treatment and Abatement Fund)
527.text: Alabama Legislature (ALISON). The enrolled text of House Bill 487, which appropriates $43,138,650 from Alabama's Opioid Treatment and Abatement Fund for the fiscal year ending 30 September 2026. The Department of Mental Health receives $26,360,000, including $8,930,000 for prevention, treatment and recovery grants, $7,500,000 for co-occurring civil-commitment beds, $4,000,000 for the 988 Crisis Line, $2,000,000 for Medicaid state match, $1,000,000 for residential detox and $1,000,000 for naloxone. Other lines include $3,000,000 to the Administrative Office of Courts for specialty courts, $2,000,000 to UAB for its psychiatry residency program and $1,500,000 to the Board of Pardons and Paroles. Section 2 moves $5,000,000 that Act 2025-255 gave the Department of Mental Health to the Department of Public Health for a therapeutic-community treatment center. The history page shows the Senate amended and passed the bill on 2 April 2026 and the House concurred on 7 April; the copy read shows no act number or signing date. (Same document as card XA-03.)

528.title: [93] House passes bill to allocate $43.1 million in opioid settlement funds
528.text: Alabama Political Reporter. A news report published 27 February 2026 on the Alabama House's unanimous passage, the day before, of House Bill 487, sponsored by Rep. Rex Reynolds. The bill sets out how $43,138,650 from the state's Opioid Treatment and Abatement Fund would be spent. The article lists the allocations, including $26.36 million to the Department of Mental Health (among them $4 million for the 988 Crisis Line and $7.5 million for co-occurring civil commitment beds), $3 million to the Administrative Office of Courts for specialty courts, $2 million for UAB's psychiatry residency and $1.5 million to the Board of Pardons and Paroles. It describes the bill as it left the House; the Senate had not yet acted.

529.title: [94] House passes $3.74 billion General Fund budget
529.text: Alabama Daily News. News report on the Alabama House's passage of the fiscal year 2027 General Fund budget. It identifies Rep. Rex Reynolds, R-Hazel Green, as chairman of the House General Fund committee. It says the Department of Mental Health will receive approximately $4 million less next year, that the House version gives the Department $325,000 more than the Senate's, and that the budget assigns the departments of corrections, human resources and mental health tasks to complete before they receive all of their 2027 funding. It does not describe those tasks or mention crisis centers.

530.title: [95] Federal Medical Assistance Percentage (FMAP) for Medicaid and Multiplier
530.text: KFF (State Health Facts). A KFF State Health Facts table of each state's standard federal Medicaid matching rate by federal fiscal year, FY2004 to FY2027. Alabama's rate is 72.63% for FY2026 and 72.55% for FY2027. The notes and sources section of the page was not in the text read.

531.title: [96] Medicaid in Alabama (state fact sheet)
531.text: KFF. A two-page KFF fact sheet dated May 2025 summarising Alabama's Medicaid program. It reports 1,097,000 children and adults enrolled, 51% of them children; total spending of $7.9 billion, of which federal funding is 78% ($6.1 billion); expansion status 'Not Adopted'; and 92,000 adults in the coverage gap. It does not discuss mental health services. The data labels of its eligibility chart and the data year of each figure were not in the text read.

532.title: [97] Alabama Section 1115 Institutions for Mental Disease Waiver for Serious Mental Illness (11-W-00371/4): monitoring-redesign overlay letter with special terms and conditions
532.text: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. CMS letter of 25 June 2025 to Alabama Medicaid Commissioner Stephanie Azar updating monitoring arrangements, followed by the demonstration's special terms and conditions (139 pages in all). The terms show approval from 20 May 2022 through 19 May 2027 and authorise federal payment for short-term stays of adults aged 21-64 with serious mental illness in IMDs located in Baldwin and Mobile counties. Enrollees may use those IMDs regardless of county of residence. The state must keep the average length of stay at 30 days or less; individual stays of up to 60 days are payable.

533.title: [98] Alabama Substance Use Disorder Demonstration (Section 1115 demonstration page)
533.text: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Medicaid.gov. Medicaid.gov's listing for Alabama's proposed Section 1115 substance use disorder demonstration. As read on 3 October 2026 the status is 'Pending'; the page links the pending application dated 14 July 2023 and CMS's completeness letter dated 28 July 2023, and shows no approval, effective or expiration date. The page itself carries no description of what the demonstration would cover.

534.title: [99] Alabama state profile
534.text: State Health Access Data Assistance Center (SHADAC), University of Minnesota. SHADAC's at-a-glance health profile for Alabama, based on its analysis of the 2024 American Community Survey public-use microdata. It puts coverage at 50.0% employer-sponsored, 20.8% Medicare, 14.7% Medicaid/CHIP, 6.2% individual market and 8.4% uninsured, alongside measures of cost, access and health outcomes compared with the U.S. It says nothing about Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama or insurer market share.

535.title: [100] Competition in Health Insurance: A Comprehensive Study of U.S. Markets, 2025 Update
535.text: American Medical Association. The American Medical Association's annual study of concentration in commercial health insurance markets, 24th edition, using enrolment data as of 1 January 2024. It lists Alabama first among the states with the least competitive commercial health insurance markets, measured by the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index for PPO, HMO, point-of-service and exchange plans combined. Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama holds 84% of that market and UnitedHealth Group, the second insurer, 6%. The Medicare Advantage tables at the end of the document were not in the text read.

536.title: [101] Alabama: Regulatory enforcement (parity)
536.text: ParityTrack (The Kennedy Forum). ParityTrack's page on enforcement of mental health parity law in Alabama. It states that the state has no published enforcement actions relating to mental health parity, and gives the Alabama Department of Insurance's complaint contacts. The page's metadata shows it was last modified on 5 March 2021, so it is not evidence of a search made in 2026.

537.title: [102] Summary of FY26 LHHS Bill: January 2026
537.text: Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO). An ASTHO legislative alert summarising the FY2026 Labor-HHS appropriations text released by the U.S. House on 20 January 2026 as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026; it was written before the bill became law. For SAMHSA it reports $7.4 billion in total, described as relatively level funding, including $2.8 billion for mental health activities (a $15 million increase) and $2 billion for the substance use block grant, and a direction that SAMHSA consult appropriators before issuing competitive funding announcements. The reorganization provision it quotes requires HHS to submit a plan 60 days before moving functions carried out by the CDC; it does not describe such a requirement for SAMHSA.

538.title: [103] Appropriations Watch: FY 2026
538.text: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. A running tracker of the twelve federal appropriations bills for fiscal year 2026. Its table shows that the Labor-HHS-Education bill passed the House as part of a package on 22 January 2026, passed the Senate 71-29 on 30 January, cleared the House in final form on 3 February and was signed by the President the same day (H.R. 7148). The page gives dates and votes only; it says nothing about SAMHSA's funding or about agency reorganization.

539.title: [104] Governor Ivey Announces Additional Alabama Rural Health Transformation Program Grants Totaling Nearly $55 Million
539.text: Office of the Governor of Alabama. A release of 1 October 2026 announcing 34 grants totaling nearly $55 million, the second round of the Alabama Rural Health Transformation Program for 2026, which it says rounds out the program's first year. The grants are grouped under seven initiatives: maternal and fetal health, EMS trauma and stroke, EMS treat-in-place, simulation training, cancer digital regionalization, rural health and rural workforce. As read, none is described as being for CCBHC certification; South Central Alabama Mental Health Board receives $840,000 for a rural care network in four counties. ADECA administers the program, which is funded from a federal award of about $203.4 million.

540.title: [105] Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics (CCBHCs) Contract Billing Manual, version 2
540.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's billing manual for clinics in the CCBHC Medicaid demonstration, version 2, effective 1 April 2026 (file dated 5 June 2026). It explains that CCBHCs are paid a PPS-1 daily rate: a single payment each day when at least one 'triggering event' service is delivered to a Medicaid enrollee. It then defines each billable service by procedure code. The Mobile Crisis Team definition (code S9485) describes a two-person team available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and allows follow-up interventions for up to 72 hours after the initial response. The text returned for this check stopped at about page 42.

541.title: [106] Postpartum Coverage Extension from 60 Days to 12 Months (provider alert)
541.text: Alabama Medicaid Agency. Alabama Medicaid provider alert of 21 March 2023 announcing that CMS approved extending postpartum coverage for pregnant Medicaid recipients from 60 days to 12 months, with an effective date of 1 October 2022. It explains that after the pandemic continuous-enrollment requirement ends on 31 March 2023, pregnant recipients keep coverage until 12 months after the pregnancy ends. The alert calls the extension a 'pilot program' whose use and maternal health outcomes the Agency plans to evaluate.

542.title: [107] Emergency Numbers for Mental Illness
542.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's list of after-hours emergency telephone numbers for mental illness, read on 3 October 2026. It gives at least one community provider and number for every one of Alabama's 67 counties, naming 25 providers in all: the community mental health centers and, mainly in the Birmingham area, other contracted providers. The page does not itself count the centers or state that they cover the whole state; that follows from the list.

543.title: [108] Mental Illness Community Program Contract Service Delivery Manual, version 05
543.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's manual defining the services it buys from contracted community mental-illness providers, version 05, dated 2 March 2026. Its stated aim is an organized community-based system of care for adults with serious mental illness and children and adolescents with severe emotional disturbance. It defines outpatient, case-management, ACT, day-program, supported-employment and first-episode-psychosis services, and twelve residential and housing categories. The table of contents and pages 1 to 41 were read for this check; the residential definitions themselves (pages 93 onward) were not reached. The title on the cover differs from the name the report's register gives it ('CMHC Contract Service Definitions Manual').

544.title: [109] First Episode of Psychosis Program
544.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's page on its First Episode of Psychosis (FEP) programs, read on 3 October 2026. It says the Department currently operates three sites providing FEP services: NOVA-Birmingham at JBS Mental Health Authority (Jefferson County), NOVA-Mobile at AltaPointe (Mobile County) and NOVA-Huntsville at WellStone (Madison County). It describes a coordinated array of recovery-oriented services for youth and young adults with early psychosis. The phrase 'coordinated specialty care' does not appear on the page.

545.title: [110] 2025 National Guidelines for a Behavioral Health Coordinated System of Crisis Care
545.text: SAMHSA. SAMHSA's 87-page national guidance on how a community behavioral health crisis system should be built, publication PEP24-01-037, updating the 2020 guidelines after the 988 Lifeline launch. It names three essential elements: someone to contact (988 and other lines), someone to respond (mobile crisis teams) and a safe place for help (crisis stabilization services). It then sets out system-building components, including community engagement, technology, financing, data and workforce. It is national guidance and does not assess Alabama.

546.title: [111] Rural Crisis Care and Mobile Crisis Teams
546.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's page on rural crisis care programs and mobile crisis teams. It explains that many people live in rural areas without easy travel to a crisis center or community mental health center, and that in fiscal year 2021 five community mental health centers were funded to start rural crisis programs and mobile crisis teams, with two more funded through FY21 federal ARPA and block-grant awards. It names the centers and the counties they serve, says three centers received state funding for five child and adolescent teams, and notes a CMS mobile-crisis planning grant received with Alabama Medicaid in FY22. It lists the services teams provide but gives no dollar amounts or numbers served.

547.title: [112] Huntsville Police co-responder program paying dividends in helping those in crisis
547.text: City of Huntsville (City Blog). City of Huntsville feature on the police co-responder programme run with WellStone. It says the City Council voted in May 2021 to fund the programme and that two full-time, master's-level mental-health professionals ride with CIT-certified Huntsville Police officers on mental-health calls. It gives anecdotes but no outcome figures, and describes the programme as it stood in early 2022.

548.title: [113] MPD and AltaPointe to strengthen police-mental health collaboration
548.text: Mobile Police Department. Mobile Police Department news item announcing that, using grant funding, it was setting up a pilot co-response team in the Third Precinct with AltaPointe Health, pairing a police officer with a mental-health clinician on crisis calls. Seven officers travelled to Houston for training. It gives no start date, staffing numbers or results.

549.title: [114] Alabama's Sixth Crisis Center Opens – SpectraCare Crisis Care Center in Dothan: Serving 20 Counties across central and southeast Alabama
549.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. An ADMH press release of 10 February 2025 on the opening of the SpectraCare Crisis Center in Dothan, the state's sixth crisis center. It says the center would be operational and open around the clock from 17 February 2025, with 15 temporary observation beds (stays of up to 23 hours) and 12 extended observation beds (one to seven days). Its headline says the center serves 20 counties, but the release does not name them; ADMH's crisis-centers page today lists five counties for the same center.

550.title: [115] Annual Report FY24: Connecting Mind and Wellness
550.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. The Alabama Department of Mental Health's annual report for fiscal year 2024, about 35 pages, posted in May 2025. Its data pages give individuals served by division (mental illness 65,115 adults and 29,796 adolescents; substance use 27,651 adults and 2,739 adolescents), state-facility counts, and revenue of $1,385,827,039. Its articles cover the Taylor Hardin expansion from 140 to 225 beds, the WellStone pediatric crisis unit in Huntsville and the 988 in-state answer rate (82.5 percent in FY24).

551.title: [116] Alabama promised to improve psychiatric care for men charged with crimes. They still wait years
551.text: WSFA (Associated Press wire story). Associated Press report, carried by WSFA on 12 November 2025, on men held in Alabama jails awaiting court-ordered psychiatric care at Taylor Hardin Secure Medical Facility. It says the waitlist had grown to 273 men per an August court filing (from about 60 in 2017), that the average wait was well over a year and more than 30 people had waited over two years. It describes the 2018 consent decree's deadlines (evaluations and reports within 60 days of a court order; transfer to Taylor Hardin within 30 days after), construction to add 80 beds to the 140-bed facility, and Commissioner Boswell's August 2024 statement, as reported by Alabama Reflector, that only about half of technician and nursing positions were filled.

552.title: [117] Children's of Alabama Expands Inpatient Behavioral Health Services
552.text: Children's of Alabama. A Children's of Alabama news release dated 9 January 2025 announcing that its behavioral health center would open 11 additional inpatient beds that month to meet rising need for child and adolescent mental health care. A reprint of the release says the new 11-bed unit mainly serves patients aged 12 to 18 and focuses on dialectical behavioral therapy. Neither the release nor the reprint states the unit's total bed count, a child/adolescent split, or that UAB's child psychiatry division staffs it. Only the opening sentence of the release body was returned from the hospital's own page; the rest was read in the Calhoun Journal reprint.

553.title: [118] Child & Adolescent Psychiatry (division page)
553.text: UAB Heersink School of Medicine, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neurobiology. The UAB Department of Psychiatry's page for its Division of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, directed by James Cullinan, D.O. It lists the division's programs, including 50 inpatient beds for evaluation and treatment (12 child and 38 adolescent), outpatient clinics at UAB and at Children's, and consultation-liaison services to Children's Hospital of Alabama, with which it describes a strong on-site affiliation. It describes a two-year, ACGME-accredited child and adolescent psychiatry residency with 8 residents in total, usually 4 per year. The page is undated and does not say where the 50 beds are, nor mention a January 2025 expansion.

554.title: [119] School-Based Mental Health Collaboration
554.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's web page for the School-Based Mental Health Program, a joint collaboration between ADMH and the Alabama State Department of Education that began in 2010. ADMH links its community mental health providers with local education agencies so that students can receive prevention, early-intervention and treatment services in school. The page says 122 school systems and 19 community mental health centers currently take part, and that ADMH has received funds to start or expand programs every fiscal year since 2018-19 except 2024-25. It gives no funding figure and does not mention the education department's Mental Health Services Coordinators. The page is undated; the partner list it links to was uploaded in December 2023.

555.title: [120] Memo FY25-2050: Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 Mental Health Services Coordinator (MHSC) Application
555.text: Alabama State Department of Education. A one-page memorandum from the State Superintendent to city and county superintendents, dated 9 June 2025, opening applications for FY2026 Mental Health Services Coordinator funding. It states that in the FY2026 Education Trust Fund budget, Act 2025-270, the Legislature appropriated $6,360,000 for local education agencies, charter schools and public independent schools to employ coordinators 'to facilitate and expand the coordination of mental health wellness supports'. Awards are 'approximately $40,000', paid quarterly, with applications due 30 June 2025 and funds available from 1 October 2025. It says nothing about the program's history, how many districts take part, or ADMH's school-based therapists.

556.title: [121] Memo FY22-2100: Mental Health Services Notification and Opt-In (Act 2022-442)
556.text: Alabama State Department of Education. A three-page memorandum from the State Superintendent to local superintendents, dated 9 September 2022 (posted 12 September), explaining Act 2022-442, codified at Code of Alabama 16-22-16.2. The Act requires every local education agency to employ a mental health services coordinator and to adopt a parental opt-in policy with annual written notice to parents, written permission from parents for students under the age of 14 to take part in ongoing counseling or mental health services, and mental-health records kept separately from academic records. 'Mental health services' is defined to include services, treatment, surveys or assessments. The opt-in does not apply where there is an imminent threat to the health of the student or others, or to occasional interventions that are regular duties of counselors; mandatory abuse reporting is unaffected. The memo does not mention grief support.

557.title: [122] Alabama (state suicide prevention profile)
557.text: Suicide Prevention Resource Center. The Suicide Prevention Resource Center's page on suicide prevention in Alabama, read on 3 October 2026. It names the state suicide prevention coordinator as a member of staff of the Alabama Department of Mental Health, lists the Alabama Suicide Prevention and Resources Coalition (ASPARC) as the state coalition, and gives the state plan as the Alabama State Suicide Prevention Plan 2021-2026. It also notes the Alabama Department of Public Health as a federal suicide-prevention grantee. The page carries no date.

558.title: [123] Vital Statistics at a Glance, Alabama 2024
558.text: Alabama Department of Public Health, Center for Health Statistics. A one-page statistical sheet from the Alabama Department of Public Health's Center for Health Statistics, marked 'Revised 04/2026', giving 2024 population estimates and headline vital statistics. In its leading-causes table it records 834 deaths from intentional self-harm (suicide) in 2024, a rate of 16.2 per 100,000 population. It has no text about suicide-prevention planning, the Department of Mental Health, the Alabama Violent Death Reporting System, overdose fatality review or maternal mortality review.

559.title: [124] Health Center Program Uniform Data System (UDS) data overview: Alabama, 2025
559.text: Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA). HRSA's summary of what federally funded health centers in Alabama reported for 2025. It shows 17 Health Center Program awardees serving 316,993 patients, of whom 15,696 (4.95 percent) were mental health patients and 3,037 (0.96 percent) substance use disorder patients. It gives patient counts only: no count of sites offering integrated behavioral health and no visit totals for these services.

560.title: [125] Total Medicaid MCOs (State Health Facts indicator)
560.text: KFF. KFF's state-by-state count of comprehensive Medicaid managed care organizations, with data for 2024. Alabama's entry is 'N/A', which the table defines as a state that had no contracts with comprehensive managed care organizations as of 1 July 2024. Comprehensive plans are defined as those covering all acute, primary and specialty medical services. The indicator says nothing about Alabama's care-coordination networks.

561.title: [126] Alabama Administrative Code rule 560-X-37-.07, Alabama Coordinated Health Network Program (in chapter 560-X-37, Managed Care)
561.text: Alabama Medicaid Agency (Alabama Legislative Services Agency, Administrative Code). Rule .07 of Alabama Medicaid's chapter 560-X-37 (the chapter is titled 'Managed Care'). It makes the Agency responsible for the Alabama Coordinated Health Network, which provides case management programs for care coordination, and states that the ACHN program operates in seven regions (Central, East, Jefferson and Shelby, Northeast, Northwest, Southeast, Southwest). It does not describe Alabama Medicaid as fee-for-service and does not address behavioural-health benefits, rates or provider qualifications. The register gives no URL for this rule; this is the chapter page on the same site.

562.title: [127] Peer Programs
562.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's page for its Office of Peer Programs. It says the Office supports people in recovery 'by training and certifying Peer Support Specialists, helping launch peer-run services, and hosting recovery conferences'. It lists two certifications: Certified Peer Specialist for people in recovery from mental illness (adult, parent and youth) and Certified Recovery Support Specialist for people in recovery from substance use disorders. As read, it does not set out training hours, examinations or other requirements, and it gives no count of certified peers.

563.title: [128] IPS WORKS ALABAMA: The Alabama Department of Mental Health Expands Program to Support Employment for Individuals with Serious Mental Illness
563.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. An ADMH press release dated 25 February 2025 announcing that the Department has expanded its Individual Placement and Support (IPS) supported-employment program for people with serious mental illness. It says IPS began in Alabama in 2014 at three locations (Central Alabama Wellness, AltaPointe Health and Carastar Health) and that the expansion adds Indian Rivers Behavioral Health in Tuscaloosa and JBS Mental Health Authority in Birmingham. It describes a partnership with the Alabama Department of Rehabilitation Services, which helps provide funding and resources such as transportation vouchers, work attire and equipment. The expansion is funded by a five-year SAMHSA grant, 'Transforming Lives through Supported Employment'; no dollar amount or number of people served is given, and the release does not use the phrase 'evidence-based'.

564.title: [129] PIRC (Psychiatric Intake Response Center)
564.text: Children's of Alabama. Children's of Alabama's page for the Psychiatric Intake Response Center, located in the hospital's Emergency Department in Birmingham. It describes PIRC as a free, confidential phone response center that helps adult callers and community providers find the appropriate level of mental health care for a child or teen, staffed by licensed mental health clinicians. It is open 8:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m., seven days a week, at 205-638-PIRC (7472). It gives no inpatient bed figures.

565.title: [130] PATHS (Pediatric Access to Telemental Health Services)
565.text: Children's of Alabama. Children's of Alabama's page for PATHS, a program to increase the capacity of primary care providers in all Alabama communities to diagnose, treat and manage mild to moderate behavioral health conditions in children and adolescents. It offers behavioral-health case consultation by phone (205-638-PATHS, Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.). The page says the project is supported by the federal Health Resources and Services Administration as part of an award totaling $2.09 million, with 20 percent from non-governmental sources. It does not mention the Alabama Department of Mental Health.

566.title: [131] Child & Family Services
566.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's page for its Office of Child & Family Services, read on 3 October 2026; Beverly Johnson is named as Director. It describes the office's program areas: adolescent substance use treatment, autism, child and adolescent mental illness treatment, infant and early childhood programs with early intervention, intensive home-based services, prevention and school-based mental health. It says treatment providers offer a continuum from crisis and outpatient to day and residential care for children with serious emotional disturbance, with one or more of these services in all 67 counties, and that 11 certified providers offer adolescent substance use treatment. It links to a Child & Family Services Resource Directory but gives no date or provider count for it, and it does not say when the office was created.

567.title: [132] 211 Connects Alabama (home page)
567.text: United Ways of Alabama. The home page of Alabama's 211 information and referral service, run by United Ways of Alabama. It says dialing 2-1-1 connects a caller with a trained specialist at any hour who can find services in the caller's community, from food and shelter to job training and senior care, and that the service is free, confidential and statewide. It gives no call volumes.

568.title: [133] QuickFacts: Alabama
568.text: U.S. Census Bureau. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table for Alabama, a living page that pulls headline figures from the Vintage 2025 population estimates and the 2020-2024 American Community Survey five-year file. As read on 3 October 2026 it gives a July 1, 2025 population of 5,193,088; 25.9% Black alone and 6.5% Hispanic or Latino; 87.5% of households with a broadband subscription (2020-2024); 88.6% high-school graduates and 28.4% with a bachelor's degree or higher among people 25 and over; median household income of $63,999 (2024 dollars, 2020-2024); and 15.2% of persons in poverty. It has no rows for rural population, rural counties, child poverty, crisis centers or transit. The companion United States table gives a national median household income of $80,734 and 91.0% broadband.

569.title: [134] Explore Rural Population in Alabama
569.text: America's Health Rankings (United Health Foundation). America's Health Rankings measure page for the share of a state's population living in a rural area, drawn from the Census Bureau's American Community Survey one-year file for 2023 and shown in the 2025 Annual Report edition. Alabama's value is 42.0% against 20.4% for the United States. Eight states have a higher share (Vermont, Maine, West Virginia, Mississippi, Montana, Arkansas, New Hampshire, South Dakota), which makes Alabama ninth highest. The page carries no population total, race or ethnicity figures and nothing about the mental health workforce.

570.title: [135] General Fund: Investments (ADMH presentation to the Joint Legislative General Fund Budget Committee, 17 July 2024)
570.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health, posted by the Legislative Services Agency. A 40-slide deck Commissioner Kimberly Boswell presented to the Joint Legislative General Fund Budget Committee on 17 July 2024, on what earlier appropriations had bought. Its workforce slides say mental health providers needed 4,678 full-time staff to be fully staffed statewide and had 752 vacancies on 30 September 2023, and that the Legislature appropriated $15,000,000 for mental-illness providers and $2,857,142 for substance-use providers for FY2024 as rate increases. It gives the average direct-support-professional wage as $9.91 an hour in FY2022, $14.21 at 30 September 2023 and $15.17 at 31 March 2024, and lists extra shift pay and attendance incentives for state-facility staff. As of 12 July 2024 it shows Taylor Hardin with 51 percent of mental health technician and 48 percent of nursing positions filled, and it reports more than 1,375 officers trained in the 40-hour Crisis Intervention Team course. Read through the fetch tool for its workforce slides (6 to 14, 32 and 36) only; the figure 3,926 does not appear in it.

571.title: [136] State-run psychiatric hospitals in Alabama show progress in staffing amid pay increases
571.text: Alabama Reflector. News report of the ADMH Board of Trustees meeting held in Montgomery on Friday 16 August 2024. It reports that 66 percent of mental health technician and nursing positions at the state's psychiatric hospitals were filled, and that Taylor Hardin was the most understaffed, with 51 percent of technician and 48 percent of nursing positions filled. It quotes Commissioner Kim Boswell as saying average pay rose from $9.91 an hour in 2023 to $15.17 in 2024, which she tied to a rate increase for direct support professionals; ADMH's own slides date the $9.91 figure to fiscal year 2022. This is the report that the Associated Press story of November 2025 relied on for the 'about half' staffing statement.

572.title: [137] Social Work Licensure Compact news
572.text: Social Work Licensure Compact Commission / CSG. The Social Work Licensure Compact's news page. Its July 2026 item says the compact has passed in 35 states (most recently Wisconsin, West Virginia and Alaska), that implementation takes about 18-24 months before social workers can apply for multistate licences, and that the Commission's data system is due for completion in spring 2027. The page does not name Alabama; the member map is an embedded graphic the reader could not open. The Council of State Governments' compact page lists 'Alabama (Joined 2024)'.

573.title: [138] New Psychiatry Residency Coming to UA
573.text: University of Alabama News Center. A University of Alabama news release of 27 February 2025 announcing that the College of Community Health Sciences is launching a newly accredited four-year psychiatry residency. It says the first class is to start in June 2026 and that the program allows for six residents each year. Training sites named are DCH Regional Medical Center and Indian Rivers Behavioral Health in Tuscaloosa, Project Horseshoe Farm in Greensboro and Bradford Health Services in Warrior. Written sixteen months before the start date, it announces a plan and cannot confirm that the residency began.

574.title: [139] NHSC Loan Repayment Program
574.text: Health Resources and Services Administration, National Health Service Corps. The federal program page for National Health Service Corps loan repayment. It says licensed primary care providers who serve in a Health Professional Shortage Area can receive loan repayment, and that licensed behavioral health providers within a mental health shortage area may also qualify. In exchange a clinician must serve at least two years at an NHSC-approved site within a shortage area; awards for non-primary-care participants run up to $55,000 for full-time service. It is a national page and does not list Alabama sites.

575.title: [140] FY26 Budget Presentation (ADMH, 2025 legislative budget hearings)
575.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health, posted by the Legislative Services Agency. A 32-slide deck in which Commissioner Kimberly Boswell presented the Department's fiscal year 2026 budget request to legislators. Its developmental-disabilities slides ask for $10 million to recalibrate residential rates and say that, after a rate increase funded by the Legislature in FY2022, the average direct-support-professional wage rose from $9.91 an hour in FY2022 to $15.17 in March 2024. It adds that Alabama was recognized as one of the states with the largest decrease in staff turnover in 2022–2023 National Core Indicators data, without giving a rate. As read through the fetch tool it has no figure for community-provider staffing or vacancies and none for state-facility staffing. Only its workforce content was read for this check.

576.title: [141] Alabama Teaches Faith Leaders How to Help People Struggling With Addiction
576.text: Governing. Governing feature on Alabama's Faith-Based Support Specialist certification. It says that since 2022 more than 400 faith leaders have been certified through two-day trainings given by the nonprofit Agency for Substance Abuse Prevention (ASAP), using a curriculum based on recovery-support training the Department of Mental Health developed in 2015; ASAP is funded in part by the Department. The training is about substance use and addiction and connects clergy to treatment providers. It does not mention Mental Health First Aid or workplaces.

577.title: [142] Regular Continuing Education Training
577.text: Alabama Peace Officers' Standards and Training Commission. APOSTC's calendar of continuing-education classes approved for credit, shown as a table of date, course, location, registration link and CEU value. On 3 October 2026 it listed six classes; one is a two-day 'Crisis Intervention Team Training' at the Cherokee County Sheriff's Office training center in Leesburg on 23-24 September 2024, worth 16 CEU, and another is a 4-CEU 'Autism & I/DD Training' on 4 November 2026. The page does not state the annual continuing-education requirement or any mandated subject.

578.title: [143] APOSTC Administrative Code (All Rules, August 2025); Chapter 650-X-12 Continuing Education Requirements
578.text: Alabama Peace Officers' Standards and Training Commission. APOSTC's rule book. The fetch layer truncated the August 2025 consolidated PDF before the text of Chapter 12, so that chapter was read from the separate Chapter 12 PDF linked on the same rule-book page (rules last amended effective 21 October 2017). It requires certified officers to complete and report 12 hours of continuing education a year (20 for police chiefs) and to pass a firearms course annually; no mental-health subject is named. Rule 650-X-3-.02 lists the basic-academy course of study only as thirteen broad subject headings without hours. The 560-hour basic curriculum itself is a scanned PDF that could not be read.

579.title: [144] CIT (Crisis Intervention Team) Division pages
579.text: NAMI Alabama. NAMI Alabama's landing page for its CIT Division, with menu links to training, regional hubs, the IACP One Mind Campaign, the strategic plan and contacts. The landing and contacts pages give no names, no list of regions and no count of officers trained; a sub-page (published July 2024) names John Hollingsworth as NAMI Alabama CIT Director, who took the Alabama Statewide CIT Administrative Coordinator post in March 2022. The strategic-plan sub-page links only the 2024-2026 plan.

580.title: [145] NAMI AL CIT Division Strategic Plan 2024-2026
580.text: NAMI Alabama. The CIT Division's three-year plan, dated 1 January 2024. It lists five current collaborative regional programs, each pairing a mental-health provider, a law-enforcement agency and a NAMI affiliate (Huntsville, Jefferson County, Tuscaloosa, Opelika, Mobile/Baldwin), with Montgomery, VA Birmingham and Probation and Parole under development. It divides the Division's regional coordinator unit into six regions matching ADMH crisis-center boundaries, promotes the IACP One Mind Campaign (100 percent of sworn personnel trained in crisis response, at least 20 percent in CIT) and seeks APOST credit for all CIT training. It gives no count of officers trained and does not state how the Division is funded.

581.title: [146] Human Resources Management
581.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's page for its human resources office, which works through personnel offices at the three state facilities in Tuscaloosa and a central office in Montgomery. It says the Department may have positions available across the state and points job seekers to its 'Careers that Count' page for 'a list of current job announcements, information on how to apply, and our application for employment'. It covers the Department's own jobs, not those of community mental health centers.

582.title: [147] Bryce Hospital
582.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's page for Bryce Hospital, read on 3 October 2026. It says Bryce provides inpatient psychiatric services for adults throughout the state and gives its address as 1651 Ruby Tyler Parkway, Tuscaloosa. It says patient care has been in the current building since 2014 and that the original building and its campus now belong to the University of Alabama. It gives no bed count.

583.title: [148] Alabama Department of Corrections: 'Reasonable concern' $1.25 billion prison will be delayed
583.text: Alabama Reflector. News report on an Alabama Department of Corrections statement of Tuesday 28 July 2026 that there is a 'reasonable concern' the opening of the 4,000-bed men's prison in Elmore County, the $1.25 billion Gov. Kay Ivey Correctional Complex, could be delayed. The contractor, Caddell, may not meet an Oct. 15 deadline to complete the work; the opening had already slipped from May to October 2026. The prison is to include a medical and mental health area with 720 beds. No new completion date is given.

584.title: [149] Alabama Community Services Information System (ACSIS)
584.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's provider-portal page for ACSIS, read on 3 October 2026. It has no descriptive text: it is a set of links to data-submission guidelines, file-format specifications (client profile, services in 837P format, staff, episode and agency files), data dictionaries, code tables and monthly community reports on mental-illness clients served. One code table is a CCBHC activity and procedure code crosswalk dated 18 September 2026. ASAIS, the substance-use system, appears only as a separate link in the site menu under substance use disorders. The register gave no URL for this source; this is the page found on ADMH's site.

585.title: [150] Alabama Substance Abuse Information System (ASAIS)
585.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's provider-portal page for ASAIS, the information system used by substance use providers, read on 3 October 2026. It has no descriptive text. It links to clinical file-upload implementation guides, submission guides, user guides for treatment, administration and billing, an 837P companion guide for claims, training videos and an end-user manual. That the system carries treatment and billing data is inferred from those documents, not stated on the page.

586.title: [151] Alabama One Health Record® Announces Intention To Participate in eHealth Exchange's QHIN
586.text: eHealth Exchange. A press release from eHealth Exchange, datelined Vienna, Virginia, 26 April 2023. It says Alabama One Health Record plans to participate in eHealth Exchange's planned Qualified Health Information Network (QHIN) if that network achieves QHIN designation under the federal TEFCA framework. At that date eHealth Exchange was one of six candidate QHINs, not a designated one. The release quotes Gary D. Parker, Alabama Medicaid chief data officer and director of One Health Record. It announces an intention, not a completed joining, and gives no go-live date or connection counts.

587.title: [152] Fact Sheet 42 CFR Part 2 Final Rule
587.text: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. The federal health department's fact sheet on its February 2024 final rule revising 42 CFR Part 2, the confidentiality rules for substance use disorder treatment records. It explains that the rule brings Part 2 closer to HIPAA: a patient may now give a single consent for all future uses and disclosures for treatment, payment and health care operations. Records still cannot be used to investigate or prosecute the patient without written consent or a court order. Those subject to the rule had to comply by 16 February 2026.

588.title: [153] Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics (CCBHCs) Quality Reporting Manual, version 3
588.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. The Department's manual on quality measurement for Alabama's CCBHCs; the version table shows version 1 on 20 October 2025, version 2 on 1 April 2026 and version 3 on 1 July 2026. It requires each clinic to keep an annual clinic-wide continuous quality improvement plan, sets five clinic-collected and twelve state-collected measures (among them seven-day follow-up after hospitalization for mental illness), and describes Netsmart's population-health platform for the data. It says the Department "will also develop an annual CCBHC Quality Report"; it does not say that results are published.

589.title: [154] Implementation of the National Suicide Hotline Act of 2018 (Fourth Report and Order, FCC 25-42), final rule
589.text: Federal Communications Commission, in the Federal Register (90 FR 44564, document 2025-17895). The Federal Register publication, on 16 September 2025, of an FCC final rule adopted on 24 July 2025 (WC Docket 18-336). It requires covered text providers to send georouting data with text messages to 988 so the Lifeline can route each text to the appropriate crisis center based on the texter's general location rather than the phone's area code. The rule took effect on 16 October 2025; nationwide wireless providers must comply within 18 months of that date and all other covered text providers within 36 months. It does not mention 988 chat or any individual state. The register lists only the NAMI page as a URL; the rule itself was found at federalregister.gov and govinfo.gov.

590.title: [155] FCC Georouting Rule Improves 988 Crisis Text Routing (NAMI statement, reposted)
590.text: NAMI Oregon (reposting a National Alliance on Mental Illness statement of 31 July 2025). NAMI Oregon's repost, dated 5 August 2025, of a national NAMI statement welcoming the FCC's 24 July 2025 vote to require wireless carriers to georoute texts sent to the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. It says nationwide carriers must georoute text messages within 18 months and smaller regional carriers have up to 36 months, and describes georouting as connecting a person to the nearest 988 call center without disclosing exact location. It gives no effective date and does not mention Alabama or 988 chat.

591.title: [156] Governor Ivey Announces Approval of Final BEAD Broadband Proposal, Awards $460 Million to Expand Access to High-Speed Internet
591.text: Office of the Governor of Alabama. A press release from Governor Kay Ivey's office dated Monday 23 March 2026. It announces that the federal NTIA approved Alabama's final Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment (BEAD) proposal and that the Governor awarded grants totaling nearly $460 million for 63 projects to reach approximately 92,000 currently unserved locations. It says 71 percent of the projects will use fiber, 24 percent low-Earth-orbit satellite and 5 percent hybrid fiber-coaxial technology, and that more than $800 million of Alabama's original $1.4 billion allocation is being saved. It gives no household broadband-subscription rates and does not mention the Black Belt.

592.title: [157] Alabama Administrative Code rule 580-2-9-.26, Indigent Drug Program
592.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health (Alabama Administrative Code, via the Legislature). The Department of Mental Health's rule on its Indigent Drug Program, part of the chapter on mental illness community programs, filed 14 June 2010 and effective 19 July 2010. A consumer in the program must be an active consumer of a community mental health center, under a physician's care and with a psychiatric diagnosis. Prescriptions filled with drugs furnished by the State of Alabama must be filled within the center or its satellites. Consumers who qualify for Medicaid, insurance or 'compassionate need programs' are not given drugs available through those sources. The rule gives no budget figure or number of people served.

593.title: [158] Alabama State Plan Amendment AL-21-0006 (medication-assisted treatment), approval package
593.text: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. The federal approval, dated 13 September 2021, of Alabama's Medicaid state plan amendment adding medication-assisted treatment for opioid use disorder as a mandatory benefit under the SUPPORT Act. The plan page says the treatment is covered for all Medicaid beneficiaries who meet medical-necessity criteria and assures coverage of naltrexone, buprenorphine and methadone in all their forms. It took effect on 1 October 2020 and, as written, ran to 30 September 2025; a later amendment (AL-25-0015) removed that end date.

594.title: [159] Alabama State Plan Amendment AL-25-0015 (medication-assisted treatment: expiration date removed)
594.text: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Medicaid.gov's entry for Alabama state plan amendment AL-25-0015, approved 6 February 2026 and effective 1 October 2025. Its summary says the amendment removes the expiration date for the medication-assisted treatment benefit for opioid use disorder. In plain terms, the benefit first added in 2020 continues without an end date. The entry gives no detail on drugs or providers.

595.title: [160] Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP)
595.text: Alabama Department of Public Health. The Department of Public Health's page for Alabama's Prescription Drug Monitoring Program, housed in the ADPH Pharmacy Division. It describes the program as set up to detect diversion, abuse and misuse of controlled-substance prescriptions under Code of Alabama 1975, section 20-2-210 and following. Anyone who dispenses Class II to V controlled substances must report dispensing to the database daily. The database is a source of information for practitioners and pharmacists about a patient's controlled-substance use.

596.title: [161] Prescriptive Authority for Psychologists: What Patients and Policymakers Need to Know
596.text: Association of State and Provincial Psychology Boards. An article from the association of psychology licensing boards, dated 31 July 2026, built around an interview with a prescribing psychologist. It says prescriptive authority for psychologists has passed into law in nine jurisdictions, with Hawaii the latest to join Colorado, Idaho, Illinois, Iowa, Louisiana, New Mexico, Utah and Vermont. Alabama is not among those listed. The article is an overview, not a legal survey of every state's code.

597.title: [162] Non-Emergency Transportation (NET) Program
597.text: Alabama Medicaid Agency. The Alabama Medicaid Agency's page on its Non-Emergency Transportation program, last revised 31 July 2023. It says the Agency's program helps eligible recipients pay for rides to doctors' and dental offices, hospitals and other medical facilities, and gives a toll-free number for the program. It does not mention a broker or contractor and does not describe how payment works.

598.title: [163] Alabama Digital Expansion Division (broadband)
598.text: Alabama Department of Economic and Community Affairs (ADECA). ADECA's broadband page, read on 3 October 2026. It describes the Alabama Digital Expansion Division, the part of ADECA charged with developing and carrying out a statewide connectivity plan. It links to the Be Linked Alabama mapping site, the Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment (BEAD) program, the middle-mile and Capital Projects Fund programs, lists of awarded projects, and plans and reports.

599.title: [164] Governor Kay Ivey Announces First Grants in Major New Rural Healthcare Program Totaling More than $144 Million
599.text: Alabama Department of Economic and Community Affairs (ADECA). A release dated 24 August 2026 announcing 138 grants worth more than $144 million to healthcare providers and institutions across the state, the first under the Alabama Rural Health Transformation Program. It says ADECA administers the program, which has 11 initiatives. The projects are paid for entirely from a federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services award of about $203.4 million.

600.title: [165] 2022 Uniform Reporting System (URS) Output Tables: Alabama
600.text: SAMHSA. SAMHSA's Uniform Reporting System tables for Alabama for 1 October 2021 to 30 September 2022. Only two rows were read for this check. The employment table gives two rates for adults: 45.5% employed as a share of those in the labor force (U.S. 51.2%) and 20.5% employed as a share of all adults with known employment status (U.S. 27.2%). The demographic table shows 37.3% of people served in Alabama were Black, against 17.4% nationally. The exact publication date was not read.

601.title: [166] 2023 Uniform Reporting System (URS) Output Tables: Alabama
601.text: SAMHSA. SAMHSA's Uniform Reporting System tables for Alabama for 1 October 2022 to 30 September 2023. Only a few rows were read for this check. The demographic table shows 36.8% of people served in Alabama were Black, against 17.3% nationally. Adult employment was 47.1% of those in the labor force and 21.9% of all adults with known employment status. The penetration rate was 18.17 per 1,000 residents (U.S. 24.50). The exact publication date was not read.

602.title: [167] Violent Death Reporting System (AVDRS)
602.text: Alabama Department of Public Health, Fatality Review. The Alabama Department of Public Health's page for the Alabama Violent Death Reporting System. It describes AVDRS as a statewide surveillance program established under a CDC grant in 2016, which uses vital statistics, law-enforcement and coroner or medical-examiner reports to record, analyze and link homicides, suicides and certain undetermined deaths across all age groups. The page sits under the Department's Fatality Review branch. It does not mention overdose deaths or an overdose fatality review.

603.title: [168] CDC-RFA-CE-23-0002 Alabama's Overdose Data to Action-State Program (award NU17CE010196)
603.text: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, TAGGS (Tracking Accountability in Government Grants System). The federal grants-tracking record for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Overdose Data to Action in States award to Alabama's state health department. The award is titled "Alabama's Overdose Data to Action-State Program", runs from 1 September 2023 to 31 August 2028, and shows $14,664,125 in funding as read. The recipient name came through the reading tool as "Alabama Department of Health".

604.title: [169] Overdose Data to Action in States
604.text: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. CDC's page for its Overdose Data to Action in States cooperative agreement. It says the agreement "funds 49 state health departments and the District of Columbia to expand drug overdose surveillance and prevention efforts", and lists surveillance infrastructure, morbidity surveillance and mortality surveillance among the required strategies. As read, the page does not list the funded states by name and does not mention the SUDORS system.

605.title: [170] Alabama Maternal Mortality Review Program
605.text: Alabama Department of Public Health, State Perinatal Program. The Alabama Department of Public Health's web page for the Maternal Mortality Review Committee, last updated 30 July 2026. Its snapshot covers deaths in 2020 and 2021: of 137 deaths reviewed, 50 were pregnancy-related; 78 percent of those were judged preventable; and the pregnancy-related mortality rate was 77.0 for Black non-Hispanic women against 28.2 for White non-Hispanic women (the page gives no unit). The leading causes listed are infection, hemorrhage and cardiomyopathy, with 28 percent due to COVID-19; the page text says nothing about mental health or substance use. It links a one-page sheet of 2022 key findings, which reports 17 pregnancy-related deaths, 82.4 percent preventable, and lists mental health conditions among the leading causes (11.8 percent).

606.title: [171] Alabama Quietly Returns CDC Funds to Administer Youth Risk Behavior Survey
606.text: Alabama Campaign for Adolescent Sexual Health. A short article published on 8 November 2023 by the Alabama Campaign for Adolescent Sexual Health, an advocacy group. It reports that Alabama has returned funding to the CDC for the biennial Youth Risk Behavior Survey, which the State Department of Education had applied for and administered. It says the survey of high-school students was last conducted in Alabama in 2021. It gives no amount, no official reason, and does not say which agency returned the money or whether the state will take part in later cycles.

607.title: [172] Alabama Kids Count (Alabama Kids Count Data Book page)
607.text: VOICES for Alabama's Children. VOICES for Alabama's Children's own page for the Alabama Kids Count Data Book, read on 3 October 2026. It announces the 32nd edition of the Data Book as "now fully digital" and says a digital platform lets VOICES share insights more often. It says this edition examines child well-being "through the lens of mental health" and offers data profiles for the state and each of the 67 counties. It links to the Alabama Kids Count Data Center on the same site and to the national KIDS COUNT Data Center.

608.title: [173] Alabama Kids Count Data Center
608.text: VOICES for Alabama's Children. The landing page of VOICES for Alabama's Children's online data center, read on 3 October 2026. It describes the "all-new Alabama Kids Count Data Center" as putting child well-being data "at your fingertips" through interactive dashboards with state and local trends. As read, the page text does not list the indicator categories, the number of indicators or a launch date.

609.title: [174] Child advocacy group launches 'living resource' for childhood well-being data
609.text: Alabama Reflector. A news report of 27 August 2026 that VOICES for Alabama's Children is moving its annual Kids Count research project to an online dashboard that can be updated as new data arrive, a "living resource". It says the Alabama Kids Count Data Book is typically released in January and includes 73 indicators of child well-being, ranging from mental health, the group's focus this year, to education, economic security and safety. It is not one of the fifteen Reflector articles in the report's source register, but appears to be the article the report meant when it cited the Reflector for this sentence.

610.title: [175] What State-Level Data is Available for the 988 Crisis Line?
610.text: Georgetown University Center for Children and Families. A September 2024 review of what 988 data states post for themselves. The author reviewed the websites of all 50 states, the District of Columbia and the territories and found that ten had a 988 data dashboard, with another six posting some other kind of state-level 988 performance review. Six states (Colorado, Georgia, Louisiana, South Dakota, Wisconsin and Wyoming) posted demographic detail. Alabama is not named among the states with a dashboard. The count is of 988 dashboards, not of wider crisis-system dashboards, and is two years old.

611.title: [176] Incident Management Plan Part B (Mental Health and Substance Use Services)
611.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health, Division of Mental Health and Substance Use Services. The Department's incident-management plan for certified community providers of mental health and substance use services. It defines a critical incident as a severe event that warrants immediate action and must be reported within 24 hours, through the Therap system. It says the Office of Quality Improvement and Risk Management compiles periodic reports of all reported incidents for the Department's senior staff and reports quarterly to the Performance Improvement Committee on all incidents and critical incidents. The cover reads "Revised: June 2024" although the file name says June 2025.

612.title: [177] Alabama Administrative Code chapter 580-2-20, Program Operation (rules 580-2-20-.06 Incident Management and 580-2-20-.07 Performance Improvement)
612.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health (Alabama Administrative Code, Legislative Services Agency). The Department of Mental Health's certification rules for community mental health and substance use providers. Rule 580-2-20-.07 says each provider "shall operate and maintain a Performance Improvement (PI) System" to identify and assess important processes and outcomes and to correct identified problems; it covers quality improvement, incident prevention and management, utilization review, recipient and family satisfaction, review of treatment plans, and seclusion and restraint. Rule 580-2-20-.06 requires each provider to follow the Department's published Incident Management Plan. Only these two rules were read.

613.title: [178] Alabama Commission on the Evaluation of Services (ACES) website
613.text: Alabama Commission on the Evaluation of Services. The home page of ACES, read on 3 October 2026. It says the Commission "was established in 2019 to advise the Governor and the Legislature" on the evaluation of services. The reports shown on the page include the preliminary evaluation of the ADMH crisis centers (4 September 2025); no later, final crisis-center evaluation is listed. The full list of publications is at evidence.alabama.gov/publications/, which was not read.

614.title: [179] What is the poverty rate in Alabama?
614.text: USAFacts. A USAFacts explainer page built on the Census Bureau's American Community Survey. It says 15.2% of Alabama's population, 760,634 people, were in poverty in 2024, the lowest rate in ACS data going back to 2010, and that poverty among children under 18 fell from 27.7% in 2014 to 20.2% in 2024. It also gives rates for working-age and older adults and by race and ethnicity. It does not give median household income, and it shows no 2025 data.

615.title: [180] Our Government
615.text: Poarch Band of Creek Indians (Poarch Creek Indians). The Poarch Creek Indians' own page on their tribal government, read on 3 October 2026. It says the Poarch Creek Indians are the only federally recognized Indian Tribe in the state of Alabama and operate as a sovereign nation with their own system of government and bylaws. It includes a short description of the Tribe's Health Department, which it says focuses on prevention and wellbeing through medical and educational programs. The page does not name the reservation's location.

616.title: [181] PCI Health Department website (home, On-Site Specialty Services and Contact Us pages)
616.text: Poarch Band of Creek Indians Health Department. The website of the Poarch Creek Indians' Health Department, read on 3 October 2026. The home page describes the Buford L. Rolin Health Clinic as a 68,430-square-foot full-service outpatient clinic owned and operated by the Tribe and partly funded through the Indian Health Service. The specialty-services page describes a Behavioral Health Department offering counseling, psychological testing and psychiatric services, some by referral only, including substance-abuse assessment and counseling. The contact page gives the address as 429 Buford L. Rolin Drive, Atmore, AL 36502. The site does not mention the Alabama Department of Mental Health.

617.title: [182] FAQ: How many veterans live in Alabama?
617.text: Alabama Department of Veterans Affairs. A one-line FAQ answer on the state Veterans Affairs site: the National Center for Veterans Analysis and Statistics estimates 377,310 veterans living in Alabama. No year is given, and the page says nothing about VA facilities, suicide or state programmes.

618.title: [183] Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics: Veterans and Members of the Armed Forces (Alabama technical-assistance deck)
618.text: Health Management Associates for the Alabama Department of Mental Health. A 2024 training deck prepared for Alabama's CCBHC programme on serving veterans. It says 303,619 veterans lived in Alabama in 2022 (7.7 percent of the population) and lists VA sites serving the state: four medical centers (Birmingham, Tuskegee, Montgomery, Tuscaloosa), two outpatient clinics (Dothan, Selma), seventeen community-based outpatient clinics (three of them in Georgia) and four Vet Centers (Hoover, Huntsville, Montgomery, Mobile).
