It has no Alabama veteran-suicide figures and does not mention the Houston Hunter Act, the $12 million plan, the Veterans Crisis Line or the Veterans Resource Center.

619.title: [184] The Alabama Community Health Resource Guide
619.text: Alabama Office of Primary Care and Rural Health (Alabama Department of Public Health) and Alabama Rural Health Association. A guide to rural community health resources published in October 2007 by the state's Office of Primary Care and Rural Health and the Alabama Rural Health Association. It states that the Office regards 55 of Alabama's 67 counties as rural and the other 12 as urban. It also says that 54 of the 55 rural counties were then short of primary-care physicians and that most rural counties had only a visiting psychiatrist for a few hours a week. It is cited here only for who classes the 55 counties as rural; its other figures are too old to describe the present.

620.title: [185] Deaf Services
620.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. The Alabama Department of Mental Health's page for its Office of Deaf Services, read on 3 October 2026. It says the Department set up the Office to better serve deaf and hard-of-hearing Alabamians through a network of regionally based staff, with clinicians and communication-access team members working out of regional offices and coordinators based in community mental health centers as the first point of contact. It mentions group homes for deaf residents in Birmingham, Mobile and near Huntsville, names the Office's director, and links to the Signs of Mental Health newsletter and to training for qualified mental health interpreters. It does not print a regional staff directory.

621.title: [186] The Alabama Department of Mental Health: 2025 Year in Review
621.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. An undated ADMH web article reviewing calendar 2025. It notes the opening of the SpectraCare crisis center in Dothan as the state's sixth, the state's first veterans mental-health plan and the Legislature's approval of $12 million for it (including a Veterans Resource Center set to open in early 2026), the Houston/Hunter Act creating the SAFER Together voluntary firearm storage program, 40,053 contacts to 988 in FY 2025, and 47,325 naloxone kits distributed in 2025. It gives no crisis-center evaluation counts, no veteran-suicide statistics and no counts of VA facilities or veterans.

622.title: [187] Gov. Ivey attends Alabama Veterans Resource Center grand opening
622.text: Alabama Political Reporter. A three-paragraph news item published 19 February 2026 (the same article as S84i). It says Governor Kay Ivey took part the day before in the grand opening of the Alabama Veterans Resource Center, a public-private partnership and statewide hub for veterans and their families, established during the 2025 legislative session. It does not name the city, the bill number or any mental health service. The address printed in the register is missing a hyphen and returns a not-found page; the working address is the one given here.

623.title: [188] Gov. Ivey signs bill to establish Alabama Veterans Resource Center
623.text: Alabama Political Reporter. A news item published 28 February 2025 reporting that Governor Kay Ivey had signed Senate Bill 70 the day before. The bill creates the Alabama Veterans Resource Center as a public corporation governed by an 11-member board. The center is tasked with offering help with benefits, employment support and mental health resources to the state's veterans. The article does not say where the center will be or when it will open.

624.title: [189] New Alabama Veterans Resource Center comes to downtown Montgomery
624.text: WAKA Action 8 News. A local television news report of 18 February 2026 (updated the next day) on the grand opening that afternoon of the Alabama Veterans Resource Center at 100 Dexter Avenue in downtown Montgomery. A speaker describes it as a one-stop shop for veterans and their families, with help on disability claims, benefits, homelessness and jobs. The report does not mention mental health services or the bill that created the center.

625.title: [190] Fox Army Health Center: Behavioral Health Department
625.text: Fox Army Health Center, Redstone Arsenal (Defense Health Agency, TRICARE site). The Behavioral Health Department page of Fox Army Health Center at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, read on 3 October 2026. It gives the department's mission as meeting the mental health needs of active-duty personnel, their family members, retirees and their families, commanders and entitled civilian employees. Services, all outpatient, include psychotherapy, medication management, groups and classes, and neuropsychological and command evaluations. The address is 4100 Goss Road, Redstone Arsenal.

626.title: [191] Medicaid Postpartum Coverage Extension Tracker
626.text: KFF. KFF's tracker of state action to extend Medicaid postpartum coverage from 60 days to 12 months, as of 15 July 2026. It explains that the option was created by the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 and made permanent by the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023. Its table lists Alabama as '12-month extension implemented' with no limits on the coverage period, population or benefits, and notes that CMS approved Alabama's state plan amendment on 13 January 2023. All 50 states and the District of Columbia are shown as having implemented the extension. Read in a browser because the table did not come through the fetch tool.

627.title: [192] Infant and Early Childhood Special Programs
627.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's page on its infant and early childhood programs, read on 3 October 2026. It describes infant and early childhood mental health consultation, delivered since 2020 by licensed therapists placed with families and with adults who work with young children in childcare, preschool and pediatric primary care. It describes PATHS, funded by a HRSA grant since October 2018 with Children's of Alabama, which gives primary care providers behavioral health case consultation, training and telemedicine. It describes PPEER, funded by a SAMHSA grant from October 2024 to September 2028, serving children from birth to 12 at risk for or engaged with child protective services in Jefferson, Jackson and Mobile counties. The page says nothing about perinatal or postpartum care or Medicaid.

628.title: [193] Alabama Chapter of Postpartum Support International
628.text: Postpartum Support International. The register gives no URL for this source; the page read is the Alabama chapter page on Postpartum Support International's chapters site. The chapter's stated aim is to increase awareness, education, prevention and treatment of perinatal mental health issues across Alabama. The page points to PSI's national HelpLine (1-800-944-4773, call or text), the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline, and PSI's national online provider directory, along with online support groups, peer mentors, awareness walks and training scholarships. It does not mention Alabama Medicaid's postpartum coverage or the Department of Mental Health.

629.title: [194] Alabama Administrative Code rule 580-2-20-.09, General Clinical Practice
629.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health (Alabama Administrative Code, Legislative Services Agency). A rule in the Department of Mental Health's chapter on program operation for mental health and substance use services, published 31 January 2023 and effective 17 March 2023. Paragraph (8) requires that free language assistance be offered to recipients with limited English proficiency or who are deaf, by qualified interpreters, with preference for Qualified Mental Health Interpreters. It allows telephone or video remote interpreting for spoken languages, bars the use of people under 18 as interpreters, and requires treatment to be offered by staff fluent in the recipient's language or through qualified interpreters. Only the language-assistance provisions were read for this check.

630.title: [195] Tribal Health Improvement Plan 2015-2020
630.text: Poarch Band of Creek Indians, Health and Elder Services Division. The Poarch Band of Creek Indians' Tribal Health Improvement Plan for 2015-2020, written after a 2016 community health assessment under a CDC grant. It names diabetes, obesity and hypertension as the top three concerns and says the steering committee left out drug abuse, which the grant did not address. Behavioral health appears as one of the services of the tribal clinic, and 'offer more emphasis on mental health awareness' is one of a numbered list of tribal recommendations. It does not mention the Alabama Department of Mental Health. No later plan was found on the Tribe's site.

631.title: [196] The Magic City Acceptance Center (home page)
631.text: Magic City Acceptance Center, a program of Birmingham AIDS Outreach. The home page of the Magic City Acceptance Center in Birmingham, read on 3 October 2026. It describes the center as an inclusive space for the LGBTQ community in Alabama that provides social and supportive programming and supports people across the state, and as a program of the nonprofit Birmingham AIDS Outreach. Its programs page refers to case management and supportive services. Neither page, as read, describes counseling or mental health treatment.

632.title: [197] NAMI Alabama Affiliates
632.text: NAMI Alabama. NAMI Alabama's list of local affiliates. On 3 October 2026 it named eleven: Baldwin County, Birmingham, Centre, East Alabama, Madison County, Mobile, Montgomery, Shelby County, Shoals, Tuscaloosa and Wiregrass, the last marked 'in progress'. The page refers to NAMI support groups and Family-to-Family and Peer-to-Peer classes but does not state a total or describe each affiliate's programmes.

633.title: [198] The State of Mental Health in America: Data & rankings (2025 web tables: Ranking the States, Adult, Youth, Prevalence, Access to Care)
633.text: Mental Health America. The web version of Mental Health America's 2025 state rankings, with the same tables as the printed report on separate pages for the overall, adult, youth, prevalence and access-to-care rankings. Read on 3 October 2026 the pages still showed the 2025 edition. The Alabama rows match the printed report. The access-to-care page prints the national rate of students with an emotional-disturbance IEP as 6.63 per 1,000 students.

634.title: [199] NAMI Alabama website: Support & Education and Advocate pages
634.text: NAMI Alabama. NAMI Alabama's own pages on its programs. The Support & Education page says it offers classes for individuals, families and friends of people with mental health conditions (NAMI Basics, Family-to-Family and Peer-to-Peer) and two kinds of free, confidential support group (NAMI Connection and NAMI Family Support Group). The Advocate page (namialabama.org/get-involved/advocate/) explains why public policy matters and links to national NAMI's policy platform; it sets out no state legislative agenda and mentions no advocacy day. The site also has an events calendar. No count of people trained or served appears on the pages read.

635.title: [200] Alabama Suicide Prevention and Resources Coalition (home and About pages)
635.text: Alabama Suicide Prevention and Resources Coalition (ASPARC). The coalition's own website. The home page says ASPARC is a nonprofit established to help prevent suicide in Alabama through education, advocacy and awareness, and that it was originally a task force of people chosen to help the Alabama Department of Public Health with suicide-prevention strategy. The About page (asparc.org/about) says it trains people in suicide prevention and response, offers packaged courses, and keeps a database of suicide-prevention resources; the site promotes free QPR training. Neither page mentions the Alabama Department of Mental Health or the state suicide-prevention plan, and neither gives a founding year.

636.title: [201] About: Alabama Council for Behavioral Healthcare
636.text: Alabama Council for Behavioral Healthcare (Alabama Council of Community Mental Health Boards). The Council's own About page. It says the Alabama Council of Community Mental Health Boards was incorporated in 1972 and represents its members in planning and developing public mental health care, acting as a liaison between its members, the Department of Mental Health, the Legislature and the federal government. It counts 22 community mental health providers, employing more than 5,200 people and assisting more than 115,000 individuals a year. The site is headed Alabama Council for Behavioral Healthcare; the page uses both names without explaining the relation. The address acmhb.org did not resolve.

637.title: [202] Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program (home page)
637.text: Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program, The University of Alabama. The Program's own home page (adap.ua.edu redirects here). It says ADAP provides legal services to Alabamians with disabilities to protect and promote their civil rights, and that its mission is legally based advocacy to protect, promote and expand those rights. It describes educating policymakers, systems-change litigation and outreach. The page does not mention the Hunter consent decree; ADAP's monitoring role there comes from the court-case record.

638.title: [203] Cover Alabama Coalition (home and About Us pages)
638.text: Cover Alabama. The coalition's own site. It describes Cover Alabama as a nonpartisan alliance of over 130 community partners, consumer groups, businesses, health care providers and faith groups pressing the state to provide affordable health coverage, and it urges Alabama to expand Medicaid to close a coverage gap of nearly 155,000 people. Alabama Arise appears in the member list; the page does not say who leads the coalition. Alabama Arise's own releases call Cover Alabama its campaign.

639.title: [204] North Alabama Mental Health Coalition website (About and Stay Informed pages)
639.text: North Alabama Mental Health Coalition. The coalition's own website; its footer credits Little Orange Fish, the publisher of this report, which is also listed among the coalition's core partners. The About page says the coalition was formed after the St. Vincent de Paul Voice of the Poor Committee raised the issue in 2015, bringing together the sheriff's department, police, emergency medical services, WellStone, city and county officials, probate judges, psychiatrists and social-service agencies. It says that in 2019 the coalition organized a petition, signed by probate judges, police chiefs and sheriffs, urging legislators to establish a mental health diversion and crisis center. The Stay Informed page says the coalition meets on the second Tuesday of every month and posts meeting minutes from January 2022 to August 2026; the site also has resources and calendar pages.

640.title: [205] MORE GOOD DAYS TOGETHER: ADMH Celebrates Mental Health Awareness Month with Resources and Support
640.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. An ADMH press release of 30 April 2026. It says that each May the Department joins organizations throughout the state and country in observing Mental Health Awareness Month, and gives the 2026 theme as 'More Good Days, Together'. It announces the 8th Annual Strike Out Stigma game on 8 May in Montgomery and the annual Capitol Art Showcase of work by people receiving mental health services. It names no partner organization, and mentions no calendar, toolkit or social-media campaign.

641.title: [206] Mental Health First Aid
641.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's page on Mental Health First Aid, an eight-hour course that teaches people to recognize and respond to someone developing a mental health problem or in crisis. It lists who should take it, including health-care staff, police officers, human resource directors, school and college staff, houses of faith and families. It says ADMH offers the training, NAMI Alabama also offers it, and more than 90 certified instructors teach classes. It gives no count of people trained in Alabama.

642.title: [207] Alabama Dept. of Mental Health asking for $18 million in 2020
642.text: WZDX News (Huntsville), reposted by the Alabama Department of Mental Health. A local television news item of 30 January 2020, reposted on ADMH's site. It reports that the Department planned to ask the state for $18 million in the 2020 legislative session, to build three new crisis centers. It quotes one Huntsville counselor in support and gives no statistics on need. It does not mention NAMI, family groups or provider associations.

643.title: [208] Crisis Diversion Centers Awards Announced (Governor Ivey Announces Awardees of Crisis Center Funding)
643.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health / Office of the Governor. The release of 28 October 2020 announcing the first three crisis centers: AltaPointe in Mobile, the Montgomery Area Mental Health Authority and WellStone in Huntsville. It says that in the 2020 session Governor Ivey made a mental health crisis continuum of care a priority, with the effort in the Legislature led by House Majority Leader Nathaniel Ledbetter, and that the centers result from an $18 million appropriation in the FY2021 General Fund budget. It describes crisis centers as resources that law enforcement, hospitals, judges, families and individuals were seeking. It does not name any advocacy organization.

644.title: [209] Peer Support
644.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's public page on where to find peer support. It says peer support for people with mental illness is provided by certified peer specialists at local mental health centers and at drop-in centers, and names Wings Across Alabama, which runs peer support groups and a round-the-clock warmline. For substance use it lists two recovery organizations, PEIR (People Engaged in Recovery) and ROSS (Recovery Organization of Support Specialists), with nine recovery community centers between them. The page is undated, gives no count of drop-in centers and does not say its list is complete.

645.title: [210] The Evolution of the System of Care Approach for Children, Youth, and Young Adults with Mental Health Conditions and Their Families
645.text: The Institute for Innovation and Implementation, School of Social Work, University of Maryland. The 2021 update of the national System of Care framework for children's mental health; it says it 'builds on the 2010 update'. It keeps three core values, now worded as family and youth driven, community based, and culturally and linguistically responsive, and lists fourteen guiding principles. The principles the 2010 version already had remain, including a comprehensive array of services, individualized planning, interagency collaboration, support for the transition to adulthood, and data-driven accountability. New or strengthened principles cover trauma-informed care, integration of health and mental health care, a public health approach with prevention and early identification, and mental health equity. It is a national framework and does not discuss Alabama; the copy read is hosted by a Pennsylvania county association.

646.title: [211] Explore Teen Suicide in Alabama
646.text: America's Health Rankings (United Health Foundation). America's Health Rankings measure page for deaths by intentional self-harm per 100,000 adolescents aged 15-19, from CDC WONDER multiple-cause-of-death files for 2021-2023. Alabama's rate is 9.9 against 10.2 for the United States, and the page ranks Alabama 12th among states.

647.title: [212] Memorandum 24-COMM-01: Office of Child and Family Services
647.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. A one-page memorandum of 21 March 2024 from ADMH Commissioner Kimberly Boswell to the Department's providers and partners. It says the Office of Child and Family Services was established in October 2023 to better coordinate services for children and families, that existing offices and programs were reorganized, and that Beverly Johnson is its Director. It refers to two attached organizational charts, which could not be read for this check; the memo text itself does not list the programs that were brought together.

648.title: [213] Therapeutic Foster Care/Therapeutic Foster Care-Enhanced Services RFP
648.text: Alabama Department of Human Resources. The Department of Human Resources' procurement page seeking vendors to provide at least 750 statewide slots of Therapeutic Foster Care and at least 100 slots of Therapeutic Foster Care-Enhanced. It describes therapeutic foster care as a time-limited, intensive intervention, usually no longer than eighteen months, for children in state custody who cannot live at home and who meet the Department's diagnostic and behavioral criteria. The page shows no posting date; a related DHR page says its Office of Resource Development approves therapeutic foster care placements and supports 'contract providers'. It shows that the service is bought by DHR from contracted providers.

649.title: [214] To improve student wellbeing, Alabama invests in mental health coordinators
649.text: The Hechinger Report. A news feature published on 29 June 2022 by The Hechinger Report on Alabama's school mental health service coordinators. It says the position started as a state-funded pilot in 102 school districts in the 2020-21 school year, with districts applying for a $40,000 grant towards the coordinator's salary, and that coordinators 'will be in every school district, charter school and statewide magnet school for the 2022-23 school year'. It describes coordinators as organising awareness events, running small groups and connecting families with professional mental health services. It was written before the 2022-23 school year began, so the full roll-out is reported as a plan.

650.title: [215] Student-to-School-Counselor Ratio 2024–2025
650.text: American School Counselor Association. A one-page chart from the American School Counselor Association giving each state's public-school enrollment, number of school counselors and students per counselor for 2024–25, from the federal Common Core of Data. For Alabama it shows 751,060 students and 1,873 school counselors, which is 401 students per counselor; the national figure is 372. The chart states that the Association recommends 250-to-1. The chart is a graphic whose underlying text is out of order, so Alabama's ratio was worked out from its student and counselor counts and the alignment checked against ratios the Association states in words for four other states.

651.title: [216] Student-to-School-Counselor Ratio 2023-2024 (alphabetical by state)
651.text: American School Counselor Association. A one-page chart from the American School Counselor Association showing, for each state, the number of public-school students, the number of school counselors and the resulting ratio for 2023-24, drawn from the federal Common Core of Data. For Alabama it shows 748,650 students and 1,880 school counselors, a ratio of 398 students per counselor; the national figure is 376. The chart states that the Association recommends a ratio of 250-to-1. The page is a graphic, and the text behind it is out of order, so the Alabama ratio was read from the student and counselor counts and checked against the ratio list.

652.title: [217] State of Alabama Department of Human Resources 2026 Annual Progress and Services Report
652.text: Alabama Department of Human Resources. Alabama's annual child-welfare report to the federal Children's Bureau, dated 30 June 2025 and posted by DHR in November 2025. It reports 5,900 children in out-of-home care on 6 May 2025, with 576 placed in the homes of relatives. In its review of federal Child and Family Services Review outcomes, case reviews for FY2024 rated the mental and behavioral health needs of the child (Item 18) a strength in 11 of 23 applicable cases, 48 percent. It says adoption savings are spent on services including a psychotropic medication review team for children in foster care, and its contents list a section on Family First Prevention Services Act transition grants at page 30. The fetch reached only about the first 30 pages, so the appendices were not read.

653.title: [218] FY 2023 Annual Report, Alabama Department of Youth Services
653.text: Alabama Department of Youth Services. The Alabama Department of Youth Services' 27-page annual report for fiscal year 2023, posted on the DYS site in December 2025. It says DYS operates three facilities (the Mt. Meigs, Vacca and Autauga campuses), contracts with 10 community programs and funds 50 diversion grant programs serving all 67 counties. For FY2023 it shows 2,629 youth in diversion programs, 78 percent successful completion, and a six-month re-offence chart in which 86 percent did not re-offend. It records that in mid-June there were 108 youth waiting for a DYS bed, most held in county or regional detention centers, because of staff vacancies. It gives no counts of mental-health, clinical or treatment services.

654.title: [219] FY 2024 Annual Report, Alabama Department of Youth Services
654.text: Alabama Department of Youth Services. The Department of Youth Services' annual report for fiscal year 2024, its fiftieth year, posted on the DYS site in June 2026. It says diversion programs served 2,430 youth in FY24 (admissions, which may count a youth more than once), that 41 of 51 programs had success rates above 75 percent, and that of 972 clients evaluated six months after discharge 845 (87 percent) had not reoffended. It lists nine contracted custodial community facilities with their capacities and reports 808 youth admitted to DYS in FY24. It mentions Dialectical Behavior Therapy and substance-use education and treatment through UAB, but gives no counts of youth receiving mental-health or clinical services. It was read through a summarising reader; text inside images may have been missed.

655.title: [220] Code of Alabama §12-5A-8 (juvenile probation officers: supervision; employees of state) and §12-5A-13 (applicability to certain counties)
655.text: State of Alabama (text as published by Justia). Two sections of the chapter of Alabama law on juvenile probation services. Section 12-5A-8 says that in counties with 99,000 or fewer people at the 1990 census, juvenile probation officers are state employees in the court system's personnel system, appointed by and under the direct supervision of the presiding juvenile court judge, with appointments approved by the Administrative Director of Courts. Section 12-5A-13 says Mobile County is to be treated as one of those counties whatever its population and that, from 1 October 2024, Shelby County is too. The sections do not list the larger counties that remain outside the arrangement or say how probation is run there.

656.title: [221] First Teacher Home Visiting
656.text: Alabama Department of Early Childhood Education. The Alabama Department of Early Childhood Education's web page for First Teacher Home Visiting, updated 22 December 2025. It says the program uses three national models (Nurse-Family Partnership, Parents as Teachers and HIPPY) and that its programs serve families in all 67 counties. Programs may enrol pregnant women and continue until the child enters kindergarten. It warns that, because of limited funding, even counties with services may have families on waiting lists, and it lists improving maternal physical and mental health as one of the program's focus areas. It gives no numbers of families served.

657.title: [222] Help Me Grow Alabama
657.text: Alabama Partnership for Children. The register gives no URL for this source; the pages read are the Alabama Partnership for Children's Help Me Grow page and helpmegrowalabama.org. They describe Help Me Grow Alabama as a program of the Alabama Partnership for Children and an affiliate of the Help Me Grow National Network: a free information and referral line connecting families of children from birth to age eight to health and developmental resources. It uses the ASQ-3 developmental screening questionnaire, and its own site advertises developmental screenings for children 1 month to 5½ years old. Neither page mentions postpartum care, Medicaid or the Department of Mental Health.

658.title: [223] 2022 Key Findings on Pregnancy-related Deaths
658.text: Alabama Department of Public Health, Alabama Maternal Mortality Review Committee. A one-page sheet of the Alabama Maternal Mortality Review Committee's findings on deaths in 2022. It says 82.4 percent (14 of 17) of pregnancy-related deaths were judged preventable and that 64.7 percent (11 of 17) were among Black, non-Hispanic women. The leading causes listed are hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (17.7 percent) and cardiomyopathy, embolism and mental health conditions (11.8 percent each). It has no line on substance use, overdose or suicide.

659.title: [224] Suicide Prevention
659.text: Alabama Department of Public Health. The Alabama Department of Public Health's suicide prevention page, last updated 10 October 2023. It directs people in crisis to 988, gives Alabama's 2021 suicide rate as 15.8 per 100,000 and lists risk factors. Its navigation includes a 'Youth Suicide Materials' page. The page does not describe a program or give youth-specific statistics.

660.title: [225] Involuntary commitment law changed in Alabama; taking effect in July
660.text: WAFF 48 News. Television news report on House Bill 70 of the 2022 session, signed by Gov. Kay Ivey. It says officers could previously transport a person in a mental-health crisis only where there was immediate danger of harm, and that under the new law an officer can transport the person to a mental health facility to be seen by a physician. It says the new law takes effect 'this July', that is, July 2022.

661.title: [226] Alabama HB70, 2022 Regular Session (bill history)
661.text: LegiScan, reproducing the Alabama Legislature's bill history. Bill-tracking page for House Bill 70 of 2022, sponsored by Rep. Rex Reynolds, described as establishing consistency in the process of commitment of individuals with mental illness (adding §22-52-10.11 and amending §§22-52-1.1, 22-52-10.2 and 22-52-91). The history shows it was enrolled, delivered to the Governor on 29 March 2022 and assigned Act No. 2022-202. The page gives no effective date. The same act number appears in the history line of Code of Alabama §22-52-10.4.

662.title: [227] Baldwin County deputies train on mental health after Alabama law concerning crisis centers goes into effect
662.text: 1819 News. News report on NAMI-led crisis-intervention training for Baldwin County deputies, with AltaPointe staff. It says legislation passed in 2022 expedited the involuntary-commitment process for officers, and quotes Rep. Rex Reynolds, the sponsor, that officers can take people to a crisis care unit instead of jail. It adds that Reynolds asked APOSTC to raise the minimum mental-health training hours. The body gives no bill number and no effective date; only the headline says the law has gone into effect.

663.title: [228] APOSTC Law Enforcement Training Curriculum Changes (effective January 1, 2018)
663.text: Alabama Peace Officers' Standards and Training Commission. A notice from the Commission recording curriculum changes adopted on 15 November 2017 and effective 1 January 2018. It says the Basic (520 hour) Law Enforcement Academy Training Curriculum was revised to expand the Mental Health Awareness block of instruction from four hours to eight. It shows that the basic academy carries a required mental-health block. It does not say how many hours the block has in the current curriculum.

664.title: [229] Mental Health Focus in the Morgan County Jail
664.text: Morgan County Sheriff's Office. Sheriff's Office release describing mental-health services in the Morgan County jail. It says the office added two full-time licensed counselors in 2023, serving inmates and officers, that mental-health staff made 6,338 inmate visits for mental-health needs in 2025, and that mental-health crisis issues 'occur to 50% of inmates'. It does not describe screening at booking and says nothing about other counties or statewide practice.

665.title: [230] 'Mental Health Court' for nonviolent offenders launches in Cullman
665.text: The Cullman Times. Local news report that a Mental Health Court program became part of Cullman County's 32nd Judicial Circuit in late May 2022. It says the court is overseen by the presiding circuit judge in partnership with other Cullman County judges and WellStone Behavioral Health. It adds that Cullman's court system already held specialized Drug Court and Veterans Court dockets for nonviolent offenders.

666.title: [231] Mental Health Court
666.text: Shelby County District Attorney's Office, 18th Judicial Circuit of Alabama. Page of the Shelby County District Attorney's Office describing the county's Mental Health Court as a specialty court program for participants with a qualifying serious mental illness who comply with treatment and other directives of the court. It sets out who is eligible. The site's menu also lists a Veteran's Court. The page is undated and does not say when either court began.

667.title: [232] Overview of Forensic Mental Health Services (Forensic Outpatient Program primer)
667.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health, Office of Forensic Mental Health Services. A primer of about 15 pages from ADMH's Office of Forensic Mental Health Services, posted in May 2025 (the file name carries the date 05/01/25; the text itself is undated), explaining to courts and attorneys how outpatient forensic examinations are ordered, tracked and carried out. It says the Office oversees and coordinates the Department's forensic services system and that ADMH contracts with JBS Mental Health Authority for full-time certified forensic examiners who conduct outpatient forensic evaluations on ADMH's behalf. It names Taylor Hardin only as the facility for male defendants. It gives no bed counts, waitlist numbers, jail-based restoration figures, forensic-navigator description or mention of Stepping Up.

668.title: [233] Stepping Up Alabama Year Four Evaluation Report
668.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health (evaluation by Urban Metrics Consultants and The Dannon Project). A 43-page evaluation of the fourth round of ADMH's Stepping Up Alabama grants, posted on the ADMH site in September 2023. It describes Stepping Up as a national initiative to reduce the number of people with mental illness in jails, sponsored by the National Association of Counties, the American Psychiatric Association Foundation and the Council of State Governments Justice Center. Year Four funded eight county sites run by four mental health centers (AltaPointe in Baldwin, Clay, Talladega and Washington; East Alabama in Tallapoosa and Russell; JBS in Jefferson; North Central in Lawrence), which began between January and July 2021. Its jail summary table shows 6,926 inmates screened for serious mental illness, 261 screening positive, 319 referred and 121 receiving case management. It says the 2018 request for proposals offered a one-time award of up to $50,000.

669.title: [234] Stepping Up counties map, 2026
669.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. A one-page county map posted on the Alabama Department of Mental Health's website in April 2026. Its legend reads 'Current Stepping Up Counties (48)' and 'Counties without Stepping Up (19)', and the map is labelled with the names of the community mental health centers. The map prints no date or author. The reading tool could not reliably tell which counties fall under which heading, so only the two totals are used.

670.title: [235] Company late paying hundreds of Alabama corrections healthcare workers
670.text: WBRC. WBRC report that YesCare, which then held the contract for medical and mental-health care in all ADOC facilities, paid hundreds of employees late in April 2026. It says the state awarded YesCare a $1.06 billion contract in 2023 running through September 2027, and reports YesCare's failed repayment agreement with creditors. The article describes the position on 14 April 2026; ADOC terminated the contract two weeks later.

671.title: [236] ADOC Terminates YesCare Contract, Signs On With NaphCare for 24 Months
671.text: Alabama Department of Corrections. Alabama Department of Corrections news release of 29 April 2026. It says the Department has terminated its healthcare services contract with YesCare for failure to adequately fulfill its contractual duties, and that it is working to execute an emergency agreement with NaphCare to provide inmate healthcare services, with the transition at midnight on 3 May 2026. The 24-month length is in the headline. As read, the release gives no dollar value and does not say separately whether mental-health care is covered.

672.title: [237] Report: At least 277 people died in Alabama prisons in 2024
672.text: Alabama Reflector. News report on an ACLU of Alabama report estimating that at least 277 people died in Alabama prisons in 2024, a figure that may be an undercount because of poor record-keeping by the Department of Corrections. Identified causes included 46 overdoses and 77 natural deaths, with 105 deaths still under investigation. It notes that conditions remain dangerous more than four years after the U.S. Department of Justice sued the state. It does not discuss mental health care or the Braggs case.

673.title: [238] Another deadly year in Alabama prisons claims 202 lives
673.text: Alabama Appleseed Center for Law and Justice. Report by Alabama Appleseed's researcher that at least 202 people died inside Alabama prisons in 2025, a figure the organization obtained through a records request to the Alabama Department of Corrections. It says this was a drop from 277 deaths in 2024 and from a record 327 in 2023, and that the state's prison death rate remains far above the national average. As read, it gives no separate count of suicides.

674.title: [239] PREP Center (location page)
674.text: Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles. The Bureau's location page for its Perry County reentry center. It gives the name and address as 'Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles PREP Center, 4805 U.S. Highway 80, Uniontown, AL 36786', with a telephone number and a hiring notice. The page does not describe the center's programs.

675.title: [240] Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles to open rehab facility for women
675.text: Alabama Reflector. News report that the Bureau of Pardons and Paroles plans a residential rehabilitation facility for women modelled on its Perry County PREP Center. Crews were preparing a site in Thomasville expected to host an initial cohort of 20 women on parole; the facility, the Central Alabama Re-Entry (CARE) Center, was expected to open the following spring. The Bureau's director is quoted as saying it will provide drug treatment, mental health treatment and job training. The article predates the planned opening and does not report that it happened.

676.title: [241] Locations
676.text: Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles. The Bureau's list of its offices and facilities, read on 3 October 2026. Under 'Day Reporting Centers' it lists Birmingham, Huntsville, Mobile, Montgomery and Tuscaloosa; under 'Day Reporting Center Lites' it lists Baldwin, Fort Payne, Jasper, Opelika, Sand Mountain and Calera. It also lists the PREP Center. No CARE Center and no Thomasville location appeared on the page on that date.

677.title: [242] New center aims to train Alabamians on parole or probation for manufacturing jobs
677.text: Alabama Reflector. News report on a new training facility that opened the week of 21 September 2026 at the Perry County Probation and Parole Re-Entry Program (PREP) Center, expanding welding and heavy-machinery training for people on parole or probation. J.F. Ingram State Technical College operates the facility in partnership with the Bureau of Pardons and Paroles, as part of the 'Re-Entry 2030' effort to reduce recidivism. The article does not name Uniontown, the Thomasville CARE Center or the day reporting centers, and gives no recidivism percentages. (The register's title for this item is taken from the URL; the published headline is as shown here.)

678.title: [243] Day Reporting Centers
678.text: Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles. The Bureau's standing page on its Day Reporting Centers (DRCs), which it describes as standalone facilities with their own staff and contracted treatment providers for high-risk probationers and parolees. It says DRCs address education, employment, substance abuse, mental health and cognitive restructuring in a three-phase programme, and names five centers: Birmingham, Huntsville, Mobile, Montgomery and Tuscaloosa. The Bureau's site separately lists six smaller 'DRC Lites' (Baldwin, Fort Payne, Jasper, Opelika, Sand Mountain, Calera). The page says nothing about Unite Us, the PREP or CARE centers or the Reentry Task Force.

679.title: [244] Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles pilot program tracks services and treatment programs
679.text: Alabama Reflector. News report on an information and referral platform run by the company Unite Us that the Bureau of Pardons and Paroles has launched to record the services and treatment received by people on probation or parole. The pilot, which began about six weeks before publication, is a collaboration between the Bureau, the Alabama Department of Veterans Affairs and the Alabama Department of Mental Health, and is available at about five of the Bureau's day reporting centers. The article's sub-headline says the software was developed with opioid-settlement money. It does not list the day reporting centers or give recidivism or parole figures.

680.title: [245] Alabama task force finalizes recidivism definition for future vote
680.text: Alabama Reflector. News report on the Tuesday 22 September 2026 meeting of Alabama's Joint Re-Entry Task Force, where a working group kept its June recommendation to define recidivism as a return to ADOC custody for a new crime within three years of release; the task force will vote on the language at its next quarterly meeting, date not yet announced. Cam Ward, director of the Bureau of Pardons and Paroles, is identified as the task force chair. Ward said Alabama's recidivism rate is 27 percent, improved from 34 percent in recent years according to the Council of State Governments Justice Center, with which the state has partnered on 'Reentry 2030'.

681.title: [246] Section 1115 Waiver Watch: Medicaid Pre-Release Services for People Who Are Incarcerated
681.text: KFF. KFF issue brief on Section 1115 'reentry' waivers that let Medicaid pay for services before release from jail or prison. It states that as of 19 August 2024 CMS had approved reentry waivers for 11 states with 13 more pending. The states are identified only in embedded figures (Figures 1 and 2), which could not be read; Alabama is not mentioned anywhere in the article's text.

682.title: [247] Medicaid Waiver Tracker: Approved and Pending Section 1115 Waivers by State
682.text: KFF. KFF's running tracker of Section 1115 Medicaid waivers, dated as of 30 September 2026 when read. On reentry waivers for people leaving incarceration, its text says the Biden administration approved 19 state waivers and the Trump administration approved four in September 2026. The states are named only in embedded tables and maps, which could not be read. Alabama is not mentioned anywhere in the page's text, under reentry or any other waiver type.

683.title: [248] Code of Alabama §22-6-12 (Suspension of Eligibility for Inmates of Certain Public Institutions; Temporary Reinstatement) and §22-6-13 (Medicaid Benefits for County Inmates and Certain Juveniles)
683.text: State of Alabama (2025 Code of Alabama, as published by Justia). Two sections of Alabama's Medicaid law. Section 22-6-12 says an inmate of a Department of Corrections institution 'shall have his or her eligibility for Medicaid suspended, but not terminated', allows temporary reinstatement for inpatient care of more than 24 hours outside the institution, and lets the institution try to establish or renew Medicaid eligibility before release. Section 22-6-13 applies the same suspend-not-terminate rule to county inmates and certain juveniles and required the Medicaid Agency and counties to set up a centralized process by 1 November 2017. The sections state the rule; they do not report how often eligibility is restored at release.

684.title: [249] 2023 Alabama Community Corrections Program by County as of April 1, 2023
684.text: Alabama Department of Corrections. A one-page ADOC county map of community corrections programs holding an ADOC contract, dated 1 April 2023 and re-posted in February 2026. Its key states that 52 counties have an established program, that there are 38 established programs (six operating as judicial-circuit or joint-county programs), and that 15 counties have none. Counties marked 'No CCP' are Cherokee, Coosa, Lee, Henry, Crenshaw, Covington, Butler, Lowndes, Conecuh, Monroe, Clarke, Choctaw, Washington, Baldwin and Houston. It carries no mental-health or caseload information.

685.title: [250] Alabama parole grant rate remains low in November report
685.text: Alabama Political Reporter. A news report published 24 December 2025 on the Bureau of Pardons and Paroles' monthly statistics for November 2025. The Board held 224 parole hearings and granted 35, a 16 percent grant rate, against a fiscal-year-to-date rate of 17 percent and 29 percent in November 2024. It also covers pardon approvals, supervision caseloads and officer staffing. It says nothing about recidivism or mental health. The page's headline now differs from the title in the register, though the web address still carries the original wording.

686.title: [251] Monthly Statistical Report, June 2026
686.text: Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles (ABPP Data Unit). The Bureau's statistical report for June 2026. It shows 128 parole hearings in the month, with 30 granted and 98 denied, a grant rate of 23 percent (p. 11). For fiscal year 2026 to date it shows 455 grants and 1,759 denials out of 2,214 decisions, a rate of 21 percent (p. 9). It gives no count of mental-health or other specialized supervision caseloads. Read through the fetch tool for those figures only.

687.title: [252] Monthly Statistical Report, August 2026
687.text: Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles (ABPP Data Unit). The Bureau's statistical report for August 2026, the most recent on its reports page on 3 October 2026. Its parole table (p. 10) shows 37 grants out of 306 decisions in August, a grant rate of 12 percent, with June at 23 percent and July at 29 percent. For fiscal year 2026 through August it shows 560 grants and 2,192 denials out of 2,752 decisions, a rate of 20 percent. It gives no count of mental-health or other specialized supervision caseloads. Read through the fetch tool for those figures only.

688.title: [253] Federal Appeals Court Finds Constitutionally Inadequate Mental Health Care in Alabama Prisons
688.text: Equal Justice Initiative. News post by the Equal Justice Initiative on the Eleventh Circuit's decision affirming that Alabama's mental health care for people in state prisons is constitutionally inadequate. It notes the court also held that ADOC is not constitutionally required to suicide-proof every cell or to fill staffing positions unrelated to mental health care. It says the suit was filed by Alabama prisoners with serious mental illness and the Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program. The post reports on the case; it does not describe the Equal Justice Initiative as a party to it.

689.title: [254] Alabama fact sheet (2024 Point-in-Time data)
689.text: National Alliance to End Homelessness. A one-page advocacy fact sheet drawn from HUD's 2024 Point-in-Time count (the date is taken from the file path; the sheet itself is undated). It says 4,601 Alabama residents experienced homelessness on any given night in 2024, 59% of them unsheltered, a 15.9% rise between 2015 and 2024, with counts for families with children, chronically homeless people, older adults and veterans. It gives no 2023 comparison and no rate per 10,000.

690.title: [255] American homelessness is on the rise, what about in Alabama?
690.text: Alabama Political Reporter. A news report published 31 December 2024 on federal housing department (HUD) figures for 2024. It says homelessness nationally grew by over 18 percent, the largest annual rise since counts began in 2007. For Alabama it says the homeless population grew by over 39 percent between 2023 and 2024 to 4,601 people, while the state remained one of only 13 with fewer than 10 homeless people per 10,000 residents (0.09 percent of Alabamians, up from 0.06 percent). It does not give the exact rates of 8.9 or 22.6 per 10,000 and does not discuss mental illness among people who are homeless.

691.title: [256] Explore Homelessness in Alabama
691.text: America's Health Rankings (United Health Foundation). America's Health Rankings measure page for people experiencing homelessness per 10,000 population, taken from HUD's 2024 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report. Alabama's rate is 8.9 against 22.6 for the United States, and Alabama ranks 8th, where rank 1 is the lowest rate. The page gives rates only: it has no count of people and no year-on-year change.

692.title: [257] Alabama fact sheet (2025 Point-in-Time data)
692.text: National Alliance to End Homelessness. A one-page advocacy fact sheet, successor to the 2024 sheet (S69c), with statistics 'drawn from the 2025 HUD Point in Time Count'. It says 4,137 Alabama residents experienced homelessness on any given night in 2025, 54 percent of them unsheltered, and that the count is up 26.9 percent between 2019 and 2025. It gives counts for people in families with children, chronically homeless people, veterans (214) and adults aged 55 and older. It gives no rate per 10,000 and no comparison with 2024.

693.title: [258] HUD 2025 Continuum of Care Homeless Assistance Programs: Homeless Populations and Subpopulations (State: Alabama)
693.text: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD Exchange). HUD's own state summary of what Alabama's Continuums of Care reported from the 2025 Point-in-Time count. It gives 4,137 homeless persons in total: 1,600 in emergency shelter, 312 in transitional housing and 2,225 unsheltered. Its subpopulation table counts 502 people as severely mentally ill (339 of them unsheltered), 374 with chronic substance abuse and 214 veterans. HUD notes that it has made a limited data-quality review but has not independently verified everything the Continuums submitted.

694.title: [259] HUD Releases 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report to Congress (HUD No. 26-037)
694.text: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. HUD's press release announcing the 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report, Part 1. It reports 745,652 people homeless on a single night in January 2025, a 3% decrease since 2024 and a 27% increase since 2013, with 266,320 unsheltered and chronic homelessness up 81% since 2013. The release gives no Alabama or other state figures and does not mention state spreadsheets; those are on HUD User, which lists a '2007 - 2025 Point-in-Time Estimates by State' file. The report itself puts the national rate at about 22 per 10,000 people.

695.title: [260] Alabama's Continuum of Care Groups (contact list)
695.text: Alabama Department of Economic and Community Affairs (ADECA). ADECA's contact sheet, dated 1 November 2024, for Alabama's nine HUD Continuums of Care, AL-500 to AL-508, giving each one's name, service area, staff contacts and address. It lists One Roof (Jefferson, St. Clair, Shelby), Homeless Coalition of the Alabama Gulf Coast (Mobile, Baldwin), Homeless Care Council of Northwest Alabama, North Alabama Coalition for the Homeless (Madison, Limestone, Morgan), Mid-Alabama Coalition for the Homeless (Montgomery and four neighbouring counties), Homeless Coalition of Northeast Alabama, West Alabama Coalition for the Homeless (Tuscaloosa County), Alabama Rural Coalition for the Homeless (balance of state) and Southeast Alabama Coalition for the Homeless. It does not describe what Continuums of Care do and does not name Housing First, Inc.

696.title: [261] 24 CFR Part 578 (Continuum of Care Program): §578.7 Responsibilities of the Continuum of Care; §578.9 Preparing an application for funds
696.text: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (Code of Federal Regulations, as published by the Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School). The federal rule that sets out what a Continuum of Care must do. Section 578.7 requires each Continuum to develop a plan that includes coordinating a housing and service system in its area and planning and conducting a point-in-time count of homeless people at least every two years. Section 578.9 requires it to run a collaborative process for funding applications and to establish priorities for funding projects in its area. HUD, not the Continuum, makes the awards.

697.title: [262] Continuum of Care (CoC) Program
697.text: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD Exchange). HUD's program page for the Continuum of Care Program. It says the program is designed to promote communitywide commitment to the goal of ending homelessness by providing funding for efforts by nonprofit providers and State and local governments, and by promoting access to mainstream programs for homeless individuals and families. It is a national page and says nothing about Alabama's nine Continuums.

698.title: [263] Emergency Solutions Grants (ESG) program page
698.text: Alabama Department of Economic and Community Affairs (ADECA). ADECA's program page for the Emergency Solutions Grants. It says the program is funded by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and administered by ADECA, and is open to nonprofit organizations and units of local government to provide transitional housing, emergency shelter and rental assistance. It links to application memos and project lists through program year 2026 and to the Continuums of Care contact list, but gives no award totals.

699.title: [264] Gov. Ivey awards $2.7 million to fight homelessness in Alabama
699.text: Alabama Department of Economic and Community Affairs (ADECA). ADECA press release of 29 December 2025 announcing $2.7 million in Emergency Solutions Grant awards, from HUD funds that ADECA administers, to local governments and nonprofits serving homeless people and those at risk. It lists eleven recipients with amounts, among them the City of Huntsville ($450,000, serving Limestone, Madison and Morgan counties), the City of Florence ($400,100), United Way of East Central Alabama ($400,000) and the City of Tuscaloosa ($220,000). The release does not itself state the number of recipients; the eleven are counted from its list, and their amounts sum to $2,710,820.

700.title: [265] A Program in Jefferson County Helped 585 People Out of Homelessness. Then the Money Ran Out
700.text: The Birmingham Times (AL.com/The Birmingham Times). A 4 December 2025 news feature on the Jefferson County Housing Authority's HUD-funded Continuum of Care program, which paid rent for formerly homeless households. It says the program once helped 370 households, 585 people including 128 children and teens. The authority wound it down in stages: a first group of 100 households was told in August 2024 that payments would stop on 1 October 2024, and in May 2025 the final group of 100 households was told the funding had run out. The authority said HUD did not provide enough funding to sustain the program.

701.title: [266] Committee approves $500,000 contract to boost affordable housing for Alabamians with mental health needs
701.text: Alabama Daily News. News report that the Legislature's Contract Review Committee approved a $500,000 Alabama Department of Mental Health contract with Navigate Affordable Housing Partners, a Birmingham non-profit. The contractor is to secure, promote, increase and facilitate statewide affordable supportive housing options for people with mental health problems who are homeless, in jails or in emergency departments. The contract runs through 30 September 2026.

702.title: [267] Birmingham Alabama's Response to Unhoused Community
702.text: UAB Institute for Human Rights Blog. A blog post of 27 February 2026 on the UAB Institute for Human Rights site, summarising the City of Birmingham Roadmap of Services for Unsheltered Residents. It says one strategy is creating 350 more beds for emergency shelters and transitional houses, and that most of the roadmap's strategies are set to be completed or go into effect by the end of 2026. It also gives 2024 counts of about 1,153 unhoused people in Birmingham. It is a secondary account; it does not give the roadmap's date or issuing office.

703.title: [268] Congressional Statistics, December 2025: Alabama
703.text: Social Security Administration, Office of Retirement and Disability Policy. The December 2025 edition of SSA's annual fact sheet of Social Security and Supplemental Security Income beneficiaries by state and congressional district; it supersedes the December 2024 edition (S71). For Alabama it shows 1,207,893 Social Security beneficiaries including 179,658 disabled workers, and 138,832 SSI recipients (7,685 aged, 1,025 blind, 130,122 disabled) receiving $102,193,000 in total monthly payments. It prints no average SSI payment; dividing payments by recipients gives about $736 a month.

704.title: [269] Congressional Statistics, December 2024: Alabama
704.text: Social Security Administration, Office of Retirement and Disability Policy. SSA's annual fact sheet of Social Security and Supplemental Security Income beneficiaries by state and congressional district, as of December 2024. For Alabama it shows 1,193,685 Social Security beneficiaries including 185,048 disabled workers, and 140,811 SSI recipients (7,680 aged, 1,028 blind, 132,103 disabled) receiving $100,693,000 in total monthly payments. It does not print an average SSI payment; dividing payments by recipients gives about $715.

705.title: [270] 2025 Annual Report
705.text: Alabama Department of Rehabilitation Services. The Alabama Department of Rehabilitation Services' annual report for 2025, as filed with the Legislature. It reports 72,236 Alabamians served by the Department in total: 45,793 by Vocational Rehabilitation Service, 15,784 by Children's Rehabilitation Service, 8,884 by Early Intervention and 1,775 by the SAIL homebound program. Vocational Rehabilitation took 9,455 new applications and closed 3,999 individual cases in competitive integrated employment. The text seen does not mention the Individual Placement and Support program or the Department of Mental Health; the fetch layer indicated the document may have been truncated.

706.title: [271] What is IPS?
706.text: The IPS Employment Center. The IPS Employment Center's description of Individual Placement and Support. It defines IPS as a model of supported employment for people with serious mental illness that helps people work at regular jobs, and says IPS refers to the evidence-based practice of supported employment. It is a general description and does not mention Alabama's program.

707.title: [272] Map the Meal Gap: Hunger & Poverty in Alabama (2024 data)
707.text: Feeding America. Feeding America's interactive Map the Meal Gap page for Alabama, 2024 data year. The text available to the reader states that the food insecurity rate in Alabama was 17.8% in 2024; the map, counts and cost figures load dynamically and could not be read. Feeding America's press release for the study that covers 2024 is titled Map the Meal Gap 2026, so the register's label 'Map the Meal Gap 2025' appears to name the wrong edition for this URL.

708.title: [273] Federal budget changes to SNAP could cost Alabama up to $261 million
708.text: Alabama Reflector. News report from a quarterly meeting of the Alabama Department of Human Resources, where SNAP Director Brandon Hardin said federal changes to SNAP will cost Alabama between $174 million and $261 million. From 1 October 2027 the state must pay 10 percent of benefits if its payment error rate is 8 to 9.99 percent and 15 percent if it is 10 percent or more; Alabama's rate was about 10 percent. Hardin said 678,278 Alabamians were enrolled, about 44,200 fewer than in October, and attributed disenrollments to federal eligibility changes including the 80-hours-a-month work requirement for able-bodied adults without dependents.

709.title: [274] Alabama officials to ask federal government for two-year delay on SNAP error rate penalty
709.text: Alabama Reflector. News report that Alabama officials approved a request for a two-year delay in the federal SNAP error-rate penalty. It says Alabama would have to pay about $174.3 million, about 10 percent of SNAP benefits, from 1 October 2027 unless its FY2026 error rate falls below 8 percent (FY2025 rate 9.52 percent); a rate of 6 to 7.99 percent would mean a 5 percent share, $87.1 million. About 650,000 people were enrolled, and the article says the 2025 federal law's tighter work requirements contributed to some of the 80,000 Alabamians who lost benefits between July 2025 and May 2026. No federal response is reported.

710.title: [275] Broadband in Alabama's Black Belt in 2025 (Issue Brief No. 65)
710.text: Education Policy Center, University of Alabama. A University of Alabama policy brief on broadband build-out in the state's 24-county Black Belt. Using the FCC's 2024 National Broadband Map, it reports that the Black Belt's average high-speed access rate (service of 100/20 Mbps available) is 76 percent, against 87 percent statewide and 94 percent nationally. The measure is availability of service to units on the FCC map, not the share of households that subscribe, so it is not comparable with the Census Bureau's 87.5 percent subscription figure.

711.title: [276] Explore Social and Economic Factors in Alabama
711.text: America's Health Rankings (United Health Foundation). America's Health Rankings page for its Social and Economic Factors category, the sum of weighted z-scores of the Annual Report's ranked social and economic measures. In the 2025 Annual Report edition Alabama ranks 44th among states with a score of -0.662. This page is not among the URLs in the register entry for S77 but is the one that carries the report's rank of 44.

712.title: [277] What is 988? (Veterans Crisis Line)
712.text: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Veterans Crisis Line. The Veterans Crisis Line's page explaining 988. It says veterans can reach the Veterans Crisis Line by dialing 988 and pressing 1, and can still use the earlier number, text 838255 or online chat; callers who press 1 are routed to trained Veterans Crisis Line responders around the clock. It is a national service page with nothing specific to Alabama.

713.title: [278] Explore Risk of Social Isolation - Age 65+ in Alabama
713.text: America's Health Rankings (United Health Foundation). America's Health Rankings measure page for the risk of social isolation among adults aged 65 and over, an index built from six factors in the American Community Survey 2020-2024 (poverty, living alone, being divorced, separated or widowed, never having married, disability, and independent-living difficulty). Alabama's value is 78 on a scale of 1 to 100, where higher means greater risk, and the state ranks 45th. The measure covers older adults only; the page gives no all-ages figure.

714.title: [279] Multifamily (Alabama Housing Finance Authority)
714.text: Alabama Housing Finance Authority. The Alabama Housing Finance Authority's multifamily page. It describes the Authority's allocations of Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (Housing Credits) and HOME loan funds to rental developments, and refers to Housing Trust Funds and other federal housing programs. As read on 3 October 2026 it does not mention Section 811, Shelter Plus Care or supportive housing.

715.title: [280] Barriers to Prosperity Data Sheet 2025
715.text: Alabama Possible. Alabama Possible's annual poverty data sheet, 2025 edition, built from Census, SAIPE, Feeding America and state data for 2023 and 2024. It reports a 15.7 percent poverty rate, more than 780,000 people including 236,000 children, child poverty of 21.3 percent, median household income of $62,248, and Alabama as the seventh-poorest state. It gives poverty by race (White 11.1, Black 25.1, Hispanic 24.6 percent), food insecurity of 17.5 percent (22.2 percent for children), and county-level poverty rates. It has no mental-health, broadband or rural-population measures.

716.title: [281] Status of State Medicaid Expansion Decisions
716.text: KFF. KFF's running tracker of which states have adopted the Affordable Care Act's Medicaid expansion. As read on 3 October 2026 it says 41 states, counting the District of Columbia, have adopted the expansion and 10 have not. The text returned did not list the ten states by name; KFF's coverage-gap brief of July 2026 names them, Alabama among them.

717.title: [282] Medicaid Income Eligibility Limits for Parents, 2002-2026
717.text: KFF (State Health Facts). A KFF State Health Facts table of each state's Medicaid income limit for parents as a share of the federal poverty level, from an annual survey with the Georgetown University Center for Children and Families. Alabama's limit is 18% of the federal poverty level in both January 2025 and January 2026. The page covers parents only: it does not give eligibility for childless adults or say how many states have expanded Medicaid.

718.title: [283] Medicaid Income Eligibility Limits for Adults as a Percent of the Federal Poverty Level
718.text: KFF (State Health Facts). A KFF table of each state's Medicaid income limits for adults, from an annual survey with the Georgetown University Center for Children and Families. For Alabama in January 2026 it shows a limit of 18 percent of the federal poverty level for parents in a family of three and 0 percent for other adults, meaning adults without dependent children cannot qualify on income alone. It does not cover eligibility through disability.

719.title: [284] ALLHealth plan proposed for Medicaid expansion
719.text: Lagniappe (Mobile). A news report of 16 December 2024 on ALLHealth, a proposal unveiled the week before by the Alabama Hospital Association and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama. The plan would use the additional federal dollars available to states that have not expanded Medicaid to put as many as 280,000 low-income residents on private insurance plans. The article says it would not need a bill and could be arranged between the federal Medicaid agency and Alabama Medicaid at the Governor's direction, and that some state leaders were skeptical of its long-term cost. It predates any decision on the proposal.

720.title: [285] Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics (CCBHCs) Demonstration Billing Manual, version 3
720.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. The current edition of ADMH's billing manual for clinics in the CCBHC Medicaid demonstration, effective 1 July 2026. It says a clinic receives one payment for each day on which at least one 'triggering event' service is given to a Medicaid enrollee, and that each clinic's rate is established from its own cost report of the total cost of operating the CCBHC. Costs of non-triggering activities, such as care coordination, are allowable in the cost report and so are built into the rate, but those activities do not trigger a payment when delivered alone. Peer support services appear among the triggering events. The text could be read to page 43; the section listing carried-cost services (p. 47) was not reached, and the phrase 'community health worker' does not appear in the pages read.

721.title: [286] Alabama Awarded Grant to Develop Statewide Criteria for Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics
721.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. An ADMH press release of 23 March 2023 announcing that SAMHSA awarded the Department a CCBHC Planning Grant of one million dollars to develop statewide certification criteria for CCBHCs. It describes a year-long planning period in which ADMH and the community mental health centers design the business model and a payment system, and says a transition to the CCBHC model will ensure statewide expansion of access to care. It also says the state has established six state-funded crisis centers to be operational in 2023.

722.title: [287] Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics (Office of CCBHC page)
722.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. The home page of ADMH's Office of Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics. It says the Office is responsible for implementing a statewide transformation of Alabama's behavioral health system using the CCBHC model of care, and that it gives training and technical assistance to the community mental health centers. It links the current provider, billing and quality manuals (third quarter 2026), the triggering-events list and the rate re-base schedule. It does not say how many CCBHCs there are or name them.

723.title: [288] FY 2026 CCBHC Triggering Events Procedure Codes
723.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health, Office of CCBHC. ADMH's list of the procedure codes that trigger a CCBHC's daily Medicaid payment, effective 1 July 2026. Triggering events include therapy, assessment, medication services, crisis intervention, the mobile crisis team, and services by certified peer specialists and certified recovery support specialists. A separate section of carved-in or carried-cost codes holds adult, child and substance-use case management, which are paid for inside the rate but do not trigger it. Assertive community treatment is listed as carved out. Community health workers are not mentioned.

724.title: [289] Prospective Payment System Re-base Schedule (memorandum to Alabama certified CCBHCs)
724.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health, Office of CCBHC. A memorandum of 9 July 2026 from ADMH's CCBHC Office to the state's certified CCBHCs on how and when their daily rates are recalculated. It says each clinic's rate will be re-based on actual cost and visit information after its second demonstration year, that cost reports are due within 90 days of the end of each demonstration year, and that Alabama Medicaid reviews the cost report with the clinic and establishes the final rate. It names no individual clinics.

725.title: [290] Alabama Medicaid Agency Section 1115 Substance Use Disorder Demonstration Application
725.text: Alabama Medicaid Agency (posted by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services). Alabama's application of 14 July 2023 for a Medicaid demonstration covering substance-use treatment. It asks for authority to pay for residential substance-use treatment in institutions for mental disease for enrollees aged 21 to 64, at ASAM levels 3.1, 3.3, 3.5 and 3.7, wherever in the state they live. It states that residential substance-use treatment is not currently covered by Alabama's Medicaid program and is available through ADMH. CMS lists the application as pending.

726.title: [291] Psychiatry | USA Health
726.text: USA Health (University of South Alabama), Mobile. The psychiatry page of USA Health, the University of South Alabama's health system in Mobile, read on 3 October 2026. It says USA Health is committed to providing supportive psychiatric care and offers outpatient care, including cognitive behavioral psychotherapy and drug therapy, for anxiety and depression. It also says the system partners with AltaPointe Health Systems to serve pediatric patients. The page gives no bed counts or patient numbers.

727.title: [292] Office of EMS
727.text: Alabama Department of Public Health. The Alabama Department of Public Health's page for its Office of Emergency Medical Services, read on 3 October 2026. It says the office is responsible for protecting the public by assuring that emergency medical services provided by ambulance services, emergency medical response agencies, training entities and EMS personnel meet or exceed established standards. It adds that the office can deny, suspend or revoke licenses where violations are substantiated. The page does not discuss mental health.

728.title: [293] Everybody's business: strengthening health systems to improve health outcomes (WHO's framework for action)
728.text: World Health Organization. WHO's catalogue page for its 2007 health-systems framework, ISBN 9789241596077, dated 7 August 2007. Only the catalogue page could be read: it gives the title and date and describes the document's aim of promoting a common understanding of what a health system is and of supporting countries in strengthening theirs. The overview as read does not list the six building blocks, and the full text on WHO's repository refused the fetch. The six blocks themselves are confirmed from WHO's 2010 handbook (S59a).

729.title: [294] WHO-AIMS Instrument Version 2.2 (World Health Organization Assessment Instrument for Mental Health Systems), WHO/MSD/MER/05.02
729.text: World Health Organization. WHO's tool for collecting essential information on a country's or region's mental health system. Only WHO's catalogue page could be read; it says the instrument has 6 domains, 28 facets and 156 items but does not name the domains. The instrument itself, on WHO's repository, refused the fetch.

730.title: [295] An overview of Ghana's mental health system: results from an assessment using the World Health Organization's Assessment Instrument for Mental Health Systems (WHO-AIMS)
730.text: International Journal of Mental Health Systems (BioMed Central / Springer). A peer-reviewed article that applies WHO's Assessment Instrument for Mental Health Systems (WHO-AIMS) to Ghana. It is cited here only for its Methods section, which describes the instrument and names its six domains: policy and legislative framework; mental health services; mental health in primary care; human resources; public education and links with other sectors; and monitoring and research. WHO's own copy of the instrument (S59b) could not be opened, so this article is the source read for the domain names. It says nothing about Alabama.

731.title: [296] Comprehensive Mental Health Action Plan 2013–2030
731.text: World Health Organization. WHO's global mental health plan, updated in 2021 and extended to 2030. Only WHO's catalogue page could be read. It lists four objectives: more effective leadership and governance; comprehensive, integrated mental health and social care services in community-based settings; strategies for promotion and prevention; and stronger information systems, evidence and research.

732.title: [297] Code of Alabama §§22-52-4, 22-52-7 and 22-52-8, and §22-52-10.4(b)–(d): representation, limits on liberty before the hearing, and hearing deadlines in civil commitment
732.text: State of Alabama (2025 Code of Alabama, as published by Justia). Four further sections of the civil-commitment article, read for what happens between the petition and the order. Section 22-52-4 says that when a petition is filed the probate judge "shall appoint a guardian ad litem to represent and to protect the rights of the respondent" (the fetch returned only part of this section). Section 22-52-7 lets the judge limit the respondent's liberty before the final hearing only where necessary to prevent a real and present threat of substantial harm or to stop the person leaving the court's jurisdiction, allows detention at a designated mental health facility or a hospital, and says "No respondent shall be placed in a jail or other facility for individuals accused of or convicted of committing crimes." Section 22-52-8 requires a probable-cause hearing within seven days whenever such a limitation or temporary treatment is imposed, and a final hearing within 30 days of service of the petition. Section 22-52-10.4(d) says nothing in that section requires "a mental health provider to expand his or her current services if necessary funding is not provided". The article's contents page lists thirty sections; the rest were not read for this card.

733.title: [298] Code of Alabama §22-52-10.2: Findings Necessary for Outpatient Treatment
733.text: State of Alabama (2025 Code of Alabama, as published by Justia). The section of Alabama's civil-commitment law that sets the test for outpatient commitment. A probate judge may order outpatient treatment on clear and convincing evidence that the respondent has a mental illness, will without treatment "suffer mental distress and experience deterioration of the ability to function independently", and "is unable to maintain consistent engagement with outpatient treatment on a voluntary basis", shown either by the person's actions in the two years before the hearing or by aspects of the clinical condition that impair decisions about treatment. Unlike the inpatient test in §22-52-10.4, it does not require a finding of a real and present threat of substantial harm. Subsection (b) sets the findings for renewing an outpatient order. Read in full through the fetch tool; this section is not among those covered by card X-d1-02.

734.title: [299] Alabama Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 11.1: Definitions (mental incompetency)
734.text: Alabama Judicial System (judicial.alabama.gov). The Alabama court rule defining incompetency to stand trial: "A defendant is mentally incompetent to stand trial or to be sentenced for an offense if that defendant lacks sufficient present ability to assist in his or her defense by consulting with counsel with a reasonable degree of rational understanding of the facts and the legal proceedings against the defendant." Only this rule was read; the rules on how evaluations are ordered and what follows a finding of incompetency (Rules 11.2 onward) were not.

735.title: [300] Everybody's business — strengthening health systems to improve health outcomes: WHO's framework for action (publication page)
735.text: World Health Organization. WHO's catalogue page for its 2007 Framework for Action on health systems, the document in which the building-blocks scheme was set out. The overview says: "A key purpose of the Framework for Action is to promote a common understanding of what a health system is and what constitutes health systems strengthening." Only the catalogue page was read; it links the 843 kB PDF, which was not opened, and the page text itself does not list the six building blocks (card S59a does, from the 2010 handbook's chapter titles).

736.title: [301] State of Alabama Executive Budget, Fiscal Year 2027
736.text: Alabama Department of Finance, Executive Budget Office. The Governor's executive budget document for FY2027, posted in January 2026. A search-engine excerpt of it reads: "The annual appropriation acts for Alabama include legally adopted budgets for the State General Fund, Education Trust Fund, and other budgeted funds." Its budget calendar gives the fiscal year as October 1 to September 30, and its contents list a Special Mental Health Trust Fund summary at page C-33, which the fetch tool did not reach. It was read only for the fiscal-year dates and the description of the appropriation acts; no dollar figures are taken from it.

737.title: [302] Community Mental Health Services Block Grant
737.text: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. SAMHSA's program page for the Community Mental Health Services Block Grant.
