The text returned by the fetch tool gave one descriptive sentence: the program "makes funds available to all 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and 6 Pacific jurisdictions to provide community mental health services". The passages on target populations and set-asides were not in the text returned, so they are not cited from this page.

738.title: [303] Code of Alabama §28-3-202: Additional 10 percent tax; Special Mental Health Fund and general welfare purposes
738.text: State of Alabama (2025 Code of Alabama, as published by Justia). A section of Alabama's alcoholic-beverage law levying an additional 10 percent tax on the selling price of liquor and wine sold by the state board. It provides that the remainder of the proceeds of one of its taxes "shall be deposited in the State Treasury to the credit of a special fund which shall be designated the Alabama Special Mental Health Fund and shall be used only for mental health purposes", including prevention, care and treatment and mental health facilities. The history line cites Acts 1959, No. 312, with amendments in 1973 and 1986. Only this section was read: it shows one source of the fund, not all of them, and the shares going to the fund were not read.

739.title: [304] Matching rates
739.text: Medicaid and CHIP Payment and Access Commission (MACPAC). MACPAC's explanation of how the federal share of Medicaid spending is set. It says the federal share for most health care services is determined by the Federal Medical Assistance Percentage, that the FMAP "is based on a formula that provides higher reimbursement to states with lower per capita incomes relative to the national average", and that there is "a statutory minimum of 50 percent and a maximum of 83 percent". It is a national page with no Alabama figure in the text read.

740.title: [305] Medicaid State Plan Amendments
740.text: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Medicaid.gov. Medicaid.gov's page on state plans. It defines a Medicaid and CHIP state plan as "an agreement between a state and the Federal government describing how that state administers its Medicaid and CHIP programs", and says that when a state plans to change its program policies or operational approach it sends a state plan amendment to CMS for review and approval. Read through the fetch tool for the two definitions only.

741.title: [306] About Section 1115 Demonstrations
741.text: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Medicaid.gov. Medicaid.gov's explanation of Section 1115 demonstrations. It says Section 1115 of the Social Security Act gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority "to approve experimental, pilot, or demonstration projects", that demonstrations must be "budget neutral" to the federal government, and that they are generally approved for an initial five-year period and can be extended for a further three to five years. Read through the fetch tool for those three points only.

742.title: [307] Payment for services in institutions for mental diseases (IMDs)
742.text: Medicaid and CHIP Payment and Access Commission (MACPAC). MACPAC's explanation of the Medicaid IMD exclusion. It defines an IMD as "a hospital, nursing facility, or other institution of more than 16 beds that is primarily engaged in providing diagnosis, treatment, or care of persons with mental diseases, which includes substance use disorders", and says IMDs have historically not been eligible for Medicaid payment for services to people aged 21 to 64. It lists the ways states can pay for IMD care, including Section 1115 waivers for serious mental illness and for substance use disorder, a state plan option, managed-care payments limited to 15 days a month, and disproportionate share hospital payments.

743.title: [308] What Is Shortage Designation?
743.text: Health Resources and Services Administration, Bureau of Health Workforce. The federal health workforce agency's page explaining shortage designations, marked as last reviewed in April 2026. It says Health Professional Shortage Areas "can be geographic areas, populations, or facilities" and that "these areas have a shortage of primary, dental, or mental health care providers". A geographic designation covers everyone in a defined area; a population designation covers a specific group within an area. Read through the fetch tool with a request for verbatim definitions; the page does not explain how the HPSA score is calculated.

744.title: [309] Federal Poverty Level (FPL) (glossary entry)
744.text: HealthCare.gov (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services). HealthCare.gov's glossary definition: "A measure of income updated each year by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) that's used to determine eligibility for certain programs and benefits, like Marketplace savings, and Medicaid and the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) coverage." The dollar table on the page was not read.

745.title: [310] The Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA)
745.text: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. CMS's page on the federal parity law of 2008. Its introduction says the Act "generally prevents group health plans and health insurance issuers that provide mental health or substance use disorder (MH/SUD) benefits from imposing less favorable benefit limitations on those benefits than on medical/surgical benefits". Read through the fetch tool for that sentence only; the page's later sections on rules and enforcement were not read.

746.title: [311] Code of Alabama §22-51-2: Incorporation of public corporations, authorized
746.text: State of Alabama (text as published by Justia). The section of Alabama law that allows regional mental health boards to be formed. It reads: "Any number of natural persons, not less than three, may form a public corporation to contract with the State Board of Health or the Alabama Department of Mental Health in constructing and operating facilities and in carrying out programs in particular areas of the state." The history line is Acts 1967, No. 310, p. 853, §2, which is the origin of the name "310 board". Only this section of the chapter was read.

747.title: [312] Recovery After an Initial Schizophrenia Episode (RAISE): What is coordinated specialty care?
747.text: National Institute of Mental Health. NIMH's description of coordinated specialty care for first-episode psychosis: "a recovery-oriented, team approach to treating early psychosis that promotes easy access to care and shared decision-making among specialists, the person experiencing psychosis, and family members". It lists the components as psychotherapy, family support and education, medication management, supported employment and education, and case management. It is a national page and does not mention Alabama's NOVA programs.

748.title: [313] Federally Qualified Health Center (FQHC) (glossary entry)
748.text: HealthCare.gov (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services). HealthCare.gov's glossary definition: "Federally funded nonprofit health centers or clinics that serve medically underserved areas and populations." The entry adds that they provide primary care services regardless of ability to pay, on a sliding fee scale.

749.title: [314] What is a Health Center?
749.text: Health Resources and Services Administration, Bureau of Primary Health Care. The federal Health Center Program's description of a health center. It says health centers are community-based and led in part by patients, "serve everyone, even if they cannot pay", "adjust their fees based on income and family size" and "have a governing board where a majority of its members are patients". The page does not use the term Federally Qualified Health Center.

750.title: [315] Mental Illness (statistics page)
750.text: National Institute of Mental Health. NIMH's statistics page on mental illness, which gives the two survey definitions used in federal data. Any mental illness "is defined as a mental, behavioral, or emotional disorder". Serious mental illness "is defined as a mental, behavioral, or emotional disorder resulting in serious functional impairment, which substantially interferes with or limits one or more major life activities". Read through the fetch tool for the two definitions only; the prevalence figures on the page were not read.

751.title: [316] Broadband Equity Access and Deployment Program
751.text: National Telecommunications and Information Administration (BroadbandUSA). The federal program page for BEAD. It describes the program as "funded by the IIJA" and as "a $42.45 billion federal grant program that aims to connect every American to high-speed internet by funding partnerships to build infrastructure". It is a national page; Alabama's allocation and projects are not on it.

752.title: [317] TEFCA (Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement)
752.text: Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (healthit.gov). The federal health IT office's page on TEFCA. It says the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement "operates in the United States as a nationwide framework for health information sharing", and that Qualified Health Information Networks "are the individual networks that make up the backbone of TEFCA", together creating a network of networks. It names The Sequoia Project as the Recognized Coordinating Entity under a contract awarded in August 2023. It says nothing about Alabama.

753.title: [318] About YRBSS (Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System)
753.text: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. CDC's description of the Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System. It says the system "measures health-related behaviors and experiences that can lead to death and disability among youth and adults", that it includes a national Youth Risk Behavior Survey of high school students in public and private schools, and that the topics covered include "mental health including suicide". The text returned did not state how often the survey is run and says nothing about Alabama.

754.title: [319] About the State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (SUDORS)
754.text: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. CDC's page describing SUDORS. It says that "49 states and the District of Columbia collect and abstract data on drug overdose deaths for entry into a web-based CDC platform", and that "data are abstracted from death certificates, coroner/medical examiner reports, and postmortem toxicology reports". The text read does not name the participating states.

755.title: [320] Crisis Intervention Team (CIT) Programs
755.text: National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI). National NAMI's description of CIT. It calls a CIT program "an innovative, community-based approach to improve the outcomes" of encounters between police and people in mental health crisis, built on partnership between law enforcement, mental health providers, hospital emergency services and people with mental illness and their families. It refers to "the 40-hour CIT training for law enforcement". It is a national page and gives no Alabama figures.

756.title: [321] Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services (CLAS)
756.text: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Minority Health (Think Cultural Health). The federal Think Cultural Health page on the National CLAS Standards. It describes them as "a set of 15 action steps intended to improve quality of care and help eliminate health care disparities by providing a blueprint for individuals and health and health care organizations to implement culturally and linguistically appropriate services". The text returned did not include the wording of the individual standards.

757.title: [322] QuickFacts: Alabama counties, the 50 states, the District of Columbia and the United States (V2025)
757.text: U.S. Census Bureau. Census QuickFacts tables for each of Alabama's 67 counties and for every state, retrieved as the Bureau's own CSV files on 3 October 2026. They give the July 2025 population estimate and, from the 2020–2024 American Community Survey and related programs, age, race and ethnicity, veterans, income, poverty, health insurance, disability, broadband subscription and education. The county populations sum exactly to the state total, which was used as a check on the retrieval. Some rows carry no data year in their label; the site shows the label as the Bureau prints it.

758.title: [323] County Health Rankings & Roadmaps: Analytic Data, Supplemental Release (25 March 2026)
758.text: County Health Rankings & Roadmaps, University of Wisconsin Population Health Institute. A supplemental data release that updates fifty County Health Rankings measures with a newer data year, for every county and state. The site takes twelve measures from it: poor mental health days, frequent mental distress, suicide and drug overdose death rates, mental health provider and primary care physician ratios, uninsured adults, excessive drinking, social associations, life expectancy, loneliness and lack of social and emotional support. Each measure has its own underlying source and years, which the site shows with the layer. Survey-based values in this release are not comparable with the 2025 annual release, which appears to use a different method.

759.title: [324] 2025 County Health Rankings Annual Data Release: analytic data (v3)
759.text: County Health Rankings & Roadmaps, University of Wisconsin Population Health Institute. The most recent annual County Health Rankings release as of October 2026; no 2026 annual release had been published. The site uses it for three measures that the March 2026 supplement does not carry: children in poverty, severe housing problems and the share of residents living in rural areas. Values are given for every county and state with the underlying source and years for each measure.

760.title: [325] Health Professional Shortage Areas, mental health: designation detail file (BCD_HPSA_FCT_DET_MH)
760.text: Health Resources and Services Administration, data.hrsa.gov. The federal file listing every mental health shortage-area designation, read on 3 October 2026 and filtered to Alabama's area-based designations. It shows that 66 of Alabama's 67 counties are whole-county mental health shortage areas, with Madison the exception, and that 21 of those designations are flagged as proposed for withdrawal. Facility designations such as health centers and prisons are left out of the county layer. Each county's score is the one printed in the file.

761.title: [326] Suicide Mortality by State: Stats of the States
761.text: CDC, National Center for Health Statistics. The National Center for Health Statistics table of age-adjusted suicide death rates and death counts by state for 2024, drawn from the National Vital Statistics System. Alabama's rate is 15.9 per 100,000, on 837 deaths. These single-year state rates are not comparable with the multi-year county rates in County Health Rankings, and the count differs slightly from the 834 in Alabama's own vital statistics summary.

762.title: [327] Drug Overdose Mortality by State: Stats of the States
762.text: CDC, National Center for Health Statistics. The National Center for Health Statistics table of age-adjusted drug overdose death rates and death counts by state for 2024. Alabama's rate is 25.0 per 100,000, on 1,211 deaths. The count is higher than the floor of 1,151 given by Alabama's Opioid Overdose and Addiction Council, which was drawn from emergency-department records and described as a minimum.

763.title: [328] Status of State Action on the Medicaid Expansion Decision
763.text: KFF (State Health Facts). KFF's table of which states have adopted the Affordable Care Act's Medicaid expansion and when coverage began, as of October 2026. Forty states and the District of Columbia have adopted it; Alabama is one of ten states that have not. The site uses it for the expansion-status layer of the national map.

764.title: [329] Section 223 Medicaid CCBHC Demonstration and State Programs
764.text: SAMHSA. SAMHSA's page on the Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic Medicaid demonstration, with a 2026 map whose text description assigns each state to one category. It lists Alabama among the states participating in the demonstration. The description gives one category per state and may not show the full history of which states joined when, so the site presents the layer as SAMHSA's wording.

765.title: Alabama Department of Mental Health (ADMH)
765.text: ADMH · Alabama Department of Mental Health · Department of Mental Health — The state agency responsible for public mental health, substance use and developmental disability services in Alabama.

766.title: State mental health authority (SMHA)
766.text: state mental health authority · state mental health agency · SMHA-controlled · SMHA — The agency in each state that is accountable for the public mental health system and reports on it to the federal government. In Alabama it is ADMH.

767.title: Commissioner of Mental Health
767.text: ADMH Commissioner · the Commissioner — The head of the Alabama Department of Mental Health, appointed by the Governor.

768.title: ADMH Board of Trustees
768.text: ADMH Board of Trustees · Board of Trustees · ADMH board — The sixteen-member board, chaired by the Governor, that oversees the Department of Mental Health and meets quarterly.

769.title: ADMH Strategic Plan 2025–2028 (and the goal codes A1 to E3)
769.text: ADMH Strategic Plan 2025–2028 · ADMH Strategic Plan · ADMH plan goals touched · ADMH's five strategic priorities — The Department's plan, built on five priorities. The codes such as A1 or B4 are this report's labels for goals under each priority.

770.title: ADMH five-year plan (February 2025)
770.text: five-year plan · five-year goal · five-year bed goal — Targets the Commissioner presented to legislators in February 2025: more civil beds, more mobile crisis teams, more crisis centers.

771.title: Legislative Services Agency (LSA) and its comparison sheets
771.text: LSA · comparison sheets · Legislative Fiscal Officer — The Legislature's staff agency. Its line-by-line budget comparison sheets are this report's source for what was appropriated.

772.title: Alabama Commission on the Evaluation of Services (ACES)
772.text: ACES · Alabama Commission on the Evaluation of Services · Commission on the Evaluation of Services · evaluation commission — A state commission, created in 2019, that evaluates whether state programs work and advises the Legislature and the Governor.

773.title: State mental health planning council
773.text: state mental health planning council · State planning council · planning council — A council every state must keep as a condition of the federal mental health block grant, with people who use services among its members.

774.title: SB101 (Act 2025-455): age of consent for treatment
774.text: SB101 · Act 2025-455 — A 2025 Alabama law raising from 14 to 16 the age at which a minor can consent alone to medical and mental health treatment.

775.title: Parental opt-in consent for school mental health services (Act 2022-442)
775.text: Act 2022-442 · opt-in — Since 2022 Alabama schools need a parent's written permission before a student receives ongoing mental health services.

776.title: SB236 (Act 2025-366): sheriffs and probate judges on regional boards
776.text: SB236 · Act 2025-366 — A 2025 law that puts a sheriff and a probate judge on the executive committee of larger regional mental health boards.

777.title: Accountability courts (SB200, Act 2025-183)
777.text: accountability courts · SB200 · Act 2025-183 · drug courts — Alabama's new name for drug courts, which since October 2025 may also take defendants with mental illness and veterans.

778.title: Specialty courts (mental health, veterans and drug courts)
778.text: specialty courts · specialty-court · mental health court · veterans court — Court dockets that put eligible defendants under supervised treatment in place of ordinary prosecution or jail.

779.title: Houston Hunter Act (SB40, 2025)
779.text: Houston Hunter Act · SB40 · firearm-hold agreements · SAFER program — A 2025 Alabama law letting a person voluntarily leave firearms with a licensed dealer for a time, as a suicide-prevention measure.

780.title: Lethal means
780.text: lethal means · lethal-means — The method a person might use to end their life. Putting time and distance between a person in crisis and a gun or drugs lowers risk.

781.title: HB487 (2026): opioid-settlement appropriation
781.text: HB487 · supplemental appropriation — The 2026 bill that appropriated $43.1 million of opioid-settlement money across agencies, most of it to ADMH.

782.title: 2025 federal budget law (H.R.1)
782.text: 2025 federal budget law · H.R.1 — The federal budget reconciliation law of July 2025, which changed Medicaid financing rules and tightened SNAP work requirements.

783.title: Civil commitment
783.text: civil commitment · civil-commitment · probate commitment — A court order requiring a person with mental illness to accept treatment because they pose a serious danger. It is not a criminal matter.

784.title: Probate court and probate judge
784.text: probate court · probate courts · probate judge · probate judges — The county court that, in Alabama, hears petitions for civil commitment. Each county has a probate judge.

785.title: Clear and convincing evidence
785.text: clear and convincing evidence — A standard of proof: stronger than "more likely than not", weaker than "beyond a reasonable doubt". Alabama requires it for commitment.

786.title: Least restrictive alternative
786.text: least restrictive alternative — The rule that a court must choose the form of treatment that limits a person's liberty no more than is needed.

787.title: Outpatient commitment
787.text: outpatient commitment — A court order to follow a treatment plan while living in the community rather than in a hospital.

788.title: Involuntary (civil-commitment) beds
788.text: involuntary beds · Involuntary bed capacity · civil-commitment beds · civil beds · civil psychiatric beds · involuntary (civil-commitment) beds — Psychiatric beds available for people under a civil-commitment order. ADMH counted 771 in January 2026.

789.title: Beds per 100,000 residents (the 30-bed benchmark)
789.text: beds per 100,000 · 30 per 100,000 · Treatment Advocacy Center — A way of comparing psychiatric bed supply with population. ADMH plans against a benchmark of 30 beds per 100,000 residents.

790.title: Forensic mental health care
790.text: forensic — Mental health services ordered by criminal courts: evaluating whether a defendant can stand trial and treating those who cannot.

791.title: Competency evaluation (competency to stand trial)
791.text: competency evaluation · outpatient forensic evaluations · competency — An examination, ordered by a criminal court, of whether a defendant understands the proceedings well enough to be tried.

792.title: Competency restoration
792.text: competency restoration · inpatient-restoration · restoration — Treatment meant to make a defendant found incompetent able to stand trial. Until it happens the criminal case is on hold.

793.title: Jail-based competency restoration
793.text: jail-based competency restoration · jail-based restoration · telehealth restoration program — Restoration treatment delivered inside a county jail, in person or by video, instead of waiting for a state hospital bed.

794.title: Forensic waitlist
794.text: forensic waitlist · waitlist — The number of people held in county jails while waiting for a court-ordered competency evaluation or a restoration bed.

795.title: Forensic navigators
795.text: forensic navigators · navigators — Department staff who work the forensic waitlist, identifying people who may be better served outside the forensic system.

796.title: Hunter v. Boswell (the Hunter consent decree)
796.text: Hunter v. Beshear · Hunter v. Boswell · Hunter consent decree · Hunter decree · Hunter timelines · Hunter timeline — A federal court settlement, in force since 2018, that limits how long people may wait in Alabama jails for competency services.

797.title: Braggs v. Commissioner (the prison mental health case)
797.text: Braggs v. Commissioner, Alabama Department of Corrections · Braggs v. Lovelace · Braggs — A federal class action in which a court found in 2017 that mental health care in Alabama's prisons was unconstitutional.

798.title: Wyatt v. Stickney
798.text: Wyatt v. Stickney · Wyatt — The 1971 Alabama case that established a constitutional right to adequate treatment for people confined in state psychiatric hospitals.

799.title: Consent decree
799.text: consent decree · decree · decrees — A settlement of a lawsuit that a court approves and then enforces as its own order.

800.title: Eighth Amendment
800.text: Eighth Amendment — The part of the U.S. Constitution that bans cruel and unusual punishments. Courts read it to require adequate health care in prisons.

801.title: State General Fund
801.text: General Fund — One of Alabama's two main state budgets. It pays for most non-education agencies, including mental health, Medicaid and prisons.

802.title: Education Trust Fund (ETF)
802.text: Education Trust Fund · ETF — Alabama's separate state budget for education. A small part of it reaches ADMH, mostly for services tied to schools and children.

803.title: Special Mental Health Fund
803.text: Special Mental Health Fund — A state fund fed by earmarked taxes that may be spent only on mental health. It supplied about a sixth of ADMH's revenue in FY2025.

804.title: Appropriation
804.text: appropriation · appropriations — The Legislature's legal permission for an agency to spend a set amount of public money in a given year.

805.title: Conditions on appropriations (withheld installments)
805.text: quarterly installments · Conditioned appropriations · appropriation conditions · FY2027 conditions — Strings the Legislature attaches to money. In FY2027 part of ADMH's crisis funding is held back until the Department reports on results.

806.title: Fiscal year (FY)
806.text: fiscal year · FY2021 · FY2022 · FY2023 · FY2024 · FY2025 · FY2026 · FY2027 — A budget year. Alabama's runs from 1 October to 30 September and is named for the year in which it ends.

807.title: Mental Health Block Grant (federal block grants)
807.text: Mental Health Block Grant · block grants · block grant · block-grant — Federal money given to each state by formula for community mental health services, with planning and reporting duties attached.

808.title: Opioid-settlement funds
808.text: opioid-settlement funds · opioid-settlement · opioid settlements · Opioid Settlement Fund · Opioid Treatment Fund · settlement funds · settlement funding — Money paid to the state under legal settlements with opioid makers and distributors, appropriated by the Legislature for treatment and prevention.

809.title: Alabama Rural Health Transformation Program
809.text: Alabama Rural Health Transformation Program · Rural Health Transformation Program · Rural Health Transformation · rural-health grants — A federally funded grant program, run in Alabama by ADECA, that began awarding money to rural health providers in August 2026.

810.title: State mental health agency spending per resident
810.text: per resident · per-capita spending — What a state's mental health agency spends in a year divided by the state's population, used to compare states.

811.title: Medicaid (Alabama Medicaid Agency)
811.text: Medicaid · Alabama Medicaid Agency · Alabama Medicaid — The public health insurance program for low-income people, paid for jointly by the federal government and the state.

812.title: Federal match (FMAP)
812.text: FMAP · federal match · Medicaid match — The share of Medicaid costs the federal government pays. Poorer states get a higher share; Alabama's is about 73 percent.

813.title: Enhanced federal match
813.text: enhanced federal match · enhanced match — A federal share of Medicaid costs higher than a state's usual rate, offered to encourage a particular service or policy.

814.title: Medicaid expansion
814.text: expanded Medicaid · non-expansion · expansion states · coverage expansion — The option, under the Affordable Care Act, for a state to cover low-income adults whatever their family or health status. Alabama has not taken it.

815.title: Coverage gap
815.text: coverage gap · coverage-gap — Adults who earn too much for Alabama's Medicaid but too little to qualify for subsidized marketplace insurance.

816.title: Federal poverty level
816.text: federal poverty level · poverty line — An income figure the federal government sets each year, by family size, and uses to decide who qualifies for programs.

817.title: Medicaid state plan and state plan amendment (SPA)
817.text: state plan amendment · Medicaid's state plan · SPAs · SPA — The state plan is Alabama's standing agreement with the federal government on how it runs Medicaid. An amendment changes it.

818.title: Section 1115 waiver
818.text: Section 1115 waiver · 1115 waiver · Section 1115 · waivers · waiver — Federal permission for a state to test a Medicaid approach that the ordinary rules would not allow, for a limited period.

819.title: Medicaid reentry waiver
819.text: Medicaid reentry waiver · reentry waiver — A Section 1115 waiver that lets Medicaid pay for some health services shortly before a person leaves jail or prison.

820.title: Medicaid suspension during incarceration
820.text: suspended, not terminated · suspends rather than terminates — Alabama pauses, and does not cancel, a person's Medicaid eligibility while they are in prison or jail.

821.title: Institution for mental disease (IMD)
821.text: institutions for mental disease — Medicaid's term for a psychiatric or substance use facility with more than 16 beds. Medicaid usually will not pay for adults' stays in one.

822.title: Fee-for-service
822.text: fee-for-service — Payment by the item: the provider bills a set fee for each visit or procedure. More services mean more payment.

823.title: Managed care
823.text: managed care · managed-care — An arrangement in which a state pays health plans a fixed amount per member and the plans arrange and pay for care.

824.title: Alabama Coordinated Health Network (ACHN)
824.text: Alabama Coordinated Health Network · ACHN — Alabama Medicaid's care-coordination program, organized in seven regions. It coordinates care but does not pay for it as a health plan would.

825.title: Medicaid rehabilitative services (rule 560-X-47)
825.text: rehabilitative mental-health and substance-use services · rehabilitative services · 560-X-47 — The Medicaid benefit that pays for community mental health and substance use treatment delivered by ADMH-certified providers.

826.title: Commercial (employer-sponsored) insurance
826.text: Employer-sponsored insurance · employer coverage · commercial market · Commercial insurance · commercial health-insurance market — Private health insurance, most often obtained through a job. Half of Alabamians are covered this way.

827.title: Health insurance marketplace
827.text: marketplace · individual-market — The federal exchange (HealthCare.gov) where people without job-based coverage buy insurance, often with a subsidy tied to income.

828.title: Provider tax
828.text: provider taxes · provider tax — A tax a state charges hospitals or other providers and uses to pay its own share of Medicaid, drawing federal match in return.

829.title: Mental health parity
829.text: mental-health parity · parity enforcement — The legal rule that an insurance plan may not limit mental health benefits more tightly than medical and surgical benefits.

830.title: Twelve-month postpartum Medicaid coverage
830.text: postpartum coverage · postpartum care — Medicaid coverage that continues for a year after a birth instead of ending after 60 days.

831.title: Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic (CCBHC)
831.text: CCBHC · CCBHCs · Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic · Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics — A clinic certified to provide nine required mental health and substance use services and paid a set daily rate by Medicaid.

832.title: Prospective payment (the CCBHC daily rate, PPS-1)
832.text: prospective payment · prospective-payment · prospective daily rate · daily prospective rate · PPS-1 · CCBHC rate · daily rate · daily payment — A payment set in advance. A CCBHC gets one fixed amount for each day it gives a Medicaid enrollee a qualifying service, whatever the service.

833.title: Cost report
833.text: cost report — A clinic's formal statement of what it costs to operate, used to set its CCBHC daily rate.

834.title: Section 223 CCBHC Medicaid demonstration
834.text: Section 223 CCBHC demonstration · Section 223 demonstration · CCBHC demonstration · Medicaid demonstration — The federal program under which selected states pay CCBHCs through Medicaid at a prospective rate. Alabama joined in June 2024.

835.title: Designated collaborating organization (DCO)
835.text: designated collaborating organizations — A separate provider that a CCBHC contracts with to deliver one of its required services.

836.title: Community mental health center (CMHC)
836.text: CMHC · CMHCs · community mental health centers · community mental health center — One of the 19 regional organizations that deliver most public outpatient mental health care in Alabama under contract with ADMH.

837.title: Regional mental health authority board (310 board)
837.text: regional mental health authority board · Regional (310) mental health authority boards · regional (310) mental health authority board · Regional (310) boards · regional "310" board · regional boards — The public corporation that governs a community mental health center. The nickname comes from Act 310 of 1967, the law that allows them.

838.title: ADMH certification
838.text: ADMH-certified · ADMH certification — The Department's approval that a community provider meets its standards. Without it a provider cannot bill Medicaid for these services.

839.title: Crisis system: someone to contact, someone to respond, a safe place for help
839.text: someone to contact · someone to respond · a safe place for help · crisis system · crisis-system — The national model for mental health crisis care, built from three parts: a line to call, a team that comes out, and a place to go.

840.title: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
840.text: 988 — The national three-digit number for a mental health or suicide crisis, by call, text or chat, at any hour.

841.title: In-state answer rate
841.text: in-state answer rate · answer rate · answer rates — The share of 988 calls from Alabama that are answered by a counselor in Alabama instead of rolling over to a national backup center.

842.title: Georouting
842.text: georoute — Sending a 988 call or text to the crisis center nearest the person's rough location, not the one matching the phone's area code.

843.title: Veterans Crisis Line
843.text: Veterans Crisis Line — The crisis line for veterans and service members, reached by dialing 988 and pressing 1.

844.title: Mobile crisis team
844.text: mobile crisis · mobile-crisis · mobile teams — Clinicians who travel to a person in crisis, at home or elsewhere in the community, in place of police or an ambulance.

845.title: Crisis diversion center (crisis center)
845.text: crisis diversion centers · crisis centers · crisis center · crisis-center · crisis stabilization — A walk-in center, open at all hours, where a person in mental health crisis can be assessed and stabilized instead of going to an emergency room or jail.

846.title: Observation beds (temporary and extended)
846.text: observation beds — Short-stay beds in a crisis center where a person is watched and treated for hours or a few days, not admitted to a hospital.

847.title: Crisis residential unit
847.text: crisis residential units · crisis residential beds · crisis residential — A small staffed residence where a person in crisis can stay for a short period as an alternative to a hospital ward.

848.title: Pediatric crisis unit
848.text: pediatric crisis unit — A crisis center for young people. Alabama has one, WellStone's 24-bed unit in Huntsville for ages 12 to 18.

849.title: Rural crisis-care programs
849.text: rural crisis-care programs · rural crisis-care · rural crisis care · rural crisis programs — State-funded programs that bring crisis response to rural counties far from any of the six crisis centers.

850.title: Diversion
850.text: diversion · diversions — Steering a person away from a costlier or more harmful setting, such as jail or an emergency room, and into care or a community program.

851.title: Co-responder program
851.text: co-responder · co-responders — A police unit in which a mental health clinician rides with or joins an officer on calls involving a person in crisis.

852.title: Emergency-department boarding
852.text: emergency-department boarding — Holding a psychiatric patient in an emergency room, sometimes for days, because no inpatient bed or placement is available.

853.title: Catchment area
853.text: catchment — The set of counties a facility is assigned to serve. It shows who is responsible for an area, not how far people must travel.

854.title: Utilization
854.text: utilization — How much of a facility's capacity is in use, usually the share of available beds that are filled over a period.

855.title: Bed-day (cost per bed-day)
855.text: per bed-day · bed-day — One bed occupied for one day. Cost per bed-day divides a facility's spending by the number of bed-days it delivered.

856.title: Continuum of mental health care
856.text: Service-Delivery Continuum · Continuum lens · National Academies' continuum · the continuum — The full range of mental health services arranged by intensity, from promotion and prevention through treatment and crisis care to recovery supports.

857.title: Beyond Beds
857.text: Beyond Beds — A 2017 national policy paper arguing that psychiatric hospital beds work only as one part of a complete range of services.

858.title: Promotion and prevention
858.text: promotion and prevention · Promotion, prevention and early intervention — The earliest part of the continuum: building mental well-being in everyone and acting before a disorder develops.

859.title: Outpatient care
859.text: outpatient — Treatment a person attends by appointment while living at home: therapy, psychiatric visits, medication management.

860.title: Step-down care
860.text: step-down — A less intensive setting a person moves to after a hospital or crisis stay, such as a staffed residence, before living independently.

861.title: Recovery supports
861.text: recovery supports — The services that help a person keep a home, a job and relationships once the acute illness is treated.

862.title: Residential services (ADMH's residential tiers)
862.text: residential tiers · residential services · residential care · adult residential care homes · semi-independent apartments — Places to live with staff support, in grades from closely supervised homes to semi-independent apartments, funded through community contracts.

863.title: Supported (supportive) housing
863.text: supported housing · supportive housing · supportive-housing · permanent-supportive-housing — An ordinary home paired with visiting support services, so that a person with serious mental illness can live in the community.

864.title: Supported employment
864.text: supported employment · supported-employment — Help finding and keeping an ordinary paid job, with a specialist who supports both the worker and the employer.

865.title: Individual Placement and Support (IPS)
865.text: Individual Placement and Support · IPS — The evidence-based model of supported employment for people with serious mental illness: a quick job search, then lasting support.

866.title: Assertive Community Treatment (ACT)
866.text: Assertive Community Treatment — A team of clinicians that brings intensive treatment to people with serious mental illness where they live, instead of waiting for clinic visits.

867.title: Case management (targeted case management)
867.text: targeted case management · case management · case managers — Help from a named worker who links a person to treatment, benefits and housing, and keeps the pieces connected.

868.title: First-episode psychosis programs (coordinated specialty care; NOVA)
868.text: first-episode psychosis · coordinated specialty care · first-episode programs · NOVA — Team-based early treatment for young people having a first psychotic episode. Alabama's three programs use the name NOVA.

869.title: Peer support specialist
869.text: peer support specialists · peer specialists · certified peer specialist · peer and family support · peer support · certified peers · peer-support · Office of Peer Programs — A person in recovery from mental illness or addiction who is trained and certified to support others going through the same.

870.title: Peer-run organization
870.text: Peer-run organizations · peer-run — An organization led and staffed by people who have themselves lived with mental illness or addiction.

871.title: Integrated behavioral health (collaborative care)
871.text: integrated behavioral health · integrated-care · collaborative-care — Mental health care delivered inside primary care, with the family doctor and a mental health clinician working as one team.

872.title: Federally qualified health center (FQHC)
872.text: federally qualified health centers · federally funded health centers · FQHC — A federally funded community clinic that provides primary care to anyone, with fees scaled to income.

873.title: Serious mental illness (SMI)
873.text: serious mental illness · severely mentally ill — A mental disorder in an adult that seriously limits daily life, such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or severe depression.

874.title: Serious emotional disturbance (SED)
874.text: serious emotional disturbance — The children's counterpart of serious mental illness: a diagnosable disorder in someone under 18 that seriously limits life at home, at school or with others.

875.title: Intellectual and developmental disabilities
875.text: intellectual and developmental disabilities · developmental disabilities · developmental-disability · intellectual-disability — Lifelong conditions that begin in childhood and affect learning and daily living, such as intellectual disability and autism.

876.title: Substance use disorder (SUD)
876.text: substance-use disorder · opioid use disorder · SUD — The clinical term for addiction: continued use of alcohol or drugs despite serious harm. Opioid use disorder is one kind.

877.title: Medication-assisted treatment (MAT)
877.text: Medication-assisted treatment — Treating opioid addiction with a prescribed medicine, such as buprenorphine or methadone, usually alongside counseling.

878.title: Naloxone
878.text: naloxone — A medicine that reverses an opioid overdose within minutes, often given as a nasal spray.

879.title: Detoxification (detox)
879.text: detoxification · detox-capable · detox — Medically supervised withdrawal from alcohol or drugs. It is the first step of treatment, not the whole of it.

880.title: State psychiatric hospital
880.text: state hospitals · state hospital · state psychiatric facilities · state facilities · state-hospital — A psychiatric hospital owned and run by the state. Alabama has three, operated by ADMH.

881.title: Taylor Hardin Secure Medical Facility
881.text: Taylor Hardin Secure Medical Facility · Taylor Hardin · forensic hospital — The state's forensic psychiatric hospital, in Tuscaloosa, for people sent by the criminal courts.

882.title: Telehealth
882.text: telehealth · audio-only · telepsychiatry · live-video — Care delivered at a distance by video or telephone. Audio-only means an ordinary phone call with no video.

883.title: Telehealth payment parity
883.text: telehealth at parity · telehealth parity · at parity — Paying a provider the same for a visit by video or phone as for the same visit in person.

884.title: BEAD (Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment)
884.text: BEAD — The federal grant program paying to bring high-speed internet to homes and businesses that have none.

885.title: One Health Record (Alabama's health information exchange)
885.text: One Health Record · health information exchange · HIE — Alabama's network for sharing patient records electronically between hospitals, clinics and other providers.

886.title: TEFCA and QHINs
886.text: TEFCA · QHIN · eHealth Exchange — TEFCA is the federal framework for sharing health records nationwide. A QHIN is one of the approved networks that carry the traffic.

887.title: 42 CFR Part 2
887.text: 42 CFR Part 2 — The federal rule that gives substance use treatment records stricter confidentiality protection than other health records.

888.title: Alabama Community Services Information System (ACSIS)
888.text: Alabama Community Services Information System · ACSIS — ADMH's reporting system for mental illness and CCBHC providers: clients, episodes of care, staff and billing.

889.title: Alabama Substance Abuse Information System (ASAIS)
889.text: Alabama Substance Abuse Information System · ASAIS — ADMH's reporting and billing system for substance use treatment providers.

890.title: CCBHC outcomes platform (Netsmart)
890.text: Netsmart · outcomes platform — The software ADMH has bought so that CCBHCs can report the outcome measures the federal demonstration requires.

891.title: Health Professional Shortage Area (HPSA)
891.text: mental health professional shortage areas · shortage areas · shortage-area · Shortage designations · HPSA — A place, population or facility the federal government has designated as having too few health care providers.

892.title: Percent of need met
892.text: need met — In federal shortage data, the share of the psychiatrists a shortage area would need that it actually has.

893.title: Mental health workforce availability (provider ratio)
893.text: workforce availability · workforce-availability — Residents per mental health provider. Mental Health America ranks Alabama last on it, at 740 residents for each provider.

894.title: National Health Service Corps (NHSC)
894.text: National Health Service Corps — A federal program that repays clinicians' student loans in return for working in a shortage area.

895.title: Interstate licensure compact
895.text: licensure compacts · interstate compacts · compacts · EMS Compact · Occupational Therapy Compact — An agreement among states that lets a clinician licensed in one member state practice in the others, in person or by telehealth.

896.title: PSYPACT (Psychology Interjurisdictional Compact)
896.text: Psychology Interjurisdictional Compact · PSYPACT — The compact that lets psychologists practice by telehealth, and for short periods in person, across member states.

897.title: Counseling Compact
897.text: Counseling Compact — The compact for licensed professional counselors. Alabama is a member, but it is not yet working in Alabama.

898.title: Nurse Licensure Compact (NLC)
898.text: Nurse Licensure Compact · NLC — The compact under which a nurse holds one multistate licence valid in all member states.

899.title: Social Work Licensure Compact
899.text: Social Work Licensure Compact — The compact for social workers. Alabama joined in 2024; multistate licences are not yet being issued.

900.title: Direct-support professional
900.text: direct-support-professional · direct-support staff · direct-support wage · direct-support — A front-line worker who helps people with developmental disabilities with daily living, at home or in a residence.

901.title: Psychiatry residency and fellowship
901.text: psychiatry residency · residencies · fellowships · fellows — The years of supervised hospital training a doctor completes after medical school to become a psychiatrist; a fellowship adds a subspecialty.

902.title: Faith-Based Support Specialist
902.text: Faith-Based Support Specialists · Faith-Based Support Specialist · Agency for Substance Abuse Prevention — A faith leader certified, after a short training, to recognize addiction and connect people to treatment.

903.title: Mental Health First Aid
903.text: Mental Health First Aid — An eight-hour course that teaches members of the public to recognize and respond to someone developing a mental health problem or in crisis.

904.title: Uniform Reporting System (URS)
904.text: Uniform Reporting System · URS · federal tables — The standard set of tables each state mental health agency files with the federal government every year, published state by state.

905.title: Penetration rate
905.text: penetration rate — The number of people the public mental health system served in a year for every 1,000 residents of the state.

906.title: Readmission rate
906.text: readmission · readmissions — The share of people discharged from a hospital who are admitted again within a set time, usually 30 or 180 days.

907.title: Reporting year
907.text: reporting year — The twelve months a set of figures covers. For the federal tables it is October to September, not the calendar year.

908.title: Consumer survey
908.text: Consumer survey · consumer-survey — A survey of people who use public mental health services, asking about access, quality and results of their care.

909.title: Rates per 1,000, per 10,000 and per 100,000
909.text: per 100,000 · per 10,000 · per 1,000 — A count divided by population so that places of different size can be compared. The base (1,000 or 100,000) is a matter of convention.

910.title: State rankings (of 51 or 52 jurisdictions)
910.text: of 52 jurisdictions · of 51 — A state's position in an ordered list. "Of 51" counts the states and the District of Columbia; "of 52" adds Puerto Rico.

911.title: All ages versus adults
911.text: all ages · all-ages — A label on a figure saying whether children are included. The same measure can differ noticeably between the two groups.

912.title: Disaggregated data
912.text: Disaggregated · Disaggregate — Figures broken down by group, such as race, county or age, so that differences hidden in a total can be seen.

913.title: Provisional figure
913.text: provisional figure — A preliminary count that is expected to change as late records arrive.

914.title: Seven-day follow-up
914.text: seven-day follow-up · seven-day follow-up-after-discharge — The share of people who see a mental health provider within seven days of leaving a psychiatric hospital.

915.title: Mental Health America (MHA) rankings
915.text: Mental Health America · MHA — A national advocacy organization whose yearly report ranks the states on 17 measures of mental illness and access to care.

916.title: Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS)
916.text: Youth Risk Behavior Survey · YRBS — A federal survey of high-school students on behaviors that affect health, including mental health and suicide.

917.title: Kids Count
917.text: Kids Count — A collection of indicators of child well-being for Alabama and each county, compiled by VOICES for Alabama's Children.

918.title: Maternal mortality review
918.text: maternal mortality review · pregnancy-related — A committee review of each death during or soon after pregnancy, to decide whether it was related to the pregnancy and preventable.

919.title: Point-in-Time (PIT) count
919.text: Point-in-Time count · Point-in-Time · PIT count — A count of everyone found homeless, in shelters and on the street, on a single night in January.

920.title: Rural (two different measures)
920.text: Census-defined rural · deemed rural · rural areas — This report uses two measures: counties classed as rural, and the share of people living in rural areas. They are not interchangeable.

921.title: Sequential Intercept Model
921.text: Sequential Intercept Model · intercepts · intercept — A map of the points at which a person with mental illness can be turned from the criminal justice system toward treatment.

922.title: Crisis Intervention Team (CIT)
922.text: Crisis Intervention Team · CIT-trained · CIT — A program that trains police officers to respond to people in mental health crisis and links police with local mental health services.

923.title: Alabama Peace Officers' Standards and Training Commission (APOSTC)
923.text: Alabama Peace Officers' Standards and Training Commission · Peace Officers' Standards and Training Commission · APOSTC · APOST — The state body that sets training and certification standards for police officers.

924.title: Stepping Up
924.text: Stepping Up Alabama · Stepping Up — A national initiative to reduce the number of people with mental illness in county jails, administered in Alabama by ADMH.

925.title: Jail mental health screening
925.text: Jail screening · booking screen · screening at booking — A short set of questions asked when a person is booked into jail, to identify mental illness or suicide risk early.

926.title: Administrative Office of Courts (AOC)
926.text: Administrative Office of Courts · AOC — The agency that manages Alabama's state court system on behalf of the Chief Justice.

927.title: Alabama Department of Corrections (ADOC)
927.text: Alabama Department of Corrections · Department of Corrections · ADOC — The state agency that runs Alabama's prisons. Its mental health care is under federal court order.

928.title: Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles
928.text: Bureau of Pardons and Paroles · Pardons and Paroles — The state agency that supervises people on probation and parole and runs reentry programs.

929.title: Parole and probation
929.text: parole grant rate · parole · probation — Probation is supervision in the community in place of prison. Parole is supervised release after part of a prison sentence is served.

930.title: Recidivism
930.text: recidivism — Returning to crime or custody after release. The rate depends heavily on how "return" is defined and over how many years.

931.title: Reentry
931.text: reentry — The return of a person from prison or jail to the community, and the services that support it.

932.title: Reentry Task Force and the Reentry Alabama plan
932.text: Reentry Task Force · Reentry Alabama — A state task force created in 2025 to carry out Alabama's plan for reducing reoffending among people leaving prison.

933.title: Day Reporting Center
933.text: Day Reporting Centers · day-reporting centers · Day Reporting Center Lite · DRCs — A facility where people on probation or parole report regularly for supervision, treatment and job help while living at home.

934.title: Community corrections
934.text: community corrections — Locally run programs that supervise people convicted of crimes in the community as an alternative to prison.

935.title: WHO health-system building blocks
935.text: — The World Health Organization's six-part description of what any health system needs, which this report adapts into eight domains.

936.title: System of Care (children's mental health framework)
936.text: System of Care framework · System of Care principles · A System of Care — A national framework holding that services for children with serious mental health needs should be family-driven, community-based and coordinated across agencies.

937.title: Social determinants of health (SDOH)
937.text: social determinants · SDOH — The conditions of daily life, such as housing, income, schooling and transport, that shape health apart from medical care.

938.title: Healthy People 2030
938.text: Healthy People 2030 — The federal government's set of national health objectives for the decade to 2030.

939.title: Trauma-informed care
939.text: trauma-informed care — An approach that assumes many people seeking help have lived through trauma and organizes services so as not to repeat the harm.

940.title: CLAS standards and language access
940.text: CLAS-standards · CLAS · language assistance · limited English proficiency · Language access — National standards for health services that respect patients' culture and language, including interpreters at no cost.

941.title: Continuum of Care (HUD homelessness planning body)
941.text: Continuums of Care · Continuum of Care · CoCs · CoC · NACH — A regional body, recognized by the federal housing department, that plans the local response to homelessness and sets priorities for federal funds.

942.title: Emergency Solutions Grants (ESG)
942.text: Emergency Solutions Grants · ESG — Federal money for emergency shelter, short-term rental help and related services, passed through the state to local agencies.

943.title: SNAP
943.text: SNAP — The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, the federal food benefit once called food stamps.

944.title: SSI and SSDI (disability income)
944.text: Social Security disability benefits · SSI/SSDI · SSI — Two federal disability payments. SSDI is insurance earned through past work; SSI is a smaller payment for disabled people with very low income.

945.title: Vocational rehabilitation (ADRS)
945.text: Department of Rehabilitation Services · Vocational Rehabilitation · competitive integrated employment · ADRS — The state program that helps people with disabilities prepare for and find work, run by the Alabama Department of Rehabilitation Services.

946.title: ADMH Office of Child and Family Services
946.text: Office of Child and Family Services · Office of Child & Family Services · Child & Family Services · Child and Family Services — The ADMH office, created in October 2023, that brings the Department's programs for children and families under one roof.

947.title: School-Based Mental Health Collaboration
947.text: School-Based Mental Health Collaboration · school-based mental health · school-based services — A program, begun in 2010, that places community mental health center clinicians in schools.

948.title: Mental Health Services Coordinator (MHSC)
948.text: Mental Health Services Coordinators · Mental Health Services Coordinator · MHSCs — A school-district employee who links students to mental health services. State law requires every district to have one.

949.title: Local education agency (LEA)
949.text: local education agencies · local education agency · LEAs · LEA — The official term for a school district: a city or county school system.

950.title: Alabama State Department of Education (ALSDE)
950.text: ALSDE · State Department of Education — The state agency that oversees Alabama's public schools.

951.title: PATHS (Pediatric Access to Telemental Health Services)
951.text: Pediatric Access to Telemental Health Services · PATHS consult line — A consultation line through which primary-care doctors can get advice from child mental health specialists at Children's of Alabama.

952.title: Infant and early-childhood mental health
952.text: infant and early-childhood mental health · infant and early-childhood programs — Support for the emotional development of children from birth to about five, delivered mainly through the adults who care for them.

953.title: Intensive in-home services
953.text: intensive in-home services · intensive home-based services — Frequent treatment delivered in the family home for a child at risk of being placed in a hospital or residential care.

954.title: Wraparound
954.text: wraparound — A way of planning care for a child with complex needs, in which one team builds a single plan around the family across all the agencies involved.

955.title: Therapeutic foster care
955.text: Therapeutic Foster Care-Enhanced · therapeutic foster care · therapeutic-foster-care — Foster care with specially trained foster parents and clinical support, for children whose needs an ordinary foster home cannot meet.

956.title: Out-of-home care (foster care)
956.text: out-of-home care · foster care — The placement of a child, by the child-welfare agency, away from the family home: with relatives, foster parents or in a facility.

957.title: Alabama Department of Human Resources (DHR)
957.text: Department of Human Resources · Alabama DHR · DHR — The state agency responsible for child protection and foster care, and for benefits such as SNAP.

958.title: Alabama Department of Youth Services (DYS)
958.text: Department of Youth Services · Alabama DYS · DYS — The state's juvenile justice agency. It holds young people committed by juvenile courts and funds local diversion programs.

959.title: Home visiting (First Teacher)
959.text: First Teacher Home Visiting · Nurse-Family Partnership · Parents as Teachers · home visiting · HIPPY — Programs that send a trained visitor to the homes of pregnant women and families with young children to support parenting and health.

960.title: Alabama Department of Early Childhood Education (ADECE)
960.text: Department of Early Childhood Education · ADECE — The state agency for pre-kindergarten and early-childhood programs, including home visiting.

961.title: Alabama Children's Policy Council and the State Team
961.text: Children's Policy Council · State Team — Two bodies set up in state law to coordinate services for children across agencies. Neither is dedicated to mental health.

962.title: Transitional-age youth
962.text: transitional-age — Young people moving from children's services to adult services, roughly from the late teens into the mid-twenties.

963.title: Alabama Department of Economic and Community Affairs (ADECA)
963.text: ADECA — The state agency that distributes many federal grants to local governments and nonprofits, from homelessness funds to broadband.

964.title: Alabama Department of Public Health (ADPH)
964.text: Department of Public Health · ADPH — The state public health agency. It is separate from ADMH and keeps the statistics on deaths, including suicides and overdoses.

965.title: VA medical centers, clinics and Vet Centers
965.text: VA medical centers · Vet Centers · community-based outpatient clinics · VA health systems · VA — The federal Department of Veterans Affairs' own health system: hospitals, outpatient clinics and community counseling centers for veterans.

966.title: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS)
966.text: CMS — The federal agency that runs Medicare and oversees each state's Medicaid program.

967.title: SAMHSA
967.text: SAMHSA — The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, the federal agency for mental health and addiction services.

968.title: NAMI Alabama
968.text: NAMI Alabama · NAMI AL · NAMI — The state organization of the National Alliance on Mental Illness, a membership group of people with mental illness and their families.

969.title: Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program (ADAP)
969.text: Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program · ADAP — A legal advocacy program for Alabamians with disabilities. It monitors the state's compliance with the Hunter consent decree.

970.title: VOICES for Alabama's Children
970.text: VOICES for Alabama's Children · VOICES Kids Count — A child advocacy organization that compiles the Alabama Kids Count data on child well-being.

971.title: Alabama Suicide Prevention and Resources Coalition (ASPARC)
971.text: Alabama Suicide Prevention and Resources Coalition · ASPARC — The nonprofit state coalition that trains people in suicide prevention and advocates for it.

972.title: Alabama Arise and Cover Alabama
972.text: Alabama Arise · Cover Alabama — A statewide advocacy organization on poverty issues, and the coalition it leads to press for wider health coverage.

973.title: North Alabama Mental Health Coalition (NAMHC)
973.text: North Alabama Mental Health Coalition · NAMHC — A regional coalition, formed in 2015, of providers, law enforcement, officials, judges and advocates in North Alabama.

974.title: Little Orange Fish
974.text: Little Orange Fish — The organization that publishes this report.

975.title: CCBHCs and prospective payment
975.text:
A clinic model paid a daily rate for a required set of services, and why Alabama is converting to it. What it is 
 Most people assume a clinic is paid for what it does, one item at a time. A therapy session has a price, a medication visit has another, and the clinic sends a bill for each. That is  fee-for-service , and it is how  Alabama Medicaid  has paid  community mental health centers : a set amount per procedure code, from the Agency's published schedule  [49] . 
 The trouble lies in what has no code. Nobody bills for ringing a client who missed an appointment, or for the hour spent finding a bed, or for keeping a crisis worker awake at three in the morning in case the phone rings. Work that earns nothing tends not to get done. So a system paid by the item ends up with plenty of items and very little joining them together. Alabama's own  CCBHC  manual makes the point from the other side when it lists care coordination as an activity that triggers no payment by itself  [285] . 
 The Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic, or CCBHC, is a federal answer to that. It has two halves. The first is a list of obligations. A CCBHC must provide nine kinds of service, among them  outpatient  treatment for mental illness and substance use, round-the-clock crisis response, primary-care screening,  case management  and  peer support   [10] , and it must serve anyone who comes, "regardless of their place of residence, ability to pay, or age"  [287] . 
 The second half is the payment. A clinic adds up what it costs in a year to run everything on the list, coordination and crisis cover included, and files that as a  cost report . Dividing the total by the clinic's daily visits gives a rate for that clinic alone  [285] . The rate is "prospective" because it is fixed ahead of time. Alabama uses the daily version, known as  PPS-1 , under which the clinic receives "a single payment each day when at least one CCBHC triggering event service is provided to a Medicaid enrollee"  [285] . One visit or four on the same day, the payment is the same. 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw two panels side by side. The left panel is headed "Fee-for-service". It shows two small boxes, "therapy session" and "medication visit", each with an arrow to a box marked "payment per procedure code"  [49] , and a third box, "care coordination and follow-up", with no arrow. The right panel is headed "Prospective daily rate (PPS-1)". At the top a wide box reads "total yearly cost of operating the clinic: triggering services plus allowable activities such as care coordination". An arrow labelled "cost report, divided by daily visits" leads down to "clinic-specific daily rate". A second arrow runs from a box reading "a day on which a Medicaid enrollee receives at least one triggering service" to "one daily payment"  [285] . A curved arrow from "daily rate" back to the top box is labelled "re-based on actual costs after the second year"  [289] . 
 How it works in Alabama 
 The federal CCBHC  Medicaid demonstration  began in 2017  [74] , and on 4 June 2024 Alabama was named one of ten states added to it  [25] . Only a community mental health center designated by the Department may apply, which keeps the model inside the existing network of 19 centers  [10]   [31] . A clinic may contract some of the nine services out to partner organizations, though it must deliver at least 51 percent of encounters itself  [10] . 
 Conversion is happening a few centers at a time. WellStone in Huntsville and AltaPointe in Mobile were certified from July 2024  [26] . Mountain Lakes received federal approval in October 2025 and Highland Health Systems in April 2026  [27] . The Department's own directory lists a fifth clinic that its May 2026 announcement does not name  [28] , and six more providers received grants in August 2026 to prepare  [29] . The Department describes its aim as a statewide transformation  [287] . 
 The details of what triggers a payment say a good deal about the model's intent. A visit with a certified peer specialist is enough to trigger the daily rate. Case management does not trigger it but is carried as a cost inside it  [288] . Fee schedules under-pay both. 
 Early evidence is thin and encouraging. The first two clinics served 30,275 people in  FY2025   [16] . At WellStone the wait for an initial evaluation fell from 18 days in January 2025 to less than one day in December 2025, by the Department's account  [30] . No clinical outcome measures, such as hospital or emergency-room use, were found in the Department's published reports as of October 2026. 
 There is one firm limit. The daily rate is paid for Medicaid enrollees  [105] . A CCBHC must still see the uninsured, and in a state that has not  expanded Medicaid  there are many of them, but the rate does not pay for their care. 
 How this report uses it 
 Section 12 sets out the model and names the clinics. Read it beside Domain 2, where the crisis services are shown living on  General Fund  lines that the Legislature can cut or attach conditions to  [17]   [18] . The report's argument is that a CCBHC moves some of that work, for people with Medicaid, inside a payment the clinic earns in the ordinary way. Domain 3 makes the companion point about hand-offs: when one clinic is paid for crisis response, outpatient care and follow-up together, the gaps between them become that clinic's problem  [10]   [105] . 
 Keep two cautions in mind as you read. The phrase "all 19 centers will convert" appears in no Department source, and the report avoids it  [27] . And a center that has received a preparation grant is not yet a CCBHC.

976.title: Civil commitment
976.text:
How a person can be ordered into mental health treatment in Alabama: who asks, who decides, on what proof, for how long, and into which beds. What it is 
 Civil commitment  is treatment ordered by a court for a person who has not agreed to it and has not been charged with a crime. Most people imagine it as a medical decision: a doctor in an emergency room signs a form and the patient is admitted. In Alabama it is a court case, heard by a  probate judge   [66] . 
 It begins with a petition. Any individual may file one, in the probate court of the county where the person is  [66] . Probate courts are the county courts most people know from wills and estates. The petition has to be sworn, and it has to describe the specific behavior that makes the petitioner believe the person is mentally ill  [66] . 
 The judge then appoints a guardian ad litem to protect the rights of the person named, who is called the respondent  [297] . If the petition asks for the respondent to be held before the hearing, the judge may allow that only to prevent a real and present threat of harm or to stop the person leaving the court's reach. Even then the law is firm on one point: "No respondent shall be placed in a jail or other facility for individuals accused of or convicted of committing crimes"  [297] . A probable-cause hearing must follow within seven days, and the final hearing within 30 days of the petition being served  [297] . 
 At the final hearing the test is strict. The judge needs  clear and convincing evidence , a standard that sits between the ordinary civil one and the criminal one. For an inpatient order four things must be shown. The person has a mental illness. Because of it he or she poses a real and present threat of substantial harm to self or others. Without treatment the person will go on deteriorating. And the person cannot make a rational decision about treatment  [66] . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw a timeline running left to right with five stations. Station 1: "Petition: sworn, filed by any person in the county probate court"  [66] . Station 2: "Judge appoints a guardian ad litem". A side branch drops from Station 2 to a box, "Temporary limits on liberty: only to prevent harm or flight; never in a jail", and an arrow from that box rejoins the line at Station 3, "Probable-cause hearing within 7 days"  [297] . Station 4: "Final hearing within 30 days of service; proof by clear and convincing evidence". Station 5 splits into three outcomes: "Petition dismissed"; " Outpatient  order, up to 150 days, only if a designated facility consents"; "Inpatient order, up to 150 days, renewable for up to one year"  [66] . Under the inpatient outcome write "771  involuntary beds  statewide, January 2026"  [30] . Over the two commitment outcomes write " least restrictive alternative  necessary and available". 
 How it works in Alabama 
 Once the test is met, the judge does not have a free hand. The statute says the order must be for the least restrictive alternative that is "necessary and available"  [66] . That can mean  outpatient commitment , where the person lives at home under an order to accept treatment. The outpatient test is different from the inpatient one. It does not require a threat of harm. The judge has to find that the person will deteriorate without treatment and "is unable to maintain consistent engagement with outpatient treatment on a voluntary basis"  [298] . There is a catch. Outpatient treatment can be ordered only if the designated facility has consented to provide it  [66] . 
 Either kind of order lasts at most 150 days. A renewal can run for up to a year  [66] . 
 The word "available" is where the law meets the budget. An inpatient order sends the person to the  Department of Mental Health , for a bed in a  state hospital  or in a facility the Department designates  [66] . In January 2026 the Department counted 771 such beds: 285 at Bryce and Harper hospitals, 234 contracted in community hospitals, and 252  crisis residential beds  at certified providers. That is 15.1  beds per 100,000  residents. The benchmark the Department uses, taken from the Treatment Advocacy Center, is 30 per 100,000, or 1,550 beds  [30] . An order does not create a bed, and the statute says as much: nothing in it requires "a mental health provider to expand his or her current services if necessary funding is not provided"  [297] . 
 So "civil-commitment beds" has become a budget line. The  FY2027   General Fund  carries $8 million for civil commitment and  residential services  and a further $2.5 million for additional beds  [18] . The Department prices closing the 779-bed gap at $226.4 million as a  five-year goal   [30] . One number is missing. Alabama publishes how many beds it has for committed people, but no annual count of commitments was found in the Department's reports as of October 2026. 
 How this report uses it 
 Domain 1 sets out the law in a paragraph, and Section 10 returns to it at  Intercept  2, where a probate petition is one of the routes by which a person in crisis ends up before a judge. Domain 3 and Domain 5 carry the bed counts. When those domains say "involuntary beds" or "civil beds", they mean beds that can receive a person under a probate order, as distinct from the  forensic  beds at  Taylor Hardin , which serve the criminal courts  [30]   [32] . 
 Probate judges appear elsewhere in the report as partners of the mental health system. A 2025 law gives a probate judge a place on the executive committee of the larger  regional boards  on which one serves  [61] . For a local advocate that matters, because the county probate court is where commitment orders are made and the state publishes no count of them.

977.title: Competency and forensic care
977.text:
What happens when a defendant is too ill to stand trial, why people wait in Alabama jails for a hospital bed, and the two federal cases that govern care in custody. What it is 
 " Forensic " simply means connected with the courts. Forensic mental health care is care for people who are in the criminal justice system, and most of it concerns one question: is this defendant able to stand trial? In Alabama an office of the  Department of Mental Health  oversees it  [232] . 
 A trial is only fair if the accused can take part in it. Alabama's court rules say a defendant is incompetent if he or she "lacks sufficient present ability to assist in his or her defense by consulting with counsel with a reasonable degree of rational understanding"  [299] . Notice the word "present".  Competency  is about the defendant's state of mind now, in the courtroom. Whether illness explains what the person did at the time of the alleged offense is a separate question, with a separate evaluation  [232] . 
 When there is enough doubt, the court orders an evaluation. If the judge then finds the defendant incompetent, and there is a substantial probability that treatment will change that within a reasonable time, the defendant is committed to the Department of Mental Health for what is called  competency restoration   [232] . Restoration is a legal goal. It aims to get the person well enough to understand the proceedings and work with a lawyer, which is not the same as recovery. Until it happens the case generally cannot move  [32] . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw a flowchart running left to right. Box 1: "Defendant charged; held in county jail". Box 2: "Doubt about competency; court orders evaluation". Box 3, a diamond: "Competent?" A "yes" arrow leads to "Case proceeds". A "no" arrow leads to Box 4: "Court commits defendant to the Department of Mental Health for restoration"  [232] . Between Box 4 and Box 5 insert a shaded box: " Forensic waitlist : waiting in county jail for a bed (291 people, July 2026)"  [32] . Box 5: "Restoration treatment:  Taylor Hardin , or a  telehealth  program in the jail". An arrow from Box 5 returns to "Case proceeds", labelled "restored". Under the arrow into Box 3 write " consent decree : 60 days"; under the arrow into Box 5 write "consent decree: 30 days", with a footnote that these are the terms as the Associated Press describes them  [116] . In a separate panel, drawn apart, put one box: " Braggs : people serving sentences in state prisons ( Department of Corrections )", labelled "a different case and a different agency". 
 How it works in Alabama 
 You might expect that a person a judge has found too ill for trial would leave jail for a hospital within days. In Alabama restoration has mostly meant a bed at Taylor Hardin Secure Medical Facility in Tuscaloosa, the state's forensic hospital, and there have not been enough beds or enough staff to run them. (The Department's own primer names Taylor Hardin for men and Bryce Hospital for women  [232] .) So people wait where they already are, which is the county jail. In 2025 the average wait was more than a year, and more than thirty people had waited over two  [116] . 
 A federal court is already supervising the problem. A class action now captioned  Hunter v. Boswell  was settled in 2018 with a consent decree, an agreement between the two sides that a judge has made binding  [11] . As the Associated Press describes its terms, the state has 60 days to complete an evaluation and 30 more to admit the person for restoration  [116] . The  Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program  monitors compliance. In March 2025 the part of the decree covering inpatient restoration was extended to 31 January 2027  [11] . 
 The list of people waiting stood at 327 in January 2026 and 291 in July, against a Department goal of 100 by the end of the year  [32] . Taylor Hardin has grown from 140 beds to 225, about 200 of which were filled in August 2026. A telehealth program restored 32 people inside county jails between the summer of 2025 and August 2026. Staff called  forensic navigators  go through the list looking for people who might be better served outside the forensic system  [32] . Beds are only useful with people to staff them, though, and in August 2024  the Commissioner  told her board that about half of Taylor Hardin's technician and nursing positions were filled  [136]   [116] .
