 Alabama has been here before. In  Wyatt v. Stickney , decided in 1971, a federal court held that people confined in the state's psychiatric institutions had a constitutional right to adequate treatment, and the Department stayed under court supervision until 2003  [67]   [68] . 
 The other live case is about a different group altogether.  Braggs  concerns people serving sentences in state prisons, which are run by the Department of Corrections. In 2017 a federal judge found the prisons' mental health care "horrendously inadequate" and in violation of the  Eighth Amendment   [71]   [69] . On 24 June 2026 the appeals court upheld that finding and the system-wide injunction. It reversed a specific staffing mandate and some requirements for suicide-resistant cells, and sent those questions back to the trial court  [69]   [70] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Section 10 has the fullest account, under  Intercept  3 for  Hunter  and Intercept 4 for  Braggs . Domain 3 gives the hospital figures, and Domain 4 explains why staffing at Taylor Hardin decides how long people sit in jail. Domain 1 makes the wider point that court orders are still doing work that policy has not done  [11]   [69] . 
 As you read, keep the measures apart. The waitlist is a count of people on a given day  [32] , while the decree's deadlines are measured in days per person  [116] . Taylor Hardin's bed count is capacity, and capacity matters only when the beds are staffed and open  [136] . January 2027 is the date to watch.

978.title: The continuum of care
978.text:
Mental health services laid out as a line from prevention to recovery, and why the rungs between a hospital bed and an ordinary life matter as much as the bed. What it is 
 When a state's mental health system makes the news, the story is usually about beds. There are too few of them, people wait in emergency rooms and jails, and replacing what was lost would cost a fortune.  The continuum  of care is a correction to that picture, and it comes from an unexpected quarter. In 2017 the national association of state mental health directors published a paper called  Beyond Beds  with the  Treatment Advocacy Center , the same group whose minimum of 30 beds per 100,000 residents Alabama uses as its planning benchmark  [30] . The paper's argument fits in a sentence: "24/7 inpatient care represents only a single component of a well-functioning  continuum of care  for any life-threatening health condition"  [3] . 
 A continuum is a line of services ordered by intensity. The National Academies' version begins before anyone is ill, with promotion aimed at everybody and prevention aimed at people at risk. It then runs through treatment to what it calls maintenance, meaning long-term care and rehabilitation  [2] . This report marks five stops along the line:  promotion and prevention ,  outpatient  treatment, crisis response, inpatient and  forensic  care, and  recovery supports  such as housing and work. 
 Two tests come with the picture, and the report borrows both. Does each level exist at enough scale? And do the hand-offs between levels work  [3] ? The second test is easy to forget. Nobody stays at one level. A person stabilized in hospital needs a clinic appointment the following week, perhaps a supervised place to live for some months, and in time a job. Take away the next rung and that person either stays put, in a bed someone else is waiting for, or leaves without support and comes back. 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw five boxes in a row, left to right: "promotion and prevention", "outpatient treatment", "crisis response", "inpatient and forensic care", "recovery supports"  [3] . Join each neighbouring pair with a two-headed arrow labelled "hand-off". Between "inpatient and forensic care" and "recovery supports", add a sixth box with a dashed outline, labelled " step-down :  residential care , intensive outpatient,  supported housing ", and mark it "the middle". Under the crisis and inpatient boxes write "built up since 2020". Under the dashed box write "no statewide count of beds published". Under "recovery supports" write "259 in supported housing, 234 in  supported employment , of 94,410 served (2025)"  [42] . 
 How it works in Alabama 
 Alabama has spent the years since 2020 building the two parts of the line that deal with emergencies. The  crisis system , which hardly existed before, now has  988  call centers,  mobile teams  and six  crisis centers   [13] . On the inpatient side the Department counted 771  involuntary beds  in January 2026 and would like about twice that, to reach the 30-per-100,000 benchmark  [30] . Those are the numbers legislators argue over. 
 The everyday level is outpatient care. It runs through the 19  community mental health centers , which are the way in for therapy, medication,  case management  and most other services  [31]   [108] . Further along, the line gets thin. In the 2025  reporting year  259 people were in supported housing and 234 in supported employment, out of 94,410 people the public system served.  Assertive Community Treatment , in which a team looks after people who would otherwise be in and out of hospital, reached 897  [42] . 
 This is what the report means when it says the middle is missing. "The middle" is not the centre of the diagram. It is everything that lies between a locked ward and a life of one's own: step-down residential care, intensive outpatient programs, supported housing. The Department does pay for a ladder of residential services through its contracts with the centers, but no statewide count of those beds was found in its published reports as of October 2026  [108] . So Alabama publishes its hospital beds to the last one and gives no figure at all for the places people go when they leave. 
 Money explains some of the pattern. In the report's reading, state dollars concentrate on crisis and inpatient care, while outpatient treatment and recovery supports depend on  Medicaid , and so on whether a person has coverage  [18] . A word of warning about vocabulary, too. Written with capitals, a "Continuum of Care" is a regional homelessness planning body recognized by the federal housing department, and Alabama has nine of them  [260] . Section 11 uses the phrase in that sense only. 
 How this report uses it 
 Domain 3 is the continuum set out service by service, so begin there. Then look for the short "Continuum lens" passage in each of the other domains, which puts the same question to money, staff, buildings and data in turn. Section 11 takes up housing and employment as systems in their own right. Section 12 explains why the new  CCBHC  payment, which pays one clinic for crisis care, outpatient treatment and follow-up together, is the report's main hope for mending the hand-offs  [10]   [105] . 
 When you read a proposal for more beds or another crisis center, ask what the report asks. Where does the person go next, and who is paid to see that they get there? At present the second question has no numerical answer: no statewide measure of follow-up within seven days of discharge was found in the Department's reports or the  federal tables  as of October 2026  [42] .

979.title: The crisis system
979.text:
Someone to contact, someone to respond, a safe place for help: the three parts of a crisis system, and how far each one reaches in Alabama. What it is 
 For most of living memory, a mental health emergency in America has been handled by whoever answers 911. Police arrive. The person ends up in an emergency room or a cell, and neither was built for them. Federal guidance issued in 2025 describes what should exist in place of that, and reduces it to three things:  someone to contact , someone to respond, and a safe place for help  [110] . 
 The first is a phone line. Since July 2022 that has meant  988 , the national three-digit number for mental health, substance use and suicide crises  [9] . The second is a  mobile crisis team , which in the guidance's words delivers "rapid, on-site interventions to de-escalate crises and connect individuals to care"  [110] . The third is a place that is neither a hospital ward nor a jail, a  crisis center  where a person can walk in or be brought and be seen straight away. 
 The guidance wants the three to work as one system serving "anyone, anywhere, at anytime"  [110] . The reasoning is practical. A call line with no team to send and nowhere to refer can only talk. A crisis center that officers have never heard of stays quiet. Each part is worth far less alone. 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw three boxes in a row. The first is "Someone to contact: 988, four in-state call centers"  [9] . The second is "Someone to respond: mobile crisis teams, 14 teams at 11 centers"  [13]   [75] . The third is "A safe place for help: six crisis centers and one pediatric unit"  [12] . Two arrows leave the 988 box, one to each of the others, both labelled "triage". Two arrows enter the crisis-center box from outside the row: "walk-in" and "law-enforcement drop-off, around the clock". A loop on the mobile-team box is labelled "follow-up for up to 72 hours". Below the row, draw two boxes with dashed outlines, "emergency room" and "jail", and label them "what crisis care is meant to relieve". 
 How it works in Alabama 
 Alabama built its crisis system almost from nothing after 2020, and it now has all three elements  [13] . That is a real achievement. The harder questions are how far each element reaches and whether anyone can show what it accomplishes. 
 Start with the phone. Four call centers inside the state answer 988, and in  FY2025  they took 40,053 calls  [9]   [16] . The figure the Department watches is the  in-state answer rate , the share of calls picked up by an Alabama counselor before they roll over to a national backup. It rose from 82.5 percent in FY2024 to 87.4 percent in FY2025, though texts and chats still went to a national center  [16] . The money is less settled than the service. The  General Fund  line for 988 call centers fell from $500,000 to zero in the FY2027 budget, and  opioid-settlement   appropriations  have carried part of the cost  [18]   [91] . 
 Mobile teams are the thinnest layer. The Department funds 14 teams at 11  community mental health centers , and five more for children and adolescents at three centers  [13]   [111] . In February 2025 mobile teams and crisis centers together covered 24 of the state's 67 counties, and the Department's plan was to grow to 23 teams  [33] . Since October 2023  Medicaid  has paid for a mobile response, defined as a two-person team available at any hour with follow-up for up to 72 hours  [75] . 
 The six crisis centers are in Mobile, Montgomery, Birmingham, Tuscaloosa, Huntsville and Dothan. They take walk-ins and police drop-offs around the clock  [12] , and since a 2022 law an officer may drive a person in crisis to a center and not to jail  [225]   [227] . The centers performed 9,929 evaluations in FY2025  [16] . Adult centers may not admit children, which leaves the 24-bed unit in Huntsville, for ages 12 to 18, as the only  pediatric crisis unit  on the Department's list  [14]   [41]   [12] . 
 Then came the argument. In September 2025 the state's  evaluation commission  reported that it "cannot verify" the emergency-room and jail  diversions  the Department had reported, because the centers counted them differently, and it put average  utilization  in FY2024 at 27 percent. The Department answered that "most centers function at capacity most days"  [14] . The Legislature tied money to reporting. As reported on final passage, the FY2027 budget holds back the last two  quarterly installments  of the $42 million for crisis centers and  rural crisis care  until the Department reports on the programs  [17] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Domain 3 takes the three elements in order and gives the figures. Domain 2 shows the budget lines. Domain 6 treats the evaluation dispute as a question about data: what counts as a "diversion", and who decides  [14] ? In Section 10 the same services come back as  Intercept  0, the point before any arrest  [4] . 
 Two habits will help as you read. When the report says a crisis center "serves" a county, remember that the Department's list assigns 60 counties to a center and leaves seven out, and that being assigned says nothing about the length of the drive  [12] . And when you meet a count of calls answered or evaluations performed, notice what kind of number it is. It tells you the door was open. Whether the person stayed out of a cell or an emergency room, and was seen by someone the following week, is the part Alabama cannot yet show.

980.title: The eight domains
980.text:
Why this report describes Alabama's mental health system by the jobs a system has to do, and where the list of jobs comes from. What it is 
 Ask most people to describe a state's mental health system and they will start drawing an organization chart, with the department at the top and its hospitals and offices underneath. The World Health Organization starts somewhere else. Its 2007 framework set out "to promote a common understanding of what a health system is", and the answer it gave was a list of jobs that any health system has to do, whoever happens to do them  [300] . 
 There are six. WHO calls them building blocks: service delivery, the health workforce, health information systems, access to essential medicines, financing, and leadership and governance  [1] . The scheme does not say which agency owns which job, and that is why it is useful. A state can be checked block by block. Is anyone governing? Is the money there, and whose money is it? Are there enough trained people to do the work? The blocks also lean on each other, so a clinic can be fully funded and still sit half empty for want of staff. 
 This report takes the six and adds two of its own. Equity asks who the system reaches and who it misses. Community engagement asks how the public shapes it. Neither is among WHO's six  [1] . Together they make the eight domains of Part II. Four more sections follow in Part III, on children and families, the justice system, housing and social conditions, and payers, because a good deal of what decides a person's care in Alabama happens outside the  Department of Mental Health . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw two rows of boxes. The top row has six boxes, one for each WHO building block  [1] . The bottom row has eight, labelled Domain 1 to Domain 8. Six arrows run downward: leadership and governance to Domain 1 (governance, policy and law); financing to Domain 2; service delivery to Domain 3; health workforce to Domain 4; access to essential medicines to Domain 5, which the report widens to technology and infrastructure; health information systems to Domain 6. Domain 7 (equity) and Domain 8 (community engagement) receive no arrow and carry the label "added by this report". To the right, a separate column of four boxes holds Section 9 (children, youth and families), Section 10 (justice), Section 11 (housing and  social determinants ) and Section 12 (payers), under the heading "systems beyond the Department". 
 How it works in Alabama 
 A map of functions suits Alabama because responsibility here is scattered. The Department of Mental Health is the  state mental health authority   [51] . But the  Alabama Medicaid Agency  sets the covered services and rates that determine what providers can bill  [49] ,  probate courts  decide civil commitments  [66] , and the Legislature writes the  appropriations  and, in its 2026 session, attached conditions to them  [17] . An organization chart of the Department would leave all of that off the page. 
 Follow one thing through the report and the design shows itself. The six  crisis centers  appear in Domain 3 as a service, a place that takes walk-ins and police drop-offs around the clock  [12] . In Domain 2 they are a $36 million line in the  General Fund   [18] . Domain 5 treats them as buildings, with capital costs the state evaluator put at between $3.3 million and $12.6 million a center. Domain 6 treats them as a measurement problem, since the same evaluator could not verify the centers'  diversion  counts  [14] . Section 10 meets them once more, as the earliest point at which someone can be steered away from jail. Five appearances, five different questions. The repetition is deliberate. 
 Each domain is also held up against two yardsticks. One is  the continuum  of care: a short "Continuum lens" passage asks where, along the line from prevention to recovery, the domain is strong or thin  [3] . The other is the state's own plan. The Department's Strategic Plan 2025–2028 has five priorities  [40] , and each domain closes with a line listing the plan goals it touches. Treat those codes, A1 to E3, with some care. They are  Little Orange Fish 's numbering, taken from its own analysis of the full plan document, and the Department's public page shows only the five priority headings   [40] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Use the domains as an index of questions. If you want to know who decides something, start in Domain 1. If you want to know why something already decided has not happened, the answer is usually in Domain 2 or Domain 4. Domain 4 says of itself that every other domain depends on it, and the  forensic hospital  shows why: in August 2024 only about half of its technician and nursing positions were filled  [116]   [136] . 
 The four sections of Part III each borrow a frame of their own, and each frame has a primer on this site. Section 9 reads children's services against the  System of Care principles   [7] , and Section 11 uses the five  Healthy People 2030  domains  [8] . Section 10 walks through the  Sequential Intercept Model   [4] . Section 12, on payers, is where the coverage questions raised in several domains are worked out in full. One caution applies throughout: the "Gaps and opportunities" bullets that close each domain are the report's own reading of the evidence, and should be quoted as analysis and not as the finding of any agency.

981.title: How Alabama funds mental health
981.text:
The streams of money behind the Department of Mental Health, which of them the Legislature votes on each year, and how conditions get attached. What it is 
 Every spring the Alabama Legislature debates how much to give the  Department of Mental Health , and a number is reported in the press. For  FY2027  it was $240.9 million  [18] . It is easy to take that for the state's mental health budget. It is about one-sixth of what the Department actually takes in. 
 The state passes two main budgets each year, one for the  General Fund  and one for the  Education Trust Fund , and an agency can spend only what those acts appropriate to it  [301] . The fiscal year runs from 1 October to 30 September, so "FY2027" begins in October 2026  [301] . An  appropriation  lasts one year. A program funded this session has no claim on the next. 
 Not all money comes that way, though. Some arrives by standing law: a tax is earmarked for a purpose and flows to it without an annual vote. Some is federal, either as the match on  Medicaid  claims or as grants. A  block grant  is a federal sum a state receives each year to spend on community mental health services, with a few obligations attached  [302] . And some is one-time money, of which the  opioid settlements  are the current example. 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw one horizontal bar labelled "Department of Mental Health operating revenue, FY2025: $1.43 billion"  [16] . Divide it into five segments, left to right: "General Fund, 16.8%", " Special Mental Health Fund , 16.5%", "Education Trust Fund, 5.5%", "other state sources", and a long final segment, "federal, local and miscellaneous, 59.1%, mostly Medicaid". Above the bar, draw an arrow into the General Fund segment from a box reading "Legislature, yearly General Fund act", and hang a tag on that arrow: "conditions can be attached"  [17] . A second arrow runs into the Education Trust Fund segment from "Legislature, yearly education budget". An arrow into the Special Mental Health Fund segment comes from "taxes earmarked by statute"  [303] . Below the bar, an arrow into the last segment comes from " federal match  on Medicaid claims, plus grants". Off to one side, a box with a dashed outline reads "opioid-settlement appropriations: one-time". 
 How it works in Alabama 
 The Department's operating revenue in FY2025 was $1.43 billion. State sources supplied 40.9 percent of it. The General Fund gave $239.8 million, or 16.8 percent, and the Special Mental Health Fund almost exactly as much, $236.4 million. The Education Trust Fund added $79.1 million. Everything else, 59.1 percent, was federal, local and miscellaneous money, and most of that was Medicaid  [16] . 
 Two things in those figures surprise people. The first is how much of the Department's budget is not about mental illness at all. Medicaid paid $568.0 million for community  developmental-disability  services, against $125.9 million for community mental-illness services  [16] . The second is the Special Mental Health Fund, which rarely makes the news. State law sends part of a liquor tax into it and says the fund "shall be used only for mental health purposes"  [303] . 
 So why the attention to the General Fund? Because it is the money with choices in it. Medicaid follows the people who are enrolled and the services it covers. In the report's reading, the General Fund pays for what Medicaid does not:  crisis centers ,  state hospital  care for the uninsured, and services for adults without coverage  [16] . In December 2024 the Department was considering a request for a General Fund increase of $68.6 million for FY2026  [21] . The enacted increase was about $4.7 million, and the FY2027 figure is lower again  [20]   [18] . 
 The 2026 session added something new. A state  evaluation commission  had reported the previous September that it could not verify the crisis centers' results  [14] . As reported on final passage, the FY2027 budget withholds the last two  quarterly installments  of the $42 million for crisis  diversion  and  rural crisis-care  centers until the Department reports the status of the programs to the budget chairs, the Finance Director and the  Legislative Fiscal Officer   [17] . An earlier Senate committee version had spelled out what to report: each center's operating expenses, employees and persons served  [19] . The comparison sheets most people consult show amounts only. The condition sits in the text of the act, which could not be read for this report. 
 Settlement money has become a second channel. Act 2025-255 directed $27.9 million of opioid-settlement funds to the Department, including $3.5 million for  988   [91] . In 2026 a supplemental bill,  HB487 , appropriated a further $43.1 million across agencies, of which $26.4 million went to the Department  [92] . Meanwhile the General Fund line for 988 call centers went from $500,000 in FY2026 to zero in FY2027  [18] . The weakness is that nothing settlement funds pay for recurs without a base appropriation. 
 Federal block grants are small by comparison, at $33.8 million in FY2025  [16] , but they carry weight. Accepting the grant obliges the state to keep a  planning council  that includes people who use services  [73]  and to file the  federal tables  on which most national comparisons of Alabama rest  [42] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Domain 2 lays out the revenue, the budget lines for FY2026 and FY2027, and the spending benchmarks. Read its table of General Fund lines beside the paragraph on settlement funds, and ask of each service which of the two is paying for it  [20]   [18]   [91] . Domain 1 treats the FY2027 conditions as a change in how the Department is governed, and Domain 6 argues that agreed measures, published in advance, would let such conditions be met with data  [17] . 
 You will also meet two cost estimates for psychiatric beds, $226.4 million from the Department and about $590 million from the House budget chair  [30]   [32] . The sources do not reconcile them, and neither is an appropriation.

982.title: Medicaid and the coverage gap
982.text:
Who Medicaid covers in a state that has not expanded it, how the federal match works, and the two ways a state changes its program. What it is 
 Medicaid  is usually described as health insurance for the poor, and in most of the country that is close enough. Each state runs its own program inside federal rules, and Washington pays a share of every dollar spent. The share is called the  federal match , or FMAP. It comes from a formula that gives "higher reimbursement to states with lower per capita incomes", with a floor of 50 percent and a ceiling of 83  [304] . Alabama's rate sits well up that range, at 72.63 percent for  FY2026   [95] . So for each dollar of Medicaid care, the state has to find about 27 cents. 
 Who may enrol is the part a state controls, and this is where expectations go wrong. The Affordable Care Act let states open Medicaid to all adults with incomes up to 138 percent of the  federal poverty level   [38] . Forty-one states, counting the District of Columbia, have done so. Alabama is one of the ten that have not  [281] . 
 The same law built the insurance marketplaces on the assumption that every state would expand. Premium subsidies were set to begin at the poverty line, because anyone poorer was supposed to have Medicaid. Then expansion became optional, and in KFF's words "poor adults living in states that decided not to expand were left without an affordable coverage option"  [38] . That hole is the  coverage gap . An adult just above the poverty line can buy subsidized insurance. One just below it cannot. 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw two vertical bars side by side, each a scale of income from 0 at the bottom to 150 percent of the federal poverty level at the top. The left bar is labelled "Alabama parent". Shade the band from 0 to about 18 percent and label it "Medicaid"  [282] . Shade the band from about 18 to 100 percent in a contrasting colour and label it "coverage gap: no Medicaid, no  marketplace  subsidy". Label everything from 100 percent upward "marketplace subsidies"  [38] . The right bar is labelled "Alabama adult without children or a disability". Here the gap band runs from 0 to 100 percent, with marketplace subsidies above it  [283] . Across both bars draw a dashed horizontal line at 138 percent, labelled "Medicaid limit in the 41  expansion states ". 
 How it works in Alabama 
 A parent in Alabama qualifies only with income up to about 18 percent of the poverty level  [282] , and an adult with no dependent children and no disability does not qualify at any income  [283] . 
 How many people are in the gap depends on who is counting.  Alabama Arise , which campaigns for expansion, puts it at up to 155,000  [36] . KFF's estimate from 2024 survey data is 86,000 uninsured adults in the gap itself and 147,000 who would become eligible if the state expanded  [38] . The larger KFF number reaches above the poverty line, to 138 percent, and so takes in people who can already buy subsidized marketplace plans. The two should not be averaged. 
 For mental health the consequence is direct. Medicaid is the largest single funder of the care the  Department of Mental Health  contracts for  [16] . A service Medicaid pays for can grow. A person Medicaid does not cover has to be paid for from somewhere else, and that somewhere is mostly the state's  General Fund . Among Alabama adults with any mental illness, 14.1 percent are uninsured, against 9.2 percent nationally  [35] . 
 When Alabama wants to change what its Medicaid program does, it has two instruments. A  state plan amendment  alters the standing agreement between the state and the federal government  [305] .  Mobile crisis  teams became a Medicaid benefit this way in October 2023  [75] . A  Section 1115 waiver  is permission to do something the ordinary rules forbid. Waivers are approved as experiments, generally for five years, and must not cost the federal government more than it would otherwise have spent  [306] . Alabama holds one. Medicaid has historically not paid for adults aged 21 to 64 in a psychiatric institution of more than 16 beds  [307] , and the waiver lifts that rule for facilities in Mobile and Baldwin counties until May 2027  [97] . A second waiver, for substance use treatment, has been pending with the federal Medicaid agency since July 2023  [98] . 
 Unlike most states, Alabama does not hand Medicaid to private health plans. It has no comprehensive  managed-care  plans and pays providers itself  [125] , which is why the state could introduce the  CCBHC   daily rate  by its own action. 
 The terms of the expansion debate shifted in 2025. A federal budget law ended, from January 2026, the temporary extra match that had been offered to states expanding for the first time  [80] . The same law limits the  provider taxes  that states use to raise their own share, and were Alabama to expand, its 6 percent hospital tax would have to fall to 3.5 percent by FY2032  [81] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Section 12 has the full account, and Domain 2 places Medicaid among the Department's revenues. Domain 7 reads it as an equity question, and Section 10 asks what happens to a person's Medicaid on the way into jail and out again. Domain 1 says of coverage policy that it affects more sections of the report than any other single decision  [36] . 
 When you read about a new service, ask which payer it belongs to. If the answer is Medicaid, check whether it arrived by state plan amendment or by waiver, since a waiver comes with an end date. If the answer is the General Fund, you are probably looking at something Medicaid does not cover, or at care for people it does not reach  [16] .

983.title: Reading the indicators
983.text:
How to read the report's rates, rankings and counts without asking them to say more than they can. What it is 
 An indicator is a number that stands in for something you cannot see directly. Nobody can watch a mental health system "reach" people, so we count the people it served and divide by the population  [42] . That fraction is the indicator. It is only as good as the choices packed inside it: who was counted on top, who was counted underneath, over which months, and by whom. 
 Those choices are easy to lose sight of, even for careful people. The 2025 edition of this report said that 17.4 percent of the people Alabama's public system served were Black. That was the national figure. Alabama's share was more than twice as high, and stood at 38.3 percent in 2025  [165]   [42] . The same edition gave an employment rate of 45.5 percent, which was the share employed among clients in the labor force. Among all adult clients whose status was known it was 20.5 percent  [165] . Neither number was invented. Each was a real figure answering a different question from the one the sentence asked. 
 Most of the comparisons in this report come from one place, the federal  Uniform Reporting System  tables. Every state files them as a condition of its  mental health block grant , and the federal agency publishes them beside national figures  [42] . Others come from organizations that rank states, from one-night counts, and from the Department's own annual report. Each kind has its own habits. 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw a large fraction in the middle of the page. The top reads "1 person readmitted within 30 days". The bottom reads "68 civil discharges from  state hospitals ". To the right, an equals sign and "1.5%"  [42] . Four labels with pointers surround it. Pointing at the bottom of the fraction: "Who is counted? Civil patients,  all ages , state hospitals only." Pointing at the whole fraction: "When?  Reporting year  2025, which is October 2024 to September 2025." Pointing at the result: "Compared with what? United States, 9.0%." Pointing at the top: "How many events? One." Beneath, in smaller type, draw the same fraction for 2024, "5 of 74 = 6.8%"  [43] , joined to the first by an arrow labelled "four fewer people". 
 How it works in Alabama 
 Start with the measure the report uses most. The  penetration rate  is the number of people the public system served for every 1,000 residents. Alabama's was 18.31 in 2025, the same as the year before, against 22.94 for the country  [42] . It is tempting to read that as unmet need. The number will not bear it. People treated through private insurance are not in it, and a low rate could reflect less need, poorer access or simply a smaller public role. 
 Small numbers are the next trap. Alabama's 30-day  readmission rate  to state hospitals fell from 6.8 percent to 1.5 percent in a year, far below the national 9.0. Behind those percentages are five readmissions among 74 discharges, then one among 68  [42]   [43] . Four people account for the whole change. 
 Rankings need a different kind of care.  Mental Health America  ranks 51 jurisdictions, and by its convention a rank near 51 is bad  [35] . Alabama is 50th on its youth measures. Look underneath, though, and the picture is more specific. About as many Alabama young people have a major depressive episode as elsewhere, 18.9 percent. What is exceptional is that 66.4 percent of them got no treatment, the highest share in the country  [35] . A rank tells you the order of the states and nothing about the distance between them, nor about which part of the measure is doing the work. 
 Then there is time. Alabama's  fiscal year  runs from October to September, and the federal reporting year covers the same months  [301]   [42] . Deaths are counted by calendar year. The same program can therefore produce two honest totals: the opioid council's report gives 48,179 boxes of  naloxone  distributed between November 2024 and October 2025, and 40,733 kits in fiscal year 2025  [76] . Some figures are also provisional. The council's 2025 overdose count of 1,052 is an early estimate, and its 2024 figure of at least 1,151 is a floor, so the pair should not be read as a decline  [76] . 
 One-night counts have their own limits. The homelessness figure comes from a count made by local coalitions on a single night: 4,601 people in 2024 and 4,137 in 2025  [254]   [258] . The federal housing department itself cautions that "the reliability and consistency of the homeless counts may also vary" from one coalition to another  [258] . 
 Last, watch the words. "Rural" means 55 of 67 counties in one sentence and 42 percent of residents in another, and those are different measurements  [111]   [134] . A county "served" by a  crisis center  has been assigned to it, which is a statement about responsibility and not about the drive  [12] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Domain 6 has the main table of federal measures and the list of what Alabama does not publish. Appendix B carries the baseline indicators. Wherever the report gives an Alabama figure it tries to give the comparison, the period and the source key beside it, so use them  [42] . 
 On the site's maps, apply the same habits. A shaded county tells you what the legend says and no more. If the legend says "assigned to a crisis center", it is not a map of access  [12] . And when a number seems to settle an argument, look for its denominator first.

984.title: The Sequential Intercept Model
984.text:
Six points between a mental health crisis and a prison sentence at which a person can be steered toward care, and who holds each one in Alabama. What it is 
 Say " diversion " and most people picture a single moment, an officer deciding not to make an arrest. The  Sequential Intercept Model  starts from the observation that there are several such moments, spread over months or years, and that each one is in different hands. Three researchers, Mark Munetz, Patricia Griffin and Henry Steadman, developed it in the early 2000s  [5] . The federal center that promotes it calls it "a conceptual model to inform community-based responses to the involvement of people with mental and substance use disorders in the criminal justice system"  [5] . 
 The model lays the justice system out as a path and marks six places along it. They are numbered from 0 to 5: community services, law enforcement, initial detention and first court hearings, jails and courts,  reentry , and  community corrections   [4] . At each place there is something that can be done. A  mobile crisis team  can go out where a patrol car would have gone. A brief screen at the booking desk, which the federal brochure says can be given to everyone by staff with no clinical training, can flag a person before the first hearing. A treatment court can supervise someone through care. A jail can plan a person's release so that medication does not stop at the gate  [5] . 
 Two things follow from drawing it this way. Earlier is better, because every intercept a person passes means more time in custody. And no single agency owns the path. Communities use the model, in its own words, to "identify gaps, resources, and opportunities at each intercept"  [5] . It is a map for finding out who should be in the room. 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw six boxes in a row, joined left to right by arrows, under a long arrow labelled "further into the justice system". Label the boxes: "0 Community services", "1 Law enforcement", "2 Initial detention and court hearings", "3 Jails and courts", "4 Reentry", "5 Community corrections"  [4] . From the bottom of each box, draw a short arrow turning downward to a band along the foot of the picture labelled "care in the community". Label the six downward arrows, in order: "crisis line, mobile team,  crisis center "; " CIT-trained  officers,  co-responders "; " screening at booking "; "treatment courts,  competency  services"; "release planning,  Medicaid  restarted"; "supervision with treatment"  [5] . 
 How it works in Alabama 
 The justice system is a regular point of contact for Alabamians with mental illness. The director of the state's Crisis Intervention Team program estimates that 20 to 30 percent of the calls law enforcement fields involve a person in a mental health crisis  [6] . Walk the six intercepts and a pattern appears. The state has built a good deal at the start of the path and is under court order further along it, and in between there is a stretch where very little is counted. 
 Intercept 0 is the  crisis system :  988 , the mobile teams, and six crisis centers that accept police drop-offs at any hour  [12] . Intercept 1 belongs to the police and sheriffs. Crisis Intervention Team training, which prepares officers to handle these encounters, is coordinated by  NAMI Alabama  and has a $1 million line in the state budget  [145]   [18] . The Department reported more than 1,375 trained officers in July 2024, and no later count was found. The state's police standards commission requires 12 hours of continuing education a year and names no mental health subject among them  [135]   [143] . 
 Intercept 2, the booking desk and the first court appearance, is the thinnest. No statewide standard for mental health screening at booking was found, and no statewide count of jail suicides. What exists is local. Morgan County's jail, to take the report's example, employs two licensed counselors  [229] . Since October 2025 the former  drug courts , renamed accountability courts, may take defendants with mental illness  [63] . 
 Intercept 3 is where the federal courts come in. Defendants whose competency to stand trial is in doubt wait in county jails for an evaluation or a  state hospital  bed, and a  consent decree  governs how long they may wait. In July 2026 there were 291 people on that list  [32] . A separate primer covers it. 
 At Intercept 4, reentry, the tools belong to the  Bureau of Pardons and Paroles , which runs five  Day Reporting Centers  with contracted mental health and substance use treatment  [243] . Alabama law suspends a prisoner's Medicaid and does not terminate it, so that coverage can resume, though how often it does at release was not found  [248] . Intercept 5 is supervision in the community. Thirty-eight community corrections programs cover 52 counties and fifteen counties have none, on a map dated April 2023  [249] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Section 10 takes the intercepts one at a time and then gathers them in a table that sets out, for each, what exists, what is measured and what is missing. Read the "published measure" column closely, because it shows how uneven the evidence is: a call volume here, a single county's example there  [229] . 
 The model also explains why the same service appears twice. The crisis centers of Domain 3 are Intercept 0 in Section 10  [12] . Domain 4 discusses officer training as a workforce matter, and here it is Intercept 1. If you work locally, use the model as it was meant to be used, as a list of who to invite: the sheriff, the  probate judge , the  community mental health center , the district attorney, the  parole  office. A 2025 law already gives the first two a place on the executive committees of the larger regional mental health boards, where they sit on the board  [61] .

985.title: System of Care and the social determinants of health
985.text:
Two frameworks that look past the clinic: one for how children's services should fit together, one for the living conditions that shape mental health. What it is 
 It is natural to think of mental health care as what happens in a clinic or a hospital. The two frameworks in this primer were both written to push against that habit. One concerns children  [7] . The other concerns everybody  [8] . 
 The System of Care idea dates from the mid-1980s, when a federal program for children's mental health services began and the concept was first set down  [7] . Its premise is that a child with serious emotional difficulties is seldom the business of one agency alone. So the framework asks for services "organized into a coordinated network", one that "builds meaningful partnerships with families and youth"  [7] . Three values sit at the core. Care should be driven by the family and guided by the young person. It should be based in the community. And it should fit the family's culture and language  [7] . 
 Under those values come working principles: a broad array of services, a plan made for the individual child, links across the agencies that serve children, early identification, and help with the move into adulthood  [7] . An update in 2021 kept all of these and added several more, among them  trauma-informed care  and the integration of mental health with physical health  [210] . 
 The second framework is wider.  Healthy People 2030 , the federal government's set of national health goals, defines  social determinants  of health as "the conditions in the environments where people are born, live, learn, work, play, worship, and age"  [8] . It sorts them into five domains: economic stability, education access and quality, health care access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context  [8] . Income, housing and schooling shape a person's health alongside anything a doctor does. 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw two panels. In the left panel, put a circle labelled "child and family" at the centre. Around it place six boxes, each joined to the centre by a line: " Department of Mental Health ", "schools", " Medicaid ", "child welfare", "juvenile justice", "early-childhood education". Place a seventh box, "pediatric medicine", just outside the ring. Join the six boxes to one another with a dashed ring labelled "coordination across agencies: the principle. No standing body dedicated to children's mental health identified in Alabama". In the right panel, put a circle labelled "person" at the centre and five boxes around it, one for each Healthy People 2030 domain  [8] . Under each domain name write the Alabama systems Section 11 files there: "economic stability: disability income,  supported employment , food assistance"; "education access and quality: school mental health services"; "health care access and quality: coverage,  telehealth , transport"; "neighborhood and built environment: housing, homelessness, broadband"; "social and community context: faith communities, veterans' network". 
 How it works in Alabama 
 Section 9 counts at least six public systems that deliver children's mental health care in Alabama: the Department of Mental Health, the schools, Medicaid, child welfare, juvenile justice and early-childhood education, with pediatric medicine alongside. That is exactly the situation the System of Care was designed for. The Department took a step toward it in October 2023, when it gathered its own children's programs into a single  Office of Child and Family Services   [212] . 
 Hold Alabama against the principles and the results are mixed. On the array of services, the Department's providers offer crisis,  outpatient , day and  residential care  for children with  serious emotional disturbance , with at least one of these in every county  [131] .  Community mental health centers  work inside 122 school systems  [119] . On coordination the report found less. State law provides a  Children's Policy Council  and a State Team for children with multiple needs, and both have remits wider than mental health  [79]   [78] . No standing body dedicated to children's mental health was identified. 
 "Family-driven" has taken a particular form here. Since 2022 a school must have a parent's written  opt-in  before providing mental health services, at first for students under 14, and since October 2025 for students under 16  [121]   [59] . Whether that has changed how many students are served is not known, because no before-and-after count was found. The state has also been without a youth survey since 2021  [171] , which matters when  Mental Health America  ranks Alabama 50th  of 51  on its youth measures  [35] . 
 A caution about the phrase. The Department's first strategic priority is also called "System of Care Transformation", and there it means the Department's service system as a whole  [40] . 
 For the social determinants, Section 11 goes through the five domains in turn, and housing is where the mental health system's own gap shows most clearly. Alabama's 2025  point-in-time count  found 4,137 people homeless, 502 of whom were recorded as  severely mentally ill   [258] . In the same year 259 people were in  supported housing  through the public mental health system  [42] . Local homelessness planning belongs to nine regional coalitions called  Continuums of Care , which are funded through the federal housing department and sit outside the mental health system altogether  [260]   [262] . No state supportive-housing subsidy program was found as of October 2026. 
 How this report uses it 
 Section 9 has a table that sets each System of Care principle beside what Alabama has. Notice which rows end with something not identified or not published  [7] . Section 11 has a matching table for the five domains, giving the Alabama system, a published measure and a gap for each  [8] . 
 The two sections also explain choices made elsewhere in the report. Schools appear in Domain 3 as part of prevention and again in Section 9 as the largest point of contact with children  [119] . When a problem seems to belong to no one, these two frameworks are usually the place to look.

986.title: Measuring the workforce shortage
986.text:
Shortage-area designations, percent of need met, provider ratios, vacancies and licensure compacts: what each number does and does not tell you. What it is 
 It would be convenient if a shortage of mental health workers were a single number. It is at least four, collected by different bodies for different purposes, and they do not always agree. Two of them put Alabama in very different places  [34]   [35] . 
 The first is the Health Professional Shortage Area, or  HPSA . The federal health workforce agency designates these, and a designation "can be geographic areas, populations, or facilities"  [308] . One designation may cover a whole county and another a single prison or clinic. The designation is a gateway. Clinicians who agree to work at an approved site in a shortage area for at least two years can have student loans repaid through the  National Health Service Corps   [139] . 
 Attached to the designations is a second number,  percent of need met . It is narrower than it sounds. The figure is the number of psychiatrists available in the designated areas divided by the number that would be needed to remove the designations, with the target set at one psychiatrist for every 30,000 people  [34] . Only psychiatrists are counted. A county full of counselors and nurse practitioners and short of psychiatrists scores badly. 
 The third measure widens the lens.  Mental Health America 's workforce ratio divides a state's population by all of its mental health providers: "psychiatrists, psychologists, licensed clinical social workers, counselors, marriage and family therapists, and advanced practice nurses"  [35] . The fourth comes from inside the system. It is the count of funded posts that employers cannot fill. 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw four boxes in a column, each with a question on the left and Alabama's answer on the right. Box 1: "Where has the federal government recognized a shortage?" and "67 mental health shortage designations covering 2,934,202 people"  [34] . Box 2: "Inside those areas, what share of the psychiatrists needed are there?" and "28.4 percent; psychiatrists only"  [34] . Box 3: "Across the state, how many residents are there for each mental health provider of any kind?" and "740, against 320 nationally; ranked 51st  of 51 "  [35] . Box 4: "In the public provider network, how many posts are empty?" and "752 of 4,678, at the end of  FY2023 ; nothing later published"  [135] . Beside the column draw a two-step ladder labelled " licensure compacts ": the lower rung reads "state has joined", the upper rung "privileges are being issued here". 
 How it works in Alabama 
 Alabama has 67 mental health shortage designations, and 2,934,202 people live in them, which is more than half the state's population of 5.19 million  [34]   [133] . The count happens to equal the number of counties. Don't read it that way, since a designation can be a population group or a facility as easily as an area  [308] . 
 Now the surprise. Alabama meets 28.4 percent of need in those areas, and the figure for the whole country, in the same federal data, is 27.3 percent  [34] . On that measure Alabama looks unremarkable. Yet Mental Health America places the state 51st of 51 for  workforce availability , with one provider for every 740 residents against one for every 320 nationally  [35] . Both are right. Alabama's shortage areas are about as short of psychiatrists as shortage areas elsewhere, and the state has far fewer mental health professionals of all kinds, taken together, for its population. Anyone who quotes only the first number will understate the problem. 
 Neither figure says anything about the public system in particular. For that there is one data point. The Department reported in 2024 that its mental health provider network had 752 vacancies at the end of FY2023, against a need of 4,678 full-time positions  [135] . No later statewide figure was found as of October 2026. The sharpest local case is the  forensic hospital , where about half of technician and nursing positions were filled in August 2024  [136]   [116] . 
 Licensure compacts are the remedy most often mentioned, and they need the same careful reading. A compact lets a clinician licensed in one member state practice in another. Alabama has joined seven. The psychology compact has been in effect here since June 2021 and the nursing compact since January 2020  [48]   [83] . The  Counseling Compact  is a different story: ten states were issuing privileges under it by 1 October 2026, and Alabama was not yet one of them  [82] . The Social Work compact, which Alabama joined in 2024, had not begun issuing multistate licenses anywhere  [87]   [137] . Membership on paper adds no clinicians. 
 The longer-term remedy is training. The University of Alabama announced a  psychiatry residency  whose first class was to start in June 2026, with six residents a year  [138] , and a 2026  appropriation  directs $2 million of  opioid-settlement  money to a psychiatry residency at UAB  [92] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Domain 4 gives all four measures in its first two paragraphs, so read them side by side there. Domain 7 adds the rural dimension, and Domain 4 itself notes that child psychiatry is the specialty most often named as short. The report's own reading is that the compacts and  telehealth  ease the  outpatient  end of the system and do nothing for inpatient units, which need staff on the ward  [34] . 
 When a workforce number is quoted to you, ask which of the four it is, what year it describes and who is counted. The ranking is from data for 2024  [35] . The vacancy count is from 2023  [135] . And Domain 4 is candid that on turnover and burnout Alabama publishes almost nothing at all.

1766.text: "Therapists" in schools, and 122 school systems as a current figure. ADMH's page says "services" and never "therapists"; its partner list dates from December 2023.

1767.title: OI-32 · Could not be confirmed
1767.text: FY2026 funding of ALSDE's Mental Health Services Coordinator program. The two official sources disagree (ruling 23).

1768.title: OI-33 · Could not be confirmed
1768.text: When and where the Commissioner pushed back on the ACES analysis. The same sentence appears in Domains 3, 5 and 6; the year is inferred from the date of the preliminary evaluation.

1769.title: OI-34 · Could not be confirmed
1769.text: The definition of the forensic waitlist (327 in January 2026, 291 in July 2026) against the Associated Press's 273 men waiting for Taylor Hardin in August 2025. The three figures are presented as one series in Domains 3 and 7 and Section 10, described in the 2026 article's own words.

1770.title: OI-35 · Could not be confirmed
1770.text: Date and number of listings of the ADMH Child & Family Services resource directory. The file was uploaded in August 2025; the reading of it was cut short, and a machine count of the partial text gave 87 names, unchecked.

1771.title: OI-36 · Could not be confirmed
1771.text: Total inpatient behavioral-health beds at Children's of Alabama. The hospital's release gives only the eleven added (ruling 41).

1772.title: OI-37 · Could not be confirmed
1772.text: Which vacancy figure "made the case" for the FY2024 workforce appropriation. The Department showed the 752 in July 2024 as context for what the funds had done; its February 2024 presentation argued from 741 vacancies in 2020 and 1,168 in January 2023.

1773.title: OI-38 · Could not be confirmed
1773.text: A rural-against-urban comparison for workforce shortage, provider supply and broadband. The cited pages give only the rural share of the population and statewide figures.

1774.title: OI-39 · Could not be confirmed
1774.text: Joining dates for two licensure compacts, and the date of the Board of Medical Examiners' release. Nothing is asserted in the text, but the citation for the medical compact is an undated release. Two source summaries also disagree on how many states the Social Work and EMS compact pages listed; neither count is in the text.

1775.title: OI-40 · Could not be confirmed
1775.text: Two key-actors rows with no source. No association is named, and none of the sources read shows a university evaluating a Department program.

1776.title: OI-41 · Could not be confirmed
1776.text: "Each CMHC runs its own electronic health record." The manual refers to each CCBHC's current record system; it does not say in terms that every center has a different one.

1777.title: OI-42 · Could not be confirmed
1777.text: How Alabama Medicaid administers non-emergency transportation. The transit study and Medicaid's own page say the agency operates its own program, without saying whether a broker is used.

1778.title: OI-43 · Could not be confirmed
1778.text: Removed sentence: "The Department participates in federal quality collaboratives." None of the Department's quality pages or manuals names one.

1779.title: OI-44 · Could not be confirmed
1779.text: ADPH overdose fatality review, and SUDORS participation. The national overdose-fatality-review site's Alabama profile reads "State OFR: No"; the federal award record shows a CDC surveillance grant but no page read names SUDORS for Alabama.

1780.title: OI-45 · Could not be confirmed
1780.text: How the 2025 edition arrived at 45.5 percent and 17.4 percent. Domain 6 used to say 45.5 percent "matches no reporting year"; it is Alabama's 2022 rate on the labor-force denominator, and 17.4 percent is the 2022 national Black share. Domain 7 and any appendix restatement should agree.

1781.title: OI-46 · Could not be confirmed
1781.text: The ADPH Office of Minority Health and its "disparity reports and programs". The Department's old address returns a not-found page and its A–Z index has no entry. Appendix tables that still name the office need the same decision.

1782.title: OI-47 · Could not be confirmed
1782.text: A Poarch Band health plan later than 2015–2020 that makes behavioral health a priority, and state–tribal coordination. The earlier statement that the plan "includes behavioral health" does not match the plan found, which lists behavioral health among clinic services only.

1783.title: OI-48 · Could not be confirmed
1783.text: The earlier statement that "families, NAMI, providers and the Department made a specific, evidenced request". It was rewritten to what is documented. The one local petition is known only from the North Alabama coalition's own website.

1784.title: OI-49 · Could not be confirmed
1784.text: NAMI Alabama as a co-organizer of May events, and its "advocacy day". The Department's release names no partner, and NAMI Alabama's home, Advocate and Support & Education pages mention neither.

1785.title: OI-50 · Could not be confirmed
1785.text: The coalition's meeting history and membership; and the independence of its website as a source. The site gives 2015 as the origin and a monthly meeting now; posted minutes start in January 2022, and its participant lists do not name educators or family members. Little Orange Fish is a core partner and built the site, which is also the only source for the 2019 petition cited in Domain 8.

1786.title: OI-51 · Could not be confirmed
1786.text: A source naming Alabama's regional mental-health coalitions. "Each regional mental-health coalition sits inside a Continuum of Care" is true by geography, but only the North Alabama coalition has a source.

1787.title: OI-52 · Could not be confirmed
1787.text: The Council's 22 members against 19 centers; the names Alabama Council of Community Mental Health Boards and Alabama Council for Behavioral Healthcare. The Council's About page gives the figure without listing the members and does not explain the two names.

1788.title: OI-53 · Could not be confirmed
1788.text: How the two statutory children's bodies work in practice; a youth or family advisory body. They are named because they qualify the finding that no standing interagency body dedicated to mental health exists (Domain 1 and Section 9). The legislative Joint Mental Health Task Force is not mentioned in that finding.

1789.title: OI-54 · Could not be confirmed
1789.text: DYS admission screening (the earlier text named the MAYSI-2) and screening in county detention and probation. Neither the agency's pages nor its FY2023 and FY2024 annual reports mention a screening instrument.

1790.title: OI-55 · Could not be confirmed
1790.text: The list of counties (Jefferson, Madison, Morgan, Montgomery, Shelby) with county-employed juvenile probation officers. The statute makes officers state employees in smaller counties and adds Mobile and, from October 2024, Shelby; it names no others.

1791.title: OI-56 · Could not be confirmed
1791.text: The NaphCare agreement: value, execution and whether mental-health care is included. The release says the Department was working to execute the agreement for inmate healthcare services, and the 24 months is in its headline only. The key-actors table places NaphCare beside prison mental health under Braggs on that basis.

1792.title: OI-57 · Could not be confirmed
1792.text: Removed sentence: "reentry programs name medication gaps at release most often". Neither the Reentry Alabama release nor the press articles on reentry say it.

1793.title: OI-58 · Could not be confirmed
1793.text: The current statewide CIT coordinator. Nothing dated 2026 confirms the name given in Section 10.

1794.title: OI-59 · Could not be confirmed
1794.text: Whether Alabama has a Section 811 PRA award or a state supportive-housing subsidy; the Shelter Plus Care reference. These remain the report's own absence findings and are not positively confirmed. The Section 11 editor notes that Shelter Plus Care was folded into the federal Continuum of Care program in 2012, which the author may wish to say; no source for that was registered. Bills for a state housing trust fund (HB401, SB244) were seen as introduced; their outcome was not checked.

1795.title: OI-60 · Could not be confirmed
1795.text: Alabama's 2025 permanent-supportive-housing inventory. Listed in the 3 October draft together with the 2025 point-in-time count. The count has since been read (4,137) and is in Section 11; the inventory has not.

1796.title: OI-61 · Could not be confirmed
1796.text: The fate of the ALLHealth proposal. The December 2024 report describes the proposal; nothing later was found.

1797.title: OI-62 · Could not be confirmed
1797.text: Employer assistance programs and TRICARE in the commercial-payers paragraph. The earlier claim that no Alabama-specific figures are published for these payers could not be supported and became a statement about this report; "at Redstone Arsenal" was dropped.

1798.title: OI-63 · Could not be confirmed
1798.text: Four capacity figures listed in the draft's Appendix D: private and community-hospital licensed psychiatric beds; opioid treatment programs; residential substance-use beds; nursing-home behavioral-health capacity. No body section makes a claim about them, so no section editor re-tested them. The body counts only the beds the Department contracts in community hospitals.

1799.title: OI-64 · Could not be confirmed
1799.text: Absence findings that were not re-tested by web search. The shared search allowance ran out. Affected: no comparable 2026 mental-health statute; no annual count of commitments; no standing cross-sector body; no alternative coverage program; the "What Alabama does not publish" list; and the Section 9 findings on school-based services, foster youth, a DHR–ADMH protocol, an advisory body and transitional-age outcomes.

1800.title: OI-65 · Not published, as far as this review found
1800.text: A current statewide count, or any count by agency, of people trained in CIT and in Mental Health First Aid. The draft said no statewide count exists. One was published, once: ADMH's presentation of 17 July 2024 (more than 1,375 officers with the 40-hour course; more than 1,250 other officers with Mental Health First Aid for first responders). Nothing later was found.

1801.title: OI-66 · Not published, as far as this review found
1801.text: The count of circuits with accountability, mental-health or veterans courts, and the Administrative Office of Courts' funding for them. The 2025 act (SB200) requires each presiding judge to report to the Administrative Office of Courts by 15 January each year, so a count may exist unpublished. When Shelby County's courts began is also not established.

1802.title: OI-67 · Not published, as far as this review found
1802.text: A verified statewide diversion total for the crisis centers; common definitions; a public crisis dashboard. The evaluator found the centers counted diversions inconsistently. The 2025 edition's statewide totals are no longer cited, and no uniform definitions of follow-up or readmission were found. The evaluator's report is preliminary; no final report was found.

1803.title: OI-68 · Not published, as far as this review found
1803.text: Staffing, vacancy and turnover figures after 30 September 2023, and a direct-support wage after March 2024. None is in the Department's annual report or its budget presentations of 2024 to 2026. The Department's FY2026 presentation cites National Core Indicators data on staff turnover, so those reports probably hold Alabama's direct-support turnover and wage.

1804.title: OI-69 · Not published, as far as this review found
1804.text: Annual civil-commitment counts; county-jail suicide counts. Neither is in the Department's reports. State law (§22-52-10.1(d)) requires probate judges to report each commitment order to the state law-enforcement agency, which is a possible route to a count; vital statistics were not examined for deaths in jails.

1805.title: OI-70 · Not published, as far as this review found
1805.text: A statewide jail mental-health screening standard; evidence on how county practice varies. The only county source describes counseling in one jail. The Department's Stepping Up page lists a validated screening tool as a criterion for participating counties, which is a program criterion, not a state standard.

1806.title: OI-71 · Not published, as far as this review found
1806.text: Mental-health supervision caseloads; Medicaid enrollment at release. State law suspends Medicaid for people in prison and jail and lets it be renewed before release (now in Section 10), but no figure on how often that happens was found; the Bureau's monthly reports carry no mental-health caseload.

1807.title: OI-72 · Not published, as far as this review found
1807.text: Current figures for the two co-responder programs. Domain 3 now says the programs were set up, not that they operate; Section 10 gives the 2022 details.

1808.title: OI-73 · Not published, as far as this review found
1808.text: A measure of, or a published source on, emergency-department boarding in Alabama. No measure was found in the Department's reports; the one hospital article read reports shorter stays, not boarding.

1809.title: OI-74 · Not published, as far as this review found
1809.text: A statewide seven-day follow-up-after-hospitalization measure. The Department's CCBHC quality manual lists the measure as one the state will collect; no published result was found.

1810.title: OI-75 · Not published, as far as this review found
1810.text: CCBHC clinical outcomes and the annual CCBHC Quality Report. The January 2026 budget presentation gives WellStone's waiting times only.

1811.title: OI-76 · Not published, as far as this review found
1811.text: Disaggregated outcomes by race, county and age; an explanation of the racial composition of people served. The federal tables break out consumer-survey results, homelessness and state-hospital readmissions by race, but not employment, and give nothing by county; the Department's own reports give no outcomes by group.

1812.title: OI-77 · Not published, as far as this review found
1812.text: Count of certified peer specialists; whether peer-run organizations are "few". The Department's peer pages name the certifications and three organizations and give no counts.

1813.title: OI-78 · Not published, as far as this review found
1813.text: A graduate-output series, and a source for the universities named in Domain 4. The absence finding was tested only against the Department's reports; either of the two unchecked datasets may be such a series.

1814.title: OI-79 · Not published, as far as this review found
1814.text: Count of integrated-care sites. The federal health-center data give patient counts, not the number of sites with integrated services.

1815.title: OI-80 · Not published, as far as this review found
1815.text: Count of ADMH-contracted residential beds; a capital program for step-down and supported housing. The contract manual lists the residential categories without numbers, and the Department's bed tables count only involuntary and crisis beds.

1816.title: OI-81 · Not published, as far as this review found
1816.text: Whether the Indigent Drug Program is still funded and how many people it serves. The rule is listed as current but dates from 2010; no budget line or served count was found, and the FY2025 annual report publishes no prescriptions count.

1817.title: OI-82 · Not published, as far as this review found
1817.text: Confirmation from the Code of Alabama that psychologists have no prescriptive authority. The 2025 edition said Alabama had enacted it; that was wrong by the association's list, a secondary source.

1818.title: OI-83 · Not published, as far as this review found
1818.text: Whether Alabama still has no published parity enforcement actions. Domain 2 and Section 12 attribute and date the finding; one web search for this review found nothing newer.

1819.title: OI-84 · Not published, as far as this review found
1819.text: A language-access plan or CLAS assessment; actual practice at the centers. "CMHCs use telephone interpretation and some employ bilingual clinicians" had no source and was replaced by the rule's requirement.

1820.title: OI-85 · Not published, as far as this review found
1820.text: Data, programs and named providers for LGBTQ+ Alabamians. "Some providers" was dropped; the organization's pages as read do not describe counseling or treatment.

1821.title: OI-86 · Not published, as far as this review found
1821.text: Alabama's mental health planning council: name, membership, minutes. Two sections rest the council's role on the federal statute alone. Two social-media posts confirm a council exists and meets but were not used as sources.

1822.title: OI-87 · Not published, as far as this review found
1822.text: Behavioral-health data and a DHR–ADMH protocol for children in state care or custody. The protocol was listed in the 3 October draft and is still not found. The findings rest on the first 30 pages of DHR's report and on two Youth Services annual reports read through a summarizing tool.

1823.title: OI-88 · Not published, as far as this review found
1823.text: The measured effect of the opt-in rule on school-based services; outcomes for transitional-age residential care. Neither the Department's nor the State Department of Education's documents report them.

1824.title: OI-89 · Not published, as far as this review found
1824.text: The anti-eviction defense program's contractor, caseload and results. It is the Department's only housing-stability line in the FY2027 General Fund.

1825.title: OI-90 · Waiting on a date
1825.text: Completion of the Governor Kay Ivey Correctional Complex by 15 October 2026; opening of the Thomasville CARE Center. The complex's deadline is twelve days after the review, and the Department of Corrections warned of delay in July. The Bureau's locations page did not list the Thomasville center; a search snippet from a 28 September 2026 newspaper report suggests it had not opened, but the report could not be opened.

1826.title: OI-91 · Waiting on a date
1826.text: Whether Taylor Hardin's last 25 of 225 beds are in use. The forecast date has arrived. The beds bear on the forensic waitlist and on the goal of 100 by the end of 2026.

1827.title: OI-92 · Waiting on a date
1827.text: When the six grant-funded centers will be certified as CCBHCs. The grants pay for preparation and do not confer CCBHC status. A second round of grants followed on 1 October 2026; as read, it contains no certification grants.

1828.title: OI-93 · Waiting on a date
1828.text: Renewal of the ADMH–Navigate contract. The term ended three days before the review. The body describes the contract in the past tense, but the summary and key-actors tables in Section 11 still list it.

1829.title: OI-94 · Waiting on a date
1829.text: The full-year FY2026 parole grant rate. Section 10 gives 20 percent for the year through August.

1830.title: OI-95 · Editorial decision (not printed in Appendix D)
1830.text: Terminology: keep "crisis diversion centers" (the state budget's term) throughout, or switch to ADMH's "crisis centers"? Nothing is unverified: the budget sheets and the Department's pages use different names, and one explanatory clause was added in Domain 3. It is a style decision for the author, so it is not printed in Appendix D.

1871.title: MHA overall rank
1871.text: National rankings. Overall ranking across all 17 MHA measures (adult and youth, prevalence and access). States with positive outcomes are ranked higher (closer to one) than states with poorer outcomes (closer to 51). The overall, adult, youth, prevalence, and access rankings were analyzed by calculating a standardized score (Z score) for each measure and ranking the sum of the standardized scores. The majority of measures represent data collected up to 2023. An overall ranking of 1-13 indicates lower prevalence of mental illness and higher rates of access to care; 39-51 indicates higher prevalence and lower rates of access. The combined scores of all 17 measures make up the overall ranking.
