2008.title: Domain 1. Governance, Policy and Legal Foundations
2008.text: Governance. Governance is the set of laws, institutions and decision rights that determine who is responsible for mental health in Alabama, how they are held to account, and what rights people with mental illness can assert. It includes the state mental health authority and its board, the Legislature's budget and policy committees, the Governor, the courts that enforce constitutional standards of care, and the interagency bodies that coordinate across health, education, justice and human services. A strong governance frame gives the rest of the system direction, legitimacy and accountability; a weak one leaves gaps that courts eventually fill.

2009.title: Domain 2. Financing and Resource Allocation
2009.text: Financing. Financing covers where the money for mental health care comes from — state appropriations, Medicaid and other federal funds, commercial insurance, local and philanthropic sources — and how it is allocated across hospitals, community programs, crisis services and the workforce. The question for planners is not only how much Alabama spends, but which payer pays for which service, because that determines which services can grow.

2010.title: Domain 3. The Service-Delivery Continuum
2010.text: Services. This domain describes what services exist in Alabama, who provides them, and how a person moves between them: from promotion and prevention, through outpatient treatment, crisis response, inpatient and forensic care, to the supports that keep recovery going. The organizing question, borrowed from the National Academies' continuum and from the state mental health directors' _Beyond Beds_ analysis, is whether each level exists at enough scale and whether the hand-offs between levels work [2] [3].

2011.title: Domain 4. Workforce Development and Well-being
2011.text: Workforce. The workforce domain covers the people who deliver mental health care — psychiatrists, psychiatric nurse practitioners, psychologists, licensed counselors and social workers, nurses, case managers, direct-support staff, peer specialists — and the pipeline, licensure, incentives and working conditions that determine how many there are and where they practice. It also covers the wider network of first responders, educators and faith leaders trained to recognize and respond to mental health needs. Every other domain depends on this one.

2012.title: Domain 5. Medicines, Technology and Infrastructure
2012.text: Infrastructure. This domain covers the physical and technical capacity behind services: hospital and crisis-center buildings, residential beds, the information systems that carry client records and claims, telehealth, broadband, and access to psychiatric medications. Infrastructure decisions are slow and expensive; they set the ceiling on what the other domains can deliver for a decade.

2013.title: Domain 6. Information, Data and Quality Improvement
2013.text: Data. This domain covers how the system knows what it is doing: the data providers report, the measures the state publishes, the surveys of people served, the evaluations that test whether programs work, and the quality processes that turn findings into change. Alabama's 2025 crisis-center evaluation made this domain the pivot of the state's mental-health politics: funding is now conditioned on reporting [14] [17].

2014.title: Domain 7. Equity, Inclusion and Cultural Responsiveness
2014.text: Equity. Equity asks who the system reaches, who it misses, and whether the care people receive fits their language, culture, disability and circumstances. In Alabama the relevant dimensions are race, rurality, income and insurance, language and hearing, veteran status, age, and involvement with the justice and child-welfare systems. This domain reports what the data show and names the programs built for specific communities; it makes no clinical claims and takes no policy position.

2015.title: Domain 8. Community Engagement, Education and Advocacy
2015.text: Community. This domain covers how the public shapes the system: awareness and anti-stigma education, training of lay and professional responders, the organizations that carry the voice of people with lived experience and their families, regional coalitions, the press, and the advocacy that moves budgets and law. ADMH's fifth strategic priority — Awareness and Knowledge — commits the Department to giving Alabamians information that raises awareness and connects them to services [40]; this report reads that as recognizing public engagement as a system function, not an add-on.

2016.title: Section 9. Children, Youth and Families: A System of Care
2016.text: Children. Children's mental health in Alabama is delivered by at least six public systems — the Department of Mental Health, schools, Medicaid, child welfare, juvenile justice and early-childhood education — plus pediatric medicine. The national System of Care framework, adopted by the federal government since the 1980s and updated in 2010 [7] and again in 2021 [210], holds that services for children should be family-driven and youth-guided, community-based, culturally and linguistically competent, and coordinated across agencies, with early identification, individualized planning and smooth transitions to adulthood [7]. The 2021 update keeps each of these values and principles, with some rewording (the first value is now "Family and Youth Driven"), and adds principles on trauma-informed care, health–mental health integration, a public health approach and mental health equity [210]. This section describes Alabama's pieces against that frame. Child and Family Services is the second of ADMH's five strategic priorities [40].

2017.title: Section 10. The Justice Interface
2017.text: Justice. In Alabama, the justice system is a regular point of contact for people with mental illness: Lee County's sheriff says some sheriffs describe their jails as a "de facto center" for people with mental-health conditions, and the director of Alabama's Crisis Intervention Team program estimates that 20 to 30 percent of the calls law enforcement fields involve a person in a mental-health crisis [6]. This section follows the **Sequential Intercept Model**, which maps the points at which a person can be diverted from the justice system into care: Intercept 0 (community and crisis services), 1 (law enforcement), 2 (initial detention and court hearings), 3 (jails and courts), 4 (reentry) and 5 (community corrections) [4] [5]. Alabama's forensic and prison mental-health systems both operate under federal court oversight [11] [69], which makes this the area where the state's obligations are most explicit.

2018.title: Section 11. Housing, Social Determinants and Community Supports
2018.text: Housing/SDOH. Mental health outcomes depend on conditions outside the clinic: housing, income and work, transport, connectivity, food, education and social connection. Healthy People 2030 groups these into five domains of social determinants — economic stability, education access and quality, health care access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context [8]. This section describes Alabama's systems in each, with a focus on housing and homelessness, where the mental health system's own gap is clearest.

2019.title: Section 12. Payers, Coverage and the CCBHC Transition
2019.text: Payers. Who pays determines what gets delivered. This section describes Alabama's payer mix — Medicaid, commercial insurance, Medicare, the marketplace, federal and state direct funding — and the single largest change in how community mental health care is paid for in a generation: the Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic model.

2020.title: Data (6) → Financing (2): Evidence justifies or withholds funds
2020.text: ACES's preliminary evaluation of September 2025 said it "cannot verify" the crisis centers' reported diversion figures [14]; the FY2027 General Fund budget, as reported on final passage, withholds the last two quarterly installments of the $42 million for crisis diversion centers ($36 million) and rural crisis care ($6 million) until the Department reports the status of the programs to the General Fund budget chairs, the Finance Director and the Legislative Fiscal Officer [17] [18]; the Senate committee's version of the bill had required reports of each crisis center's operating expenses, employees and persons served [19]

2021.title: Financing (2) → Services (3): Money sets capacity
2021.text: The Department's draft FY2026 request of December 2024 — $68.6 million more from the General Fund, including $23.4 million for civil-commitment beds and $11.5 million toward a goal of eleven crisis centers — was not funded on that scale [21] [20]: the FY2026 General Fund rose by about $4.7 million, with $8 million for civil-commitment and residential services and the six existing crisis centers at $36 million [20]. FY2027 kept the crisis-center ($36 million) and rural crisis-care ($6 million) lines and the $5 million child-and-adolescent mobile-crisis pilot level [20] [18], added $2.5 million for civil-commitment beds [18] and cut the 988 call-center line from $500,000 to zero [18]
